concepts/armed-neutrality-1800.title: The Armed Neutrality of 1800
concepts/armed-neutrality-1800.content:
The Armed Neutrality of 1800
The Rupture with Russia
The defection of Russia from the Second Coalition in the autumn of 1799 was the first crack in the alliance that had seemed, for a moment, capable of crushing the French Republic. By the end of that year the Czar Paul I, whose armies had fought alongside the Austrians under Suwarrow in Italy and Switzerland, had become bitterly disillusioned with his allies. He blamed Austria for the reverses suffered by his troops — particularly the disaster that befell Korsakoff at Zurich while Suwarrow struggled through the Alpine passes — and he saw in the policies of Vienna and London less a zeal for the restoration of legitimate thrones than a cold calculation of territorial advantage. The unbalanced temper of the Czar, at once chivalrous and reckless, turned rapidly from coolness to active hostility.
Into this widening breach Bonaparte inserted himself with characteristic adroitness. From the moment he became First Consul he had fixed his gaze upon Russia as the key to a continental combination against Great Britain. As early as June 1800, while marching toward Marengo, he wrote to Talleyrand that if Paul turned his attention toward the decaying Ottoman Empire, French and Russian interests would become common. By July he had dispatched a letter to the Czar offering to surrender Malta — which he knew he could not hold — into Russian hands, appealing directly to Paul’s vanity as the self-styled protector of the Knights of St. John. The offer was carefully worded to distinguish the Czar from the other enemies of the Republic, who fought, Bonaparte wrote, from “a vile love of gain.”
Paul was captivated. The prospect of becoming Grand Master of the Knights of Malta, of seeing his flag fly over that fortress-island, was precisely the kind of grand gesture that appealed to his romantic and autocratic nature. He designated a general to proceed to Paris, take command of French prisoners of war, and with them repair to Malta.
The Neutral Rights Question
While Bonaparte worked upon the Czar, a more immediate quarrel was brewing between Great Britain and the Baltic powers over the ancient and vexed question of neutral rights — the same question that had produced the original Armed Neutrality of 1780 under Catherine the Great. Denmark in 1799 had adopted the policy of convoying her merchant vessels by ships of war, and claimed that a statement from the senior naval officer — that the cargoes contained nothing forbidden by the law of nations — exempted the convoy from the belligerent right of search. British statesmen denied that a conceded belligerent right could be nullified by any regulation a neutral might choose to adopt. The dispute was sharpened by a fundamental divergence over the definition of contraband: Great Britain classed naval stores — timber, hemp, iron, tar — as contraband of war, since they were essential to the construction and maintenance of warships; the Baltic states, whose economies depended upon the export of these very articles, insisted they were innocent goods in peaceful trade.
Two hostile encounters followed. In December 1799 a Danish frigate resisted search, and in July 1800 a second clash left several dead on both sides, the Danish frigate being carried into the Downs as a prize. The British government, seeing the storm gathering, acted swiftly. An ambassador was sent to Copenhagen supported by nine sail-of-the-line and bomb vessels, and on August 29 a convention was signed: Denmark agreed to suspend her convoys pending future discussion, and the immediate crisis passed.
But the damage had been done. Paul I seized upon the affair as a pretext for sequestrating all British property in Russia, to be held as a guarantee against the future action of Great Britain. A second order of September 10 announced that “several political circumstances induced the emperor to think that a rupture of friendship with England may ensue,” and directed a concentration of Russian troops. The sequestration was briefly lifted on September 22, but the fall of Malta — which had surrendered to the British on the 5th of that month — brought matters to a head. The Czar, who had so eagerly accepted Bonaparte’s offer, learned in early November that the island was now in British hands and would not be yielded to him. In a fury he again decreed the sequestration of British property. Some three hundred British merchant ships were seized, their crews marched into the interior, and seals placed on all warehouses containing British goods. The Czar declared the embargo would not be removed until his rights to Malta, as Grand Master of the Order, were acknowledged.
The Northern League
The breach between Russia and Great Britain had now opened wide enough for Bonaparte to drive through. Prussia, which since 1795 had maintained a rigorous neutrality, felt encouraged to stir. The commerce of the Continent had poured through the North German states — by the Ems, the Weser, and the Elbe, through Hamburg and Bremen — and the tonnage clearing from Great Britain alone to North Germany had risen from 120,000 in 1792 to 389,000 in 1800. Prussia took the lion’s share of this traffic and was loath to see it disturbed. Yet her ambition to play a leading part in Europe, her jealousy of Austria, and the hope of one day annexing Hanover — the German possession of the British king — pulled her in the opposite direction.
The incident that decided her course occurred in October 1800. A British cruiser seized a Prussian merchantman attempting to enter the Texel with a cargo of naval stores. The captor, driven by weather, took his prize into Cuxhaven, a port at the mouth of the Elbe belonging to Hamburg. Prussia demanded its release; the Hamburg senate hesitated; Prussia ordered two thousand troops to take possession of the port. The senate bought the prize and delivered it to Prussia, and the British government — conciliatory in the face of the gathering storm — directed its restoration. It was, as Fox later taunted the ministry, a concession of principle dictated by the fact that Prussia, while capable of doing much harm to Great Britain, could not be reached by the British navy. The concession availed nothing. The Prussian minister informed the British ambassador that the occupation of Cuxhaven, having been ordered, must proceed.
On December 16, 1800, a treaty renewing the Armed Neutrality of 1780 was signed at St. Petersburg by Russia and Sweden. Denmark and Prussia immediately adhered. Its leading affirmations struck at the heart of British maritime practice: neutral ships were free to carry on the coasting and colonial trade of belligerents; enemy’s goods under the neutral flag were not subject to seizure; blockades, to be respected, must be supported by a force sufficient to make entry actually hazardous; naval stores were excluded from the definition of contraband; and vessels under convoy of a ship of war were not liable to belligerent search. Each of these propositions contested a claim upon which British sea power rested. The consenting states bound themselves to maintain their positions by force if necessary.
The Baltic was thus closed. The strategic danger to Great Britain was acute. From the Baltic states came the naval stores without which the British navy could not operate: the great masts of Riga, the hemp of Russia, the iron of Sweden, the tar and pitch that preserved the hulls of the fleet. Without these, the dockyards would fall silent and the ships would rot at their moorings. Bonaparte’s conception was realized: there was not only a naval combination against Great Britain but also an exclusion of her trade from one of its chief markets.
The British Response
Great Britain was left alone, and for the moment against all Europe. The ministry met the emergency with vigor. An armed negotiation with the Baltic powers was determined upon, and a fleet of eighteen sail-of-the-line with thirty-five smaller vessels was assembled at Yarmouth on the east coast of England. Rapidity of movement was essential: the Baltic ice was breaking up, and the British fleet had to strike before the hostile navies could concentrate. The chief command was given to Sir Hyde Parker, a gallant and respectable officer of the old school, with Nelson as his second-in-command. The choice of Parker over Nelson was a mistake — one that would not have been made by Lord St. Vincent, who succeeded Spencer as First Lord a few weeks later. Nelson was still among the junior flag-officers, and his erratic conduct in the Mediterranean under the influence of Lady Hamilton had perhaps excited doubts about his fitness for a command requiring delicacy of discretion as well as vigor. But withholding the chief command from him unquestionably weakened the expedition from the start.
The fleet sailed from Yarmouth on March 12, 1801. By the 19th, despite a heavy gale that scattered the ships, nearly all were collected off the Skaw, the northern point of Jutland. The wind was fair for Copenhagen, and Nelson, had he been in command, would have advanced at once with the ambassador on board. “While the negotiation is going on,” he said, “the Dane should see our flag waving every moment he lifted his head.” As it was, the envoy went forward with a frigate alone while the fleet waited.
On the 21st the fleet was off Elsinore, where the envoy rejoined: Denmark had rejected the British terms. This amounted to an acceptance of hostilities, and it only remained to act at once, for the wind was favorable — an advantage that at any moment might be lost. Nelson addressed a letter to Parker summing up the situation with luminous clarity. “Not a moment should be lost in attacking,” he wrote. “We shall never be so good a match for them as at this moment.” He pointed out that the fleet ought to have been off Copenhagen, not at Elsinore, when the negotiation failed — then the Danish fleet could have been destroyed and the capital made so hot that Denmark would listen to reason. “Almost the safety, certainly the honor, of England, is more entrusted to you than ever yet fell to the lot of any British officer,” he concluded.
The Plan of Attack
Copenhagen lies on the east coast of the island of Zealand, fronting Sweden across the Sound. Before the city, shallow flats extend for half a mile from the shore, and in the Sound itself, little more than a mile out, lies a long shoal called the Middle Ground. Between these two bodies of shallow water runs the King’s Channel, through which heavy ships could sail. At the northern end of this channel, a deep pocket stretches toward the harbor, defended by powerful works rising on piles out of the shoal water — the formidable Three-Crown Batteries. The Danes had moored a line of armed hulks and floating batteries along the inner edge of the King’s Channel, covering the front of the city.
The natural point of attack appeared to be from the north, but Nelson pointed out that not only was the head of the line exceedingly strong, but the wind that was fair to attack would be foul to return. A disabled ship would have no escape but by running the gauntlet of the entire Danish line, separated from her fleet. He dismissed this approach as “taking the bull by the horns.” More importantly, he argued that so long as the British fleet remained in the Sound without entering the Baltic, the way was left open for the Swedes and Russians to join the Danes. He therefore advised that a sufficiently strong force should attack the southern end of the Danish line, interposing between Copenhagen and the Baltic.
Nelson’s letter of March 24, 1801, is a masterpiece of military reasoning. He concluded with a suggestion worthy of Napoleon himself: “Supposing us through the Belt with the wind first westerly, would it not be possible to go with the fleet, or detach ten ships of three and two decks, with one bomb and two fire-ships, to Revel, to destroy the Russian squadron at that place? I do not see the great risk of such a detachment, and with the remainder to attempt the business at Copenhagen. The measure may be thought bold, but I am of opinion the boldest are the safest; and our country demands a most vigorous exertion of her force, directed with judgment.”
He saw the Northern League as a tree, with Paul the trunk and Sweden and Denmark the branches. “If I can get at the trunk and hew it down, the branches fall of course; but I may lop the branches and yet not be able to fell the tree, and my power must be weaker when its greatest strength is required.” At Revel lay twelve Russian ships-of-the-line — fully half their Baltic fleet. Their destruction would have paralyzed the naval power of the empire. But Parker was determined not to leave Denmark hostile in his rear — a reason whose technical accuracy under the circumstances was nothing short of pedantic. He adopted Nelson’s plan for the attack on Copenhagen but not the broader strategic stroke.
The Battle of Copenhagen
The nights of March 30 and 31 were employed sounding the King’s Channel. On April 1 the fleet moved up to the north end of the Middle Ground, about four miles from the city. That afternoon Nelson’s division — to which Parker had assigned twelve ships-of-the-line, two more than asked — got under way, passed through the outer channel, and anchored off the southeast end of the shoal, two miles from the head of the Danish line. The enterprise was perilous, not so much from the force to be engaged as from the extreme difficulties of navigation. The pilots were mostly mates of merchantmen trading with the Baltic, and their experience in vessels of three or four hundred tons did not fit them for the charge of heavy battleships. They betrayed throughout great indecision, and their imperfect knowledge contributed to the principal mishaps of the day.
On the morning of April 2 the wind came fair from the south-southeast. At half-past nine the signal was made to weigh. The ships were soon under sail, but the difficulties of pilotage were immediately apparent. The Agamemnon, of sixty-four guns, was unable to weather the point of the Middle Ground and had to anchor out of range, taking no share in the battle. The Bellona and Russell, seventy-fours, the fourth and fifth in the order, kept too far to the eastward and ran ashore on the farther side of the channel — upon the Middle Ground itself. They were not entirely out of action, but were beyond the range of efficient gunnery under the conditions of that day. Nelson’s flagship passed clear, as did the rest of the heavy ships, but the loss of these three vessels from the line exposed the northern part of the British order to a weight of fire disproportioned to its strength. A body of frigates very gallantly undertook to fill the gap.
The battle was at its height by half-past eleven. There was no more maneuvering — only the simple question of efficient gunnery and endurance. Around two in the afternoon, a great part of the Danish line had ceased to fire, and the flagship Dannebrog was in flames. During the action, Danish crews were frequently reinforced from the shore, and in several cases, new arrivals reaching ships that had already struck renewed the fight, either through ignorance or indifference. The land batteries fired on British boats trying to take possession.
Nelson seized on this circumstance to bring the affair to a conclusion. He wrote a letter addressed “To the brothers of Englishmen, the Danes,” and sent it under a flag of truce to the Crown Prince: “Lord Nelson has directions to spare Denmark when no longer resisting; but if the firing is continued on the part of Denmark, Lord Nelson will be obliged to set on fire all the floating batteries he has taken, without having the power of saving the brave Danes who have defended them.” The letter was sent ashore by a British officer who spoke Danish. The engagement continued until about three o’clock, when the whole line of floating defenses southeast of the Crown Batteries had either struck or been destroyed.
It was at some point during this action that the famous episode of the blind eye occurred. Parker, lying four miles off with the reserve division, saw the smoke and confusion of the battle and concluded that Nelson was being overwhelmed. He hoisted signal No. 39 — the signal of recall. Nelson, aboard the Elephant, was informed. He raised his telescope to his blind eye and, turning to his flag-captain, Thomas Foley, said: “I really do not see the signal.” The signal remained flying; Nelson remained in action. It was an act of deliberate disobedience that has become the emblem of his genius — the recognition that at a certain point in a battle, the commander on the spot, who sees the situation with his own eyes, must overrule the distant judgment of the commander-in-chief.
The Crown Prince demanded the precise purport of Nelson’s first message. Nelson took a high hand. He had destroyed the part of the enemy’s line he had attacked, but it was now important to withdraw his crippled ships — and with the existing wind, that could only be done by passing the Crown Batteries, which had been but little injured. He wrote a second letter, politicly ignoring this danger: “Lord Nelson, with humble duty to His Royal Highness, begs leave to say that he will ever esteem it the greatest victory he ever gained, if this flag of truce may be the happy forerunner of a lasting and happy union between my most gracious Sovereign and His Majesty the King of Denmark.” Having written the letter, he referred the bearer for definite action to Sir Hyde Parker, some four miles off — foreseeing that the long pull there and back would give time for the leading ships, much crippled, to clear the shoals, though their course lay close under the Crown Batteries. Thus the exposed part of the British fleet was successfully withdrawn. Three out of five ships-of-the-line that had taken the heaviest punishment grounded on the shoals during the retirement, and only the respite gained by the flag of truce saved them from destruction by the shore batteries.
The Armistice and the Death of Paul
The result of the battle was to uncover the front of Copenhagen and lay it, with its dockyards and arsenals, open to bombardment. The bomb vessels could now be placed safely in the King’s Channel. Denmark had to decide whether fear of her powerful allies and zeal for neutral claims should lead her to undergo further punishment, or whether the suffering already endured was excuse enough for abandoning the coalition.
Nelson conducted the negotiations himself. He insisted upon an armistice of fourteen weeks, after which hostilities could be resumed on fourteen days’ notice. This would assure Parker complete immunity for his communications and leave Nelson free to act against the Russian fleet. Fear of Russia long deterred the Danes from this concession, which Nelson frankly told them he must have, so as to be at liberty to act against the Russian fleet and return to them; and he made it the indispensable requisite to sparing the city. During the discussions, however, the Crown Prince received news of the Czar’s death. Paul I had been murdered by a body of conspirators on the night of March 23, 1801. The Danish government concealed the tidings, but the departure of the soul of the confederacy relieved their worst fears and encouraged them to yield to Nelson’s demands.
The armistice was signed. Denmark’s part in the Armed Neutrality was suspended.
The Dissolution
Among the first measures of the new Czar, Alexander I, was the release of the British seamen imprisoned by his father, an order dated April 7. On the 12th the British ships entered the Baltic — much to the surprise of the Northern Powers, who had thought their heavy draught would prevent it. The three-deckers had to remove their guns to pass some shoal ground ten miles above Copenhagen. Parker anchored in Kioge Bay, off the coast of Zealand, there awaiting further instructions; the Russian minister at Copenhagen having informed him that the new Czar would not go to war. Nelson entirely disapproved of this inactivity. Russia might yield, but she would be more likely to do so if the British fleet lay off Revel.
The British ministry, however, had at last taken the measure of Parker. On April 17, four days after news of the victory reached London, orders were issued modifying his instructions: if Alexander removed the embargo and released the seamen, all hostile movements were to be suspended; if not, the Revel division must be prevented from joining that at Cronstadt. Four days later, orders were issued relieving Parker and leaving Nelson in command. Taken only a week after a victory, this could scarcely be construed as anything but an implied censure. “They are not Sir Hyde Parker’s real friends who wish for an inquiry,” Nelson wrote. “His friends in the fleet wish everything of this fleet to be forgot, for we all respect and love Sir Hyde; but the dearer his friends, the more uneasy they have been at his idleness, for that is the truth — no criminality.”
Nelson’s first signal upon receiving command was to hoist the boats aboard and prepare to weigh. On May 7 the fleet left Kioge Bay, and on the 12th appeared off Revel. But the Russian division had sailed three days before and was now safe under the guns of Cronstadt. From Revel, Nelson dispatched very complimentary letters to the Russian minister of foreign affairs, but received in reply the message that “the only proof of the loyalty of his intentions that the czar could accept was the prompt withdrawal of his fleet; and that until then no negotiation could proceed.” “I do not believe he would have written such a letter,” said Nelson, “if the Russian fleet had been in Revel.” But the bird was flown, and with a civil explanation he withdrew from the port. He remained in the Baltic, awaiting the issue of negotiations. Russia meant peace: on May 17 the Czar ordered the release of the embargoed British ships. On June 4 Great Britain released the Danes and Swedes detained in her ports. Russia and Prussia had already agreed, on April 27, that hostile measures against England should cease, Hamburg and Hanover be evacuated, and the free navigation of the rivers restored.
On June 17, 1801, a convention was signed at St. Petersburg between Russia and Great Britain, settling the points in dispute. The question of Malta was tacitly dropped. On neutral claims, Russia conceded that the neutral flag should not cover enemy’s goods. While she obtained the formal admission that articles of hostile origin which had become bona fide neutral property were exempt from seizure, she yielded the critically important exception of colonial produce: this, no matter who the owner, could not be carried by a neutral direct from the colony to the mother country of a nation at war. Great Britain conceded the right of neutrals to carry on the coasting trade of a belligerent and agreed that naval stores should not be classed as contraband of war. As for the right of search under convoy, Russia yielded the principle, and Great Britain accepted methods that would make the process less offensive.
Sweden acceded to these terms on October 23, 1801, Denmark on March 30, 1802. The Baltic states renewed among themselves the principles they had relinquished in their convention with Great Britain — that neutral flags should cover enemy’s property and that convoy should exempt from search — but these were now merely declarations of principle, without force of arms to support them. The Armed Neutrality of 1800 was dead.
The Meaning of the League
Thus had fallen resultless, as far as the objects of the First Consul were concerned, the vast combination against Great Britain which Bonaparte had fostered in the North. The dissolution of the Armed Neutrality demonstrated a fundamental truth about sea power. The Northern League had seemed formidable on paper: the combined fleets of Russia, Denmark, Sweden, and Prussia outnumbered the British squadron sent to confront them. But the coalition was held together by no common interest of sufficient weight. The commerce of the Baltic states depended upon the British market; their carrying trade had flourished during the war precisely because of the protection of British naval supremacy. The interests of the Northern powers lay in yielding the points in dispute, while those of Great Britain lay in not yielding. The coalition required only a decisive demonstration of British naval force — or the death of Paul I — to dissolve.
The Czar was the only man wholly embarked in the quarrel, the only one deaf to the call of clear interest. Bonaparte, who had fostered the combination with such skill, underestimated the vitality of a state whose power rested not merely on ships but on a far-reaching commercial system. He had shown wonderful skill at this critical period in combining against his principal enemy an opposition for which Prussia afforded the body and the hot temper of the Czar the animating soul. But he never fully understood the maritime problems with which he had to deal. He underestimated the vitality of a state upon which centred a far-reaching commercial system, and in valuing naval power he did not appreciate that a mere mass of ships had not the weight he himself was able to impart to a mass of men.
The Baltic campaign was one of Nelson’s finest achievements — not for the battle alone, but for his clear reading of the political and military situation. He had lifted on his shoulders the dead weight of his superior, had seen that the trunk of the tree was Paul and Russia, and had never for one moment lost sight of the key to the whole. Had Nelson been given the command from the start, the twelve Russian ships at Revel would have been destroyed, the League would have been shattered at its source, and the whole course of the naval war might have been altered. As it was, the Armed Neutrality of 1800 remains a classic demonstration of the difficulty of combining continental and maritime powers against a state that commands the sea. British sea power had dispersed the Northern coalition, commanded the friendship of the great continental states, retained control of the Mediterranean, reduced Egypt to submission, and forced even the invincible Bonaparte to wish for a speedy cessation of hostilities.

concepts/continental-system.title: The Continental System
concepts/continental-system.content:
The Continental System
The Prelude: Commerce Raiding and the Road to Economic War, 1793–1806
The war against commerce during the French Revolution and Empire was marked from its opening by the same passionate vehemence that characterised the political and military enterprises of the period. Both France and Great Britain, in their effort to bring the commerce of the whole world under the yoke of their respective policies, swayed back and forth in a deadly grapple that trampled under foot the rights and interests of every weaker party. The question between Napoleon and the British people became simply one of endurance: like two infuriated dogs, they had locked jaws over commerce as the decisive element in the contest.
At the outbreak of war in 1793, both sides issued the customary instructions to commanders and privateers to seize enemy merchant vessels and neutrals violating international law. The sea swarmed with hastily equipped cruisers. But while the great British fleets gradually established a distinct preponderance over the masses of the enemy, France was quickly reduced to the ordinary operations of commerce-destroying — the guerre de course — a policy to which both national tradition and the opinion of many eminent naval officers particularly inclined. By 1795 the Directory formally abandoned the policy of keeping great fleets together and committed France wholly to the war against commerce.
To these raids upon their shipping the British opposed a twofold system. The first was the convoy system: merchant vessels bound to different quarters of the globe were gathered in specified ports and sailed together under the protection of ships of war. From two to three hundred ships was not an unusual gathering; five hundred or even a thousand were at times seen together in the Chops of the Channel or the entrance to the Baltic. The second was the system of patrol: fast frigates and sloops-of-war, with a host of smaller vessels, were disseminated over the ocean upon the tracks that commerce followed. The Convoy Act of 1798 compelled the taking of convoy and the payment of a sum for protection; in its first year this tax brought in £1,292,000 to the Treasury while resulting in a yet greater saving of insurance to owners.
The losses on both sides were substantial but never decisive. Over the twenty-one years of war approximately eleven thousand British vessels were captured — an annual average of about 524 ships, representing roughly two and a half per cent of British commerce. This loss, while painful, was partially offset by prizes taken by British cruisers and by the enormous expansion of British trade carried on under neutral flags. The British merchant marine, with its enormous tonnage and global reach, absorbed losses that would have shattered any smaller trading nation. Meanwhile French commerce was annihilated: in 1799 the Directory admitted that not a single merchant ship carrying the French flag remained on the sea. French exports to Asia, Africa, and America together amounted in 1800 to less than $56,000.
The neutral carriers — particularly the United States, whose merchant tonnage exploded from 355,000 tons in 1790 to 799,304 in 1801 — stepped into the gap. But this neutral carrying trade provoked escalating restrictions from both belligerents. Great Britain enforced the Rule of 1756, forbidding neutrals from carrying trade in peacetime that was closed to them; France, through the Directory’s law of January 18, 1798, subjected neutral vessels to seizure and condemnation. By 1806, both belligerents had moved far beyond the Law of Nations as it had been understood in 1793. The war was consuming the legal order as surely as it consumed men and treasure.
The Berlin Decree
On November 21, 1806, from the Prussian capital that he had entered after the battle of Jena, Napoleon issued the Berlin Decree. Its essential underlying idea was to crush the commerce of Great Britain by closing the entire European continent to her products of every kind. The pretext was found in the British Order in Council of May 16, 1806, issued by the ministry of Grenville and Fox, which had placed the coast of the Continent from Brest to the Elbe under blockade. Napoleon asserted — falsely — that the right to blockade applied only to fortified, not to commercial, ports; and argued, with some plausibility, that the united forces of Great Britain were unable to maintain so extensive an operation.
Retaliating an alleged abuse with a far greater excess, the Berlin Decree began by declaring the British Isles blockaded — at a time when the emperor could not keep a ship at sea except as a fugitive from the omnipresent fleets of his enemy. From this phantom blockade it followed that all commerce with the British Isles was forbidden; all merchandise exported from them became good prize; vessels from Great Britain could not be admitted into French ports. Not only was the property of individual Englishmen on the Continent to be seized, but also that of individual neutrals, if of British origin. The preamble ended with a clause defining the decree as a fundamental principle of the Empire, to remain in force until England acknowledged that the law of war was one and the same on land as on the sea — that it could not be extended to private property of whatever kind, nor to the person of individuals not in the military profession.
Having launched his missile, Napoleon immediately engaged in the campaign against Russia. The bloody and doubtful battle of Eylau was fought on February 8, 1807, and for the next several months the emperor was too busily engaged holding on by his teeth on the banks of the Vistula to superintend the working of his decree. The whole edict remained a dead letter until the struggle with Russia was decided. American vessels continued to trade freely with the Continent, and British merchants, at first desisting from sending goods, soon resumed shipments by neutral vessels as briskly as before. The decree would remain inoperative until Napoleon could enforce it by military control of the entire European coastline.
The British Response — Orders in Council (1807, 1809)
While the Berlin Decree lay dormant, negotiations were proceeding in London between the United States envoys and the British ministry concerning matters in dispute between the two countries. On December 31, 1806, a commercial treaty was signed, but it was not ratified by the United States government.
Meanwhile the British ministry determined to retort by a measure of retaliation. On January 7, 1807, an Order in Council was issued by the Whig ministers. Citing Napoleon’s decree, it avowed his Majesty’s unwillingness to carry retaliation to extremes and for the present went no further than to forbid all trade by neutral vessels from one hostile port to another — that is, the coastwise trade of France and her allies. This bore particularly hard upon American ships, which were in the habit of going from place to place in Europe seeking the best markets. Under this order American trade in the Mediterranean was swept away by seizures and condemnations.
A change of ministry in March 1807 brought back into power the party that had been in opposition since the death of Pitt. The Berlin Decree had remained inoperative through Napoleon’s absence in Poland, but the emperor’s return to Paris in the summer of 1807 presaged a new phase of the economic conflict. On November 11, 1807, were published the great retaliatory measures of Great Britain — the Orders in Council of that date — which for the moment filled the cup of neutrals to overflowing.
Setting forth the Berlin Decree as their justifying ground, the Orders proclaimed a paper blockade of the barest form and most extensive scope: all ports of France and her allies, and all other ports in Europe from which the British flag was excluded, were declared subject to the same restrictions as if actually blockaded in the most strict and rigorous manner. All trade in hostile colonial produce was likewise declared unlawful for neutrals.
The object of the Orders was twofold: to embarrass France by the prohibition of direct import and export trade, and at the same time to force into the Continent all British products and manufactures that it could take. “No trade except through England” was the formula: neutrals might not trade directly with any ports in Europe not open to British ships, but they might trade with them by first going to a British port, landing their cargo, reshipping it subject to certain duties, and then proceeding to a hostile port. The same process was to be observed on the return voyage. The commerce of the Continent thus paid toll going and coming.
Anything more humiliating and vexatious to neutrals could scarcely be conceived. The Orders trampled upon all previously received law, upon men’s inbred ideas of their rights, by sheer uncontrolled force. Yet they were a very real and severe measure of retaliation. The additional expense entailed upon every cargo that reached the Continent after passing through British ports — the expenses of delay, unloading and reloading, wharfage, licenses, maintenance — fell chiefly upon the continental consumer. And Great Britain, while unable to blockade every individual French port, was able to make the approach to the French coast exceedingly dangerous. In the English Channel she controlled the approaches from the Atlantic to all the northern continental ports; at Gibraltar she controlled those to the Mediterranean. The Orders were by no means an empty threat.
The Milan Decree
Napoleon was not the man to accept the Orders in Council silently. On October 27, 1807, he signed the treaty of Fontainebleau with Spain, arranging the partition of Portugal and taking the first step in the invasion of the Peninsula. On November 16 he left Fontainebleau to visit his kingdom of Italy. From the capital, Milan, on December 17, 1807, he issued the decree that bears its name.
Alleging the Orders as its motive, the Milan Decree declared that any ship that submitted to search by a British cruiser was thereby “denationalised” — outlawed — and liable to arrest as a vagrant. The decree further declared that all vessels going to or sailing from Great Britain were for that fact alone good prize, a point that under the Berlin Decree had been left open. French privateers were still sufficiently numerous to make these regulations a great additional danger to ships at sea; and the decree added that when vessels came under the previous provisions, they should be seized whenever they entered a French port.
The two belligerents had now laid down the general lines of policy on which they intended to act. Napoleon never revoked his Berlin and Milan Decrees, although by a trick he induced an over-eager President of the United States to believe that he had done so. The Orders in Council received various modifications over the following years, but the entire series was finally withdrawn only in June 1812 — too late to avert the war with the United States that was declared in the same month.
The System in Operation
The Continental System, once Napoleon had the military power to enforce it, extended over the entire coastline of Europe from the Baltic to the Adriatic. Its operation was shaped not merely by decrees but by the interaction of naval power, geography, and human ingenuity.
The Portuguese Court’s Flight to Brazil
In July 1807, while still at Dresden, Napoleon notified Portugal that she must choose between war with France or with Great Britain. A French corps under Junot assembled in the south of France to invade Portugal. The British government, which had received certain information of the secret articles agreed to at Tilsit, foresaw the danger. A squadron appeared off Lisbon at the critical moment, and its presence determined the vacillating Portuguese regent to withdraw to Brazil. When Junot’s army — which had made a march of extreme suffering with great rapidity, losing most of its numbers by privation, exposure, and straggling — entered Lisbon on November 30, 1807, it found the Portuguese fleet gone and the court and its treasure departed with it.
The Second Copenhagen Expedition
Simultaneously, Napoleon moved against Denmark. The British ministry had received intelligence of the secret articles of Tilsit and understood the danger of allowing the Danish and Portuguese navies to fall into the emperor’s hands. Early in August 1807, twenty-five sail-of-the-line entered the Baltic, convoying transports with twenty-seven thousand troops. The island on which Copenhagen stands was invested by the ships and the town by the army. The Danish government was summoned to surrender its fleet into British safe keeping, with a pledge that all maritime equipment delivered would be held as a deposit and restored at a general peace. The offer being refused, the city was bombarded from September 2 to September 5, after which the Danes yielded. The British took possession of eighteen sail-of-the-line and a number of frigates, stripped the dockyards of their stores, and returned to England.
Though foiled in his endeavours to seize the fleets, Napoleon had succeeded in formally closing the ports of both Denmark and Portugal to British goods. The bombardment of Copenhagen served as a pretext for Russia’s declaration of hostility against Great Britain on October 20, 1807. Prussia, under the compulsion of the two empires, closed her ports against British commerce by a proclamation on September 2. Austria acceded to the Continental System and excluded British goods from her borders. In Italy, the kingdom of Etruria showed little zeal in enforcing Napoleon’s commands; the British carried on commerce at Leghorn as freely as at any port in their own country. By the emperor’s orders the viceroy of Italy therefore took possession of the city, while French detachments entered the Papal States, occupied their coasts, and drove the British from them. With Joseph Bonaparte already king of Naples, Napoleon’s control extended over both coasts of Italy. Turkey, being involved in hostilities with Great Britain, completed the ring.
The System’s Economic Effects
The effects of this vast closure on the European economy were profound. Ports rotted idle. Colonial goods — sugar, coffee, cotton, tobacco — vanished from the continental markets or reached them only through channels of desperate ingenuity. Smuggling became a universal industry. The coasts of the North Sea, between the mouths of the Ems, the Weser, and the Elbe, and those of Danish Holstein — low-lying, difficult of approach for large vessels, favourable to small boats — fostered clandestine trade. The British seized Heligoland in September 1807 and converted it into a depot for goods waiting to be introduced into Germany and Holstein. A garrison of six hundred men defended the island while ships of war cruised continually in its neighbourhood; from there contraband traders obtained merchandise with which they supplied the Continent. Between five and six hundred women were employed by the merchants of Hamburg daily to convey into the city, each of them, fourteen pounds of coffee and other produce concealed beneath their garments.
In Holland, where Napoleon had placed his brother Louis on the throne in 1806, the king sought from the first to identify himself with his new subjects and constantly withstood Napoleon’s commands in favour of their maritime commerce. Evasions were frequent; the decrees were openly disregarded on various pretences. From Holland goods found their way without great difficulty into France, though on two occasions Napoleon punished Holland for her waywardness by closing the frontier against her.
In the Baltic the effectiveness of the system depended upon the heartiness of the czar in the cause. Decrees of great severity were issued, and the British flag was honestly excluded; but the quick mercantile intelligence of the era soon detected that no ill-timed curiosity as to ships’ papers would be exercised. British commerce was carried on in Russian ports by neutrals armed with British licenses. The czar had never promised to exclude neutrals or to forbid all export and import; it was none of his business to pry behind the papers that covered transactions essential to his people.
American Neutrality and the Embargo
The United States was caught between the two belligerents. Napoleon’s decisions of September 18, 1807, communicated to Congress on December 18, together with a British proclamation directing the impressment of British seamen found serving on foreign merchant ships, moved President Jefferson to recommend an embargo to keep American vessels in their own ports. An Act of Embargo was approved on December 22, 1807, forbidding all registered United States vessels to depart from the ports in which they were then lying.
The Embargo continued in force throughout 1808 and until March 1, 1809, when it was repealed and replaced by a Non-Intercourse Act that allowed American merchant ships to go abroad but forbade them to trade with Great Britain, France, or their colonies. This was the law governing American intercourse with the two great belligerents until May 1810.
Napoleon, meanwhile, had in April 1808 issued an order directing the sequestration of all American ships entering the ports of France, Italy, Holland, and the Hanse towns, on the ground that since the Embargo prevented them from having lawfully left their own country, their papers must be fabricated and they must really have come from England. Under this ruling sequestrations continued until March 23, 1810, when the Decree of Rambouillet confiscated the vessels and cargoes thus seized.
The Expansion and Cracking of the System
Tilsit: Russia Enters the System
The battle of Friedland, fought on June 14, 1807, resulted in the total defeat of the Russian army. An armistice was signed on June 22, and on June 25 Alexander and Napoleon had their first interview upon the raft in the Niemen. On July 8 was concluded the remarkable and threatening Treaty of Tilsit. The czar recognised all the new states created by the emperor and ceded to him the Ionian Islands and the mouths of the Cattaro in the Adriatic; in return, Napoleon acquiesced in Russia’s taking Finland from Sweden and, under certain conditions, the European provinces of the Turkish Empire as far as the Balkans. A further clause bound Russia to adopt the Continental System — to close her ports against British commerce and join the economic war against England.
The two empires had divided Europe between them. For Napoleon, this was the moment when the Continental System ceased to be a paper project and became the dominant economic fact of European life. From the Sound to the Hellespont, every port was nominally closed to British trade.
The Peninsular War Begins (1808)
In 1808 Napoleon’s purpose to overthrow the Spanish monarchy and place one of his own family upon the throne finally matured. He left Paris on April 2, reached Bayonne, and there engineered the resignation of the Spanish king. But on May 2 an insurrection in Madrid was followed by spontaneous popular risings throughout Spain. On July 21 an army corps under General Dupont was cut off by insurgents in Andalusia and surrendered at Baylen, eighteen thousand strong. On July 29 the new king of Spain, Joseph Bonaparte, fled from Madrid.
On August 1 a British fleet appeared off the coast of Portugal bearing the first division of troops destined to act in the Peninsula under Sir Arthur Wellesley. On August 21 the battle of Vimiero was fought, resulting in the defeat of Junot, who by the Convention of Cintra was permitted to evacuate Portugal and was conveyed to France in British transports. Portugal was wholly lost, and the French army in Spain fell back to the line of the Ebro.
Napoleon realised the necessity of suppressing the general uprising and determined to take the field in person. But before removing to this distant scene of action, he confirmed his understanding with the czar at a second meeting at Erfurt in September 1808. The alliance formed at Tilsit was renewed. The czar had already begun hostilities against Sweden; Denmark had declared war against Sweden as well; Prussia closed her ports against Swedish commerce. The vital importance of the Baltic to Great Britain — as the source of naval stores and a channel for commerce into the Continent remote from Napoleon’s vigilance — imposed upon her the necessity of supporting Sweden. A fleet of sixty-two sail, of which sixteen were of the line, was sent through the Sound under Sir James Saumarez.
The Peninsular War proved to be a catastrophe for the Continental System. The Spanish uprising gave Britain a foothold on the Continent and, for the first time, a continental army that she could supply and sustain entirely by sea. The French could not turn the British flank because they could not control the sea; they could not starve the British army because it was fed by sea. Wellington’s army in Portugal and Spain was supplied, reinforced, and sustained entirely by maritime power, and the Peninsular War became the final demonstration of what sea power meant: not a weapon of conquest but the condition that made endurance possible.
Austria’s Revival (1809)
Austria, since the Peace of Presburg in 1805, had been quietly engaged in restoring her military strength. The destruction of Prussia, the establishment of the Confederation of the Rhine, the foundation of the Duchy of Warsaw, and her own territorial losses had left Austria in a position she could not possibly accept as final. Napoleon undertook his Spanish enterprise with the full knowledge that his absence in the Peninsula must be short; he understood that a prolonged stay there would give Austria the opportunity she needed. This hope was frustrated by the action of Sir John Moore, whose daring move to the north in December 1808 turned Napoleon from his projected march on Lisbon and forced him into a winter campaign in northwestern Spain.
The year 1809 therefore opened with the prospect of war between France and Austria. Napoleon, at the head of eighty thousand men, was driving some twenty thousand British troops through the snows of northwestern Spain — but Austria was arming. The war that followed — the campaign of Essling and Wagram — absorbed Napoleon’s attention for the rest of the year, and in his absence trade with the North Sea ports went on almost as in time of peace.
The License System
Among the multiplied impediments to commerce there arose an extensive usage of licenses — individual permissions to carry on traffic forbidden by the existing laws of the issuing authority. The British government adopted the license system in 1808, immediately after the Orders in Council and the alliance of Russia with Napoleon. The numbers grew from 2,606 in 1807 to over 15,000 in 1809 and over 18,000 in 1810. The licenses, which protected against British cruisers, were primarily used for trade to the Baltic ports, though they also covered voyages to Holland, France, Spain, and other continental countries. After 1810 there was a rapid falling off — not from a change of system, but from the bitter discovery that the license that protected against a British cruiser did not save the ship upon arrival in a port under Napoleon’s control, when the emperor at last devoted his indomitable energy to the thorough enforcement of his decrees.
Growing Russian Tensions
In the Baltic, the czar was wearying of his engagements with France. He had adhered faithfully to the letter of his bargain and refused admission to British ships, but he would not open his eyes to the fact that British commerce was being carried on in his ports by neutrals with British licenses. The imports to Great Britain of naval stores, mainly from the Baltic, more than doubled from 1808 to 1809. The czar’s nobles disapproved of the French alliance; the distress of his subjects from the cessation of trade with Britain was palpable. Napoleon, by demanding ever stricter enforcement — by pressing for measures that would close Russian ports to neutral carriers entirely — was pushing Alexander toward the breaking point.
The Continental System, which had seemed Napoleon’s masterstroke, was creating the conditions for his eventual downfall. It alienated the populations and rulers he needed to keep the system closed. It forced the Spanish people into a national insurrection that Britain could support. It strained the alliance with Russia beyond endurance. And it gave Britain — which commanded the sea and had access to world markets — the strategic advantage of time. The system could not defeat a nation with command of the sea; it could only impoverish the continent that had to enforce it.
By 1810 the cracks were spreading. The Peninsular War bled French resources. Austria had risen and been beaten but was gathering strength. The czar’s compliance was visibly flagging. Napoleon’s own letters from this period reveal the strain: the emperor wrote to his brother Louis of Holland that he could close the Rhine, the Weser, the Scheldt, and the Meuse to Holland and place her in a position more critical than by declaring war. He threatened to reunite Holland to France. The system was devouring its own children.
The Balance of the System
The Continental System inflicted serious hardship on Britain. The exclusion from continental markets was real and painful; British exports to Europe fell sharply in certain years; the distress among manufacturing districts was at times acute. The financial strain was severe, and the years 1810–1811 witnessed a protracted commercial crisis in which British merchants groaned under the weight of accumulated inventories and restricted markets.
But the system did not bring Britain to terms — nor, on the evidence, could it have done so. The British merchant marine, protected by convoy and by the commanding position of the Royal Navy, carried on a global commerce that sustained British credit, taxation, and subsidy capacity. British exports found their way into Europe through every chink in Napoleon’s wall: through Heligoland, through the Baltic neutrals, through the license system, through the corruption of customs officials, through the smuggling networks that implicated entire populations. The continental peoples, with few exceptions, resented the French blockade and co-operated with the evaders. The British instinctively understood that the hearts of the continental peoples were with them rather than with Napoleon — for much the same reason that the United States, contrary to the general interests of mankind, sided upon the whole against Great Britain: the immediate oppressor was the object of hatred.
For Napoleon himself, the system was a trap. It demanded the absolute closure of the entire European coastline — a task that required military control of every port from the Baltic to the Adriatic, the co-operation or subjugation of every continental power, and the suppression of a universal instinct for commerce that no decree could eradicate. To maintain the system he had to extend his dominion further and further — into Spain, into Portugal, into the Papal States, into Holland, into the Hanseatic cities — each extension provoking new resistance, each conquest demanding new garrisons, each enforcement breeding new resentment. When Russia, the indispensable linchpin of the system in the east, finally defied the blockade by reopening her ports to neutral shipping in 1810, Napoleon had only one answer: war. The invasion of Russia in 1812 was not merely a punishment for Russian defiance; it was the logical consequence of a system that could tolerate no exception and no neutrality.
The Continental System thus accomplished what no British fleet could have achieved by itself: it created the conditions for Napoleon’s destruction. The Peninsular War bled France of men and prestige; the Russian campaign consumed the Grand Army; the coalitions that finally defeated Napoleon in 1813–1814 were sustained by British subsidies drawn from the very commerce the system had tried to destroy. The system that was meant to starve Britain instead starved the continent of everything except the will to resist the emperor who had impoverished it.

concepts/court-at-versailles.title: The Court at Versailles
concepts/court-at-versailles.content:
The Court at Versailles
The Living Machine
The court at Versailles under Louis XVI was not a museum of bygone splendour, nor was it merely the king’s residence. It was the central nervous system of the French monarchy — a vast, intricate, and unceasingly active institution that governed how power was distributed, how patronage flowed, how the nobility justified its privileges, and how the Bourbon dynasty presented itself to the world. Between 1774, when the young king ascended the throne, and October 1789, when the Parisian mob dragged the royal family back to the Tuileries, the court functioned according to a rhythm and logic that had been refined over more than a century. It was a world of relentless ceremony, ferocious ambition, private pleasures, and public display — and it was dying even as it danced.
The palace itself was the most visible expression of this system. Built to house the entire apparatus of governance and to cage the nobility in plain sight of the sovereign, the château of Versailles contained within its walls not only the royal apartments but the offices of ministers and secretaries of state, the military household, the stables, the kitchens, the chapel, the theatre, and the endless galleries and antechambers where courtiers spent their lives waiting — waiting for an audience, for a favour, for a pension, for a word from the king that might change their fortunes. The town of Versailles, which had grown up around the palace, housed the thousands of functionaries, servants, merchants, and hangers-on whose existence depended on the court’s appetite.
The physical scale was staggering. The main château stretched nearly a quarter-mile along the terrace, its five thousand rooms spread over four floors. The Marble Court, the Royal Court, the Ministers’ Wings — each space had a precise social gradient, from the public outer courts where any well-dressed person might wander, to the Oeil de Boeuf antechamber where only those with the grandes entrées might penetrate, to the intimate apartments of the king and queen where only the family and a handful of privileged servants might enter. The park stretched for miles, its groves and fountains designed for promenades, hunts, and clandestine rendezvous. Beyond the park lay the Grand Trianon, a palace of rose marble built for private retreat, and further still the Petit Trianon, the queen’s domain. At the Petit Trianon, Marie-Antoinette had created the Hamlet — a rustic village of thatched cottages, a working farm, a mill, and a lake — where she could escape the suffocating formality of the main court and play at being a milkmaid with her closest friends.
The Etiquette System
Every moment of the day at Versailles was governed by a code of precedence and procedure so detailed that it bordered on the liturgical. The etiquette system, inherited from Louis XIV and refined by a century of practice, determined who might hand the king his shirt in the morning, who might sit on a tabouret in the queen’s presence, who might accompany the royal hunt, and who might embrace the queen when she was enceinte. It was not mere fussiness: in a world where favour and fortune depended entirely on proximity to power, the procedures that controlled access were the very mechanisms of distribution.
The king’s day began with the lever, a highly structured ceremony that unfolded in stages. At the appointed hour, the first valet de chambre woke the king. The petit lever admitted only those with the entrées de la chambre — the princes of the blood, the highest officers of the crown, the gentlemen who held the most coveted positions. As the king was washed and shaved, these privileged courtiers might exchange a few words with him, present a petition, or simply stand in attendance, their presence a visible claim on the monarch’s attention. The grand lever followed, opening the doors to a wider circle: the military officers on duty, the gentlemen of the wardrobe, the physicians, the courtiers of sufficient rank. The king dressed, each garment handed to him by the officer whose privilege it was to hold that particular piece of clothing. The shirt was the great prize — only the highest-ranking prince present had the right to present it.
The queen’s lever was similarly elaborate, though Marie-Antoinette came to chafe against its rigours. Madame Campan, her première femme de chambre, recorded the precise order in which the queen’s toilette unfolded. The princesses of the blood and the duchesses had the right to attend, to hand the queen her shift, her handkerchief, her fan. The entrées to the queen’s toilette were jealously guarded; to be admitted was a mark of favour, to be excluded a public slight. Marie-Antoinette, increasingly impatient with these formalities, would sometimes slip away to the Petit Trianon precisely to avoid them — a retreat that the court, and eventually the public, read as an affront to the established order.
The grand couvert was the public meal, held in the king’s antechamber, where any properly dressed person might watch the royal family eat. It was not a private affair but a performance of kingship — the king’s appetite, his table manners, his casual remarks to those standing nearby were all observed and reported back to Paris. The Sunday chapel was a major ceremonial event, the royal family processing through the galleries in full court dress, the king taking his place in the royal tribune while the courtiers filled the nave below. The hunt was perhaps the most important social event of the court calendar: the king rode out with a vast retinue of mounted nobles, and the invitation to join the hunt was one of the surest marks of favour. Louis XVI, whose passion for hunting bordered on the obsessive, spent more time in the saddle than he did in council.
Presentations at court followed a formidable ritual. A noblewoman presented for the first time had to be sponsored by a lady already presented, had to wear the prescribed costume — the grand panier hoopskirt, the elaborate headdress, the train of precisely regulated length — and had to execute a series of reverences before the king and queen, backing out of the presence without once turning her back. A single misstep could ruin a family’s hopes for years. The honneurs de la cour, the right to be presented, belonged only to families who could prove their nobility back to 1400 — a requirement that excluded the newer nobility of the robe and kept the court a preserve of the ancient sword nobility.
The Factions
The court was a battlefield of factions, their alignments shifting with the marriages, deaths, and disgraces that punctuated court life. Under Louis XVI, the most significant division was between the party of the old Choiseul faction and the Polignacs, who rose with the queen’s favour.
The Duc de Choiseul, minister under Louis XV, had been the great patron of a generation of nobles, military officers, and philosophers. Though disgraced in 1770, his network survived him, clustering around the hope of his return. The Choiseul party — or what remained of it — was associated with the reformist, anti-clerical, pro-Austrian policies of the previous reign. They looked to the king’s minister Maurepas with suspicion and to the rising Polignac circle with outright hostility.
The Polignac faction was the queen’s party. The Comtesse Jules de Polignac, a woman of charm, beauty, and exquisite manners, had become the queen’s favourite in the late 1770s, displacing the Princesse de Lamballe, who held the revived office of Surintendante of the Queen’s Household. Campan describes the Polignacs as a clan rather than a couple — the countess, her husband, her brother-in-law the Comte d’Artois’s governor, and most notably the Vicomte de Vaudreuil, a brilliant and dangerous figure who dominated the circle. The queen showered the Polignacs with favours: the comtesse received a pension of 400,000 livres, her husband became the premier écuyer, their friends and relatives received sinecures, offices, and benefices. The court groaned under the weight of this obvious partiality. Besenval, a court insider who observed the factional struggles from close range, noted that the queen’s preference for the Polignacs over the Lamballe circle created a lasting wound in the court’s fabric — and, by extension, in the monarchy’s moral authority.
The Mesdames — Louis XV’s daughters, Adélaïde, Victoire, Sophie, and Louise — formed a separate, devout, influential bloc. They had survived their father’s reign and the ascendancy of Madame du Barry; they now occupied a secure place in the court hierarchy, wielding quiet but persistent influence over ecclesiastical appointments and devotional policy. They lived in a separate wing of the château, maintaining their own ceremonial and their own networks. To the queen, they were figures of respect but also of constraint — they represented the old piety, the old formality, the old way of being royal, which the young queen’s innovations seemed to threaten.
The princes of the blood — notably the Comte de Provence (the king’s brother, later Louis XVIII), the Comte d’Artois (later Charles X), and the Duc d’Orléans — were themselves centres of faction. Provence was clever, ambitious, and, it was widely suspected, waiting for his brother to stumble. Artois was frivolous, spendthrift, and devoted to the queen’s social circle. Orléans was worst of all — a prince of the blood who had been alienated by the queen’s coldness and who cultivated popularity among the Parisian bourgeoisie, frequenting the Palais-Royal and positioning himself as an alternative to the king’s authority. The queen, Campan notes, always kept Orléans at arm’s length; the estrangement became a political weapon in his hands.
Daily Life at Court
The king’s routine was that of a methodical, private, somewhat melancholy man. Louis XVI rose early, heard mass, attended council on appointed days, dined in public, hunted, and spent his evenings in his private apartments where he pursued his two great passions: locksmithing and geography. He had a forge set up in the mezzanine above his cabinet, where he worked with iron and tools, often in the company of his locksmith, Gamin. The court found this habit undignified; pamphleteers would eventually use it as evidence of the king’s unfitness — a monarch who preferred tinkering with locks to governing his kingdom. But for Louis XVI, the forge was a refuge from a world he never quite mastered.
The queen’s life followed a different rhythm. Marie-Antoinette had been a child of fourteen when she came to France; as queen, she threw herself into pleasure with an energy that the court alternately admired and condemned. Her days were filled with gaming — faro, lansquenet, cavagnole — often until the early hours of the morning. She attended the opera and the theatre, both at the court and in Paris. She gave balls, masked balls, private concerts. She filled the Petit Trianon with a society of her choosing, a closed circle that excluded many of the highest-ranking courtiers and that became, in the public imagination, the scene of nameless debauchery. The Queen’s Hamlet was the final expression of this need for escape — a fantasy of rural simplicity, complete with a working dairy, a dovecote, a mill, and a lake, where the queen and her friends could dress as peasants and forget that they were the centre of the most scrutinised court in Europe.
For the ordinary courtier — the six hundred families who were expected to maintain a presence at Versailles — life was a perpetual, grinding pursuit of favour. To be noticed by the king, to be greeted by the queen, to receive a pension, a benefice, a regiment, a governorship, a ribbon of an order — these were the prizes for which a family might devote generations. The cost was enormous. A courtier needed an apartment in the château or a hôtel in the town, a carriage, servants in livery, costumes for ceremony after ceremony, and the endless round of gifts, bribes, and gambling losses that oiled the social machine. Many nobles ruined themselves in the attempt. Those who succeeded found themselves no more than glorified attendants, standing in galleries for hours, hoping for a nod.
Montesquieu had written that the court was the natural element of the monarchy, the place where honour was the principle of government. But by the 1780s, the court had become synonymous with waste and frivolity. The pensions paid to courtiers consumed a staggering portion of the royal budget. The Polignac circle alone absorbed millions of livres. The queen’s building projects at Trianon, her theatricals, her gambling — each was a drop in a bucket that was already overflowing with the debts of the American war.
The Political Function
Despite its reputation for triviality, the court remained the seat of government. The Council of State met in the king’s cabinet at specified hours — the Conseil d’En Haut for the most sensitive matters of state, the Conseil des Dépêches for internal administration, the Conseil Royal des Finances for the budget that was always on the edge of crisis. Ministers came to Versailles to report, to receive instructions, to negotiate with the king and, increasingly, with the queen. It was here that Necker was summoned, dismissed, and recalled; here that Calonne presented his doomed plan for tax reform; here that the Assembly of Notables met in 1787, hoping to stave off the financial collapse that would trigger the Revolution.
Ambassadors were received in the Salon de la Paix or the Salon d’Apollon, where the throne was placed on a dais beneath a ceiling painting of the Sun God. The reception of ambassadors was a piece of theatre designed to display French power to the world — the king seated, the ambassador approaching through a double line of courtiers, the ceremonial bowing, the exchange of speeches in a language that both sides understood to be about the relative standing of their sovereigns.
Patronage was distributed through the court, and patronage was the substance of politics. A minister who lost the king’s ear ceased to be able to reward his clients; a minister who could not reward his clients lost his faction; a faction that lost its cohesion could not govern. The court was therefore the mechanism through which the entire edifice of the French state was held together — and the mechanism through which it was finally torn apart. When the king could no longer satisfy the demands of those who depended on him for place and pension, the loyalty of the nobility began to fray.
The Breakdown
The fiscal crisis of the 1780s exposed the court to a scrutiny that it could not survive. The deficit, the failure of successive ministers to reform the tax system, the summoning of the Estates-General — each blow diminished the court’s legitimacy. The nobility had been expected to sacrifice their privileges to save the state; they had refused. The court’s profligacy was now held up as evidence that the monarchy itself was unreformable. The pamphlets that flooded Paris — Les Nuits de Versailles, the endless libelles against Marie-Antoinette — turned the court into a symbol of everything that was rotten in France.
The October Days of 1789 were the end. On 5 October, a crowd of Parisian women — and men in women’s clothing, and National Guardsmen — marched on Versailles, demanding bread and the king’s return to Paris. The château was invaded; the queen’s apartments were stormed; two guardsmen were killed and their heads paraded on pikes. Lafayette, who commanded the National Guard, persuaded the king to return to Paris. On the morning of 6 October, the royal family climbed into a carriage and began the slow journey to the Tuileries. Behind them, the vast, empty palace stood as a monument to a world that had already ended.
The court would never return.
