concepts/sea-power-as-concept.title: Sea Power as a Concept
concepts/sea-power-as-concept.content:
Sea Power as a Concept
Mahan’s Retrospective Thesis
The argument that sea power determined the outcome of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars belongs, in its fully developed form, not to the eighteenth century but to the 1890s. It is the creation of Rear Admiral Alfred Thayer Mahan, an American naval officer writing at the United States Naval War College a century after the events he analysed. Mahan’s great work, The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812 (1892), is not a naval history in the ordinary sense. It is a sustained theoretical argument, using the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars as a case study to demonstrate a universal proposition: that control of the sea is the decisive factor in the outcome of great conflicts.
It is essential to understand what this means — and what it does not mean. The men who fought the Revolutionary Wars did not think in terms of ‘sea power’ as Mahan defined it. Nelson, Pitt, Bonaparte, and the statesmen of the era understood that the navy was important; they did not possess a systematic theory of maritime supremacy as a unified force encompassing commerce, colonies, naval strength, and national character. Mahan’s framework is a retrospective construct, imposed upon the events of 1793–1815 to reveal a pattern that contemporaries saw only dimly and in fragments. This page presents Mahan’s framework as he himself presented it: not as ‘how the revolutionaries understood the sea’ but as ‘how sea power, rightly understood, determined what happened to the revolutionaries.’
The central proposition, in Mahan’s own account, is this: a nation that controls the sea controls the terms of the conflict. It can strike where it chooses, supply its allies, starve its enemies, and prevent invasion of its own shores. Its commerce flourishes while that of its adversary withers; its credit remains sound while the enemy’s treasury empties; its people are sustained by the resources of the whole world while the enemy’s are confined to what lies within reach of his armies. The nation that loses control of the sea may still win battles, may still conquer territory, may still compel the submission of continental states — but it does so at an ever-mounting cost, and in the end it cannot prevent the maritime power from assembling against it a coalition that it cannot defeat.
This was the fate that overcame France. The Revolution produced the most formidable army Europe had seen since the Roman legions; it conquered Belgium, Holland, the Rhineland, Italy, Switzerland, and Egypt; it overthrew every coalition that the powers of the Continent could mount against it; and under Napoleon it dominated Europe from the Atlantic to the Niemen. But it never succeeded in challenging British control of the sea after the first years of the war, and that failure proved ultimately fatal. The French army could not cross the Channel; the French treasury could not draw upon the colonies once the navy was destroyed; the French people could not obtain the colonial products and raw materials that their economy required; and the French government could not prevent British subsidies from keeping continental armies in the field against it. Sea power, in Mahan’s reading, was the foundation upon which the entire edifice of resistance to the Revolution and the Empire was built.
The Definition of Sea Power
Mahan’s first move is to define his central term. ‘Sea power’ in his usage is not synonymous with naval strength. It is a broader concept encompassing three elements that together form a unified system: the merchant shipping that carries a nation’s trade, the colonies that produce the commodities that trade requires, and the navy that protects both. These three elements are interdependent. A nation without merchant shipping cannot develop a navy, because it has no pool of trained seamen; a nation without colonies cannot generate the wealth to sustain a navy in peace and war; a navy that cannot protect the merchant marine and the colonies is worthless. Sea power, in Mahan’s conception, is the capacity of a nation to deploy all three elements in a coherent strategy that serves its national interests.
This definition is retrospective. When Mahan applies it to the French Revolutionary Wars, he is not describing how the French or British governments understood their situation in 1793. He is measuring their actions against a theoretical standard that did not yet exist. The value of the definition lies not in its faithfulness to contemporary thinking but in its analytical power: it allows Mahan to explain why certain policies succeeded and others failed, in terms that the actors themselves could not have articulated.
The Six Elements Affecting Sea Power
Sea power does not arise spontaneously. It is not the product of a single decision or a single generation’s effort, but the result of a combination of conditions that together create the capacity for maritime strength. Mahan distinguishes six such elements, each contributing in its way to the whole.
Geographical Position
The first and most fundamental element is the position that a nation occupies upon the globe. An island or an archipelago is, other things being equal, better situated for sea power than a continental state — not because the islanders are more sea-minded, but because an island has no land frontier to defend and therefore can concentrate its military resources upon the sea. A continental state, by contrast, must maintain a standing army against its neighbours; its naval effort is always competing with the claims of its land frontiers for money, men, and attention.
From this alone, Mahan argues, it follows that Great Britain enjoyed a structural advantage over France in the struggle that opened in 1793. France was the most naturally powerful of the continental states, with long coastlines on three seas and a fine inheritance of harbours and seafaring populations. But France also had frontiers on the Rhine, the Alps, the Pyrenees, and the North Sea coast; it had to maintain the largest army in Europe; and its navy was therefore always the competitor of its army for resources, rather than the primary arm of the state. This was not a matter of choice but of geography: a state with a land frontier must guard it.
Geographical position also determines the strategic relationship between a nation and the great trade routes of the world. A nation placed athwart the principal lines of commerce can exert upon them an influence far out of proportion to its naval strength. The British Isles lie across the approaches to the Baltic, the Channel, and the Atlantic — the three great arteries of European maritime trade. Every vessel trading between northern and southern Europe, between Europe and America, between the Baltic and the Mediterranean, passes within reach of the British coast. This position gave Great Britain, even before she possessed the world’s largest navy, an enormous advantage in the control of commerce.
Physical Conformation
The physical shape of a country, and particularly the character of its coastline, constitutes the second element. A coast that provides good harbours, deep-water anchorages, and sheltered inlets offers facilities for both commerce and naval operations that a coast lacking these cannot match. The British Isles, with their numerous deep estuaries, their natural harbours at Portsmouth, Plymouth, and the Medway, and their sheltered anchorages along the Channel coast, were ideally suited to the maintenance of a great navy. The French coast, though not deficient in good harbours — Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, Cherbourg — was less favourably disposed in two critical respects: the Atlantic ports faced the prevailing westerly winds, making it difficult to sail out against a blockading force, and the Mediterranean and Atlantic fleets were separated by the Spanish peninsula and the Strait of Gibraltar, so that they could not easily combine.
Physical conformation also determines the interior communications of a country. A nation with good internal waterways can move goods and men more cheaply than one dependent upon roads. The British coal trade, carried by sea from Newcastle to London, was the foundation of British industrial strength; the French road system, though the best in Europe, could not match the cheapness of water carriage for heavy goods.
Extent of Territory
The third element is the extent of territory, but not in the sense that mere size confers sea power. The relevant measure is the length of coastline relative to the total land frontier and the productive interior. A country that is very large in area may be so largely continental in character that its maritime resources are stretched thin over a vast extent; its navy must defend a long coastline while its army guards an even longer land frontier. France, with its compact shape and its nearly equal land and sea frontiers, was in this respect better situated than Russia, with its enormous land mass and its limited access to the sea. But the comparison that matters is between France and Great Britain, and here the British advantage was clear: the whole of the British Isles was accessible to sea-borne commerce; there was no interior so remote that it could not be reached by water. France, by contrast, had large inland regions whose only contact with the outside world passed through ports that could be blockaded.
Population
The fourth element is the size of the population, but again with a qualification. The relevant population is not the total number of inhabitants but the number available for maritime employment — for the navy, the merchant marine, and the fishing fleets that together constitute the seafaring community. A large agricultural population is of little use for sea power if it has no maritime tradition and no access to the sea. The French population in 1793 was roughly twice that of Great Britain, but the proportion of Frenchmen who lived by the sea was much smaller; the British seafaring population, including the fishermen of the North Sea and the Channel, the crews of the merchant marine, and the Thames watermen, was probably at least as large as the French, and certainly better trained.
The relationship between the population of the seafaring class and the total population is also important for the mobilisation of naval reserves. In Great Britain, the merchant marine and the fisheries provided a constant stream of trained seamen who could be taken into the navy in time of war; the press-gang, brutal as it was, drew upon a deep reservoir of men who already knew how to handle a ship. In France, the system of maritime conscription — the inscription maritime — had been established by Colbert and maintained by the old monarchy, but it was disrupted by the Revolution and never fully restored. The French navy in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic period was chronically short of trained seamen, and the quality of those it had declined steadily as the war continued.
National Character
The fifth element is the character of the people, and especially their aptitude for commerce and their willingness to engage in maritime enterprise. A nation whose people are naturally inclined toward trade, toward risk-taking, and toward the kind of disciplined enterprise that seafaring requires will develop sea power almost unconsciously; a nation whose people prefer the security of the land and the settled life of the farmer will find sea power an unnatural growth that requires constant artificial support.
The British people, Mahan argues, possessed precisely the character that sea power requires. Commerce was not a mere occupation in Great Britain; it was the ruling passion of the nation, pursued by all classes from the aristocracy to the labourer. The British merchant marine was not a state creation but the spontaneous product of individual enterprise; the Navigation Acts might have shaped its course, but they did not create its impulse. The French, by contrast — while they had produced many of the finest navigators and naval officers of the eighteenth century — were on the whole a continental people whose genius turned toward the land. French commerce was more dependent upon state direction, French maritime enterprise more subject to bureaucratic regulation, and French seafaring less widely diffused through the population than in Great Britain.
National character also affects the quality of the navy in action. The British naval tradition, built up over centuries of maritime war, had produced an officer corps that combined professional skill with an extraordinary capacity for independent action in battle — a capacity that reached its highest expression in Nelson, but that was present in many lesser commanders as well. The French naval tradition, though it had produced brilliant officers in the age of Suffren, was destroyed by the Revolution, and the quality of French naval leadership never recovered.
Character of Government
The sixth element is the character of the government, and especially its capacity to pursue a consistent maritime policy over a long period. Sea power cannot be built in a single parliament or a single reign; it requires sustained investment in ships, dockyards, and training, and a strategic conception that outlasts the changing moods of public opinion and the turnover of ministries.
The British government, for all its faults, provided this consistency. The system of parliamentary government, however turbulent it appeared, produced a remarkable continuity of naval policy across the eighteenth century. The navy estimates, the dockyard programmes, the promotion system, and the strategic habits of the service were maintained through changes of ministry and fluctuations of public favour. In France, by contrast, the Revolution destroyed the continuity of naval administration along with the officer corps. The Committee of Public Safety, the Directory, the Consulate, and the Empire each reorganized the ministry of marine, each changed the system of promotion and training, and each began again from the beginning. The French navy never had the time — or the stable political environment — to develop the institutional memory and professional tradition that British sea power took for granted.
The Twofold Aspect of Sea Power
Mahan distinguishes two aspects of sea power in war, each requiring separate consideration. The first is the effect of sea power considered as a thing in itself — as a faculty that a nation possesses, a natural force that operates independently of the wisdom or folly of those who direct it. The second is the use made of sea power by statesmen and commanders — the strategy of the war, the direction given to naval operations, the decisions that determine whether the faculty is employed wisely or squandered.
The first aspect is the more fundamental. A nation that possesses sea power — that has the ships, the seamen, the commercial base, and the geographical position to control the sea — will produce certain effects simply by existing. The enemy’s commerce will wither, not because anyone in particular has decided to attack it, but because the ships that carry it cannot go where they need to go. The enemy’s colonies will be isolated and captured, not because a strategic decision has been made to take them, but because the sea power that protects them has disappeared. The enemy’s finances will be strained, not because of any particular financial operation, but because the revenues that flow from overseas trade have been cut off. These are the unconscious workings of the faculty, and they operate whether the government that possesses it is wise or foolish, active or passive.
The second aspect — the intelligent use of sea power — is what distinguishes a successful war policy from an unsuccessful one. A nation may possess overwhelming sea power and yet fail to use it effectively, as France failed under Napoleon to use what remained of its navy, or as Spain failed for a century and more. The question of how sea power should be directed is the question of naval strategy: where to concentrate force, when to seek battle, when to blockade, when to convoy, when to attack colonies, when to support allies.
The Seven Functions of Sea Power in the Revolutionary Wars
In the concluding chapter of his two-volume work, Mahan synthesises his argument by identifying seven distinct functions that British sea power discharged in the war against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France. These functions are not presented as a description of British strategic planning — Mahan is clear that the British ministry often acted without a coherent overall conception — but as an analytical framework for understanding how sea power actually contributed to the defeat of France.
Strategic Mobility
The first function of sea power was the capacity to shift military force from one theatre to another faster than any continental power could march its armies. The British army was small by continental standards, but it could be landed anywhere the navy could reach: the West Indies, the Mediterranean, Portugal, Holland, the Peninsula. This mobility gave Britain a flexibility that the French, bound to the roads and rivers of the Continent, could not match. A British expeditionary force could appear off the coast of Holland one season and in the Tagus the next, forcing the French to disperse their forces to guard against threats that might materialise anywhere along thousands of miles of coastline.
Economic Pressure on France
The second function was the economic strangulation of the enemy. British control of the sea cut France off from its colonial revenues, destroyed its overseas trade, and forced the French treasury to rely on continental exactions and plunder — a method that worked in the short term but exhausted the territories subjected to it. By 1799 the French Directory was forced to admit that not a single merchant vessel remained on the sea carrying the French flag. French exports to Asia, Africa, and America together amounted in the year 1800 to less than $56,000. The French merchant marine was annihilated, not by any particular campaign or battle, but by the simple fact that a French ship could not sail without encountering a British cruiser.
Sustaining the Coalitions
The third function was the financial and material support of continental allies. The British government, its own commerce flourishing under the protection of the navy, was able to raise enormous sums by taxation and borrowing. These sums were distributed as subsidies to Austria, Russia, Prussia, and the lesser European states, enabling them to maintain armies in the field against France. Without British gold, Mahan argues, no continental coalition could have sustained a war against the Revolution or the Empire for more than a single campaign. The navy thus functioned not only as a fighting force but as the guarantor of the financial system that made the coalitions possible: because British commerce was safe, British credit was good; because British credit was good, British subsidies could flow; because British subsidies flowed, the continental powers could fight.
The Blockade of French Naval Ports
The fourth function was the continuous watching of the French naval arsenals. The close blockade of Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, and later Cadiz was the most persistent and grinding operation of the war. It prevented the French fleet from concentrating, exercising, or intervening decisively in any theatre. The blockades were not passive but aggressive: they forced the French to sea at disadvantage, or kept them in port where they could not influence events. The strain on the blockading squadrons was immense — winter gales, lee shores, endless patrolling — but the effect on the French navy was far worse: its ships rotted at the quays, its crews never trained at sea, its officers never learned to handle a squadron under sail in all weathers. By the time the French fleet did venture out, as at the First of June (1794) or Trafalgar (1805), its seamanship and gunnery were so far inferior to the British that the outcome was all but foreordained.
Direct Naval Action
The fifth function was the destruction of the enemy’s organised naval forces in fleet actions. The three great battles of the war — the Nile (1798), Copenhagen (1801), and Trafalgar (1805) — each destroyed an enemy fleet and each had immediate strategic consequences far out of proportion to the numbers engaged. The Nile trapped Bonaparte’s army in Egypt and made possible the formation of the Second Coalition. Copenhagen broke the Armed Neutrality of 1800, restoring British access to the Baltic in a single morning. Trafalgar destroyed the Franco-Spanish combined fleet and made the invasion of England impossible forever.
But Mahan is careful not to overstate the importance of fleet actions. The blockades, he notes, were as destructive in their cumulative effect as any single battle. The French navy was destroyed not primarily by Trafalgar — though that was the culminating blow — but by the cumulative pressure of blockade, demoralisation, and the inability to maintain its personnel in a state of readiness. By 1805 the French navy was a shadow of what it had been in 1793, and after Trafalgar it never again attempted to contest the control of the sea in a line-of-battle engagement.
Protection of British Commerce
The sixth function was the preservation of the trade that underlay the entire British war effort. The convoy system, enforced by the Convoy Act of 1798, gathered merchant vessels in specified ports and sailed them under the protection of warships. Flotillas of two to three hundred ships were not unusual; five hundred or even a thousand were at times seen together in the approaches to the Channel or the Baltic. Fast frigates and sloops-of-war patrolled the trade routes, and a network of smaller vessels watched the approaches to enemy ports. The system was not perfect — approximately eleven thousand British vessels were captured over the twenty-one years of war, an annual average of about 524 ships — but the losses were absorbable. The British merchant marine, with its enormous tonnage and global reach, weathered a level of attrition that would have shattered any smaller trading nation. And because British commerce survived, British credit survived, and with it the capacity to finance the coalitions.
The Peninsular War as Culminating Demonstration
The seventh function, and for Mahan the culminating demonstration of what sea power meant, was the Peninsular War. The British army under Wellington in Portugal and Spain was supplied, reinforced, and sustained entirely by sea. The French could not turn the British flank because they could not control the sea; they could not starve the British army because it was fed by sea; they could not cut its communications because its communications were the ocean. The Peninsular War thus became, in Mahan’s reading, the most complete demonstration of sea power’s essential character: not a weapon of conquest but the condition that made endurance possible against a superior land power. The French army in Spain was steadily consumed by a foe it could not reach; the British army grew stronger as it was fed by the sea; and the French Empire was drained of men and resources in a theatre that should have been a sideshow but became, because of sea power, the wound that never healed.
Retrospective Framework versus Contemporary Understanding
It is worth pausing to emphasise the distance between Mahan’s framework and the thinking of the men who actually fought the war. The British government in 1793 did not possess a systematic theory of sea power. Pitt the Younger had reduced naval estimates in the years before the war, expecting a long peace; the mobilisation of 1793 was improvised, not the execution of a coherent maritime strategy. The great blockades of Brest and Toulon were not planned by a central strategist but developed piecemeal as local commanders did what seemed necessary. The convoy system was adopted in response to losses, not as the application of a pre-existing doctrine. Even Nelson, the greatest practitioner of sea power the age produced, thought in tactical rather than strategic terms; his genius lay in the handling of a fleet in action, not in the theoretical elaboration of maritime supremacy.
Mahan’s achievement, in his own view, was not to discover something that the actors had known but to make explicit what had been implicit — to extract from the events of 1793–1815 a pattern that explained why things had happened as they did, and to present that pattern as a general theory applicable to other conflicts and other nations. The six elements, the twofold aspect, and the seven functions are all analytical devices, retrospective constructs that Mahan imposes on the historical material to reveal its underlying logic. They are not descriptions of how the war was planned or understood by its participants; they are explanations of why it turned out as it did.
The Limits of the Thesis
Mahan himself acknowledged the limits of his argument. Sea power could not win battles on land; it could not prevent the French army from conquering most of Europe; it could not, by itself, bring Napoleon to his knees. That required the armies of Russia, Prussia, Austria, and Sweden, and the leadership of statesmen who could hold the coalition together against the centrifugal forces of national interest and mutual suspicion. What sea power could do — and what Mahan argued it did — was to make possible the conditions under which the continental powers could eventually combine to defeat Napoleon. It provided the financial sinews of war; it protected the base from which the Peninsular campaign was launched; it kept open the Baltic and the Mediterranean to British trade and allied supplies; it prevented Napoleon from concentrating his whole force against any single enemy; and, above all, it gave Britain the capacity to endure. In the long grinding struggle of attrition between two forms of power, the form that could draw upon the resources of the whole world — the form whose commerce was protected, whose credit was sound, whose people were safe from invasion — was the form that in the end prevailed.
Conclusion
The French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars constitute, in Mahan’s analysis, the most complete demonstration ever given of the power of maritime supremacy. They demonstrated that a nation which controls the sea can, if it has the patience and the political wisdom to use its advantage correctly, defeat a power that dominates the land. They demonstrated that sea power is not merely a military force but an economic and political instrument of the first order — that it can, by its pressure on commerce, colonies, and credit, impose upon the enemy a constant drain of strength that no victory on land can permanently repair. And they demonstrated that the elements from which sea power is built — geographical position, national character, governmental policy, commercial enterprise, and professional naval tradition — are not the products of any single moment of decision but the slow accumulation of centuries.
This was Mahan’s thesis. It was not the thesis of the age he studied, and he never pretended otherwise. The value of his framework lies precisely in its retrospectivity: looking back over twenty-three years of war from the vantage of the 1890s, Mahan could see patterns that the participants could not, and could articulate a theory of sea power that would shape naval thinking for generations to come.
Sources

















SourceDescriptionMahan, A.T., The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812, Vol. I (1892)Mahan’s theoretical framework applied to 1793–1801. Chapters I–II establish the six elements of sea power and the institutional destruction of the French navy. The Preface states the work’s central argument.Mahan, A.T., The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812, Vol. II (1892)Covers 1801–1812. Chapter XIX — ‘Summary — The Function of Sea Power and the Policy of Great Britain in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars’ — contains the seven-function synthesis and Mahan’s final statement of his thesis.

concepts/the-chouannerie.title: The Chouannerie
concepts/the-chouannerie.content:
The Chouannerie
I. Two Faces of the Same Resistance
The Chouannerie was never one thing. It was two — a southern movement and a western one, separated by geography, by chronology, and by circumstance, yet united by a single thread: the refusal of rural France to accept the Revolution. Ernest Daudet, in two works composed fourteen years apart, traced this double history. His Histoire des Conspirations Royalistes du Midi (1881) examined the southern variant from 1790 to 1793 — the Camp de Jalès, the Saillans conspiracy, the Charrier uprising — a movement driven by religious hatred and aristocratic intrigue in the sun-baked valleys of the Gard, the Ardèche, and the Lozère. His La Police et les Chouans sous le Consulat et l’Empire (1895) took up the western variant from 1800 to 1815 — the Clément de Ris kidnapping, the Aché-De Combray conspiracy, the English agencies, the final rising of the Hundred Days — a guerrilla war fought in the misty hedgerows of Brittany, Normandy, and Maine against the police state of Napoleon Bonaparte. Between them, these two books trace a continuous arc of rural royalist resistance that ran from the first stirrings of counter-revolution in 1790 to the last campfires of 1815.
II. The Midi: Religion and Royalism in the South (1790–1793)
The southern Chouannerie was born not of peasant loyalty to the seigneur but of fire and blood between Catholics and Protestants. In the Midi, the Revolution had reopened wounds that had been healing for a century. The Protestants of Nîmes, Montauban, and the Cévennes embraced the Revolution as their deliverance from Catholic domination; the Catholics, in turn, saw the Revolution as a Protestant conspiracy against throne and altar. The result was massacre.
On 13 June 1790, violence erupted in Nîmes. Protestant National Guards, armed and organised under revolutionary authority, fell upon the Catholic quarter. Houses were pillaged and burned, hundreds of Catholics were killed in the streets, and the municipal authority collapsed. The Catholic notables fled the city, and the survivors were left with nothing but the memory of the slaughter and a thirst for vengeance. It was this thirst that filled the first Camp de Jalès.
In the summer of 1790, in the solitary plain of Jalès in the Ardèche, the royalists of the Midi attempted what the Vendée would later achieve: to raise a mass army for the king. The pretext was a federal gathering of the National Guards of the Vivarais, summoned to renew the civic oath. But the National Guards who assembled around an altar erected near the château of Jalès heard mass, and passed resolutions that amounted to a declaration of war on the Revolution. A permanent Committee of the Camp of Jalès was established, composed of elected delegates, which from that day coordinated the royalist movement in the South.
The first assembly of Jalès dispersed without action. The conspirators lacked arms, lacked unity, and lacked a commander. But the idea did not die. Through 1791 and into 1792, the Committee maintained its correspondence with the émigré princes, who were gathering at Coblentz for the invasion of France. The princes, for their part, saw the Midi as a diversion — a second front that would draw republican forces away from the eastern frontier. They authorised the comte de Saillans, a major in the regiment of Roussillon, to return to France in disguise and take command of the southern rising.
Saillans arrived in the Ardèche in the spring of 1792, a man of undoubted energy but fatal arrogance. He clashed immediately with the local royalist leaders, who resented his authority and suspected his motives. The second assembly of Jalès, convened in July 1792, brought together perhaps thirteen hundred men — a thousand of them National Guards from the Catholic parishes of the Vivarais. Saillans issued a manifesto calling for the restoration of the monarchy and marched from Alais toward Saint-Ambroix.
It was too late. The revolutionary authorities had been forewarned by their own intelligence networks. The columns of National Guards that marched to meet Saillans were stronger and better armed. The rising was crushed almost as soon as it began. Saillans himself was killed or captured — the sources are ambiguous — and his papers, seized by the Directory of the Ardèche and printed, revealed the full scope of the conspiracy, implicating priests, nobles, and merchants across the Midi. The Camp de Jalès was finished.
But the Midi was not pacified. In the winter of 1792–1793, a new leader emerged from the mountains of the Lozère. Marc-Antoine Charrier, a notary of Nasbinals and a former deputy to the Estates-General, was a man of a different stamp from the aristocratic Saillans. He had fled to the high plateaus of the Aubrac after the failure of an earlier conspiracy in Mende, and there, in a landscape of frozen moors and wolf-haunted forests, he gathered around him the Catholic peasantry of the region. In March 1793, Charrier raised the banner of revolt. He rallied several hundred men and held the field against the republican army under General Carteaux for weeks, operating in the high country between the Lozère and the Aveyron. He captured Mende, marched on Marvejols, and attempted to coordinate with the Lyonnais federalists who had risen against the Convention.
It was the last serious royalist rising in the Midi before the Terror. Charrier was eventually defeated, captured, and executed. The republicans responded with pitiless repression: the refractory priests were driven out, the châteaux of the nobles were pillaged, and the bands of armed patriots roamed the countryside burning feudal titles. The southern Chouannerie was crushed, but the religious hatreds that had fuelled it remained, waiting to reignite at the next opportunity. Daudet’s judgment was clear: the Midi was not the West, and never could be. The open plains of Languedoc and the broad valleys of the Rhône did not favour the hit-and-run tactics of the hedgerow fighter. The southern movement had burned hot and died young, destroyed by its own internal divisions, by the lack of popular depth, and by the effectiveness of republican intelligence.
III. The West: The Chouannerie Under the Consulate and Empire (1800–1815)
The western Chouannerie was a different phenomenon entirely. Where the southern movement had been a series of convulsive risings, the West sustained a permanent guerrilla war for a generation. The geography of Brittany, Normandy, and Maine — the sunken lanes, the dense hedgerows, the forests, the endless coastline of coves and inlets — was made for the partisan. The social structure was different, too: the West was a region of deeply rooted Catholic piety, where the non-juring priest was more influential than the revolutionary official, and where the peasant fought for his faith as much as for his king.
When Bonaparte became First Consul in November 1799, the West was still in arms. Cadoudal commanded in Brittany, Bourmont in Maine, Frotté in Normandy, Châtillon in the Vendée. The Consulate’s first task was to pacify this region, and Bonaparte pursued a dual strategy: military pressure combined with amnesty offers. Frotté was lured into negotiations and then executed by General Guidal in a treacherous ambush that stained the new regime’s reputation. Cadoudal was courted, offered command in the republican army, and refused. The negotiations produced a fragile peace, but it was a peace built on police surveillance rather than genuine reconciliation.
The kidnapping of Senator Clément de Ris in September 1800 demonstrated how fragile that peace truly was. On the evening of 19 November 1800 — the date is fixed in Daudet’s narrative — a band of about thirty armed men, remnants of the Chouan bands who had turned to banditry, seized the senator from his château in the Touraine. They dragged him from his house before the eyes of his terrified wife and son and vanished into the darkness of the surrounding woods. The kidnapping of a senator — a former member of the Council of Five Hundred, a supporter of Bonaparte — was an act of spectacular audacity, a direct challenge to the authority of the new regime.
Fouché and Bonaparte mobilised the full machinery of the state. The prefect of Indre-et-Loire, the gendarmerie, and the military authorities all threw themselves into the pursuit. The kidnappers held Clément de Ris for several weeks at the château de Saut-de-Sabot, demanding a ransom. The affair was resolved when the police tracked down the kidnappers and liberated the senator. But the consequences were far-reaching. The kidnapping hardened Bonaparte’s attitude toward the West, confirmed his conviction that only relentless policing could break the Chouan resistance, and inaugurated an era of special military commissions operating without restraint.
The same month saw another Chouan blow against the revolutionary order: the assassination of Yves Audrein, the constitutional bishop of Quimper. Audrein was an old man, a former Oratorian, a deputy to the Convention, a regicide who had voted for the death of Louis XVI under three different names. He was the most hated figure in Brittany, the living symbol of the constitutional church that the peasantry despised. On the night of 19 November 1800, as Audrein travelled by diligence from Quimper to Morlaix, the carriage was stopped on the road by a band of armed men. A man in the typical dress of a Chouan — blue blouse, red waistcoat, leather-trimmed trousers — climbed into the carriage, seized the old bishop by the collar, held a lantern to his face, and pronounced his death sentence for the triple vote of regicide. Audrein was dragged from the carriage and shot dead on the road. The killers were never caught.
The Clément de Ris affair and the Audrein murder, occurring almost simultaneously, revealed the two faces of the western Chouannerie in the Napoleonic period: on one hand, the organised political conspiracy aimed at destabilising the state; on the other, the popular religious vendetta that needed no organisation at all. Both were beyond the reach of Fouché’s police to prevent, though both triggered crackdowns that progressively reduced the Chouan networks.
IV. The Aché-De Combray Conspiracy and the English Agencies
The most elaborate of the Napoleonic conspiracies was that of the vicomte d’Aché and the chevalier de Combray. D’Aché, a grandson of the admiral of that name, had emigrated in 1792, served under the princes, and fought in the bands of Frotté. After Frotté’s death, he returned to Normandy, where he became the organising centre of royalist resistance in the Calvados, moving through the countryside under assumed names — Deslauriers, Alexandre — sheltered by a network of sympathisers that the police could never fully penetrate. In 1802, he entered into relations with De Combray, a naval officer, and together they formed a conspiracy to raise the West. The plan was audacious: to seize a port on the Norman coast, open it to an English landing, and simultaneously raise the Chouan legions of Brittany and Normandy. The comte d’Artois, the Bourbon prince in exile, promised — as he had promised many times before — to come and take command in person.
The conspiracy was penetrated by Fouché’s police. Daudet, working from the police dossiers, reconstructs the slow accumulation of evidence: the intercepted couriers, the raided safe houses, the betrayals that gradually exposed the network to the authorities. D’Aché was arrested, imprisoned, and subjected to the full rigour of the imperial police. Even in prison, he remained defiant, but the conspiracy was broken. The Aché-De Combray affair was the last serious attempt to organise a general rising in the West during the Empire. After its failure, the Chouannerie in Normandy subsided into isolated acts of brigandage.
What had sustained the western movement through all these years, through the defeats and the betrayals and the executions, was English support. Daudet devotes his longest chapter to the Jersey agency, the nerve centre of Chouan operations after 1800. From the island of Jersey, British officers, French émigré intermediaries, and a network of smugglers and fishermen maintained a constant flow of correspondence, money, and arms across the Channel. The English agency in Bordeaux performed a similar function for the South, channelling English gold through the great Atlantic port into the Midi. The utility of this support was questionable — the sums of money were never enough, the arms shipments always too small, the promised English soldiers never came. But without English money, the Chouannerie would have died in 1796. English support gave the insurrection the means to survive, even if it could never give it the means to win.
V. The Last Campfire: The Rising of 1815
When Napoleon returned from Elba in March 1815, the Chouannerie of the West had been dormant for a decade. The old leaders were still alive — d’Autichamp, Suzannet, d’Andigné, Sapinaud — but they were no longer young men. They had accepted the Bourbon restoration of 1814, had received military ranks from Louis XVIII, and were living in honourable retirement. The return of the Emperor threw them into confusion. Suzannet rushed to Paris to offer his services to the king, but found only paralysis at the Tuileries. The duc de Bourbon was dispatched to the West, but without a plan. The Chouan leaders were left to improvise.
And improvise they did. In May 1815, the West rose for the last time. D’Autichamp raised five thousand men in Anjou, d’Andigné thirteen thousand on the right bank of the Loire, Suzannet, Sapinaud, and Charette in the Vendée, De Sol de Grisolles in the Morbihan. A council of war was held at Cholet. The plan was to drive the imperial troops out of the West and to coordinate with the expected arrival of English arms and Bourbon princes.
The reality was a disaster of miscommunication and false hope. The promised English flotilla arrived at Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie on 16 May — with only two thousand muskets and a few barrels of powder instead of the fourteen thousand muskets, cannon, and ammunition that had been promised. A second convoy on 2 June was no better. There was no money, no cannon, no English soldiers. The Chouans fought with hunting rifles and pitchforks against the veterans of the imperial army.
General Travot struck first at Aizenay, scattering Suzannet’s corps in a night attack. Charette was mortally wounded. The Chouan bands, poorly armed, poorly supplied, and torn by rivalries between their commanders, were defeated in a series of obscure skirmishes across the West. By the end of June, the rising was over. Napoleon had been defeated at Waterloo, but the Chouans had played no part in his downfall. Thousands of imperial troops pinned down in the West — men whom Daudet notes might have turned the tide at Waterloo — had been held away from the decisive theatre by the last, futile convulsion of the Chouannerie.
With the second Bourbon restoration, the surviving Chouan leaders were rewarded with ranks and pensions. The peasants of the West returned to their fields. The hedgerows and forests that had sheltered the Chouans for a generation fell silent. The war that had begun in 1790, that had burned in the South and smouldered in the West, was finally over.
VI. The Thread
Daudet’s two books, read together, reveal the Chouannerie as a continuous thread running through the entire revolutionary and Napoleonic period — a thread that connected the Camp de Jalès of 1790 to the final campfire of 1815. The southern and western variants were different in character: the one religious and convulsive, the other social and enduring. But both were expressions of the same refusal: the refusal of rural France, Catholic France, royalist France, to accept the Revolution and its works. The Chouannerie failed. It never came close to restoring the Bourbons, never seriously threatened the republic or the empire. But it lasted, and its longevity was a reproach to the Revolution’s claim to have united the nation. For twenty-five years, a substantial part of the French people remained in arms against the state. That fact, which Daudet documents with the patience of the archival historian and the vividness of the novelist, is the true significance of the Chouannerie. It was not a war that could be won, but it was a war that could not be ended — not by massacre, not by amnesty, not by the most sophisticated police system in Europe. It ended only when the men who had fought it were too old to fight any longer.

The Directory Government
The Constitution of the Year III
The Constitution of the Year III, ratified in August 1795, was the most elaborate political mechanism the Revolution had yet produced — an attempt to give France a stable government after the Terror by dividing authority so minutely that no faction could ever again seize the state at a stroke. The framers, the Commission of Eleven chosen by the Thermidorian Convention, had drawn the lesson that absolute power, whether lodged in a single assembly or a single man, led inevitably to catastrophe. They designed a republic of checks so carefully distributed that in practice they could scarcely move at all.
Executive power was vested in a Directory of five members, elected by the two legislative councils from a list drawn up by the Council of Five Hundred. One director retired each year, replaced by a newly elected member, the order determined by lot. Each presided in rotation for three months; decisions were by majority; no director could be removed except by slow impeachment. The Directory appointed ministers and generals, conducted diplomacy, and executed the laws — but could not initiate legislation.
Legislative power was divided between two chambers: the Council of Five Hundred, which proposed laws, and the Council of the Ancients — two hundred and fifty members, all married or widowed men over forty — which approved or rejected them. Neither could dissolve the other. The electoral system was indirect and property-weighted: only citizens who paid a direct tax equivalent to three days’ labour could vote in the primary assemblies; only those who paid the equivalent of one hundred and fifty days’ labour could serve as electors. The deputies themselves had to meet still higher property qualifications. It was a republic of the propertied, designed by men who believed that the Terror had its roots in the participation of the propertyless in politics.
The two-thirds decrees, adopted before the Constitution took effect, required that two-thirds of the first legislative corps be drawn from the sitting Convention. This self-protecting measure was a confession of fragility: the framers dared not trust the electorate to choose a republican majority on its own. The Constitution was ratified by plebiscite with an overwhelming majority, but the abstention rate was enormous. The country was exhausted; what it wanted was simply an end to convulsions.
From the first, the Constitution bore the mark of the fear that had produced it. It was a document that trusted no one and nothing — not the people, not the executive, not the legislature. It created a government that was strong enough to be dangerous but not strong enough to be effective.
The Five Directors
The first Directory, chosen in November 1795, reflected the cross-currents of the Thermidorian reaction. Louis-Marie de La Révellière-Lépeaux was a regicide of the Convention, a provincial lawyer from Anjou, a fervent deist who dreamed of founding a national cult of theophilanthropy. Jean-François Rewbell, a former deputy of the Third Estate from Alsace, was coarse, energetic, domineering, his bluntness masking a shrewd political intelligence — he was, by general agreement, the most capable of the five. Étienne-François Letourneur, a military engineer and a constitutional monarchist of the 1791 school, had made his peace with the Republic. Paul Barras, the nobleman turned revolutionary, a man of pleasure and intrigue, governed through corruption, mistresses, and favours; his venality was already legendary. Lazare Carnot, the Organizer of Victory — the austere mathematician and military strategist who had directed the war from the Committee of Public Safety — commanded the respect of the army as no other civilian could.
The Directory was split from its first session. La Révellière-Lépeaux, Rewbell, and Barras formed a loose alliance of the republican left, determined to suppress Jacobins and hold royalists at bay. Carnot and Letourneur inclined toward the moderate right, favouring conciliation with constitutional monarchists and relaxation of the laws against émigrés and priests. This division between the three — the dominant faction, increasingly associated with Barras — and the two persisted until the final convulsions of the regime.
The Babeuf Conspiracy
The first great crisis of the Directory came not from the royalists but from the extreme left. Gracchus Babeuf — François-Noël Babeuf by birth — was a journalist and agitator of formidable energy who had emerged from Thermidor as the apostle of a new revolution, more radical than the first. His newspaper, Le Tribun du Peuple, preached the abolition of private property and the establishment of a true community of equals — a doctrine he called absolute equality. He gathered around him a circle of former Jacobins, Montagnard deputies proscribed after Thermidor, and disaffected army officers: Filippo Buonarroti, the Italian revolutionary and former agent of the Committee of Public Safety; Sylvain Maréchal, the atheist philosopher; Darthé, the former juror of the Revolutionary Tribunal; Rossignol, the general of the Vendée.
Fantin-Desodoards, writing in 1801, gives the fullest account of the conspiracy among our sources. He notes that Babeuf himself was “only the obscure and secondary agent of a faction of whose secrets he perhaps himself knew only a part.” The operational structure was elaborate: a secret directory of public safety directing the movement, with agents in each of Paris’s twelve arrondissements who reported on food stores, arms depots, workshops, and workers’ numbers; compiled lists of well-off patriots who could house provincial militants; organized subscriptions to fund the insurrection; and formed teams of groupeurs who circulated daily in the Tuileries gardens reading patriot journals aloud to crowds.
The conspiracy was betrayed by an agent of the Directory, Georges Grisel, who infiltrated the inner circle. On the night of 21 Floréal, Year IV — May 10, 1796 — the police struck. Babeuf, Buonarroti, Darthé, and the principal conspirators were arrested in their lodgings. Seized in Babeuf’s rooms was the complete archive of the conspiracy: lists of adherents, correspondence, plans for the insurrection, drafts of proclamations. The trial at Vendôme began in February 1797 and dragged on for months. Babeuf conducted his own defence with extraordinary eloquence, turning the courtroom into a tribune. He was condemned to death and guillotined on 27 May 1797. Buonarroti, whose life was spared, would write a history of the conspiracy in prison that became a sacred text for the revolutionary movements of the nineteenth century.
Fantin quotes at length from a letter found at Babeuf’s address in which Babeuf defended the Robespierre Terror as correct in principle: “I think that government was the one best suited to make a revolution succeed. A regenerator must see on a grand scale; his duty is to mow down everything that hinders him, everything that obstructs his passage — scoundrels, idiots, the presumptuous alike, it is all the same; too bad for them, why were they in the way?” This was not the voice of a single fanatic; it was the ideology of a faction that had never accepted that the Terror was wrong, only that it had failed.
The Elections of Year V and the Royalist Resurgence
Barely had the Babeuf conspiracy been crushed when the Directory faced a threat from the opposite direction. The elections of Germinal, Year V — March–April 1797 — to renew one-third of the legislative councils resulted in a stunning victory for the royalist and constitutional monarchist opposition. The Clichyens — so called because they gathered at the Club de Clichy in Paris — were not openly royalist in the sense of demanding the immediate restoration of Louis XVIII; they were rather a coalition of constitutional monarchists, moderate royalists, and conservative republicans who wanted to roll back the Revolution’s most extreme measures. They demanded freedom for the royalist press, relaxation of the laws against émigrés and refractory priests, and an end to the Directory’s financial mismanagement.
The new third of the councils included figures of known royalist sympathies: General Pichegru, the conqueror of Holland who had returned from exile and was elected president of the Council of Five Hundred; the abbé Brottier, a former agent of the princes; and a substantial minority that looked to the restoration of the monarchy as the only way to end the Revolution. The effect was immediate. A state of war established itself between the legislative and executive powers. The royalist deputies attacked the Directory’s financial administration, demanded the repeal of the laws against the émigrés, and manoeuvred to remove the directors allied with Barras.
The government was in a precarious position. The treasury was empty. The armies were unpaid. The Clichyen press grew bolder by the day. Pichegru, who had been secretly in correspondence with the Bourbon princes, was manoeuvring to become a figurehead of the restoration. In the councils, motions were introduced to recall the proscribed priests, to reopen the churches, to revise the laws against the émigrés. The Republic seemed to be dissolving from within.
The Coup of 18 Fructidor
The three directors who formed the governing core — Barras, La Révellière-Lépeaux, and Rewbell — resolved to strike. They had the support of the army, and they had the precedent of every revolutionary government before them: when the constitution failed to protect the Republic, the Republic must protect itself by extra-constitutional means. General Augereau, a rough and energetic commander of the Army of Italy, was brought to Paris by Bonaparte and placed in command of the military forces of the capital. On the morning of 18 Fructidor, Year V — September 4, 1797 — Augereau’s troops surrounded the Tuileries. Carnot, forewarned, escaped through a window and fled to Switzerland. Barthélemy, who had replaced Letourneur, was arrested. The royalist deputies — Pichegru and the leaders of the opposition — were seized in their seats and sent to the Temple prison.
The Directory then unleashed a package of repressive measures. The elections of forty-nine departments were annulled. A hundred and seventy-seven deputies were deprived of their seats; fifty-three were condemned to deportation to Guiana. The laws against émigrés and refractory priests were revived with new severity; all unauthorized returnees were given two weeks to leave France on pain of death. The royalist press was suppressed; a dozen newspapers were closed, their editors deported. Constitutional guarantees of personal liberty were suspended; administrative arrests were authorised on the order of the Directory alone. Carnot and Barthélemy were proscribed as directors.
Fantin gives the full sequence: the Directory’s intelligence about royalist contacts with the Bourbon pretender (the Duverne de Presles revelations), the Directory’s session of 10 Fructidor, the coup itself, the permanent session of the surviving councils, the deportation law. He is critical but not simplistic — he accepts that a genuine royalist threat existed while questioning whether the Directory’s methods were constitutional.
Constant, who had watched the events unfold from his retreat at Hérivaux, was caught between his principles and his fears. He had argued, in De la force du gouvernement actuel (1796), that the Directory was strong enough to govern legally, without recourse to arbitrary power — that its real strength lay in the material interests created by the Revolution: the purchasers of national lands, the holders of Republic-issued contracts, the new class of proprietors who had no stake in a royalist restoration. The arbitrary power had come, nevertheless, and Constant, fearing a royalist restoration more than he feared despotism, accepted the coup as a necessary evil. But the necessity was a confession of failure: the Directory had proven that it could not govern through the Constitution. The resort to force was the strategy of a regime that had lost its political legitimacy.
Constant’s Analysis
Benjamin Constant’s three pamphlets of 1796–97 constitute the most sustained contemporary analysis of the Directory’s constitutional predicament. In De la force du gouvernement actuel, Des réactions politiques, and Des effets de la terreur, he developed a double argument: the Directory had genuine sources of strength in the new property settlement, but it was destroying those sources by its own recourse to arbitrary power.
The first argument was sociological. The Revolution had created interests — in land, in contracts, in careers — that were now widespread and could not survive a restoration. The purchasers of biens nationaux, the army officers who had risen from the ranks, the civil servants of the Republic, the suppliers who had grown rich on war contracts — all these men had a material stake in the Republic that no ideology could match. The Directory’s real base, Constant argued, was not the theory of republicanism but the practice of property. This was a brilliant insight: it grounded the Republic not in abstract principle but in the concrete interests of a new ruling class.
The second argument was a warning. The Directory was destroying this base by its own methods. When it resorted to arbitrary arrests, to annulled elections, to military force against its political opponents, it reproduced the logic of the Terror in the name of opposing it. “What did France the most harm,” Constant wrote, “the harm most difficult to repair, was precisely the impatience to do good.” When honest Thermidorian men used revolutionary means against revolutionary brigands, they consecrated illegality by making it serve good purposes — thereby destroying the only moral argument against illegality: that it always produces harm.
In Des effets de la terreur, Constant attacked a doctrine he saw spreading: that the Terror had been justified by its outcomes — that its violence had saved the Republic at its moment of maximum external danger. His refutation had two parts. First, the factual claim was false: the Republic was saved by the armies, by geography, and by the incompetence of the coalition — not by the guillotine. Second, and more important, even if the Terror had beneficial effects, accepting it as justified set a precedent that destroyed constitutional government: any emergency could be used to justify any measure, and once that principle was accepted, there was no logical stopping point. The Directory was proving the point by its own actions.
The deepest argument in Constant’s analysis was structural: the Directory was a government that tried to be constitutional while governing through coups. It had no popular base of its own — it was neither Jacobin nor royalist, neither democratic nor monarchical — and it had no way to acquire one without abandoning the very centre ground it claimed to occupy. The revolutionary mean was not a stable equilibrium; it was an unstable oscillation where each resort to force narrowed the base of support on which the regime rested.
The Coup of Floréal Year VI
The elections of Floréal, Year VI — April 1798 — produced the next crisis. This time, the danger came from the left. The neo-Jacobins, taking advantage of the discredit into which the royalists had fallen after Fructidor, won a substantial number of seats in the renewed third of the councils. The Directory, once again unwilling to accept a result that threatened its control, resorted to extra-constitutional action. On 22 Floréal — May 11, 1798 — a law was passed by the purged councils annulling the elections in twenty-six departments and excluding a hundred and six deputies from their seats.
The coup of Floréal was different in character from Fructidor. It was not a military operation but a legislative manipulation, carried out by a commission of the Ancients that examined the electoral returns and struck out the names of Jacobins on grounds of illegality. But its effect was the same: the Constitution was violated, the will of the electorate was set aside, and the regime’s already slender claim to legitimacy was further eroded. Pagès, in his Histoire secrète de la Révolution, notes the irony: those who had regarded the Republic’s institutions with indifference now aspired only to be masters of them, and the Directory had taught them that the only way to be master was to cheat.
The Coup of Prairial Year VII
The third and final coup — 30 Prairial, Year VII — June 18, 1799 — marked the disintegration of the regime. The elections of Year VII had returned a strengthened neo-Jacobin minority to the councils, and the military disasters of 1799 — the defeat of Jourdan at Stockach, the loss of Italy to Suvorov’s Russian army, the financial collapse — had destroyed what remained of the Directory’s prestige. The legislative councils turned on the executive.
In a single session, the councils forced the resignation of three directors: Treilhard (who was replaced on a technicality regarding his eligibility), La Révellière-Lépeaux, and Merlin de Douai. Only Barras remained of the original governing core. Sieyès, who had been elected to the Directory in May 1799, now became the dominant figure — and he brought with him a conviction that the Constitution of Year III was a dead letter that needed to be replaced entirely, not reformed.
The coup of Prairial was the reverse of Fructidor and Floréal: this time it was the legislature that purged the executive, not the executive that purged the legislature. The neo-Jacobins in the councils pushed through a forced loan on the rich, a law of hostages against the Chouan insurgents, and a revival of revolutionary taxation. The Directory, now headed by Sieyès, resisted these measures passively, refusing to enforce what it could not openly oppose. The government had ceased to function. Paganel, writing in 1815 from inside the French state apparatus, describes this period as one of accelerating dissolution: the treasury empty, the armies unpaid, the departments in insurrection, and the generals — Bonaparte above all — watching from afar as the civilian regime consumed itself.
The War and the Generals
While the Directory struggled with its internal contradictions, the war created the forces that would destroy it. Bonaparte’s Italian campaign of 1796–97 — the crossing of the Alps, the victories at Lodi, Castiglione, Arcole, Rivoli, the Treaty of Campo Formio — had made the Republic the dominant power on the continent. The spoils of Italy filled the empty French treasury. The prestige of the army sustained the government against its domestic enemies.
But the war also created a new set of problems. The generals had become independent political actors. Bonaparte had signed the preliminaries of Léoben without consulting the Directory, and the directors had been forced to accept the fait accompli. The condition of the Republic depended on the goodwill of men whose power was military in origin and whose ambitions were personal. The Egyptian expedition, launched in May 1798, was at once a strategy of imperial expansion and a means of removing Bonaparte from the political stage. The Directory, alarmed by the general’s popularity, was happy to see him depart for the Orient. But Nelson destroyed the French fleet at Aboukir Bay, and Bonaparte was stranded — watching from Cairo as the Republic drifted, but also gathering the prestige of a conqueror in the East.
The Second Coalition — England, Austria, Russia, Naples, the Ottoman Empire — formed against France in 1798, and the Republic suddenly found itself fighting on six fronts with its best general trapped in Egypt. The war turned decisively against the Directory in 1799. Masséna was defeated in Switzerland; Schérer was routed in Italy; Suvorov’s Russian army swept across the Po valley undoing all of Bonaparte’s conquests. The Republic was threatened with invasion. The departments of the west rose in a new Chouan insurrection; the south was ravaged by brigandage. The regime seemed to be dying by inches.
The Financial Collapse
The Directory inherited a fiscal catastrophe and made it worse. The assignats had depreciated to virtually nothing by February 1796 — a one-hundred-franc note worth barely five sous in coin. The government attempted a drastic remedy: a new paper currency, the mandats territoriaux, exchangeable for national lands. They were issued in March 1796 to the value of two billion four hundred million francs. Within six months, they had followed the assignats into the abyss. On February 4, 1797, the fabrication of paper money was definitively abandoned. France returned to a metallic currency — but there was almost none in circulation.
The bankruptcy was declared on September 30, 1797. The consolidated debt was reduced to one-third of its nominal value, payable in bonds that could be used to purchase national lands. The rentiers, the widows and orphans whose annuities had been paid in assignats and then in nothing, were ruined. The state had defaulted on its obligations, and the financial confidence that is the foundation of any stable government was destroyed for the remainder of the Directory’s existence.
The consequence was that the state came to depend on the army for its survival — not merely for defence against foreign enemies, but for its daily bread. The military commanders financed their operations by requisitions, contributions, and outright plunder, remitting a portion to the empty treasury in Paris. This arrangement kept the state afloat, but at a terrible cost: it made the civilian government a pensioner of its own generals, and it placed in the hands of men like Bonaparte a power that no constitution could contain.
The Political Factions
The Directory was perpetually caught between three political forces that it could neither absorb nor destroy. On the left, the neo-Jacobins — survivors of the Montagnard party, Jacobin club militants, and radical democrats — demanded the revival of revolutionary taxation, the prosecution of the remaining émigrés, and the defence of the Republic by any means necessary. On the right, the Clichyens — constitutional monarchists, moderate royalists, and conservative republicans — pressed for peace with the European powers, the return of the émigrés, and the restoration of Catholic worship. In the centre, the Directorials — the men who actually held power — had no program beyond survival. They governed by playing the extremes against each other, but the game required periodic coups to correct the election results, and each coup alienated the very interests that Constant had identified as the regime’s natural base.
The regime could not expand its support because it dared not trust the electorate. Every election between 1795 and 1799 produced the “wrong” result: first a royalist majority, then a neo-Jacobin resurgence, then another leftward shift. The Directory responded each time by annulling the elections it did not like. It was a republic that could not win a popular mandate and could not govern without one. Pagès, in his synthetic volume (Tome VI), notes the extreme penury of the national treasury — needs so great and pressing that the Directory could not borrow at any interest. A state that cannot borrow has no future; a government that cannot trust its own elections has no legitimacy.
The Approach of Brumaire
By the summer of 1799, the Directory was in its death agony. Sieyès, now the dominant figure, concluded that a new constitution was necessary — and that a new constitution required a new executive, with concentrated powers, backed by the army. He began to search for the “sword” — a general who would lend his military prestige to the enterprise of overthrowing the Directory. Paganel, in his Histoire de Napoléon Bonaparte (1815), gives the sharpest contemporary account of what followed. Bonaparte had returned from Egypt in October 1799, landing at Fréjus and travelling to Paris through crowds that hailed him as the saviour of the Republic. He was young, famous, ambitious, and loyal to no regime. Paganel insists that the coup was a personal political achievement of extraordinary craft: Bonaparte cultivated Sieyès not as a collaborator but as an instrument he intended from the first to use and discard. He “attached himself to Sieyès to deceive him; he deceived him in order not to have to fear him.”
Paganel’s sharpest observation is about the reception: military glory was the avowed title of Bonaparte’s elevation; “fear and venality were its true causes.” The Directory had governed for four years by the periodic resort to force; now force had found a face, and the regime that had lived by the army would die by it.
The conspirators — Sieyès, Talleyrand, Fouché, Lucien Bonaparte — laid their plans through the autumn. The coup was fixed for 18 Brumaire, Year VIII — November 9, 1799. The Council of Ancients was persuaded to transfer the legislative sessions to Saint-Cloud and to appoint Bonaparte commander of the military forces of the capital. The directors were dealt with one by one: Sieyès and Ducos resigned; Barras was persuaded to resign by Talleyrand; Gohier and Moulin were placed under house arrest. The Directory was finished.
The drama at Saint-Cloud on 19 Brumaire was less smooth. Bonaparte’s attempt to address the Council of Five Hundred degenerated into chaos — the deputies shouted “Down with the dictator!” and Bonaparte was manhandled. It was Lucien Bonaparte who saved the situation by calling in Murat’s grenadiers, who cleared the hall with fixed bayonets. That night, a rump of the Council voted the abolition of the Directory and the establishment of the Consulate.
The Verdict
The Directory had governed France for four years — from November 1795 to November 1799. It had preserved the Republic against the royalists, crushed the Babeuf conspiracy, maintained the war effort, and given France the most brilliant military victories of the Revolution. But it had failed to establish any durable foundation for republican government. The Constitution of the Year III, the most carefully designed of the revolutionary constitutions, had been violated by its own executives — elections annulled twice, a military coup once, a legislative purge once more — and finally collapsed into the personal rule of a general.
The verdict of the period sources is remarkably consistent. Constant’s analysis — that a government which governs through arbitrary power destroys the only foundation on which a durable republic can rest — proved prophetic. Fantin’s narrative shows a regime perpetually reacting to crises it could not prevent. Pagès, in his synthetic volume, catalogues the corruption of the directors, the penury of the treasury, the moral exhaustion of the nation. Paganel traces the logic by which a republic that could not govern itself produced a general who would govern instead.
The Directory expired without convulsions, its end scarcely noticed by the inhabitants of Paris, who watched the military promenade of Brumaire with the indifference of a people that had seen too many revolutions to be surprised by one more. It had been, in its mortal illness, a government that could neither live by the law nor openly abandon it — a regime caught between the Constitution it could not make work and the coup it could not stop making.
