concepts/the-emigres.title: The Émigrés
concepts/the-emigres.content:
The Émigrés
The Flight of the Princes
On the night of July 16, 1789, two days after the fall of the Bastille, the comte d’Artois — the younger brother of Louis XVI and the most hated man in Paris after the queen — slipped out of Versailles with a handful of companions. The king himself had ordered his departure, fearing for his life. Accompanied by the prince d’Hénin, the comte de Vaudreuil, and a few gentlemen of his household, Artois rode first to Chantilly, where the prince de Condé’s carriage awaited them, then pressed on toward Valenciennes and the frontier. Behind him came Condé himself with his son the duc de Bourbon and his grandson the duc d’Enghien. Behind them poured the great families of the court: the Lauzuns, the Villequiers, the Durases, the Polignacs, the Broglies — all fleeing what they took to be a passing storm, convinced they would be home within three months.
“Nous rentrerons dans trois mois,” Artois told the comte Eszterhazy, the governor of Valenciennes, with characteristic insouciance. It was the universal conviction of the first émigrés. None paused to settle their affairs or secure resources beyond a few weeks. They departed as if for a country excursion, in carriages and fiacres, with their mistresses and their jewel-cases, certain that the revolutionary tempest would soon blow over and that the old order would reassert itself with a minimum of fuss.
From Valenciennes, Artois made his way to Turin, the capital of his father-in-law Victor-Amédée III, king of Sardinia. The journey took him through Brussels — where the Austrian governor, the archduchess Marie-Christine, ordered him to move on at her brother Joseph II’s command, lest his presence provoke the French government — and across Germany and Switzerland. By mid-September he was installed at Moncalieri, the Sardinian summer residence, with his wife and children, the three Condés, and a suite of eighty-two persons. The court in exile had begun.
Even as Artois settled in Piedmont, the emigration gathered momentum. The October Days — the march on Versailles and the forcible transfer of the royal family to the Tuileries — unleashed a new wave. The duc d’Orléans fled to England; nobles from Provence and Dauphiné poured into Chambéry and Nice. After the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in 1790, priests and bishops swelled the exodus. Entire families, from the greatest lords down to the shopkeepers and seamstresses who had served them, took to the roads, choking the post-roads from Paris to the frontiers, begging for horses at every relay, camping in barns and village inns, sustained by the illusion that their exile would be brief.
Turin and the Concert of Europe
At Turin, the comte d’Artois expected that the crowned heads of Europe would fly to his brother’s aid. He was quickly disabused. The courts of Europe had their own calculations, and the French Revolution, for all its alarming novelty, was not yet seen as a mortal threat to the monarchical order.
The emperor Joseph II, absorbed in his projects of aggrandizement in the east, regarded the weakening of France with something close to satisfaction. His successor Leopold thought similarly: neither would move against the Revolution except on terms that gave Austria territorial advantages. Prussia, under Frederick William II, was fixated on Poland and on keeping Austria in check; the French imbroglio was a distraction. William Pitt’s England, still recovering from the American war and focused on commercial recovery, remained studiously neutral. Catherine the Great, though she thundered against revolutionary ideas and took sanitary measures to keep French propaganda out of Russia, was consumed by the war with Turkey and the final partitions of Poland. Only Gustavus III of Sweden, a romantic enthusiast for royal legitimacy, offered spontaneous support — but Sweden was distant and weak.
The one power that might have acted, Spain, where a Bourbon still reigned, proved maddeningly elusive. The comte d’Artois bombarded Madrid with appeals; Florida Blanca, the Spanish minister, responded with polite silence. The prince de Condé, whose correspondence with his agent Larouzière provides the most intimate record of these months, wrote in February 1790: “We will not have a single foreign soldier if Spain is not at the head of everything.”
To direct the diplomacy of the emigration, Artois turned to Calonne, the former controller-general of finances, who had installed himself in London. Calonne was the fatal man of the emigration — presumptuous, credulous, convinced of his own infallibility. He dictated the first approaches to Vienna and Berlin, both of which failed. The emperor’s answer, Condé reported, was “affreuse, repoussante, insultante même.” The Prussian response was hardly better.
Money, meanwhile, was already running out. The comte d’Artois had arrived in Turin with no more than pocket-money. The king of Sardinia would feed and lodge his daughter and son-in-law, but he would not finance a war against France. Loans were sought from the treasury of the Grande Chartreuse and the rich abbeys; nothing came of them. The year 1789 ended with the princes’ treasury empty and their diplomacy barren.
Worse still, the first seeds of discord between the émigrés and the king they professed to serve had already been sown. From the Tuileries, Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette watched their brother’s activities with mounting alarm. Every letter from Turin — and there were many, for the émigrés observed no discretion — seemed designed to compromise the royal family further. “Le comte d’Artois excédé de toutes les lettres qu’il reçoit,” Condé wrote in January 1790. The king reproached; the queen pleaded. From Turin, the response was defiance: “Secourez-les malgré eux,” as Madame Élisabeth herself wrote. “Labourer la terre, gagner mon pain à la sueur de mon front, périr enfin, fût-ce de misère,” Artois wrote to the bailli de Crussol, “voilà ce que je préférerai toujours à un accommodement quelconque.”
Coblentz and the Army of the Princes
By the summer of 1791, the center of gravity of the emigration had shifted from Turin to the Rhineland. In June, Louis XVI’s failed flight to Varennes demonstrated — if demonstration were needed — that the king was a prisoner and that a counter-revolution could not wait upon his pleasure. The comte de Provence, the king’s elder brother, who had escaped separately and successfully, reached Brussels and then joined the émigré gathering on the Rhine. The electoral court of the archbishop of Trier, at Coblentz, became the headquarters of the emigration.
It was at Coblentz that the émigré enterprise assumed its most characteristically theatrical form. The princes established a court in miniature, with chancelleries, uniforms, regiments, and a ceaseless traffic in deputations, intrigues, and memoranda. The Army of the Princes — the émigré military force — was assembled, its officers drawn from the noblesse of France, its rank and file from a miscellany of German adventurers, Swiss mercenaries, and discharged soldiers. Its uniforms were magnificent; its discipline was not.
The politics of Coblentz were those of intransigence. The princes and their circle — Calonne among them — insisted on the complete restoration of the old order: the monarchy of 1788, the privileges of the nobility and clergy, the abolition of everything the Revolution had done. Any talk of compromise, of a constitutional monarchy on the English model, was treated as treason. The “monarchiens” — Malouet, Mounier, Lally-Tollendal, Montlosier, Cazalès — who had tried to steer the Revolution toward a moderate settlement, were regarded by the Coblentz émigrés with a hatred scarcely less intense than that reserved for the Jacobins. D’Antraigues, the most violent of the ultras, declared: “Je ferai tomber cent mille têtes — et la sienne la première,” speaking of Montlosier.
From Coblentz, the princes conducted their diplomacy. Austria, Prussia, and the smaller German states were canvassed for support. The Declaration of Pillnitz, issued in August 1791 by Leopold II and Frederick William II, was the result — a cautiously worded statement that the restoration of order in France was “a matter of common interest to all sovereigns of Europe,” but hedged with conditions that made immediate action impossible. The émigrés read it as a blank cheque; it was nothing of the kind.
Nevertheless, by the spring of 1792, the coalition had taken shape. Austria and Prussia agreed on war. The Brunswick Manifesto — the famous declaration threatening Paris with “exemplary and never-to-be-forgotten vengeance” if the royal family were harmed — was drawn up by a French émigré, the marquis de Limon, and issued on July 25, 1792. It was intended to terrify the Revolution into submission. It had precisely the opposite effect. The invasion that followed, under the duke of Brunswick, was a series of humiliations: the cannonade of Valmy on September 20, the retreat of the Prussian army, the dissolution of the invasion as a fighting force. The Army of the Princes, which had accompanied the main force, melted away. The first military effort of the emigration was over, and in its wake came the September Massacres in Paris, the fall of the monarchy, and the establishment of the Republic.
The émigrés scattered. The Army of the Princes, reconstituted under the prince de Condé and maintained first by Austria and then by England, continued to fight — but always as a subsidiary force, a political ornament to the campaigns of the great powers rather than an independent military instrument. Condé’s army would see action on the Rhine in 1793, in the disastrous campaign of 1796, and again in 1799, but it never again approached French territory in force. It was a symbol, a standard around which the fading hopes of the royalist cause gathered, but a standard that receded ever further from the frontiers of France.
Hamm and Verona: The King in Exile
On January 21, 1793, Louis XVI was guillotined. The comte de Provence, who had been living quietly at Hamm in Westphalia since his escape from France, proclaimed himself Regent for the imprisoned Louis XVII. When the child-king died in the Temple in June 1795 — from neglect, disease, or worse — the comte de Provence declared himself Louis XVIII, king of France. The emigration now had a sovereign, but one without a throne, without an army, and without a territory.
The first years of Louis XVIII’s reign in exile were spent at Verona, in the territories of the Republic of Venice. There he established a court, appointed ministers — the comte d’Avaray as his closest confidant, the duc de La Vauguyon as foreign minister — and issued his first proclamation to the French people. It was uncompromising: a return to the “antique constitution” of the kingdom, the restoration of the three orders, the maintenance of the Catholic religion as the religion of state, and severe punishment for the regicides. “I abandon to all the severity of the judgments they deserve,” the declaration read, “all those who, when I pardon, would abandon themselves to sentiments of vengeance.” But it excepted from clemency “the assassins of the king my brother, of the queen, of Madame Élisabeth.”
This was not the language of a prince seeking reconciliation with his people. The émigré court at Verona was consumed — as it would be for the next twenty years — by two obsessions: the problem of finance, which was never solved, and the problem of the comte d’Artois, which was more intractable still.
Quiberon
The most tragic episode of the emigration was Quiberon. In the summer of 1795, the British government — eager to exploit the royalist insurrection in the Vendée and Brittany — launched a combined naval and military expedition to land émigré troops on the Breton coast. The plan had been pressed by the comte de Puisaye, a former constitutionalist turned royalist organizer, who had won the confidence of the British war minister Windham. The comte d’Artois was to follow with a second wave; the Breton chouans, under Charette and Stofflet, were to rise in concert.
On June 27, 1795, an émigré force of some three thousand men landed at Carnac, on the Quiberon peninsula. A second landing at Auray, under the chevalier de Tinténiac, penetrated inland. For a few weeks, the royalists held the peninsula. Then the republican army under General Hoche arrived.
On July 16, the royalist sortie from the peninsula was crushed at Sainte-Barbe. The survivors fell back into the trap of the peninsula itself, hemmed between Hoche’s advancing columns and the sea. On the night of July 20-21, during a violent storm, republican grenadiers, guided by deserters from the royalist ranks, scaled the cliffs of the fort of Penthièvre and seized it in a coup de main. The peninsula was overrun. The British squadron, under Admiral Warren, could do little but pick up survivors from the water.
The scene at Port-Halliguen, at the tip of the peninsula, was one of unspeakable horror. Officers, soldiers, and peasants — men, women, and children — threw themselves into the sea, trying to reach the English boats that the violence of the waves prevented from approaching the shore. Hundreds drowned. Others were pulled into overloaded boats, whose first passengers beat back those who tried to climb aboard. Some, seeing no escape, threw themselves from the cliffs or fell on their own swords.
Sombreuil, the young general who had commanded one of the émigré regiments, held out with his legion on the rocks of the Fort-Neuf until surrender was the only option. Hoche, who admired his bravery, promised — or was understood to promise — that the prisoners would be treated as prisoners of war. Sombreuil handed over his sword after kissing the blade. But the Convention, which had sent commissioners to the scene, was in no mood for clemency. Seven hundred and fifty-one émigrés were executed by military commissions in the weeks that followed. Sombreuil himself was shot at Vannes on July 28, along with the bishop of Dol and thirteen priests.
The British squadron, carrying the survivors — among them Puisaye himself, who had made his way to the flagship Pomone early in the battle — sailed for England. Puisaye, who had abandoned his men, wrote to Windham blaming the émigrés for the disaster: “The greatest number, especially those paid too dearly by you, did not bring among us the spirit one might have expected after six years of exile and misfortune.” Calonne, writing from Southampton, was more measured but no less damning: “A lack of vigilance, which does great harm to M. de Puisaye’s reputation, delivered them to treachery.”
The comte d’Artois, who had been expected to lead the second wave, arrived at Portsmouth on August 7 to learn that the expedition had been crushed. He was kept in England; the British government, sobered by the catastrophe, abandoned further landing attempts. From the island of Yeu, where he was briefly stationed, Artois attempted to coordinate with Charette, but the opportunity had passed. Charette was captured and executed the following year. “Sire,” he was supposed to have written to Louis XVIII, “the cowardice of your brother has lost everything.” Whether he wrote those exact words is uncertain, but the sentiment was widely shared.
Émigré Politics under the Directory and Consulate
The failure of Quiberon marked the end of the émigrés’ military hopes. From 1795 onward, the struggle became one of conspiracy, diplomacy, and the slow, grinding war of influence at Europe’s courts.
Louis XVIII was expelled from Verona in April 1796 at the demand of the Directory, which threatened Venice with French invasion. He fled to the Army of Condé at Riégel, in Baden, but the Austrians would not tolerate his presence there. He searched for a fixed residence — first at Blankenberg, in the duchy of Brunswick, where he stayed from 1796 to 1798; then at Mitau, in the Russian Baltic, to which Tsar Paul I invited him in 1798. There he remained until Paul’s murder in 1801, when Alexander I, the new tsar, reluctantly asked him to leave under French pressure. He spent the next years in Warsaw, then at the invitation of Frederick William III of Prussia at Memel, and finally, from 1807, at Hartwell in England.
These were years of endless negotiation, of agents sent and missions failed, of plots discovered and betrayed. The royalist network inside France — the “Agence de Paris,” directed by Brottier, Duverne de Praile, and Despomelles — was uncovered and broken in January 1797. The arrest of its leaders in the École Militaire, after a colonel named Malo whom they had tried to recruit betrayed them to the Directory, was a devastating blow. In its wake came the coup of 18 Fructidor (September 4, 1797), which purged the government of royalist sympathizers, annulled elections, and reimposed the Terror by other means. All the patient work of infiltration and subversion — the cultivation of the moderate deputies, the secret correspondence with generals like Pichegru — was undone in a single stroke.
The conspiracy of the Rue Saint-Nicaise, a bomb attack on Napoleon as he drove to the Opéra on Christmas Eve 1800, was the work of royalist plotters from the west. It failed, killing several bystanders but leaving Napoleon unhurt. The response was ferocious: the deportation of 130 Jacobins implausibly blamed for the attack, the execution of the real conspirators, and the intensification of police surveillance over the surviving royalist underground.
The Cadoudal-Pichegru conspiracy of 1803-1804 was the most ambitious attempt to assassinate the First Consul and restore the Bourbons. Georges Cadoudal, the Breton chouan leader, crossed the Channel with a band of accomplices; General Pichegru, the former commander of the republican Army of the Rhine who had turned royalist, returned from exile to join him. The plot extended to the highest levels: the comte d’Artois was to appear on the frontiers of France the moment Napoleon was eliminated. But the police, directed by Fouché, had penetrated the conspiracy from the start. Cadoudal was captured and executed; Pichegru was found strangled in his prison cell — whether by his own hand or by agents of the state was never clearly established. The due d’Enghien, the young Bourbon prince whom Napoleon suspected of involvement, was seized from neutral Baden, tried by military commission, and shot in the ditch of the Château de Vincennes. It was the most controversial act of Napoleon’s career, and it sent a shudder through every royalist court in Europe.
Mitau, Warsaw, Hartwell
The assassination of the due d’Enghien convinced Louis XVIII that his cause could not be advanced by conspiracy alone. From Hartwell, the modest English estate where he installed himself in 1807, he pivoted to a strategy of patience. The European war would, he believed, eventually produce circumstances favorable to the Bourbon restoration — if only he could survive, maintain the unity of his family, and avoid the fatal lure of premature action.
The court at Hartwell was a curious affair: a little Versailles in Buckinghamshire, complete with the arcana of etiquette, the distribution of empty honors, and the perpetual struggle for the king’s favor. The comte d’Avaray, Louis’s devoted companion, was the most trusted figure — until his health collapsed and he was forced to retire to Madeira in 1810, dying there the following year. The comte de Blacas succeeded him as the king’s right hand. The correspondence between Blacas and Joseph de Maistre, the Savoyard philosopher who served as the king’s eyes and ears in St. Petersburg, provides the most vivid record of these years: the intellectual excitement of the European struggle, the long intervals of despair, the gradual, almost imperceptible accumulation of hope.
The Russian campaign of 1812 transformed everything. Napoleon’s Grande Armée was destroyed in the snows. The prisoners-of-war taken by the Cossacks, the accounts of cannibalism in the retreat, the burning of Moscow — all of it was reported to Hartwell by de Maistre in letters of savage joy. “Bonaparte n’a plus d’armée,” he wrote on November 13, 1812. But the Allies, though they defeated Napoleon in Germany in 1813, were in no hurry to restore the Bourbons. The emissaries Louis XVIII dispatched to the camp of the sovereigns — Alexis de Noailles, the comte de La Ferronnays, the comte de Bouillé — were received with courtesy and given nothing. Alexander I was sympathetic but non-committal; Metternich was hostile; Bernadotte, the former revolutionary general who now ruled Sweden, was pursuing his own ambitions. “Le moment n’est pas encore propice,” was the invariable reply.
The Return
The moment came at last in the spring of 1814. The Allies entered Paris on March 31. The due d’Angoulême — the comte d’Artois’s elder son — landed at Bordeaux, where the city received him with acclamations. The comte d’Artois himself entered Paris as lieutenant-general of the kingdom. On April 2, the Senate proclaimed the deposition of Napoleon; on April 6, it offered the crown to Louis XVIII, on condition that he accept a constitution.
Louis XVIII landed at Calais on April 25, 1814 — twenty-four years after he had fled France, a fugitive. He entered Paris on May 3, passed through crowds that shouted “Vive le roi!” from the same streets that had roared for the guillotine a generation earlier. The emigration was over.
But it had left its mark. The years of exile had not softened the émigrés. They returned — those who survived — with their grievances intact, their estates sold, their châteaux in ruins, their world turned inside out. The comte d’Artois had learned nothing and forgotten nothing. The prince de Condé was old and broken, mourning the wife he had married at last after forty-five years of devotion. The Army of the Princes was a memory. The great names of the emigration — the Polignacs, the La Trémoïlles, the Noailles — came back demanding restitution, demanding revenge, demanding the restoration of everything the Revolution had taken.
Louis XVIII, wiser than his followers, knew that such a restoration was impossible. “Bien rétablie — cela dépend,” he said to the duc de Duras on the eve of his departure from England. He gave France the Charter of 1814, which preserved the essential achievements of the Revolution — equality before the law, religious liberty, the Napoleonic Code — while restoring the monarchy. It was a compromise, and like all compromises, it satisfied no one fully. The émigrés of the old school thought it a betrayal; the liberals thought it insufficient. The king walked a narrow path between them, and it was not enough to save his dynasty. But for a moment, in the spring of 1814, the long exile was over. The Bourbons had come home.

concepts/the-meaning-of-terror.title: The Meaning of 'Terror'
concepts/the-meaning-of-terror.content:
The Meaning of ‘Terror’
The word itself was not new. Long before 1793, la terreur had named the shudder that seizes a people before arbitrary power — the cold that descends when law gives way to will, when the state’s hand can reach anyone, anywhere, without warning or reason. What was new was the claim that such a state might be legitimate. The Terror of 1793–1794 was not, to those who lived through it, primarily a quantity of executions or a list of laws. It was an experience: the experience of living under a government that governed without fixed law, that defined safety as total submission, and that demanded the inner life of every citizen as the price of survival.
The Theory of Arbitrary Government
Benjamin Constant, writing in the aftermath of Thermidor, recognized that the Terror had been not merely a series of violent episodes but a coherent claim about how power could be exercised. Its defenders said — and during 1793–1794 many said it openly — that the Republic was at war, that normal constitutional forms were a luxury the emergency could not afford, that the survival of the state justified any measure. To Constant, this argument was more dangerous than the guillotine itself. Once the principle was accepted that safety could come from arbitrary violence, there was no logical stopping point. Any emergency could justify any measure; any faction could declare itself the embodiment of the nation’s will; any individual could be declared an enemy of the people. The Terror had not saved the Republic, Constant insisted. The Republic was saved by its armies, by geography, by the incompetence of the invading coalition — not by the Revolutionary Tribunal. But the deeper damage was cultural. The Terror had taught French men and women that power could operate without law, that the state’s survival justified individual destruction, that suspicion was a sufficient basis for condemnation. A generation grew up knowing that the authorities could reach them at any hour, without charge, without trial, and that the only safety lay in invisibility.
The logic of revolutionary government, as its own advocates formulated it, inverted every principle of constitutional order. Where constitutional government defined and limited power, revolutionary government declared that power must be unlimited because the danger was total. Where constitutional government required fixed procedures and known laws, revolutionary government operated through committees, surveillance, and denunciation — procedures that could change direction at any moment. Where constitutional government protected individual rights as inviolable, revolutionary government treated every citizen as a suspect until proven otherwise. This was not, to Constant, a temporary expedient that had gotten out of hand. It was a distinct form of government, with its own logic, its own justification, and its own corruptions. The Terror was not the absence of government; it was government of a particular kind — a government that ruled through fear because it had abandoned the only legitimate foundation of rule, which was law.
The psychological corruption was the worst of it. Constant observed that arbitrary government corrupted even those who benefited from it, because it made all relationships — between citizen and state, between individuals — dependent on favor rather than right. Under such a system, no one was safe. The man who denounced his neighbor today could be denounced tomorrow; the revolutionary committee that ordered arrests could itself be purged; the most ardent patriot could become the most dangerous suspect. The effect on the human character was devastating. Men learned to say what was required, to conceal their thoughts, to watch their friends for signs of hesitation. The habit of truthfulness — that slow, difficult achievement of civilized life — dissolved in a few months. The Republic that Constant wanted to build could not rest on such a foundation. A republic required citizens capable of independent judgment, of public speech, of trust in institutions. The Terror had produced something else: subjects trained in concealment, their moral muscles atrophied by fear.
The Streets of Paris Under Surveillance
In the streets of Paris, the Terror was not a theory but a texture — the quality of light and sound and human contact in a city where every public space had become a theater of suspicion. The Palais-Royal, which in 1789 had been the great open-air forum of the Revolution, the place where crowds gathered, speeches were made, and the future was debated aloud, had become something else by 1794. Its cafés and galleries were still full, but the conversations had changed. Men spoke in lowered voices, watching who approached. The words that had been shouted in ‘89 — liberty, rights, the nation — were dangerous now if attached to the wrong person or the wrong faction.
The police reports from these years, preserved in the archives, give a precise picture of what surveillance meant at street level. The agents of the secret police moved through the crowds of the Palais-Royal, the gambling dens, the brothels, the food lines, noting what was said, who said it, and what mood the people were in. One agent, Pourvoyeur, filed daily reports during the spring of 1794. On 14 February, standing on the Place de la Révolution — the former Place Louis XV, renamed for the regime that now executed its enemies there — he noted what the crowd said as they watched the guillotine work: “When will the guillotine end? Is it not tired of guillotining every day?” Men asked this of each other in low voices, careful not to be heard by the wrong person. The women, Pourvoyeur observed, had become the most ferocious. He reported that “the people said they had noticed that women had become bloodthirsty, that they preach only blood, that there is among them a certain quantity of women who never leave the guillotine nor the Revolutionary Tribunal.”
The brothels and gambling dens that clustered around the Palais-Royal were not merely places of vice; they were nodes in the surveillance network. The police knew that men spoke freely in such places, that the combination of drink, sex, and the illusion of privacy loosened tongues. The agents noted the prostitutes who might be useful informants, the clients whose opinions might be reported, the assignats changing hands at gambling tables that revealed where wealth was flowing. The Palais-Royal, which had been the Revolution’s nursery, had become its confessional — a place where everything was seen and nothing was safe to say.
The food lines were another theatre of surveillance. In the winter of 1793–1794, when bread was scarce and the assignats buying less every week, men and women stood for hours in the cold, their patience fraying. The police listened to what they muttered. Defeatism, criticism of the committees, nostalgia for the king — any of these, overheard and reported, could be fatal. The Convention had decreed the Law of Suspects in September 1793, which defined who could be arrested: those who by their conduct, their connections, their speech, or their silence showed themselves to be enemies of liberty. The definition was deliberately vague; it had to be, because the purpose of the law was not to define crimes but to authorize suspicion. Under this law, a woman complaining about the price of bread, a man grumbling about the length of the queue, a former noble who had kept his head down — any of them could be denounced and imprisoned on the word of a neighbor, a servant, a spurned lover.
The public executions were the culmination of this system, its visible, ritualized face. The guillotine was not hidden away; it stood in the Place de la Révolution, where the crowds could gather, where the daily spectacle was open to all. The Conventionnel Philippe Drulhe, who had seen enough of the crowds to judge them, wrote that “an immoral and wicked being alone can rejoice” at the fall of the blade — but that it was women, above all, who seemed to feel the attraction. “If one sometimes encounters this ferocious sentiment,” he wrote, “it is hardly ever except in women. In general, they show themselves more avid than men for these bloody scenes; they watch without trembling the play of this modern blade, whose mere description made the Constituent Assembly cry out in horror — but it was an assembly of men; women are a hundred times more cruel.”
The women who gathered daily at the guillotine — the tricoteuses, the knitters, who brought their work to the Place de la Révolution as other women brought it to the fireside — were the Terror’s most visible audience. They sat through the cartloads, through the reading of the sentences, through the fall of the blade. They counted the heads. They knew the faces of the executioner’s assistants. They were, in their way, the perfect citizens of the Terror: they had internalized its logic so completely that the death of others had become a form of entertainment, a daily ritual, a way of passing the time until dinner.
The Prison
Madame Roland arrived at the Abbaye prison on the first of June 1793. The arrest had been a formality — the warrant bore no charge, no evidence, not even a plausible accusation. She was detained “by order of the revolutionary committee,” and that was sufficient. The Abbaye was an old prison, built for criminals, not political prisoners, and its routines had not changed. The concierge, a woman named Lavacquerie, received her with a certain professional courtesy: she showed her to a room, promised that a bed would be arranged, told her that she had many people to accommodate and hoped she did not mind sharing.
Roland sat down in her cell and experienced, in the first moments of imprisonment, something she would later describe among the most valuable of her life. She took stock: her past actions, her present situation, her future prospects. She found nothing to regret and nothing to fear. “I devoted myself voluntarily to my destiny, whatever it might be,” she wrote. “I established myself in that disposition where one seeks only the good use of the present, without further anxiety.” This was the moral composure of the Stoic — the attitude of a woman who had read Plutarch and Seneca and meant to live by what she had read — but it was also a specific act of defiance. The Terror demanded fear; to refuse fear was to refuse the system’s most essential demand.
She wrote at once to the Convention, protesting that she had been arrested without any charge being stated, that she was “presumed guilty in the eyes of the public,” that she had been taken through the streets in the midst of an armed force while “some individuals sent me openly to the scaffold, without anyone being able to indicate to anyone, nor announce to me, upon what I was presumed such, and treated accordingly.” The letter went unanswered. The Convention was itself under armed siege, its deputies arrested at the bar, its will no longer its own. No one in the Assembly could protect her; some had signed the warrants.
Prison life under the Terror had its own rhythms. The prisoners formed a society of their own — men and women thrown together by the same arbitrary power, sharing the same uncertainty, the same dwindling hope. They talked, they read, they wrote letters that might or might not be delivered. They watched who arrived and who was taken away. The atmosphere was poisoned by the knowledge that among them, almost certainly, were informers — prisoners who had been offered their freedom in exchange for reports, men and women who listened and remembered and passed on what they heard. The Revolutionary Tribunal did not need evidence gathered in the usual way; it needed denunciations, and prisoners could provide those as well as anyone. To speak freely in the prison yard was to court death. To trust your cellmate was an act of faith that the system was designed to destroy.
Roland was transferred from the Abbaye to Sainte-Pélagie, where conditions were harsher and the regime stricter. She was allowed no contact with the outside world except through heavily censored letters. She lived under the constant threat of transfer to the Conciergerie — the holding prison for those about to be tried — which was, in most cases, a transfer to death. The trial, when it came, was a formality. The Revolutionary Tribunal had been created precisely to produce convictions, and its procedures were designed to ensure them. There was no jury of peers; there were no rules of evidence; there was no appeal. The accused were brought before the court, a list of charges was read, and the verdict — always the same — was pronounced. Roland was condemned not for anything she had done but for who she was: the wife of a proscribed minister, a woman of intelligence and influence, a witness to the crimes of those who now judged her.
She drafted a defense that she was not permitted to deliver. In it, she traced the logic by which the Revolution had consumed its own children: first the king, then the Girondins, then — she predicted — the Montagnards themselves. “The tigers are going to tear each other apart,” she wrote from her cell, watching the factional struggles that would eventually bring down Robespierre. “They will perhaps forget us, unless the fury of their last moments carries them to exterminate everything before their own defeat.”
On 8 November 1793 — 18 Brumaire, Year II — she was taken from Sainte-Pélagie to the Conciergerie, tried, condemned, and executed on the same day. She went to the scaffold in a white dress, her hair cut, her hands tied behind her. A story — perhaps true, perhaps invented — says that before the blade fell, she asked for pen and paper to record the last thoughts of a woman about to die. The request was denied.
The Fugitive
While Roland faced the Revolutionary Tribunal, her friends were dying differently — slowly, in hiding, in the cold of forests and the dark of caves, alone with the fear of betrayal. Buzot and Louvet, both proscribed after the June coup, both Girondin deputies, both men who had voted for the king’s death and then found themselves hunted by those who had done the same, experienced the Terror as a narrowing of the world: a progressive contraction of space, of options, of hope.
Buzot fled Paris in the first days of June 1793, making his way toward Normandy, where he hoped to rally resistance. The federalist uprising in Caen — the attempt by Girondin-allied departments to march on Paris and restore the Convention’s independence — failed at the Battle of Pacy-sur-Eure in July. After that, there was no organized resistance left, only flight. Buzot went to Brittany, then to Bordeaux, then to the wine country of the Gironde, where a handful of the proscribed deputies gathered at Saint-Émilion. They lived in a single house, hidden by a sympathetic republican, their existence known to only a few. They did not dare to show themselves in daylight. They cooked their own meals, slept in shifts, and waited.
The waiting was its own kind of torture. The news that reached them in the wine cellars of Saint-Émilion was always bad: Brissot condemned, Vergniaud condemned, the Revolutionary Tribunal working through the list of Girondin names. The friends they had known, the colleagues they had worked beside, the men who had shared their hopes for the Republic — one by one, they were called before the Tribunal and sent to the scaffold. The fugitives could do nothing. They could not show themselves to defend the accused; they could not write letters that would not be intercepted; they could not even die with them.
The fear of denunciation was constant. Buzot wrote bitterly about the friends who had refused them shelter — men who had been protected by the Girondins for months, who owed their positions to Girondin patronage, who had sworn eternal gratitude, and who now would not open their doors for a single night. “Friends ferocious through pusillanimity,” Louvet called them, “would refuse to recognize their friend… friends of twenty years would drive you from their door, repulse you to the foot of the scaffold.” The system worked not only through the police and the committees but through the atomization of trust. When every man feared his neighbor, no man could help another.
Louvet’s experience was even more stark. After the failure at Caen, he fled through Brittany and the Gironde, always a step ahead of the searches, always dependent on the mercy of strangers. His wife Lodoïska accompanied him, sharing his dangers, managing a bookshop in Paris while he was in hiding — a cover that allowed her to pass messages and money. In April 1794, they took refuge in the Jura mountains, in a limestone cave that Louvet described as “the grottos of the Jura.” There, in the cold, with inadequate food and whatever light the day offered, he wrote his memoirs. He did not expect to survive. His prefatory note, dated 19 April 1794 — 30 Germinal, Year II — explains the conditions under which he wrote: “Here, as there, time fails me. I throw down notes, and that is all. Do not expect either stylistic concision or abundance of detail. Truly, I am writing neither history nor what is called memoirs. I am recording notes that may help me, if some day of genuine leisure is given to me — or help someone else, if I do not survive.”
The cave was not a metaphor. He was physically present in it, cold and hungry and isolated, the sound of wind in the trees the only sign of a world that had forgotten him. He wrote for the record — for the truth, as he said, which alone could justify the Girondin cause. “It is the truth, it is she alone that can destroy this immense scaffolding of absurd and atrocious calumnies with which they have overwhelmed us, in order to assassinate us afterwards.”
The political experience of the fugitive was distinct from that of the prisoner. The prisoner at least knew where she stood: the cell, the trial, the scaffold — there was a sequence, a dreadful clarity. The fugitive existed in a state of permanent suspension, never safe, never at rest, never able to resume normal life. Every knock on the door might be the gendarmes; every stranger who looked too long might be an informer; every friend might be a man who had already broken. Louvet wrote of the seven proscribed deputies who had fled together to the Gironde — himself, Buzot, Pétion, Barbaroux, Salles, Guadet, and Valady — and of what happened to them. Guadet and Salles were captured and guillotined. Barbaroux shot himself through the head, survived the wound, and was guillotined. Pétion and Buzot were found dead in a field near Saint-Émilion, their bodies partly consumed by wolves — whether by poison, starvation, or exposure, no one could say with certainty. Of the seven, only Louvet survived, and he survived because he had gone to the Jura while the others stayed in the Gironde. “I left them by a temerity that was my salvation,” he wrote. “They remained by a confidence that destroyed them.”
What the Terror Meant
To those who lived through it, the Terror was not an abstraction — not a period, not a policy, not a quantity of deaths. It was a condition of existence, a way that power pressed on daily life. It meant that the law could not protect you because the law was whatever the committees said it was. It meant that your neighbor might be an informer, your maid might be a spy, your friend might be a man who would sacrifice you to save himself. It meant that the state could reach into your home, your bed, your mind, and demand that you prove yourself innocent of thoughts you had never thought.
It meant the streets of Paris where the police listened to every murmur. It meant the Place de la Révolution where the blade fell every afternoon and the women knitted while they watched. It meant the prison where you shared a cell with a stranger who might be reporting your words to the committee. It meant the cave where you wrote your memoirs by candlelight because you would not live to see them published.
Constant understood that the Terror was not primarily a matter of individual cruelty — though there was cruelty enough — but of institutional logic. The revolutionary government needed suspicion because suspicion legitimated its power; it needed denunciation because denunciation kept the population divided and compliant; it needed the guillotine because the guillotine was the visible proof that resistance was futile. The system was not a machine that had malfunctioned; it was a machine that had worked exactly as designed.
When Louvet, writing from his cave, addressed the Convention that had proscribed him, he called on the survivors to recognize what had been done: “These crimes were not those of the republic! They never permitted us to establish it! It was to debase it, to make it hateful, to destroy it forever, that they constantly mixed its name with their cruel turpitudes.” The Terror, in this telling, was not an excess of revolutionary zeal but a betrayal of the Revolution itself — the substitution of arbitrary will for constitutional law, of the committee for the assembly, of the police for the citizen. It was, in the deepest sense, counter-revolutionary.
But the word itself — terror — resisted any single definition. To Constant, it was a political method, a form of government. To the women of the Palais-Royal, it was the quality of the air they breathed. To Madame Roland, it was the moment she heard the lock turn behind her and understood that the law had abandoned her. To Buzot, dying in a field near Saint-Émilion, it was the silence of friends who would not open their doors. To Louvet, it was the cold of the Jura cave and the knowledge that he was writing for a posterity he might never see.
The Terror was all of these things, and the sum of them was greater than any single part. It was the experience of living in a world where power had become arbitrary, where the state had become a predator, and where the only safety — if any existed — lay in being forgotten. That was what the word meant in 1794, and that was what it continued to mean for those who survived to tell the story.

entities/besenval.title: Pierre-Victor, baron de Besenval
entities/besenval.content:
Pierre-Victor, baron de Besenval
He was born in 1721 in Soleure, the capital of the Swiss Catholic cantons, into a patrician family of Savoyard origin that had served the French crown for generations. His father had been sent by Louis XIV as an envoy to Charles XII of Sweden and Augustus of Poland, then returned to the military career natural to his station, dying as a lieutenant-general and colonel of the régiment des Gardes Suisses. The boy was destined for the same path. At nine years old, he entered the régiment des Gardes as a cadet, and at thirteen he made his first campaign.
The Switzerland of his childhood was not the neutral, banking Switzerland of a later century. It was a rugged confederation of cantons whose principal export to the great powers of Europe was soldiers — hard, reliable infantry who fought for whoever paid them and whose loyalty was proverbial. The Besenvals, as officers in the French service, belonged to the military aristocracy that bridged the two worlds: Swiss by birth and loyalty, French by profession and culture. Young Pierre-Victor learned early that he was expected to be fearless, faithful, and clever, and he managed to be all three.
The Soldier
He made his name at the attack on a redoubt during one of the campaigns of the 1740s. The position was critical; the French had lost many men trying to take it. The general resolved to make one more assault with the elite of the grenadiers. Besenval, still a young officer, obtained permission to join the force. The Swiss grenadiers advanced under terrible fire, approached the redoubt, plunged into the ditch, and tried to scale the parapet. Besenval reached the front rank, climbed the wall with his bare hands, his palms bleeding from the sharp rocks. At the crucial moment, he turned to the men behind him and called out, with the particular kind of gaiety for which he became famous: Morbleu! camarades, cette situation-ci n’est pas commode; savez-vous bien que s’il n’y avoit pas des coups de fusil à gagner, on n’y tiendroit pas! The grenadiers, who had been faltering, surged forward; the redoubt was taken; Besenval was the first man over the wall.
The story, which his biographers repeated and which he himself seems to have encouraged, defined his public character: the brave, witty Swiss officer who could make men laugh while they were dying, who combined the solidity of the mercenary tradition with the lightness of the French court. He was promoted rapidly — maréchal-de-camp by the time of the Seven Years’ War, in which he served as aide-de-camp to the duc d’Orléans, the grandfather of the future Philippe-Égalité. He fought at Hastenbeck (1757) and Villinghausen (1761), and served in the campaign of 1757 alongside the officer-academicians of Drévenich — that curious literary academy formed by French generals in the field, where Besenval first tried his hand at writing prose and verse.
He was never wounded. It became a point of pride, almost a superstition. In a lifetime of exposing himself to fire, he came through untouched; and those who knew him attributed it to something more than luck. There was a quality about Besenval that danger could not quite reach, as if the same sanguine temperament that made him incapable of sustained resentment also made him proof against lead.
The Courtier
The peace brought him to Versailles, where his name and his position in the Swiss Guards naturally drew him. He became a fixture at court in the last years of Louis XV — that strange, decadent, brilliant world of the 1760s and early 1770s when the monarchy was still absolute in form but already eroding in fact. Besenval had the right combination of qualities for the place: a fine figure, a quick wit, a talent for friendship, and enough violence in his character to keep people uncertain of what he might do next. His temper was legendary — he admitted it himself, saying that he had tried to master it in his youth, found it impossible, and resolved to give way to his passions freely, like attacks that could not be repressed and that it was better to discharge quickly. But the fury passed as fast as it came, leaving no trace of resentment, and the man who had been the object of his rage often found himself suddenly the object of his caresses and his generosity.
The story told of his old valet Blanchard captures the man exactly. Besenval had a servant who had been with his father before him, an old man of eighty who lived in the house more as a friend than a domestic. One day Besenval received a beautiful jasmine from the Cape, intended for the queen; he entrusted it to Blanchard with instructions to water it. The old man dropped the pot. Besenval returned, saw the wreck, and flew into a fury that lasted the rest of the day. By nightfall the anger had passed and he was anxious about Blanchard’s distress. The next morning the old servant asked permission to retire to his family. Besenval exploded again: You want to leave me? You will stay, monsieur; we must live and die together. The old man insisted he was becoming odious, that his slowness provoked too much violence. Besenval, tears in his eyes, replied: You were with my father, your wife nursed me, you are more ancient in this house than I am. It is I who must leave. He took his hat and cane and made for the door. Blanchard threw himself at his feet; Besenval lifted him up, embraced him, and they swore never to part.
His intelligence was of the practical, worldly kind — more brilliant than deep, more natural than cultivated. He had a subtle and fine tact that served him as well as any education, and he believed, perhaps too readily, that a man of the world could dispense with formal instruction. He applied the same instinct to the arts, which he loved passionately but without the patience to study them properly. Yet his taste was so sure that he formed a superb cabinet of paintings and sculpture, and as an honorary member of the Académie de Peinture, he was often consulted by artists who found his advice surprisingly valuable. Sculptors, painters, and architects admitted that they owed ideas and successes to his counsel.
The Kingmaker
The court of Louis XV and the early reign of Louis XVI were a labyrinth of factions, and Besenval navigated them with the skill of a man who understood power without being consumed by the desire for it. He was a friend of the duc de Choiseul during that minister’s ascendancy, and he watched Choiseul’s fall in 1770 with the clear-eyed disillusionment of a man who knew how the game was played. He was present at the deathbed of Louis XV, saw the smallpox that killed the king and the stunned reaction of the court, and lived through the transition to the reign of Louis XVI.
His greatest political achievement was the elevation of his friend the maréchal de Ségur to the Ministry of War in 1780. Besenval had worked for years to prepare the ground, persuading everyone who could influence the appointment that Ségur was the only man capable of rescuing the French military from the chaos into which it had fallen. Ségur proved him right: he reformed the army, introduced Prussian-style discipline and manoeuvres, established permanent camps for training, and overhauled the administration of supplies and hospitals. The two men corresponded incessantly, and Besenval’s long letters to Ségur — preserved in his memoirs — are among the most detailed contemporary analyses of the French military system in the 1780s, covering everything from the drill regulations and the officer corps to the corruption of the forage contractors.
He was also the intimate friend of Chrétien-François de Lamoignon, the président à mortier of the Parlement of Paris who became Keeper of the Seals in 1787. It was Besenval who urged Lamoignon, during a famous conversation in the magistrate’s study, to undertake the reform of judicial abuses in the Parlement. Looking at the portrait of the great Lamoignon (the seventeenth-century premier président), Besenval had asked: Does he never speak to you? Lamoignon replied that he often heard the portrait telling him to try to become worthy of him. Well then, answered Besenval, isn’t that telling you that it is not enough to be a good father, a good husband, a good friend, a good magistrate — that when you bear such a name and occupy a place where you can make yourself useful, you must not content yourself with the virtues of an obscure citizen? The speech worked. Lamoignon undertook the reform, and when he finally became garde-des-sceaux in 1787, Besenval was the man who had put him on the path.
The Crisis
By 1787, Besenval was in his mid-sixties, a lieutenant-general, a grand’croix of the Order of Saint-Louis, governor of Haguenau, and commander of the provinces of the interior — a vast jurisdiction covering the Île-de-France (excluding Paris itself), the Soissonnais, the Berry, the Bourbonnais, the Orléanais, the Touraine, and the Maine. He had also been lieutenant-colonel of the Swiss Guards since 1764, second-in-command of the Swiss regiments in French service. He had reached the summit of a career that had begun with a nine-year-old cadet in Soleure.
The crisis of 1787-1789 unfolded before him with the terrible clarity of a tragedy whose every act he could foresee and whose outcome he could not prevent. He watched the Assembly of Notables fail to solve the financial crisis. He saw Calonne dismissed, Brienne appointed, Lamoignon made Keeper of the Seals, the Parlement exiled, the May Edicts imposed, the Cour plénière established, the provinces of Brittany and Dauphiné in revolt, the treasury empty, Brienne dismissed, Necker recalled. He wrote in his memoirs that he had predicted the catastrophe years before — that the morality of the philosophes, which tended only to destroy every principle of religion and subordination, could only end in ruin. But what he could not have foreseen was the point to which things actually came: the unheard-of, innumerable faults of the ministers, the weakness of the king, the decay of the nobility, the hypocrisy and clumsiness of the clergy, the insolence and cupidity of the faction that seized control of the National Assembly.
In April 1789, the comte d’Affry, colonel of the Swiss Guards, suffered a grave accident that nearly killed him. As lieutenant-colonel, Besenval was obliged to replace him, taking on the detail of Paris — the command of the troops responsible for maintaining order in the capital — in addition to all his other responsibilities. It was a burden that would have crushed a younger man. Besenval, at sixty-eight, bore it without complaint. The grain shortages that spring had set off riots across his command; the Réveillon uprising in the faubourg Saint-Antoine in April had already shown how fragile order was. He spent his days managing the distribution of troops to protect markets and grain convoys, and his nights at the assembly of the lieutenant of police, trying to ensure the arrival of wheat for the subsistence of Paris.
And then July came.
The July Days
On 12 July 1789, the news reached Paris that Necker had been dismissed. The insurrection that followed took an alarming character from the first hour. Besenval, commanding the troops at the Champ de Mars and the various posts around the capital, faced an impossible situation. The regiments under his orders — the Swiss Guards, the hussards de Berchiny, the dragons de Choiseul, the regiment of Salis-Samade — were concentrated on the Place Louis XV (the modern Place de la Concorde) and in the Champs-Élysées. He had four pieces of cannon. As the crowds grew and the violence spread, his troops were assailed with insults, stones, and pistol shots. Several men were seriously wounded. Not a single soldier made a threatening gesture. Besenval had given strict orders: not a drop of the citizens’ blood was to be spilled.
It was the decision that defined his place in history, and the one for which he was later nearly hanged.
As the disorder increased hour by hour, Besenval debated his options. If he ordered the troops into Paris, he would start a civil war. Blood would flow on both sides, and nothing useful would be accomplished for the public tranquillity. The troops were being seduced before his eyes; he received warnings about their loyalty. Versailles — the court, the ministers, the king — sent him no orders. They persisted in regarding three hundred thousand mutinous men as a mere mob, and the Revolution as a riot. His couriers to the maréchal de Broglie went unanswered. A second courier was intercepted by spies of the popular army.
At one in the morning on 13 July, Besenval made his decision: he withdrew the troops from the capital and left Paris to itself.
The 13th and 14th of July were a nightmare. Besenval moved his headquarters to the École Militaire and then to the Invalides, where the governor, de Sombreuil, showed him the arsenal. Thirty-two thousand muskets were stored in the cellars. The Invalides themselves — the veteran soldiers who guarded the building — had been corrupted. For ten days, money had been filling their pockets. A cripple had been discovered smuggling in packets of licentious and mutinous songs. Sombreuil told him that if the cannoneers received the order to load their pieces, they would turn them on the governor’s own apartment. Besenval wrote to Broglie again, reporting these facts. He received no reply.
At five in the morning on 14 July, a man entered Besenval’s room. He had inflamed eyes, rapid and abrupt speech, an audacious bearing, and something eloquent about him that struck the old officer. Monsieur le baron, the man said, you must be warned, to prevent a useless resistance. Today the barrières of Paris will be burned. I am sure of it, and can do nothing to stop it, nor can you. Do not try to prevent it. You will sacrifice men, and not extinguish a single torch. Besenval did not have him arrested. He let him go.
Between nine and noon, the arsenal of the Invalides was pillaged. Thirty or forty thousand men entered through every door and armed themselves with whatever came to hand. The soldiers of the Hôtel not only failed to resist — they helped. By noon the Bastille had fallen. De Launay, the governor, was dead. Besenval had warned Broglie eight days earlier that de Launay should be replaced — the man’s nerve was gone, his head troubled by noise. The proposal was rejected on grounds of equity, and the Bastille was taken.
A council of general officers at the École Militaire concluded that the effervescence was impossible to repress. The troops were visibly wavering; a colonel assured Besenval, with tears in his eyes, that his regiment would not march. Besenval ordered a retreat to Sèvres. As the troops began to move, he finally received Broglie’s order: he was to make his retreat. It was not troubled by the people.
The Scapegoat
He went directly to Versailles and reported to the king. It was the first time Louis XVI had heard the full story of what had happened. For three days, Besenval was almost the only minister-level figure at the king’s side. Louis came to Paris on 17 July, submitted to the new municipal authority, wore the tricolour cockade, and confirmed Bailly as mayor. The monarchy had capitulated.
Besenval had become the object of the Revolution’s hatred. The faction in Paris believed — or claimed to believe — that he had planned to massacre the city. He was the visible symbol of the military repression that had failed, and the victors needed a scapegoat. The king, warned that his life was in danger, ordered him to leave for Switzerland. Besenval resisted; the king insisted.
He left Versailles at dusk on the night of 19 July, disguised in the uniform of the maréchaussée des chasses, with two cavalrymen as escort. The disguise, which he accepted only after his friends begged and wept, humiliated him. This precaution that smacks of fear, he wrote later, cost my character a great deal. It was perhaps the first time I let myself be led. He was right to be sceptical. The next morning, stopping at an inn in the village of Villegruis near Provins, he was recognised. He had made the mistake of consulting a map in public and asking about the road to the frontier. The tocsin sounded; the inn was surrounded by two or three hundred armed peasants. He was arrested.
The commissioners sent from Paris to collect him told him the story of Foulon — the old intendant of finances who had been hanged from a lamppost, his head paraded on a pike — and gave him to understand that a similar fate awaited him. Necker, learning of the arrest, intervened and saved his life. Besenval never forgot it. I do not know and see only one thing: M. Necker saved my life. Without changing my opinion on his political operations and his errors — let us say the word — I vow to him, until my last day, attachment and gratitude.
Mirabeau, vexed that Necker had scored a point, had the decision reversed. Besenval was sent to Brie-Comte-Robert, to a ruined medieval fortress that was hastily repaired to receive him. His gaoler was a procureur named Bourdon — the same Bourdon who would later sit in the Convention as Bourdon de l’Oise, the man who voted for the king’s death and who was eventually deported to Cayenne. Besenval, with the sangfroid that was his peculiar gift, treated the whole thing as a farce. Bourdon strutted about in epaulettes, convinced that Besenval had plotted to besiege Paris with red-hot shot and grills. Commandant, Besenval told him, I have never known anything but the ruses of war. I am ignorant of those of the law. But I know enough not to be taken in by them.
He spent three months at Brie-Comte-Robert, playing trictrac with a village curé who panicked every time a drum sounded, entertaining himself with the pranks of the Bazoche (the young clerks who guarded him), and watching Bourdon’s burlesque authority with the same detached amusement with which he had once watched the court at Versailles. In November, he was transferred to the Châtelet in Paris, the abominable prison where he spent the winter awaiting trial. Mobs gathered under his window shouting for his head. He received four anonymous notes: They will come; but I will be there. He never discovered who sent them.
The Trial and the End
His trial before the Châtelet, constituted as the tribunal for crimes of lèse-nation, began in the early months of 1790. The committee of research of the Commune of Paris had assembled a hundred and fifty witnesses. Among the prosecutors were Brissot — the future Girondin leader — and other figures who would dominate the Revolution’s first years. The accusation was as simple as it was absurd: that Besenval had planned to massacre Paris. His defence, equally simple, was unanswerable: he had been ordered to suppress the insurrection and had found it impossible to do so.
His advocate was a certain Desèze, the same man who would later defend Louis XVI before the Convention. Desèze’s eloquence was enough. On 1 March 1790, the tribunal acquitted him. His friends, who had filled the courtroom every day of the trial, surrounded him as he walked free.
There is a story that his editor tells, and it is worth recording for what it reveals of the man. During the preparation of his defence, Besenval’s lawyers discovered a written order from the king, dated 12 July 1789, bearing the words: The baron de Besenval will repel force by force. It was a complete defence — a royal order that justified everything he had done and could not have done. His lawyers brought it to him exultantly. Besenval read it, tore it up, and threw it into the fire. What! I would use such an order, which would be turned against this unhappy prince! No, messieurs, save me without that, if you can. He laughed at the consternation of his procureur, who understood nothing of heroism.
He returned to his house, to his friends, to the remnants of a life that the Revolution had shattered. He was not well. During one of the trial sessions, leaving a hearing of witnesses called in his defence, he had suffered the first attack of the illness that would kill him. He knew it. This is the disease that will kill me, he said. It did.
He died in 1791, at the age of seventy, at the very moment when the last things he had loved — the monarchy, the army he had spent his life serving, the world of ordered hierarchy and personal honour that had been the air he breathed — were being swept away beyond any hope of recovery. His memoirs, entrusted to his executor A. J. de Ségur, were nearly lost during the Terror, when Ségur was imprisoned and the manuscript narrowly saved from seizure. They were finally published in 1805, fourteen years after his death.
He left no heir. He left no great political legacy. He left nothing but the memoirs — four volumes of sharp, negligent, brilliant prose that captured the voice of the old regime’s military aristocracy in its last generation: brave, loyal, corrupt, witty, violent, generous, and utterly unable to understand the forces that were destroying it. It is the voice of a man who fought a revolution with nothing but a bad temper and a sense of honour, and who, when he could fight no longer, sat down to write about it.
