entities/bonaparte.title: Napoleon Bonaparte
entities/bonaparte.content:
Napoleon Bonaparte
Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–18??), First Consul of the French Republic and Emperor of the French, dominated European affairs from 1796 through 1815. His career is the story of a man of immense military genius whose ambition consumed all other qualities, who dismantled the French Republic that had raised him, and who finally exhausted the nation that had sustained him.
1. Character
Bonaparte possessed a rich fund of positive science, a vast genius, and a character marked by cold resolution and enterprise. He had the intellectual equipment of a great commander — the scientific knowledge of his profession, the rapidity of judgment, the capacity to hold vast quantities of operational detail in his mind without confusion.
What he lacked was the moral equipment of a great statesman. He had no sensitive soul, no calmer head, no harmony between his passions and his reason. A single passion — ambition — absorbed all the others and gave his career its long brilliance, sustained by a succession of spectacular successes. But this same passion made him incapable of the retreat and consolidation that might have preserved his empire. The contrast with General Moreau is instructive: Moreau’s Rhine retreat of 1796 showed the art of the strategically wise withdrawal — an art Napoleon never possessed and never valued.
His birth had originally placed him among the subaltern officers of an artillery regiment. The Revolution gave him a stage; his genius gave him victories; but his character — ambition without limit, intelligence without moral counterweight — gave Europe twenty years of war and France a regime that exhausted everything it touched.
2. Italian Campaigns, 1796–1797
The Italian campaign of 1796–97 was the making of Bonaparte’s reputation. He took command of the Army of Italy, a force that had been neglected and undersupplied, and in a single year destroyed four Austrian armies, conquered Lombardy, and forced Austria to sue for terms.
The campaign opened with a series of rapid victories that separated the Austrian and Sardinian armies. The Sardinians were forced to a separate peace; the Austrians fell back on Mantua, the great fortress city that commanded the approaches to the Tyrol and the Austrian heartland. Field Marshal Wurmser descended from the Alps with a relieving army; Bonaparte abandoned the siege of Mantua, massed his forces against the Austrian columns, and defeated them at Castiglione in August 1796. The victory re-established the siege and sent captured Austrian flags to the Directory in Paris.
A second Austrian attempt at relief, under Field Marshal Alvinzi, culminated in the three-day battle of Arcola in November 1796 — a contest fought in the marshes and canals between the Adige and the Brenta, described by the marshal Trivulzio as a battle of giants. Bonaparte himself was knocked into a marsh by Austrian fire and had to be pulled from the water by his staff. The French flanked the Austrian position and Alvinzi withdrew.
A third Austrian effort, again under Alvinzi, was crushed at Rivoli in January 1797 in Bonaparte’s most complete Italian victory. The Austrian army was destroyed; the road to Vienna lay open. Mantua surrendered in February 1797, Wurmser capitulating with his garrison after a six-month siege. Bonaparte then drove through the Norican Alps to Klagenfurt and Leoben, within a hundred miles of Vienna. Austria signed the preliminaries of Leoben in April 1797.
The British Mediterranean position became untenable precisely because Bonaparte’s Italian victories cut off the Austro-Sardinian forces on which British strategy depended. The British fleet under Jervis withdrew from the Mediterranean in 1796, a strategic retreat made necessary by land victories that sea power could not prevent.
3. Egyptian Expedition, 1798–1799
Bonaparte’s Egyptian expedition was two things simultaneously: a genuine strategic ambition and a flight from the Directory’s accumulating failures. The Orient was conceived as the road to India; Egypt was to be the base from which France could threaten the richest of Britain’s possessions and sever the commerce of the East. Bonaparte presented it as the great blow against England on its most vulnerable flank.
The fleet that sailed from Toulon in May 1798 carried an army of some 35,000 men and a commission of savants and artists. But the ships were ill-supplied: almost without spare rigging or stores, three of thirteen ships-of-the-line not fit for sea. The entire operation depended on avoiding Nelson’s Mediterranean squadron long enough to land the army. Nelson twice misguessed the expedition’s destination, searching first at Alexandria and then ranging eastward, before returning to find the French fleet anchored in Aboukir Bay.
The Battle of the Nile, August 1, 1798, was the decisive event. Nelson attacked without waiting for tactical formation, sending ships inside the French line as well as outside. Thirteen of seventeen French ships-of-the-line were taken or destroyed; Admiral Brueys was killed. The army in Egypt was cut off absolutely from France. The Nile was the battle that made Waterloo possible — it demonstrated that sea power could isolate any expeditionary force, regardless of its land strength.
Bonaparte had to choose between watching France drift from Egypt or returning through a British-dominated sea. He chose to return, slipping through the blockade in a fast frigate — a personal gamble that succeeded and that he later represented as a strategic necessity. The Syrian campaign that preceded his departure had failed at Acre, where the British naval squadron under Sidney Smith supplied the garrison with naval artillery and intercepted Bonaparte’s siege train at sea.
4. 18 Brumaire 1799
The coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799) was a personal political achievement of extraordinary craft, not a rescue of France from the Directory’s collapse. Bonaparte cultivated the Abbé Sieyès, the most influential intellectual of the Revolution’s constitutional phase, as his instrument. He attached himself to Sieyès to deceive him, and deceived him in order not to have to fear him. He regarded his future colleagues as coarse and inert mud, deprived of feeling, ideas, and will.
The coup itself succeeded because military glory was the avowed title of Bonaparte’s elevation. But the true causes were fear and venality. The deputies who abandoned the Republic did so not from conviction but from a calculation of personal advantage and a terror of the alternatives. The court of courtiers that immediately formed at Bonaparte’s headquarters and at the Luxembourg Palace was composed of those who saw in the general their path to favour.
The Constitution of Year VIII that emerged from the coup was a design in which nothing was lacking to guarantee the citizen’s liberty except everything that was lacking in the men who would execute it. The Senate’s anticipated devotion confirmed a servility already inherent in the structure. Everything seemed arranged, men and things, for the advantage of a single man.
The obstacles that had stopped or slowed great captains during several campaigns were finally overcome — the path was clear for the consolidation that followed.
5. The Consulate, 1799–1804
The Consulate was a period of genuine achievement and deepening corruption — each feeding the other. Bonaparte as First Consul undertook immense public works: canals, roads over the Mont-Blanc and the Simplon, the harnessing of mountain rivers for Paris’s water supply. The civil and criminal codes were framed under his direction, consolidating the legal reforms of the Revolution. The education law under Fourcroy established a system of state-controlled secondary and higher education. The Legion of Honor was created, merging military and civil service in a single order of merit — a gesture genuinely philosophical in its conception.
The Concordat with the Papacy (1801) restored Catholic worship to France after the dechristianisation of the Revolution. But the measure carried a darker edge: restoring the Church was necessary; making the clergy agents of the state’s social-control apparatus was something else. The Senate’s self-abasements revealed the mechanism by which the Republic was dismantled within constitutional forms. The Senate doubled the duration of the Consulship before it had fairly begun; it proclaimed the Life Consulship; it erected dictatorial authority by a single sénatus-consulte without the authentic concurrence of the people. The chiefs of intrigue pressed these accelerations on Bonaparte before he could demand them, assuring themselves thereby of the first dignities and the favour of the master.
The Saint-Domingue expedition of 1801–02 exhibited the pattern that would define the Empire: ambition disregarding consequences, announced with the imposing apparatus of dictatorial authority against a public opinion that clearly disapproved. The expedition was a disaster: the army melted in the tropical climate, the colony was lost, and the financial and military cost were enormous at the moment France most needed to prepare for the renewal of war with England.
The Peace of Amiens (1802–03), the fourteen-month interval of peace between Britain and France, was never a real peace. Bonaparte used the truce to consolidate French domination of the Continent: French troops remained in the Batavian Republic, the Italian Republic was established with Bonaparte as its president, and Piedmont was annexed outright. The treaty was an armed interlude in which both sides prepared for the next round.
6. The Empire, 1804–1812
The Empire was proclaimed in December 1804. The atmosphere was one of singular epidemic — not merely the vulgar who always create supernatural powers for their rulers, but the educated classes, senators, and men of letters who proclaimed Napoleon’s fortune a certain sign of divine vocation to universal empire. The coronation ceremony at Notre-Dame revealed the new emperor’s character with perfect clarity: Pope Pius VII consecrated the crown; Napoleon took it from the altar and placed it on his own head. The contrast was devastating: Charlemagne had received the crown from Rome as a favour from the Church; Bonaparte, recognizing no intermediary between himself and Providence, commanded.
The military achievements of the Empire’s first years were unparalleled. Austerlitz (December 1805), fought on the anniversary of Napoleon’s coronation, destroyed the combined Austro-Russian army and shook the throne of Emperor Francis. Napoleon harangued his army with the confidence that inspires certainty of victory, entered Vienna abandoned by its government, and reassembled the Austrian monarchy by signing peace at Pressburg. Austerlitz was made possible by the strategic failure of Napoleon’s naval combinations. The Trafalgar campaign — the invasion of England abandoned when Villeneuve’s fleet took refuge in Cadiz instead of proceeding to Brest — forced Napoleon to turn the Army of England eastward. Trafalgar, fought on October 21, 1805, destroyed the combined Franco-Spanish fleet and broke Napoleon’s naval arm for the rest of the war. Unable to fight Britain at sea, he turned to the economic warfare of the Continental System.
Jena-Auerstedt (October 1806) was the most complete and rapid of Napoleon’s victories: Berlin occupied, Prussian fortresses falling in sequence. The Treaty of Tilsit (July 1807) with Alexander I marked the height of Napoleon’s power. The Continental System against Britain — the Berlin Decree of November 1806 and the Milan Decree of 1807 — declared the British Isles in a state of blockade and prohibited all commerce with them. The system was a strategic conception that was not absurd but was impossible to execute without a continental compliance Napoleon could not maintain. The Spanish ulcer, the Austrian marriage of 1810 — the moment when Napoleon’s pride reached the point of delirium, manipulated by Vienna’s calculated humiliation — and the growing tension with Russia over the blockade’s enforcement all pointed toward the crisis of 1812.
7. The Decline, 1812–1815
The Russian campaign was defined by the political failure that preceded the military catastrophe. Napoleon entered Russia without having resolved the Polish question. If he had organised the government of Poland, fixed its borders, armed it, and made it capable of defending itself, Russia would have been forced to respect the barrier. The opportunity was lost because the glory of creating a people held few attractions for a man who found peoples to subjugate and states to conquer. The retreat from Moscow was less a meteorological catastrophe than the consequence of a campaign that had no exit: having sought a battle the Russians refused to give and an occupation the inhabitants burned rather than concede, Napoleon found himself deep in Russia with an army impossible to feed and a political situation impossible to manage.
The 1813 campaign in Germany opened with successes that proved a deceptive prelude to the reverses fortune was preparing. A peace was available on terms that, while not restoring the pre-1812 position, would have preserved France and its emperor. Austria offered itself as mediator between Napoleon its son-in-law and the allied powers. Napoleon could have concluded a treaty no less advantageous than honorable; but he claimed to dictate peace, not negotiate it.
The battle of Leipzig (October 1813) broke the Empire’s hold on Germany. The 1814 campaign in France — fought on French soil for the first time since 1792 — produced some of Napoleon’s most brilliant tactical improvisations. But the fundamental political decision to reject Austrian mediation and refuse the Frankfurt peace terms made the military brilliance irrelevant. The abdication at Fontainebleau in April 1814 was the deserved consequence of a politics in opposition to the lights of the time, the dispositions of the peoples, and local conditions.
The Elba episode and the Hundred Days followed. Napoleon returned to France in March 1815, landing at Cannes and marching through mountain roads to avoid the Rhône valley. At Grenoble, the battalion sent to arrest him was won over at pistol range; Lyon fell; Paris opened its gates as Louis XVIII fled. The men who rallied to Bonaparte did so for different reasons: some moved by genuine military devotion, some by hatred of the Bourbons, some by personal advantage. These three motives were not equivalent.
The Acte Additionnel of April 1815 — Napoleon’s proclaimed return to constitutional principles — was a clandestine work written by valets under the master’s dictation, in which despotism veiled itself with some modesty and pushed to its last terms the doctrine of Machiavelli. Waterloo (June 18, 1815) ended the Hundred Days. The rout of the French army, Napoleon’s return to Paris, and his second abdication — this time in favour of his son Napoleon II, a constitutional fiction the Chambers declined to accept — closed the military career.
8. Final Judgment
The final judgment on Napoleon is contained in a single sentence that serves as the epigraph to his entire story: Napoleon Bonaparte was a great error of nature that she cannot commit twice. He had no model; he will have no imitators. His system of politics, strongly conceived, was outside human proportions and almost ideal in its coherence — but ideal for whom? For the man who would rule without consent, without law, without the harmony of passion and reason that makes political life possible.
The ambition that consumed all other qualities, the cold resolution that operated without the check of a sensitive soul, the vast intelligence applied without moral direction — these made him the greatest commander of his age and the worst statesman. He destroyed the Republic that had raised him, exhausted France in wars that could not be won, and left Europe in ruins and his dynasty extinct. The history of Napoleon Bonaparte, as written by the men who lived through his rise and fall, is the history of a genius without character, a soldier without a statesman, and a revolution that devoured its own children.

entities/gouverneur-morris.title: Gouverneur Morris
entities/gouverneur-morris.content:
Gouverneur Morris
He arrived in Paris in February 1789 with the ink barely dry on the Constitution of the United States — a document he had written with his own hand as chairman of the Committee of Style, the man who gave the world the words “We the People.” He was thirty-six years old, tall, commanding, with a wooden leg below the left knee (lost when a runaway horse overturned his phaeton in a Philadelphia street in 1780), and a New York Federalist’s deep suspicion of enthusiasm in politics. He came on commercial business for Robert Morris, the financier of the American Revolution — no relation, but the man who had been his chief in the Superintendent of Finance office during the war. The business was the tobacco contract with the Farmers-General of France, a tangled inheritance from the old system of monopoly that was unraveling even as he stepped off the ship at Havre.
But within weeks of his landing, the world he had come to negotiate in began to dissolve.
The Green Diary
On his first days in Paris, Morris visited the shop of one Marquis, at À l’Espérance, rue Neuve des Petits Champs, and bought a blank-book bound in apple-green vellum. On March 1, 1789, he made the first entry. The diary that followed — written in a terse, precise hand, no paragraph breaks, business and politics and weather and women all in the same breath — became the most sustained American eyewitness account of the French Revolution ever written. He kept it for nearly four years, through the fall of the Bastille, the October Days, the flight to Varennes, the storming of the Tuileries, and the September Massacres. After August 10, 1792, when his house on the rue de la Planche became a refuge for royalists fleeing the insurrection, the diary fell silent. But by then the record was already extraordinary.
That first entry ran: “This Morning employed in Writing after my Return from M! Le Nd with whom I breakfasted and conferred on the Means of proceeding further with Respect to the Tobacco. I suggested to him a Plan for drawing Silver from Havanna which he did not seem to like… Dine with M! Du Molley. Madame wishes some American Plants and Seeds. Go to the french Theatre. The Misanthrope is acted with great and deserved Applause.” Already the pattern was set: business, society, observation — the three threads of his Paris life wound together on the same page, each given the same weight.
Business in Revolutionary Paris
The tobacco contract with the Farmers-General was the surface reason for Morris’s journey. Robert Morris, the Philadelphia merchant-prince whose wealth had helped finance the Revolution, had negotiated a monopoly on supplying the French tobacco market. The contract was now in dispute: the American end had been undercut by a competing agreement, the French end was tangled in the Farm’s labyrinthine bureaucracy, and the political crisis was making everyone reluctant to pay. Morris spent his first year in Paris shuttling between Le Couteulx et Cie (the bankers who acted as intermediaries), Le Normand (the Farm’s representative), and an endless series of dinners and conferences at which nothing was quite decided.
“Paris is if possible a worse place for Business than Virginia,” he wrote early on. “Every Body here has his Country Seat and comes to Town to do Business once in three or four Days and then works not to finish but to get Rid of Work that he may again get out of Town. Indeed Pleasure is the great Business.” He pressed, cajoled, drafted memoranda, wrote sharp letters, and slowly extracted concessions. The tobacco negotiations would run for years, interleaved with the Revolution’s convulsions; he was still trying to collect payment when the monarchy itself had ceased to exist.
The same commercial thread ran through every phase of his time in France. He worked the whale oil trade (a major American export), the tariff rates under debate in the Assembly committees, the Dutch banking houses for loans to develop the Delaware ironworks at Trenton, the London bankers for Robert Morris’s sprawling credit network. He lobbied ministers, drafted memorials, calculated exchange rates, and recorded the assignat’s accelerating depreciation with the precision of a man watching his own money evaporate. The diary in 1791 has a section the editor titled “Whales and Nicotine” — two weeks of concentrated lobbying on both commodities at once, the commercial and the diplomatic merging into a single daily round.
The Salons and the Louvre
No account of Morris’s Paris years can separate the business from the social, and no social thread ran deeper than his connection with Adèle de Flahaut. He met her in March 1789 at a dinner at the Comte d’Angivillier’s — the Superintendent of the King’s Buildings, who had given her rooms in the Louvre. “She speaks English and is a pleasing Woman. If I might judge from Appearances, not a sworn Enemy to Intrigue,” he wrote. She was twenty-eight, married at eighteen to the fifty-three-year-old Comte de Flahaut, and the acknowledged mistress of Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord, then Bishop of Autun, by whom she had a young son. Her apartment in the Louvre — the blue room, as the diary calls it — became Morris’s fixed social coordinate in Paris, a place of refuge, conversation, and politics, where the news of the Revolution arrived before it reached the newspapers.
The triangle with Talleyrand gave the relationship its peculiar tension. The Bishop of Autun — lame, cynical, visionary, the man who would become the diplomat of diplomats — was Morris’s rival and his intellectual companion simultaneously. They dined together at Madame de Flahaut’s table, debated constitutions and finance, visited painters’ studios, and maintained a surface of civilized ease that did not quite conceal the competition beneath. “The eternal triangle was squared,” the editor observed: “there were pretty lady, antique husband, brilliant official lover, and triumphant newcomer.”
Morris’s other great social subject was Lafayette — the hero of two worlds, the man who had fought for American liberty and now commanded the National Guard of Paris. Morris studied him with the clinical attention of a portraitist who admires his subject and sees through him at the same time. Lafayette told him, in a moment of confidence, that he had “had the utmost Power his Heart could wish and is grown tired of it. That he has commanded absolutely an hundred thousand Men, has marched his Sovereign about the Streets as he pleased, prescribed the Degree of Applause which he should receive, and could have detained him Prisoner had he thought proper.” Morris’s private verdict: “He wishes therefore as soon as possible to return to private Life. In this last Expression he deceives himself or wishes to deceive me; a little of both perhaps. But in Fact he is the Lover of Freedom from Ambition, of which there are two Kinds, the one born of Pride, the other of Vanity and his partakes most of the latter.”
Jefferson was a regular presence — the American Minister, with whom Morris visited the National Assembly, exchanged political analyses, and compared notes on Parisian life. Their relationship was cordial but not warm; Jefferson’s enthusiasm for the Revolution was something Morris could not share, and the tobacco dispute that had brought Morris to France had originated in part from Jefferson’s role in dismantling the Morris monopoly. Still, they dined together, consulted on commercial questions, and maintained the mutual respect of two men who understood that they disagreed on fundamentals.
Observer of the Revolution
Morris watched the Revolution unfold with the same compressed precision he gave his business accounts. The entries for July 12–14, 1789 — the days the Bastille fell — are among the most vivid in the diary.
On July 12, Necker was dismissed. Morris was dining with the Maréchal de Castries when the Marshal took him aside and told him. The news broke Paris open. Morris rode through the city and witnessed a cavalry charge in the Place Louis Quinze — sabres drawn, stones thrown, pistols fired without effect. “The People are employed in breaking open the Armorers’ Shops,” he noted, “and presently a large Body of the Gardes Françoises appear with Bayonets fixed, in the Garden, mingled with the Mob.” He predicted what was coming: “If the Representatives of the Tiers have formed a just Estimate of their Constituents, in ten Days all France will be in Commotion.”
On July 13, he walked to the Louvre with a green bow in his hat — “the Fashion of the Day which every Body is obliged to comply with who means to march in Peace. It is somewhat whimsical that this Day of Violence and Tumult is the only one in which I have dared to walk the Streets, but as no Carriages are abroad but the Fiacres I do not hazard being crushed, and I apprehend nothing from the Populace.” He recorded the forced prisons, the seized grain from the Monastery of Saint-Lazare (“on every Cart a Friar”), the rumors from Versailles.
July 14 was in some ways the quietest of the three days in his telling — he was detained by business with Nesbitt at the Temple, stopped twice for weapons searches — but the entry for July 22 is the one that stops the reader. Walking under the arcade of the Palais-Royal, he saw the head and body of Foulon, the old minister, carried through the streets on a pike, the body dragged naked on the earth, and then Bertier his son-in-law, also torn to pieces. “Gracious God what a People!” he wrote.
Lafayette gave him a passport to visit the Bastille on July 21. Morris went with Madame de Flahaut, the Abbé Bertrand, and Capellis. The stench was terrible — “more than I wish to see,” he wrote. The same day, visiting a painter’s studio, he saw a canvas titled Love Escaped from His Cage and proposed a different subject: the guardsman who, seizing the Bastille gate and unable to bring it down, cried to his comrades to pull on his legs, and held while a dozen men pulled him like a rope, racking his joints, until the gate gave way. “To represent him drawn out of Joint with his Head turned round, encouraging them to draw still harder, must I think have a fine Effect.” The Bishop of Autun — Talleyrand — agreed entirely.
The Secret Royalist
Throughout 1791 and 1792, as the Revolution radicalized, Morris’s position shifted from observer to participant in a clandestine and ultimately tragic royalist operation. His sympathies had always been with constitutional monarchy — he had helped write an American constitution with a strong executive, and he watched the French fumble toward a unicameral assembly with a powerless king and predicted failure from the start. “I preach incessantly Respect for the Constitution under which we live and for that which is forming here,” he wrote. But by 1792, preaching was no longer relevant. The king’s flight to Varennes in June 1791 had changed everything. Morris’s analysis was cold and clear: “He changed every Thing and now the general wish seems to be for a Republic, which is quite in the natural Order of Things.”
The royalist counter-conspiracy of 1792 drew him in through a chain of contacts: the Comte de La Marck, the former minister Montmorin, and the Provençal agent Brémond. The scheme was to organize armed men inside Paris who would rally to the king’s defense at designated points in the event of an insurrection. Morris held 5,000 louis d’or in his house — gold coins earmarked for paying reliable men when the moment came. The money had been paid out of royal funds through Brémond; the purses of twenty louis were divided and kept at Morris’s house pending activation of the network.
The moment never came. On August 10, 1792, the insurrectionary sections stormed the Tuileries before the network could be activated. The Swiss Guard was massacred. The king took refuge with the Assembly. The monarchy fell. Morris’s house on the rue de la Planche became a shelter for former minister Monciel and his family, along with others implicated in the royalist resistance. The diary was suppressed — it would have been a death warrant for everyone under his roof if discovered.
The 5,000 louis became a prolonged ordeal. Brémond had removed the gold to Swiss bankers and Morris spent years afterward pursuing its recovery, finally rendering an account to Madame Royale — the Princess Marie-Thérèse, Louis XVI’s daughter — after her release from the Temple prison. The accounting survives in the diary’s appendix: a document of remarkable clarity and moral seriousness, tracing what had become of every coin.
The American Minister
In May 1792, despite French republican protests — the Girondins knew his monarchist sympathies — Washington appointed Morris as United States Minister to France. The appointment was controversial. Morris had been too candid about his views; he had written to Washington that the Revolution was devouring itself; the French foreign ministry had lobbied against his accreditation. But Washington trusted him, and Jefferson as Secretary of State supported the appointment for reasons of policy if not personal sympathy.
Morris presented his credentials and entered the diplomatic corps at the worst possible moment. Within weeks, the June 20 invasion of the Tuileries forced the king to put on a red cap and drink to the nation from a bottle handed to him by a rioter. Within two months, the monarchy was gone. Within three, the September Massacres had killed Montmorin — the minister with whom Morris had dined and corresponded — and filled the streets of Paris with bodies.
After August 10, Morris’s dispatches to Jefferson became the primary American channel for information about the collapsing French state. He reported on the abolition of the monarchy, the proclamation of the Republic, the formation of the National Convention, the trial of the king. His position required diplomatic restraint, but his private assessments can be read between the lines of his official correspondence. He watched Robespierre survive Louvet’s accusation in the Convention — “Robespierre has got thro his Affair with Éclat” — and noted the rise of the Jacobins with the same cold eye he had turned on Lafayette’s vanity.
The Diarist’s Voice
What makes Morris’s diary extraordinary is not merely the events it records but the voice that records them. He writes in short, declarative sentences, each fact standing alone, business and atrocity and the weather given the same flat emphasis. He is laconic about violence: the heads on pikes are recorded in the same paragraph as the price of dinner. He is ironic about human weakness, including his own: “I have never yet mentioned to you that M! Jefferson… commands very much Respect in this Country and which is merited by good Sense and good Intentions,” he wrote to Robert Morris. “The french, who pique themselves on possessing the Graces, very readily excuse in others the Want of them; and to be an Étranger (like Charity) covers a Multitude of Sins.”
He is precise about business: the tobacco prices, the exchange rates, the discount on bills, the calculations of profit and loss that run like a double-entry ledger through the revolutionary turmoil. He is tender with Madame de Flahaut and dry with Lafayette and sharp with the politicians he sees making a constitution that cannot work. He is, above all, a man who refuses to be swept along by the emotional currents of his time. “I apprehend nothing from the Populace” — the sentence could stand as his motto through the whole four years.
The diary was published in 1939, edited by Beatrix Cary Davenport, who wove editorial commentary and connecting letters into the text. The original manuscript — written in a blank book bought at À l’Espérance — is the record of a man who went to Paris to negotiate a tobacco contract and ended up holding royal gold in his house while the monarchy fell around him, writing it all down in a voice so distinct that two centuries later it still sounds like a man speaking directly across a dinner table.
He left France in 1794, recalled by Washington, the United States having recognized the Republic. He returned to Morrisania — the manor on the Harlem River where he had been born in 1752 — and spent his remaining years as a farmer, a Federalist senator, and a determined opponent of Jefferson’s embargo. But the French years stayed with him. The green diary, the Louvre salon, the heads on pikes on the rue Saint-Honoré, the 5,000 louis that never bought what it was meant to buy, the king he had tried to save — they formed the great subject of his life, and he knew it.

entities/louis-xvi.title: Louis XVI
entities/louis-xvi.content:
Louis XVI
Character and Personality
Louis-Auguste de France, who ascended the throne as Louis XVI on 10 May 1774 at the age of nineteen, carried into kingship a temperament singularly ill-suited to the times that awaited him. He was a man of genuine goodness — a quality on which virtually every observer agreed — but his virtues were those of a private gentleman rather than a sovereign. His reign would become a tragedy of character meeting circumstance at the worst possible hour.
He was a big man, tall and heavily built, with a thick neck and a phlegmatic constitution that gave him an appearance of dullness. In his youth he had been awkward and shy, uncomfortable in the elaborate rituals of Versailles, preferring the company of a few trusted servants to the ceaseless performance of court life. An operation performed in 1786 — a fistula or some related complaint, kept largely secret — left its mark on him. His gait became irregular, his speech slightly thickened, and those who saw him in the years that followed often remarked on a certain heaviness of movement and hesitation of utterance that compounded the impression of sluggishness. By 1789, American minister Gouverneur Morris, who observed the king at close quarters during the critical months, noted frankly that the king was already in physical decline — a man whose body seemed to be failing him even as his throne began to shake.
The king’s piety was deep and sincere. He attended mass daily, observed the full liturgical calendar of the Church, and confessed regularly. This religious devotion, however, was of a simple, almost peasant-like quality — it was not the intellectual faith of a theologian but the unquestioning belief of a man who had been raised to see the altar and the throne as twin pillars of the same divine order. It gave him steadiness of conscience but not flexibility of mind. When the Revolution eventually demanded that he choose between his crown and his salvation, his piety would paralyse him rather than guide him.
His private tastes ran to the mechanical and the physical. He was an enthusiastic hunter — perhaps the only arena of life in which he displayed genuine vigour and decisiveness — and he spent as many days as possible in the saddle pursuing stag and boar through the forests around Versailles. The hunt was his escape, his one reliable pleasure, and he resented any interruption of it with a petulance that surprised those who saw only his usual placidity. More unusually for a king, he had a passion for locksmithing. He maintained a private forge and workshop at Versailles, where he spent hours working with iron and steel, fashioning locks and mechanical devices under the tutelage of a skilled locksmith named Gamin. The Comte de Saint-Germain is said to have remarked that the king would have been happier as a locksmith than as a monarch — an observation that captured something essential about the man’s misfit with his destiny.
Those who saw him daily at court, like the queen’s first lady-in-waiting, noted his reserve and his difficulty with emotional expression. He was not unfeeling — his correspondence with his ministers shows genuine distress at the suffering of his people — but he lacked the easy warmth that inspires loyalty. His marriage to Marie Antoinette, initially cold and unconsummated for seven years due to a physical condition that was eventually corrected by a minor surgical procedure, had settled into a relationship of mutual if undemonstrative affection by the 1780s. The king was devoted to his children, especially the Dauphin, and his family life at Versailles was the one domain where he seemed genuinely at ease.
To the Swiss commander the Baron de Besenval, who had observed the court for decades, the king appeared as a man constitutionally incapable of the kind of decisive action that monarchy required. Besenval, who commanded the royal troops in Paris and saw the king’s hesitation during the early crises, concluded that Louis possessed every private virtue — honesty, frugality, kindness, modesty — but lacked entirely the public qualities of a ruler: the capacity to command, to threaten, to punish, and, when necessary, to shed blood for the preservation of order. The king shrank from violence with a physical revulsion that Besenval found admirable in a man but disastrous in a king.
Jean-François Marmontel, the historian and moralist who watched the Revolution unfold from a constitutional-monarchist perspective, drew much the same portrait. In his memoirs he described a king whose intentions were uniformly good, whose heart was just, but whose understanding of power was so rudimentary that he could not conceive of men acting from base motives. Louis believed, Marmontel wrote with a mixture of affection and despair, that if he simply explained his difficulties honestly to his people, they would respond with the same goodwill he felt toward them. This naivety — this assumption that the world was as honest as himself — was the fatal flaw that his enemies calculated with precision.
The Crisis 1787–1789
The fiscal crisis that forced the king’s hand was of long gestation. The American War of Independence, in which France had played a decisive role in humbling Britain, had left the treasury exhausted. Year after year, expenditure outstripped revenue, and by 1786 the deficit had reached a point where even the most optimistic ministers could see no way forward without fundamental reform of the tax system. The problem was not merely arithmetic: it was political. The privileged orders — the clergy and the nobility — were exempt from the principal taxes, and any attempt to make them pay provoked immediate resistance from the Parlements, the sovereign courts that registered royal edicts and claimed a constitutional voice in the nation’s affairs.
The king’s first response, characteristically, was to seek counsel. He summoned an Assembly of Notables in February 1787 — a hand-picked body of 144 princes, dukes, magistrates, and clergymen — to approve a package of reforms proposed by his controller-general, Calonne. The centrepiece was a universal land tax that would fall on all landowners regardless of status. The Notables, many of whom were themselves the principal beneficiaries of the tax exemptions, refused. Calonne was dismissed. His successor, Brienne, attempted to force the reforms through the Parlement of Paris, but the Parlement declared that only the Estates-General of the realm — the ancient representative assembly that had not met since 1614 — could consent to new taxes.
The king’s position throughout this struggle was curiously passive. He alternated between yielding to the Parlement and attempting to coerce it, never fully committing to either course. He exiled the Parlement to Troyes, then recalled it; he attempted a lit de justice to browbeat the magistrates, then gave way; he dismissed one minister after another — Turgot, Necker, Calonne, Brienne — each time hoping that a new face would resolve what was fundamentally a crisis of authority rather than of personnel. The court watched his vacillations with growing alarm. Besenval, from his command post in Paris, saw the king’s authority eroding month by month and wrote despairingly of a sovereign who could neither impose his will nor choose a course and stick to it.
Finally, in the summer of 1788, the king capitulated to the logic of events. He agreed to summon the Estates-General, hoping that this ancient body would somehow restore the harmony that his ministers had failed to achieve. The decision was taken with the same good faith that characterised all his public acts. He genuinely believed that the representatives of the three orders — clergy, nobility, and commoners — would join with him in a common effort to restore the kingdom’s finances and address the grievances of the people. What he did not understand — what no one at Versailles fully understood — was that the act of summoning the Estates-General after 175 years of disuse had unleashed forces that no king could control.
The question of how the Estates-General should be constituted became the explosive issue of the winter of 1788–1789. The Third Estate — the commoners — demanded that their representation be doubled to match that of the two privileged orders combined, and that voting should be by head rather than by order. The Parlement of Paris, in a moment of disastrous misjudgement, ruled that the Estates-General must follow the forms of 1614, which would have given the clergy and nobility an automatic majority. The resulting outcry swept through France. Pamphlets, petitions, and demonstrations multiplied. The king, after weeks of indecision, accepted the principle of doubling the Third Estate but left the question of voting method unresolved — a compromise that satisfied no one and merely postponed the confrontation.
In the streets of Paris, the agitation grew steadily through the spring of 1789. The winter had been the harshest in decades; bread prices had risen to levels that the urban poor could not afford. Hungry crowds gathered in the Palais-Royal, the great arcaded square owned by the king’s cousin, the Duke of Orléans, where orators harangued them daily against the aristocracy, the clergy, and the court. The king, still at Versailles, received reports of these disturbances with genuine distress but without any corresponding sense of urgency. He continued to hunt, to work at his forge, to attend mass, to preside over the endless ceremonies of the court, as though the crisis were a temporary misunderstanding that would resolve itself in time.
March–July 1789
The Estates-General opened on 5 May 1789 in a vast hall at Versailles, with all the pomp that the court could muster. The king appeared before the assembled deputies in full regalia, accompanied by the queen, his brothers, and the princes of the blood. To the historian Marmontel, who was present, he seemed at that moment every inch a sovereign — dignified, earnest, visibly moved by the occasion. His speech, which he delivered in a simple, unornamented style that was entirely his own, spoke of his love for his people and his hope that the Estates would bring about a new era of happiness and prosperity. He promised reform, economy, and justice. Many of those present wept.
But within weeks the atmosphere had soured irrevocably. The Third Estate, having waited in vain for the privileged orders to join them in a common assembly, declared itself on 17 June to be the National Assembly — the sole legitimate representative of the French people. The king, pressed by the court party that surrounded the queen, responded by closing the hall where the Third Estate met. The deputies, led by Jean-Sylvain Bailly and the Comte de Mirabeau, reconvened in a nearby indoor tennis court and swore the famous oath: they would not disperse until they had given France a constitution.
The king hesitated. He announced a Royal Session for 23 June at which he would present a reform programme of his own, but his plans were undermined by the growing radicalism of the Third Estate and by the incompetence of his advisers. When the Royal Session was held, the king declared the acts of the Third Estate null and void and ordered the deputies to separate by order. The Third Estate refused to budge. When the master of ceremonies repeated the royal command, Mirabeau uttered his thunderous reply: “Go tell those who sent you that we are here by the will of the people, and that we will not leave except at the point of the bayonet.”
The king, faced with open defiance, did nothing. He could have ordered the troops to clear the hall; he could have dissolved the Estates-General by royal decree; he could have retreated to a provincial stronghold and raised the standard of civil war. Instead, he yielded. On 27 June, he ordered the clergy and nobility to join the National Assembly. The Revolution had its first victory, and the king had revealed the full extent of his weakness.
Through July, the crisis deepened. The king dismissed his popular minister Necker on 11 July — a move dictated by the queen’s circle, which blamed Necker for encouraging the Third Estate. The news of Necker’s dismissal reached Paris on 12 July and ignited an explosion of popular fury. Crowds gathered, orators inflamed them, troops under the Prince de Lambesc charged a gathering in the Tuileries Gardens, and by the morning of 14 July the city was in open insurrection. The mob seized arms from the Invalides and marched on the Bastille, the ancient fortress-prison that symbolised royal authority in the heart of Paris.
The Bastille fell after a brief and confused fight. Its governor, the Marquis de Launay, was murdered along with several of his officers. The heads of the dead were paraded through the streets on pikes. When the news reached Versailles, the king is said to have asked: “Is it a revolt?” The Duke of La Rochefoucauld replied: “No, Sire, it is a revolution.”
The king’s response was characteristic. He appeared before the National Assembly on 15 July, accompanied only by his brothers, and announced that he had ordered the troops to withdraw from Paris and Versailles. The following day, he went to Paris in person — a journey that had been arranged by the revolutionaries to demonstrate his submission. At the Hôtel de Ville, the new mayor, Bailly, presented him with the tricolour cockade — the blue, white, and red badge that had been adopted by the revolutionary militia. The king accepted it and pinned it to his hat. The crowd cheered. He returned to Versailles as a constitutional monarch in name, but the power had already shifted.
In the weeks that followed, the National Assembly worked through the nights of August to dismantle the entire structure of the old regime. On 4 August, the deputies voted to abolish feudalism, seigneurial rights, tithes, and all the privileges of the nobility and clergy. On 26 August, they published the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which proclaimed the sovereignty of the nation and the natural rights of every man. The king, who had accepted the tricolour under duress, delayed ratifying these decrees. He could not bring himself to approve the abolition of a system that had consecrated the throne for a thousand years. His hesitation would cost him dearly.
October 1789
By the autumn of 1789, Paris was hungry and suspicious. The bread shortages that had plagued the spring had not been resolved; the harvest of 1789 was poor, and grain did not flow freely into the capital. Rumours spread that the court at Versailles was stockpiling flour, that the queen was plotting a counter-revolution, that foreign regiments were being summoned to crush the National Assembly. On 1 October, a banquet was held in the opera house at Versailles for the king’s bodyguards. When the royal family appeared, the officers tore off the tricolour cockades and trampled them underfoot, replacing them with white cockades — the colour of the Bourbon monarchy. News of this incident reached Paris and detonated the smouldering tension.
On the morning of 5 October, a crowd of women — fishwives, market women, working-class mothers — gathered at the Hôtel de Ville, demanding bread. They were joined by men armed with pikes and muskets, and by detachments of the National Guard under the Marquis de La Fayette. The mob, thousands strong, began the twelve-mile march from Paris to Versailles in the rain.
The king was hunting at Meudon when word reached him. He returned to Versailles to find the palace grounds filling with the ragged, angry crowd. Throughout the night, deputations of women came before the king and the Assembly, demanding bread and the royal family’s return to Paris. The king, exhausted and overwhelmed, promised to ratify the August decrees and to provide food for the capital. The crowd was not satisfied.
At dawn on 6 October, a group of the more determined rioters forced their way into the palace. They surged through the marble corridors, killing two bodyguards whose heads they mounted on pikes. The queen, awakened by the uproar, fled barefoot through a secret passage to the king’s apartments. La Fayette finally restored order, but the mob had achieved its aim. The king appeared on the balcony with the queen and the Dauphin. The crowd shouted for them to come to Paris.
Louis XVI agreed. That afternoon, the royal family left Versailles — the great palace that had been the seat of French monarchy since Louis XIV — never to return. The procession wound its way slowly to Paris, the king’s carriage surrounded by a shouting, singing multitude carrying the heads of the murdered guards on pikes. Behind the carriage followed wagons laden with flour from the palace stores. The king and his family were installed in the Tuileries Palace, a dilapidated royal residence that had stood empty for years. They were, to all intents, prisoners.
The Constitutional Monarchy 1789–1791
The two years that followed the October Days were a strange interregnum in which the forms of monarchy were preserved while the substance of power drained away. The king lived at the Tuileries, venturing out occasionally for state ceremonies or for walks in the Tuileries Gardens, where the Parisians could see him and — for a time — still cheer him. He continued to perform the routine duties of a sovereign: he reviewed the National Guard, received ambassadors, affixed his signature to laws passed by the Assembly. But his heart was no longer in the enterprise.
The National Assembly, meanwhile, was engaged in the vast project of remaking France. It reorganized the country into eighty-three departments, abolished the ancient provinces, suppressed the religious orders, nationalized church lands, and — most controversially — imposed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, which required all priests and bishops to swear allegiance to the state rather than to the Pope. The king’s conscience revolted. He was a devout Catholic, and he could not accept a law that he believed would divide the Church and damn the souls of those who obeyed it. He delayed his assent for months, and when he finally gave it in December 1790, he did so with a heavy heart — a gesture of surrender that satisfied no one and alienated the pious clergy who had remained loyal to him.
Throughout this period, the king maintained a secret correspondence with foreign monarchs — his brother-in-law, the Emperor Leopold II of Austria; the King of Prussia; the King of Sweden — begging them to intervene on his behalf. He had become, in effect, the prisoner of a revolution he could neither accept nor resist, and his only hope was that foreign armies would restore him to his rightful authority.
This double game — public acceptance of the Revolution, private plotting against it — culminated in the disastrous flight to Varennes.
Flight to Varennes
The plan was simple in conception: the royal family would escape from the Tuileries in disguise, travel by carriage to the eastern frontier, and place themselves under the protection of the royalist army commanded by the Marquis de Bouillé. From there, the king would issue a proclamation rejecting the Revolution and calling for the restoration of the monarchy on his own terms. The queen, who had been the driving force behind the plan, organized the details with the help of the Swedish Count Axel von Fersen.
On the night of 20 June 1791, the plan was put into action. The king, disguised as a valet, the queen as a governess, and the Dauphin as a girl — the elaborate disguises that were meant to deceive the sentries — slipped out of the Tuileries one by one and made their way to a waiting carriage on the boulevard. By midnight, the royal family was on the road east, heading for the fortress of Montmédy.
The escape went smoothly for the first twelve hours. The great berlin carriage, drawn by six horses, lumbered through the summer night. The king, who had brought his maps and travel guides, was in good spirits — perhaps the happiest he had been since the fall of the Bastille. But delays accumulated. The carriage lost time at almost every relay station. By the time they reached the small town of Sainte-Menehould, they were hours behind schedule.
There, the postmaster, Jean-Baptiste Drouet, recognized the king from his portrait on an assignat — a revolutionary banknote — and raised the alarm. The carriage rolled on toward Varennes, a walled town on the River Aisne, where the horses were to be changed for the last stage of the journey. But the relay had been sabotaged; the horses were not ready. When the king’s party arrived at Varennes after midnight, they found the bridge blocked and the town in arms. The local officials confronted the king. He identified himself, produced his passport — which identified him as the Baron de Korff, a Russian nobleman — and tried to brazen it out. But the game was up. By morning, the National Guard had arrived from the surrounding towns, and the royal family was escorted back to Paris, a slow, humiliating procession through crowds that had transformed overnight from subjects into captors.
The king’s attempt at escape destroyed what remained of the popular trust in the monarchy. The Jacobin clubs, led by Robespierre and Desmoulins, called for the abolition of the monarchy and the establishment of a republic. The Assembly, still dominated by moderates, temporized: it suspended the king from his functions, declared him temporarily incapacitated, and began to consider the future of the monarchy. For six weeks, Louis and his family remained virtual prisoners in the Tuileries while the Assembly debated.
In the end, the Assembly produced an elaborate fiction: the king had not fled; he had been abducted. He was restored to the throne on 14 September 1791, having sworn an oath to uphold the new Constitution that the Assembly had finally completed. The Constitution of 1791 made France a constitutional monarchy. The king retained the title of King of the French — no longer King of France — and a suspensive veto over legislation, but his powers were sharply circumscribed. He could not dissolve the Assembly, could not declare war or make peace without its consent, could not command the armed forces directly. The experiment of limited monarchy had begun.
The Fall 1792
The constitutional monarchy lasted less than a year. The sources of tension that had produced the Revolution did not disappear with the adoption of the Constitution. The émigrés — the nobles and clergy who had fled France — gathered in the German states and agitated for foreign intervention. The revolutionary factions in Paris, led by the Jacobins and the more radical Cordeliers, denounced the king as a traitor and demanded a republic. The European monarchies, Austria and Prussia foremost, viewed the Revolution with growing alarm and issued increasingly bellicose declarations.
The king was caught between forces he could neither control nor conciliate. In March 1792, under pressure from the Assembly, he accepted a ministry dominated by the Girondins, the faction that favoured war with Austria. The king himself favoured war, hoping that a French defeat would lead to the collapse of the Revolution and his restoration by foreign arms. On 20 April 1792, he appeared before the Assembly and proposed a declaration of war against Austria. The Assembly voted overwhelmingly in favour.
The war went badly from the start. French armies fled before the Austrian advance. The king exercised his veto to block two key measures: the decree that would have summoned a provincial army of twenty thousand National Guards to defend Paris, and the decree that would have exiled the refractory priests who had refused to swear allegiance to the Civil Constitution. His vetoes were constitutionally valid, but they confirmed the popular suspicion that he was in league with France’s enemies. The sections of Paris — the popular assemblies of the city’s forty-eight districts — began to prepare for insurrection.
On 20 June, a crowd of several thousand armed Parisians invaded the Tuileries Palace, demanding that the king recall the decrees he had vetoed. The king received them with what many observers considered remarkable composure. He submitted to their shouts and threats for several hours, drinking to the health of the nation, accepting a red cap of liberty, and allowing himself to be harangued by a succession of popular orators. He refused, however, to revoke his vetoes. The crowd eventually withdrew, having accomplished nothing except to demonstrate the impotence of the monarchy.
The decisive blow came on 10 August 1792. The Paris Commune — the revolutionary municipal government that had formed in the aftermath of the 20 June demonstration — ordered the tocsin to be rung. The sections of Paris mobilized their National Guard battalions. A vast armed column, estimated at twenty thousand men, marched on the Tuileries. The king, at the last moment, abandoned the palace and sought refuge with the Legislative Assembly, which was sitting in the nearby Riding School. He brought his family with him. As they crossed the garden, they could hear the firing begin.
The Swiss Guard, left to defend the palace without clear orders from the king, fought bravely but was overwhelmed. Hundreds of Swiss were massacred in the palace courtyards and the gardens — shot down as they tried to surrender, their bodies stripped and mutilated. The Assembly, sitting in continuous session, heard the roar of the crowd and the crackle of musket fire. Finally, the president announced that the royal family would be lodged in the reporters’ box, where they could hear the debate. The king sat in silence, the Dauphin on his knee, as the Assembly voted to suspend him from his functions. The monarchy was over.
The royal family was transferred to the Temple, a medieval fortress in the eastern quarter of Paris that the revolutionaries had converted into a prison. Here, in the tower where the Knights Templar had once been held, Louis XVI — no longer king, now simply Louis Capet — began his final confinement.
The Trial and Execution
The National Convention, which succeeded the Legislative Assembly in September 1792, proclaimed the Republic on 21 September. The question of what to do with the former king hung over its proceedings from the very first sessions. The Jacobins, led by Robespierre and Saint-Just, demanded his immediate trial and execution. The Girondins, more cautious, argued that the inviolability of the king’s person was guaranteed by the Constitution of 1791 and that he should be deposed and exiled rather than tried. The debate raged for weeks.
In November, a remarkable discovery was made: a secret iron chest in the Tuileries, which the king had built for his locksmithing work — the very hobby that had marked him as a man of the people — was found to contain a cache of incriminating documents. The correspondence revealed the king’s secret dealings with foreign powers, his denunciations of the Revolution in his private letters, and his plans to restore his absolute authority by force of arms. For the Jacobins, this was the proof they needed. The king was a traitor who had conspired against the nation while pretending to accept its laws.
The trial began on 11 December 1792, when Louis was brought before the Convention for the first time. He was questioned for hours by Bertrand Barère, the president of the Convention, in a proceeding that was as much political theatre as judicial process. The king answered with composure. He denied the authenticity of some of the documents, explained others as expressions of his true feelings at a time when he was not free, and refused to recognize the Convention’s authority to try him. “I was your king,” he told them, “and you have no right to judge me.”
The king’s defence was conducted by three lawyers: Chrétien de Malesherbes, a former minister who had once been the king’s censor — and had, ironically, helped to disseminate the Enlightenment writings that had undermined the monarchy — along with Guillaume-Chrétien de Lamoignon de Malesherbes and Raymond Desèze, the latter a renowned orator from Bordeaux. Desèze delivered the principal defence on 26 December. It was a long, eloquent, and ultimately futile speech. He argued that the king could not be tried under the Constitution of 1791, which had declared him inviolable; that the Convention had no power to act as both prosecutor and judge; and that Louis had never knowingly betrayed a nation that he had always loved.
The Convention was not moved. On 15 January 1793, the deputies voted on three questions. First, was Louis Capet guilty of conspiracy against the public liberty and of attacks against the general security of the state? The vote was overwhelming: 693 in favour, none against (with some abstentions). Second, should the verdict be submitted to the people for ratification? The Girondins had proposed a referendum, hoping to save the king through popular mercy. The Convention voted it down, 424 to 287. Third, what punishment should be inflicted? This was the roll-call vote that would determine the king’s fate.
For three days, from 16 to 18 January, each of the 721 deputies mounted the tribune in alphabetical order and pronounced his verdict. It was a harrowing spectacle. Some deputies wept as they voted. Others, notably the Duke of Orléans — the king’s own cousin, who had taken the revolutionary name Philippe Égalité — voted for death. In the end, 361 deputies voted for death without conditions, 334 for death with a stay or for imprisonment, and 26 for various other penalties. The majority was a single vote — 361 to 360 — when the ambiguous votes were counted. The king of France was condemned to die.
On Sunday, 20 January, the Convention’s delegation came to the Temple to inform the king of his sentence. He received the news with greater calm than many of those who brought it. He asked for a three-day reprieve to prepare his soul; it was denied. He requested permission to see his family; this was granted. That evening, he met with his wife, his sister, and his two children for the last time. The interview lasted an hour and three-quarters. When it was over, the queen and the children were led away. The king spent the night in prayer and confession with the Abbé Edgeworth de Firmont, an Irish priest who had been smuggled into the Temple to administer the last rites.
The morning of 21 January 1793 was cold and grey. The king was awakened at five o’clock. He heard mass, received communion, and prepared himself for death. At around eight o’clock, the guards arrived. The king handed them his will, a packet of personal effects for his family, and his wedding ring. He was taken to a closed green carriage, which rolled slowly through the silent, heavily guarded streets to the Place de la Révolution — today’s Place de la Concorde — where the guillotine had been erected.
The carriage halted at the foot of the scaffold. The king emerged, pale but composed. He attempted to address the crowd, shouting in a voice that carried across the vast square: “I die innocent of all the crimes of which I am accused. I pardon the authors of my death, and I pray to God that the blood you are about to shed may never fall upon France…” The drummers, under orders to drown out any speech, began to beat. The king was seized by the executioner, Charles-Henri Sanson, and his assistants. His coat was removed, his hands were tied behind his back, his hair was cut. For a moment, he resisted — a brief, instinctive struggle — but then he submitted. He was strapped to the plank and thrust under the blade.
The guillotine fell. Sanson lifted the severed head by the hair and displayed it to the crowd. The onlookers — many of whom had been kept at a distance behind a line of soldiers — erupted in shouts of “Vive la République!” The head of Louis XVI, the seventy-seventh king of France in the direct Capetian line, rolled into the basket.
Gouverneur Morris, who had remained in Paris through the darkest months of the Revolution, recorded the event in his diary with characteristic bluntness. He had seen the king often, had watched him decline from a good-natured if inept sovereign to a prisoner who could not save himself. He had warned of the coming catastrophe and had been ignored. Now, he noted simply the fact of the execution — a single line in his journal for 21 January 1793 — and recorded that the news had reached the American legation with the speed of a spreading stain. The monarchy had ended not with a battle but with a single swing of the blade, and the king who had been too weak for his throne had faced the scaffold with a dignity that had eluded him in life.
