entities/madame-roland.title: Madame Roland
entities/madame-roland.content:
Madame Roland
Marie-Jeanne Roland de la Platière (1754–1793) was the intellectual centre of the Girondin circle. Her husband Jean-Marie Roland served twice as Minister of the Interior; their apartment and salon in the Hôtel Britannique on the rue Guénégaud was the meeting place of the leading Girondins throughout 1791–1793. She was not merely a political hostess: she drafted many of her husband’s ministerial letters, conducted her own correspondence with deputies and writers, and formed sharply independent judgments on every figure she encountered. In the Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie prisons between August and November 1793, she wrote the memoirs that would become the definitive first-person account of the Girondin experience.
Early Life and Formation
She was born on 17 March 1754, the daughter of Gratien Phlipon, an engraver and goldsmith whose workshop on the Pont-Neuf employed a number of workers. Her father was active and vain about his appearance, fond of jewellery, ambitious in commerce beyond his craft, and ended by ruining himself. Her mother, Marguerite Bimont, was a patient and tactful woman who protected her daughter’s intellectual development without appearing to do so — permitting access to whatever books the girl could reach while maintaining the form of parental supervision.
Her access to books was early and intensive. At nine years old she carried Dacier’s translation of Plutarch’s Lives to church in place of a prayer book, and from that experience, she later wrote, dated the impressions and ideas that made her a republican without her knowing what the word meant. She read Fénelon’s Télémaque, Tasso’s Jerusalem Delivered, Voltaire’s Candide (reprimanded for it by a neighbour, unperturbed by her mother), Fénelon’s Treatise on the Education of Girls, and Locke on child education.
At eleven years and two months (May 1765) she entered the Convent of the Congrégation des dames on the rue Neuve-Saint-Étienne, faubourg Saint-Marcel. She had asked to go herself. The religious life was intense and genuinely felt; the convent was not oppressive but nourishing. She describes individual nuns with the same precision she later applied to political figures. The friendship with a nun called Sainte-Agathe outlasted the convent.
After the convent years her reading continued intensively: Saint Francis de Sales, Saint Augustine, Bossuet’s works of religious controversy — which, though written to defend Catholicism, acquainted her with objections to it and set her on the path of reasoning her belief. She passed successively through Jansenism, Cartesianism, Stoicism, deism, and finally to a scepticism tempered by her discovery of Rousseau. Of this progression she wrote wryly: “What roads, to end up with patriotism, which has put me in irons!”
Her mother’s death when Roland was twenty-one was the decisive emotional event of her young womanhood. An abscess in the head, unrecognised until the final effusion; Roland was away two hours on the afternoon of the day it happened and returned at five-thirty to find her mother struck. The grief was violent and physical: fainting, rigidity, loss of the faculty of attention, seeming derangement. The abbé Legrand, visiting, had the insight that she needed to talk about her mother rather than avoid the subject; he led her through conversations that gradually brought other thoughts alongside. When he judged her ready for a book, he brought her Rousseau’s Héloïse. “Its reading was truly my first distraction. I was twenty-one years old. Rousseau made on me then an impression comparable to what Plutarch had made at eight years old.”
Marriage and the Roland Household
She met Jean-Marie Roland through a correspondence that preceded their meeting. He was a manufacturing inspector in the Lyon generality, contributing to the Encyclopédie méthodique, whose brother came to see her one day bearing notes Roland was sending from his Italian travels. She read his travel journals and found his soul, his austere probity, his rigorous principles, his knowledge and taste appearing undisguised. She was thirty-two; he was forty-six. The marriage produced one daughter, Eudora.
The Salon and the Girondin Circle
The Rolands’ apartment in Paris became the nerve-centre of the Girondin network from 1791. Brissot came to visit them in February 1791 — the first meeting after a long correspondence. She describes his simple manners, his frankness, his natural negligence, in perfect harmony with the austerity of his principles — but found in him a kind of levity of spirit and character that did not suit the gravity of philosophy. “The best of men, good husband, tender father, faithful friend, virtuous citizen… confiding to the point of imprudence, gay, naïve, ingenuous as one is at fifteen, he was made to live with sages and to be the dupe of the wicked.”
Through Brissot’s circle the Rolands became part of the wider Girondin network. The apartment on the rue Guénégaud received Buzot, Vergniaud, Pétion, Barbaroux, Guadet, Gensonné, Louvet, and many others. The meetings were not formal salons in the ancien régime sense but political gatherings in a domestic space, at which Madame Roland was a full participant. It was in this setting that the political positions of the Girondin faction were formed: the war policy against Austria, the defence of constitutional legality against the Commune’s arbitrary power, and the conviction that the Revolution could be consolidated only through order.
The First Ministry (March–June 1792)
When the Girondins formed a cabinet in March 1792 under the constitutional monarchy — Dumouriez at Foreign Affairs, Servan at War, Clavière at Finance — Jean-Marie Roland was named Minister of the Interior. The appointment was of a genuine reformist administrator with deep expertise in French industry and commerce.
The ministry attempted to govern constitutionally under a king who accepted his ministers but did not support them. The most significant act of this period was Roland’s letter to the king in June 1792, which Madame Roland substantially drafted. The letter called on Louis XVI to promulgate the decrees he had vetoed — on the deportation of refractory priests and on the establishment of a camp of federal volunteers near Paris — and warned him that constitutional resistance was dangerous to the monarchy itself. The king’s response was immediate: dismissal of Roland and his Girondin colleagues.
The Second Ministry and Danton (August 1792 – January 1793)
After the insurrection of 10 August 1792, Roland was recalled to the Interior in the reconstituted council. The critical and contested element of this second ministry was the inclusion of Danton at the Ministry of Justice.
She had warned that placing Danton in the government was to inoculate the body politic with men who torment a government when excluded and degrade it when they participate in it. Danton came frequently to her apartment during this period, arriving a little before council time and staying after with Fabre d’Églantine. She watched him closely: his repulsive and atrocious face, the violence of brutal passions half-veiled by an air of joviality, the affectation of frankness and a kind of good nature. Her imagination placed him a dagger in hand, inciting assassins. His biographical arc, as she traced it: a miserable lawyer, burdened with debts, rising through his district section by force of his lungs, a great partisan of the Orléanists, acquiring ease without visible work, becoming substitute prosecutor of the Commune.
She recorded his conduct during the September Massacres without mitigation. While the prisons were being attacked, Danton was at the Commune’s surveillance committee, from which the arrest orders were flowing. He had just embraced Marat there after a feigned twenty-four-hour quarrel. The warrant for Roland’s arrest was issued; Danton took it, showed it to the mayor Pétion, and on Pétion’s instruction did not execute it. Roland records the scene at the council table late that night when a citizen came to Danton recounting his attempts to protect prisoners from the massacres. Danton, irritated, cried out: “I don’t give a damn about the prisoners! let them become whatever they will!”
The Portraits
In twenty-two days in August 1793, she wrote portraits of fifteen individuals she had known.
Buzot — the longest and most personal portrait. Elevated character, proud spirit, boiling courage, sensitive, ardent, melancholic, and lazy — prone to extremes. The gentlest man in the world with his friends and the most formidable adversary of scoundrels. His parliamentary works are praised in detail: his report on the departmental guard, his law against inciters to murder, his motion for the banishment of the Bourbons, his opinion on the trial of the king. Accused of royalism, calumniating Paris, aristocracy, federalism — all for insisting on legality in a revolution that had abandoned it. “Buzot professed the morals of Socrates and preserved the politeness of Scipio,” for which his house was razed and his goods confiscated.
Pétion — a true honest man and a good man, incapable of wounding probity. The serenity of a good conscience, mildness of an easy character, frankness and gaiety distinguished his face. A cold orator and slack in prose style. A prudent mayor and faithful representative, but too trusting and too peaceful to foresee storms. “Made to practice the virtues in a republic, and not to found such a government among a corrupt people who regarded him for a time as their idol, and rejoiced at his proscription as at an enemy’s.”
Marat — known through anecdote rather than direct meeting. A Toulouse woman detained at Sainte-Pélagie described Marat receiving her: boots without stockings, old leather breeches, filthy open shirt exposing a yellowing chest, long dirty nails — received in a salon of blue and white damask furniture, silk curtains, a brilliant chandelier, superb porcelain vases full of natural flowers. He led her to a voluptuous ottoman, listened, kissed her hand, squeezed her knees, promised to free her cousin — and within twenty-four hours wrote to the husband demanding a reciprocal service. Not a disorganised lunatic but a deliberate political operator who extracted personal favours through fear.
Vergniaud — the most double-edged assessment. Perhaps the most eloquent orator in the Assembly, whose prepared speeches were strong with logic, burning with warmth, full of substance. “However, I do not love Vergniaud; I find in him the egoism of philosophy. Disdaining men, certainly because he knows them well, he does not trouble himself for them.” The moral consequence she drew was strict: “What a pity that a talent such as his was not employed with the ardor of a soul devoured by the love of the public good.”
Pache — the sustained anatomisation of betrayal. The Tartuffe of politics. He arrived every morning at seven with a piece of bread in his pocket, refused all pay and title, seeming attentive, prudent, zealous. Roland recommended him as his own successor at the Interior. The unmasking: Pache at the War Ministry began receiving Fabre, Chabot, and Montagnards while refusing Roland’s dinner invitations. As War Minister: 130 million livres in accounts impossible to render; in the twenty-four hours after he was forced to resign, appointments to sixty positions including his son-in-law made an ordonnateur at 19,000 livres and his hairdresser made a war commissary.
Barbaroux — painters would not disdain his features for a head of Antinous. Active, hardworking, frank, brave, with the vivacity of a young Marseillais. Love of pleasure adjacent to love of glory. Paired with Buzot as Nisus and Euryalus: “may they have a better fate than those two friends.”
Louvet — small, slight, poor-sighted, with a neglected coat — appearing nothing to the vulgar who do not remark the nobility of his brow and the fire in his eyes. Known for his Faublas novels, he had proven his hand could alternately shake the bells of folly and launch the thunderbolts of eloquence. Impossible to unite more wit with less pretension and more good nature.
Guadet and Gensonné — a complementary pair. Guadet impetuous, Gensonné cold. Guadet dissipated in brilliant but short bursts; Gensonné lost through deliberation the time for action. Both were tender husbands, good fathers, excellent citizens. They “succumbed under the accusation of conspirators only for having failed to coalesce themselves in favor of the good cause.”
The Fall and the Flight to the Convention
The coup of 31 May 1793 caught the Rolands at home. Madame Roland was preparing to leave Paris with her daughter when a colic attack put her to bed for six days. On 31 May the tocsin sounded. At five-thirty in the evening six armed men arrived with a warrant from the revolutionary committee to arrest Roland. He refused to recognise the authority: “I know no law that constitutes the authority you cite, and I will not comply with orders emanating from it.”
Roland immediately understood he needed to denounce this publicly. She had a letter written to the Convention president, called a cab, and went alone. The Tuileries courtyard was full of armed men. She passed through them “jumping like a bird.” At the Convention doors she used a trick — adopting the tone of a devotee of Robespierre — and was admitted. Inside the petitioners’ hall she waited an hour for Vergniaud, who finally came: “In the state the Assembly is in, I cannot flatter you, and you can barely hope; the Convention can no longer do anything.”
Roland fled that night.
The Imprisonments
She was arrested on 1 June 1793 and taken to the Abbaye prison. The arrest order bore the signature of Dorat-Cubières, the verse-writer who had tried to ingratiate himself with her through flattery when Roland was minister. She examined the warrant, found it defective in form, and refused to accompany the commissioners until they returned with a properly-executed order. She then went without protest.
From the Abbaye she wrote to the Committee of General Security asking to know on what grounds she was held: “I have no offenses to reproach myself; those who speak worst of me have never seen me… I am a mother, this title imposed duties I cannot fulfil.”
After a brief release, she was re-arrested and transferred to Sainte-Pélagie — the second and final imprisonment.
In Sainte-Pélagie she observed the factional struggle beginning to devour the Montagnards themselves: “Robespierre jealous rises against Danton; the Cordeliers and Jacobins are ready to divide. Grand spectacle preparing for us victims: the tigers are going to tear each other apart; they will perhaps forget us, unless the fury of their last moments carries them to exterminate everything before their own defeat.”
The Last Writings and Execution
She wrote four texts in her final weeks at Sainte-Pélagie: Mes dernières pensées, the Observations rapides sur l’acte d’accusation contre les députés, notes on her interrogation, and a projected defence she was not permitted to deliver.
Mes dernières pensées opens with Shakespeare’s Hamlet: “To be or not to be: it is the question. It will soon be resolved for me.” She asks forgiveness of Roland, of her daughter, of her friends. She states directly why she will not wait for the Revolutionary Tribunal’s procedures: “this vain formula of judgment is only an insulting apparatus from which, for the victims, they take care to remove the faculty of expressing oneself.” Her harshest words are for the twenty-two Girondin deputies who did not act decisively on 2 June: “Why did they not do themselves justice by falling on the monsters to annihilate them, rather than receive their verdict from them?”
She was condemned by the Revolutionary Tribunal on 18 Brumaire, Year II (8 November 1793), sentenced to death, and executed the same day in the Place de la Révolution. Her last words, addressed to the statue of Liberty in the square: “Oh Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!”
Jean-Marie Roland, learning of her execution, left Paris and died by his own hand on a road near Rouen, a sword-cane beside him.
The Buzot Question
Madame Roland’s relationship with Buzot — whether it was a romantic attachment or a close intellectual friendship — was hinted at in a footnote by the editor Champagneux, who preserved her private confession that she had a personal reason for wanting to leave Paris that “the time to publish has not yet come.” The full nature of the relationship was never publicly acknowledged in her lifetime or in the 1823 edition of her memoirs. Buzot’s own account, written in hiding, treats the matter with a delicacy that leaves the question unresolved.
Sources
The principal sources for Madame Roland’s life are her own memoirs in two volumes, written in the Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie prisons between August and November 1793 and published posthumously in 1823. Volume I covers her childhood, convent, intellectual formation, her marriage, and the first Roland ministry. Volume II covers the second ministry, the imprisonments, the portraits of her political contemporaries, the last writings, and a documentary appendix. Supplementary accounts appear in the memoirs of Buzot, Louvet, and Brissot.

entities/marie-antoinette.title: Marie-Antoinette
entities/marie-antoinette.content:
Marie-Antoinette
Marie-Antoinette (1755–1793), Archduchess of Austria and Queen of France as wife of Louis XVI, was the most controversial woman of the French Revolution. From her arrival in France in 1770 as a fourteen-year-old bride through her execution in October 1793, she was the subject of more sustained public fascination, rumour, and hostility than any other figure at court. The figure that emerges from the records of those who knew her — her first lady-in-waiting, the American diplomat Gouverneur Morris, and the Swiss officer the Baron de Besenval — is sharply at odds with the legend that grew around her.
The Arrival at Versailles
She was met on the river island of the Rhine between Kehl and Strasbourg. All of France seemed to be gathered: Bernese, Austrian, Alsatian officers mixed with the crowd; women of Strasbourg with uncovered hair and flowers in their hats; silk weavers bringing her their best; a crowd so dense that the carriages could barely push through. In Strasbourg she learned that she was grown too tall for the new style of hairdressing: the dresser found nothing ready. The court of Louis XV was not what she had imagined: Marie-Antoinette found the young king awkward and silent, the king’s daughters remote, the king’s mistress Madame du Barry — a woman who had risen from the streets to the king’s bed — at the centre of every political calculation. The dauphine refused to speak to the favourite, citing protocol. The Austrian ambassador Mercy d’Argenteau and her mother Maria Theresa in Vienna both counselled her to comply.
The Young Queen’s Circle
After her accession in 1774, Marie-Antoinette surrounded herself with a small group of intimates: the Princesse de Lamballe (superintendent of her household), the Comtesse de Polignac (governess of the children), the Duc de Coigny, her page the Comte d’Artois, and the Duc de Guiche. The king’s aunts (Mesdames Adélaïde, Victoire, and Sophie) resented the queen’s separation of her circle from theirs and the queen’s independence from the forms of the court. The king’s brothers showed ambivalence: the Comte de Provence silent and watchful, the Comte d’Artois openly affectionate.
The queen built the Petit Trianon as a private retreat — a separate household within the larger court — where she could live without the ceremonial of Versailles. Her intimacy with the Polignac circle and her private amusements at Trianon became the material for the libelles: pamphlets printed in English-controlled presses in Paris and the Netherlands, depicting the queen as sexually corrupt, conspiring against France in Austrian interests, and indifferent to the sufferings of the people.
The Diamond Necklace Affair (1785–1786)
The affair of the diamond necklace is the decisive event in the destruction of the queen’s public reputation. The cardinal de Rohan, ambitious and debt-ridden, was deceived by a woman calling herself the Comtesse de la Motte-Valois into believing the queen had secretly authorised him to purchase a diamond necklace worth 1,600,000 livres on her behalf. The cardinal, who had been estranged from the queen since his time as ambassador to Vienna, was eager to believe the queen’s favour was returning. He did not deal with the queen directly but with an intermediary who forged her signature and produced — for a single night — a woman impersonating her in the gardens of Versailles.
The fraud was discovered when the cardinal tried to negotiate the necklace with the jewellers Boehmer and Bassenge. The queen, on learning she was implicated, insisted on a prosecution. The Parlement of Paris tried the cardinal and acquitted him — a verdict that was also a judgment on the queen. She was innocent of the fraud but publicly implicated in a scandal that confirmed the worst assumptions of her enemies: that her circle trafficked in secret negotiations, that she was allied with men disloyal to the monarchy, and that the royal family’s reputation was so damaged that a cardinal could be acquitted for defrauding the crown. The Affair became a fixture of revolutionary rhetoric — invoked as proof of the depravity of the court.
The High Summer of the Monarchy (1786–1789)
The queen’s diaries show her absorbed in the life of the court and the children, at Trianon and at Versailles, during the years when the fiscal crisis of the monarchy was deepening. Her brother the Emperor Joseph II visited her at Versailles (the journey improvised after a stay with the Comte d’Artois), and the correspondence with Vienna shows that Maria Theresa’s death in 1780 had removed the one figure who could command the queen’s obedience. The king’s gradual physical decline from the illness that would kill him — a tubercular condition that affected his gait and his speech after an operation in 1786 — was recorded without editorial emphasis by those close to the court.
The king’s younger brother, the Comte d’Artois, was the queen’s most consistent confidant among the king’s family. He alone of the princes shared and sustained her circle’s attitudes. The king’s older brother, the Comte de Provence (the future Louis XVIII), was perceptive enough to see the danger of the royal response to the growing political crisis. The king’s aunts (Mesdames) maintained a residence at Belle-Vue and exercised influence through their confessors.
The October Days (5–6 October 1789)
The women’s march to Versailles and the royal family’s forced transfer to Paris is the critical turning point in Marie-Antoinette’s revolutionary history. The Flanders Regiment had arrived at Versailles on 23 September, and the officers were entertaining the royal bodyguards. The queen’s appearance at the window with the dauphin — holding him out to the regiment’s view — showed the soldiers a woman in distress, appealing to their loyalty.
On 5 October, the Parisian women arrived at Versailles in the afternoon. The queen was advised not to receive a delegation of the insurgents. She stood at the balcony of her apartment — the Hall of Mirrors — with the king and the royal children. The crowd demanded that the king remove to Paris. He agreed.
The queen could not sleep during the night of 5–6 October. She spent the hours moving between her apartment and the king’s, waiting for decisions, while the court descended into chaos. Through it all she maintained her composure and the forms of dignity. Then came the night attack on the queen’s apartment — the mob breaking through the guards — and her escape through the Œil-de-Bœuf to the king’s chambers, the most dramatic incident of the October Days.
The Tuileries (October 1789 – August 1792)
At the Tuileries the queen’s life changed fundamentally. The palace was cramped, cold, and overlooked by the Parisian crowd. The queen’s circle shrank as émigration pruned the court. She had lost the use of Trianon; her intimate society had scattered to the frontiers. She had become instinctively a resister.
The king’s acceptance of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the constitutional oath in July 1790 marked the moment when the queen ceased to hope. Her correspondence from this period with Mercy and with her brother Leopold II in Vienna shows her increasingly desperate and isolated. Gouverneur Morris, the American diplomat who moved in court circles, saw her as a figure of tragic dignity and felt sympathy for her impossible political position, though his judgment of the court’s conduct was often severe.
The Flight to Varennes (June 1791)
The royal family’s attempted escape from Paris was planned in the queen’s apartments at the Tuileries with the Comte de Fersen, a Swedish officer and one of the queen’s closest friends. The plan called for the family to leave separately, rendezvous at Bondy, and proceed by heavy carriage to Montmédy on the frontier, where royalist troops under Bouillé were to receive them. The queen spent the last weeks before the flight shipping her diamonds to Brussels through intermediaries.
The flight failed at Varennes: the carriage was recognised and stopped, the king identified from his portrait on an assignat, and the family returned to Paris under escort, silent and still dressed in the clothes of the servant’s family they had meant to use as disguises. The return journey through the villages — the crowds silent, the mayor of each commune receiving the procession — was the greatest single blow to the monarchy’s popular standing before August 1792.
The Fall of the Monarchy (10 August 1792)
The assault on the Tuileries by the sections of Paris, coordinated with the Jacobin club and the Commune, drove the royal family to seek refuge in the National Assembly. That morning the women of the court sewed uniforms, the Swiss Guards stood at their posts, and the king reviewed the troops. Then the royal family walked from the Tuileries through the gardens to the Riding School where the Assembly sat — the queen carrying the dauphin, the king quiet, the princesse de Lamballe and the duchesse d’Angoulême following.
The subsequent massacres of the Swiss Guards and of the queen’s servants — the Princesse de Lamballe killed in the September Massacres, her head carried on a pike to the Temple — marked the threshold between the queen as a political figure and the queen as a prisoner.
The Temple Prison (August 1792 – August 1793)
The family was transferred to the Temple, the medieval fortress of the Knights Templar, on 13 August 1792. They were given three floors of a tower: the king on one floor, the queen on another, the children and the king’s sister Madame Élisabeth on a third. The family was permitted to keep some servants and the freedom of the tower’s rooms and garden. The king spent his time reading and teaching the dauphin, bearing the accelerating isolation with quietness. In the autumn of 1792 the remaining servants, including the queen’s first lady-in-waiting, were dismissed.
The Conciergerie and the Trial (August – October 1793)
After the king’s execution in January 1793, the queen was separated from her son in July and transferred to the Conciergerie — the prison of the Revolutionary Tribunal — on 2 August. She was confined in a cell that was damp, narrow, and opened onto the women’s courtyard. The guards were instructed not to speak to her. Her health deteriorated.
The trial opened on 14 October 1793 before the Revolutionary Tribunal, presided by Herman, with the prosecutor Fouquier-Tinville conducting the case. The indictment charged her with treason, conspiracy with foreign powers against the French Republic, and corruption of public morals — including the specific accusation by Hébert that she had sexually abused her son. The queen’s response to this accusation was the most dramatic moment of the trial: asked to answer, she stood and said that if she had not answered the charge it was because nature itself refused to answer such an accusation against a mother — appealing to every mother in the hall. The audience was moved; the judges did not stop the trial.
She was condemned on 15 October and executed on 16 October 1793. Her last letter — to Madame Élisabeth, the king’s sister, written the morning of her death — was not delivered.

entities/marmontel.title: Jean-François Marmontel
entities/marmontel.content:
Jean-François Marmontel
He was born in 1723, in the last years of the Regency, in a small town in the Massif Central called Bort-les-Orgues, where his father was a poor draper with thirteen children. The landscape of his childhood — the black volcanic cliffs of the Dordogne valley, the organ-pipe basalt formations that gave the town its name — stayed with him for the rest of his life, and he wrote about it in the opening pages of his memoirs with the precision of a man who had spent sixty years away from it and had never stopped seeing it in his mind. He was the eleventh child, and the family was too poor to feed him; his mother, who emerges from his account as the decisive figure of his early life, managed to get him into the Jesuit college of Mauriac on a charity placement, because the Jesuits ran a system of free education for promising boys from the provincial poor. He was eleven years old and he walked there barefoot.
The Jesuit Formation
The college at Mauriac was a rough school by the standards of the time: the boys slept in dormitories with broken windows, ate soup made from boiled chestnuts in winter, and were beaten regularly by the régents. But the education was real. Marmontel learned Latin verse composition, rhetoric, and philosophy in the classical Jesuit curriculum, and he discovered that he had a facility for writing that set him apart from the other boys. He was not a naturally gifted student — he admits in his memoirs that his memory was poor and that he had to compensate with sheer stubbornness — but he had a talent for imitation and adaptation that made his verses admired by his teachers.
His father died when Marmontel was still an adolescent. He describes the scene in the memoirs: the boy, seventeen years old, returning from a walk to find his father dead in the house, and collapsing into a fever that nearly killed him. The death left the family destitute. Marmontel was taken out of school and placed with a merchant in Clermont-Ferrand — a commercial apprenticeship that lasted exactly as long as it took him to realise he would rather starve than spend his life counting bolts of cloth. He ran away back to college, announced that he had a religious vocation, and took minor orders.
For several years he drifted through a series of positions typical of the provincial cleric-intellectual: preceptor in the château of Linars, where he taught the children of a noble family and wrote Latin verses in praise of the local seigneur; a brief stay at the seminary of Limoges, where he discovered that the directors were more interested in his literary abilities than in his piety; and a return to the Jesuits in Toulouse, where he was offered the chance to enter the novitiate. He consulted his mother by letter. She wrote back: do not become a Jesuit, you are not made for it. It was the first of several moments in his life when he followed her judgment and was saved by it.
In Toulouse he began to make his way as a man of letters. He competed in the Floral Games — the ancient academy of Toulouse that awarded prizes for poetry — and won. Voltaire heard of him through a mutual acquaintance and wrote him a letter of encouragement. The letter, which Marmontel kept all his life, was the turning point. A young man from the provinces, with no family connections and no money, had been noticed by the most famous writer in Europe. In 1745, at the age of twenty-two, he took the road to Paris.
Paris and Voltaire
He arrived in Paris with almost nothing — a few coins, a letter of introduction to Voltaire, and the manuscript of a tragedy. Voltaire received him in the manner for which he was famous to promising young writers: with immediate warmth, practical advice, and the offer of a room in his own house. Marmontel became part of Voltaire’s circle at a time when Voltaire was at the height of his fame but not yet at the height of his fortune — the years between the success of Mahomet and the move to Ferney. Voltaire read his tragedy, told him it was not good enough, and set him to work writing verse epistles and literary criticism.
The mentorship was the making of him. Voltaire introduced him to everyone who mattered in Paris: the salons of Madame de Tencin, the theatre world of the Comédie-Française, the philosophical circle of d’Alembert and Diderot that was then forming around the Encyclopédie. Marmontel absorbed the intellectual culture of the French Enlightenment at its source. He was not a revolutionary thinker — his mind was too moderate, too classical, too attached to order to embrace the radical implications of the philosophy he was learning — but he was the perfect literary craftsman of the movement: capable of turning any idea into elegant prose, any philosophical argument into a readable story.
His first major success came in 1748 with Denys le tyran, a tragedy that was performed at the Comédie-Française and ran for several months. The play was conventional — classical verse, moral theme, the rehabilitation of a tyrant through the power of clemency — but it hit the public taste at exactly the right moment. Marmontel followed it with Aristomène (1749) and Cléopâtre (1750), both successful, and for a few years he was the most performed tragic playwright in Paris after Voltaire himself.
The theatre brought him into the world that would define his life: the actresses, the patrons, the courtiers, and the salonnières who controlled literary reputation in France. He had an affair with Marie Verrière, an actress who was the mistress of the Maréchal de Saxe; the Maréchal discovered it and threatened to have him killed, an episode that left Marmontel terrified and discreet for the rest of his life. He became a regular at the salon of Madame de Tencin, the former nun turned political fixer whose Thursday dinners were the crossroads of literary and ministerial France. It was at Madame de Tencin’s that he discovered the secret fireplace through which she listened to the conversations of her guests — a discovery that did not endear him to her.
The Salon Years
Through the 1750s and 1760s, Marmontel moved from the theatre into the broader world of letters. He contributed articles on literary subjects to the Encyclopédie — not the great philosophical articles of Diderot or d’Alembert, but the competent, clear, readable entries on poetry, tragedy, and rhetoric that helped make the work accessible. He was appointed secretary of the Bâtiments du Roi under the Marquis de Marigny, Madame de Pompadour’s brother, which gave him a position at Versailles and a comfortable income. He moved between worlds with an ease that few of his contemporaries managed: the court at Versailles in the morning, the philosophe salons in the evening, the theatre at night.
Madame de Pompadour liked him. She found him useful, polite, and without the prickly vanity that afflicted so many of the literary men she patronised. He wrote libretti for the court opera, occasional verses for the king’s entertainments, and a steady stream of literary criticism. In 1758, when the Mercure de France — the official literary journal of the kingdom — needed a new editor, the position was offered to him. He transformed it from a dry collection of official announcements into a real literary review, commissioning work from the best young writers he could find and building it into the most widely read periodical in France.
His Contes moraux, published in the Mercure and then collected in book form, made him famous across Europe. These were short, elegant tales in the classical French tradition — La Fontaine updated for the eighteenth century — each with a moral point lightly carried by the narrative. They were translated into every European language, read by Catherine the Great in Russia, Frederick the Great in Prussia, and every literate person between them. Marmontel became the representative French man of letters of his generation: not a genius like Voltaire or Diderot, but the kind of writer who defined the standard of good taste for an entire age.
In 1763, he published Bélisaire, a philosophical novel set in the Byzantine Empire that used the story of the blinded general Belisarius to advance arguments for religious toleration and enlightened monarchy. The Sorbonne condemned it for its heretical propositions — fifteen specific propositions were extracted and denounced — and the Archbishop of Paris, Christophe de Beaumont, threatened him with excommunication. Marmontel defended himself with a mixture of deference and firmness that was characteristic of his entire career: he would not retract the book, but he would not attack his persecutors either. The affair made him a hero to the philosophe party without making him a martyr; he had the rare ability to be both principled and prudent.
The Académie and the Historian
In 1763, the same year Bélisaire appeared, Marmontel was elected to the Académie Française. The election was contested — there were factions who thought him too much a philosophe and others who thought him too much a courtier — but he was admitted, and the Académie became the centre of his institutional life for the next thirty years. He was also appointed Historiographer of France, a position that gave him access to the state archives and a mandate to write the history of the reign of Louis XV.
The history was never written — the material was too vast, the Revolution too disruptive, the task too daunting — but the preparation for it gave Marmontel an intimate knowledge of French political life at the highest level. He read the memoirs of Saint-Simon in manuscript, consulted the ministers who had served under Louis XV, and accumulated the documentary base that would later make his account of the Revolution so well-informed.
In 1783, he was elected Secrétaire Perpétuel of the Académie Française — the permanent secretary, the most senior administrative position in the institution, responsible for its records, its correspondence, and its public face. It was the summit of a literary career in the ancien régime. Marmontel delivered the éloges of deceased academicians in the annual public sessions, and his speeches became literary events in their own right — the synthesis of the classical French style at its most polished, celebrating the lives of writers and statesmen whose world was about to end.
The Revolution: Electoral Politics
When the Estates-General were convoked in 1788, Marmontel was sixty-five years old. He had spent his entire life in the service of the monarchy and the institutions of the ancien régime, but he was not a reactionary. He believed in constitutional reform, in the principles of the Enlightenment, in the possibility of a rational and ordered liberty that would preserve the monarchy while transforming the state. In the spring of 1789 he became a member of the primary assembly of the district of the Feuillants — the ancient monastery in Paris where the electors of the Third Estate met — and then of the electoral assembly that chose the deputies for Paris.
The electoral assembly of Paris in 1789 was one of the most extraordinary political gatherings in French history: six hundred men from the Third Estate of the capital, meeting not in a royal building but in a former monastery, electing deputies who would go to Versailles to remake the kingdom. Marmontel sat among lawyers, merchants, academics, and men of property, many of whom had never participated in politics before. He describes the scene in his memoirs with a mixture of hope and unease: the eloquence of the young advocates, the energy of the debates, the growing influence of men like Adrien Duport who were already thinking beyond constitutional monarchy to something more radical.
He stood for election himself. The assembly needed to fill forty seats for the Paris deputation. On the first ballot, he placed high enough to be in contention. On the second, he was defeated — the seat went to Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès, the man who had just written What is the Third Estate? and whose name was on every tongue in France. Marmontel withdrew from the contest with dignity. He was too old, too moderate, too identified with the institutions of the old world to command the confidence of a body that was inventing a new one.
The Revolution: Witness
From the summer of 1789 onward, Marmontel watched the Revolution unfold from the best possible vantage point — and from the worst. He was a witness to the great events: the fall of the Bastille reached him through the streets of Paris; the October Days he saw from his house near the Tuileries; the king’s flight to Varennes, the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August 1792, the September Massacres — each event registered in his mind with the accuracy of a trained observer. But he was also a victim of the Revolution, and the two perspectives are interwoven in his account in a way that gives his memoirs their peculiar tension.
He had been a man of the ancien régime — a pensioner of the crown, a member of the Académie, a beneficiary of the system of patronage and privilege that the Revolution was dismantling. The loss of the Mercure de France deprived him of his principal income. The suppression of the academies in 1793 deprived him of his institutional identity. The law of suspects, the proscription of ex-nobles, and the attacks on ex-priests touched his family directly: his brother-in-law was arrested, his friends were executed, his world was systematically destroyed.
He did not flee France. He stayed in Paris through the first years of the Revolution, moving between his house in the city and a small property at Saint-Brice, north of Paris, where he tried to keep his head down and his family safe. In 1793, as the Terror deepened, he withdrew more completely. He had been proscribed by name as a former noble — not by blood, but by association with the Académie and the court — and he lived in daily expectation of arrest.
The Memoirist in Retirement
The memoirs were written in this period of hiding and waiting. Marmontel conceived them as a testament for his children — Mémoires d’un père pour servir à l’instruction de ses enfans — a record of a world that had vanished and a life that had crossed the entire span of the Enlightenment, from the provincial poverty of Bort to the heights of the Académie Française, from the reign of Louis XV to the Terror. He wrote in the measured, classical prose that had been his trademark for fifty years, but the tone is different from his earlier work: more reflective, more melancholy, more aware of the ironies of a life that had been lived at the centre of events and had ended in impotent observation.
The memoir is not a political tract. Marmontel was a constitutional monarchist to the end, but his account of the Revolution is less concerned with justifying his politics than with recording what he saw. He gives extended portraits of the figures he knew: Louis XVI, whom he describes with a sympathy that is all the more striking for being unillusioned; Necker, whose miscalculations he analyses without rancour; Mirabeau, whose genius he recognised and whose corruption he deplored; the deputies, the ministers, the king’s councillors, the revolutionaries, all drawn from a lifetime of observation in the salons and the corridors of power.
The most remarkable section of the memoirs is the account of the fall of the Bastille as told to him by Élie, one of the vainqueurs de la Bastille — the insurgents who stormed the fortress on 14 July 1789. Marmontel met Élie in the days after the event and took down his narrative directly. It is one of the very few eyewitness accounts from the insurgent side, preserved within the memoirs of a moderate constitutionalist who could not have been more different from the men who took the Bastille, but who had the historian’s instinct to record what he heard.
The Last Years
In 1795, with the Terror over and the Thermidorian Reaction in progress, Marmontel moved his family to Abbeville, in Picardy, where he had inherited a small property from his wife’s family. He lived there in retirement, completing the memoirs and writing educational works for his children: a course in grammar, a course in logic, a course in metaphysics and morality — the curriculum of the Enlightenment reduced to its essentials for the private instruction of one family.
He died on 31 December 1799, the last day of the eighteenth century, at his house in Abbeville. The coincidence was not lost on those who knew him. He had been born in 1723, in the France of Louis XV, when the philosophes were still a scattered group of writers without influence, when the Encyclopédie did not exist, when the monarchy seemed as eternal as the seasons. He died in 1799, on the eve of the Consulate, having seen the monarchy fall, the republic rise and fall, the Terror consume his friends, and the institutions of his life — the Académie, the Mercure, the salons, the system of royal patronage — swept away by forces that he had helped to set in motion without knowing what they were.
The memoirs were published posthumously in 1804. They became one of the most-read accounts of the Revolution from the moderate constitutionalist perspective, valued as much for their portrait of the eighteenth-century literary world as for their account of the revolutionary years. Marmontel had been the perfect representative of his age — not its greatest writer, not its boldest thinker, but the man whose life trajectory traced the curve of the French Enlightenment from its origins to its collapse, and who had the sense, in his final years, to write it all down.

entities/the-girondins.title: The Girondins
entities/the-girondins.content:
The Girondins
The Girondins — also called Brissotins by their enemies — were the leading republican faction in the Legislative Assembly (1791–1792) and the National Convention (1792–1793). They are known to history by the name of the department of the Gironde, from which several of their principal speakers were elected, though many of their leaders came from other parts of France: Brissot from Chartres, Roland from Lyon, Buzot from Évreux, Louvet from Orléans, Pétion from Chartres, Barbaroux from Marseilles. The name was given to them by their enemies in the Jacobin clubs — the deputies of the Mountain — and accepted by them reluctantly, as a designation that misrepresented the scope of their support.
The Girondins left an unusually rich documentary record: memoirs written in hiding or in prison after their proscription, speeches and published writings, and the records of the Convention itself. These are not the work of detached observers but the documents of a defeated party, written by men who expected to die, and they preserve the Girondin understanding of the French Revolution as it was happening.
The Circle and Its Formation
The Girondins never constituted a formal party with a programme, a whip, or a coordinated discipline. They were a network of deputies who met in one another’s houses — principally at the apartment of Jean-Marie Roland and his wife Madame Roland on the rue Guénégaud in Paris, and at the house of the deputy Pierre Vergniaud in Versailles. The connections that became the faction formed gradually through 1791 in the Jacobin Club of Paris, where Brissot, Buzot, Pétion, and others were active members before the schism.
The sociological core of the group was provincial, professional, and intellectual. Brissot was a journalist. Roland was a manufacturing inspector and administrator. Buzot was a lawyer from Évreux. Vergniaud was a lawyer from Bordeaux. Louvet was a novelist turned journalist. Guadet and Gensonné were lawyers from the Bordelais. Barbaroux was a lawyer from Marseilles. Pétion had been the mayor of Paris. They were not nobles; they were men of the Third Estate, risen through talent and ambition in the decade before the Revolution.
The War Policy
The Girondins’ signature policy was the war against Austria. From the autumn of 1791 through the spring of 1792, Brissot’s speeches in the Legislative Assembly argued that the Revolution could not be secure while Austria and Prussia were arming and threatening the frontiers, that war would rally the nation to the Revolution, and that the king’s court would be forced to show its hand. The war was declared on 20 April 1792 — a war that went badly for France at first, that produced the invasion crisis of the summer, and that ultimately brought down the monarchy on 10 August 1792.
Brissot’s reasoning on the war was not purely ideological. He argued that Austria’s position in the Netherlands (Belgium) was the strategic key to French security: as long as Austria held the Scheldt, France was vulnerable to invasion from the north. The war policy also served a domestic purpose: it forced the issue of the king’s loyalty, dividing the court from the Revolution.
The Girondins and the Convention
By the time the National Convention met in September 1792, the Girondins were the dominant faction. They held the ministry. They had led the call for the republic. Their orators dominated the Convention debates. The Mountain — the Jacobin deputies on the upper benches who had been allied with the Commune of Paris and with the insurrection of 10 August — was numerically weaker but organised, ruthless, and allied with the Paris sections.
The conflict between the Girondins and the Mountain was not about the form of government (both were republican) or about the war (both supported it) or about the trial of the king (most Girondins voted for death). It was about the revolutionary process: whether the Revolution could be consolidated through constitutional order or whether it required permanent popular insurrection.
The Conflict with the Mountain
The most systematic Girondin analysis of the struggle came from Buzot. The true causes of Girondin proscription, he insisted, were not the public charges — royalism, federalism, counter-revolution, corruption by foreign gold — but the Girondin insistence on order, legality, and constitutional procedure at a moment when the Mountain’s power depended on maintaining popular agitation. Since the monarchy had been annihilated, Buzot argued, the insurrectional movement had to cease: where there is no tyranny to overthrow, there should be no force in insurrection; where one is only building, one needs order and reason.
The Mountain, according to the Girondins, used the Jacobin Club as a parallel power structure. The affiliated clubs in the departments let the Mountain mobilise public opinion against the Convention itself. The Commune of Paris — controlled by the radical sections — provided armed street pressure at key moments. The press — Marat’s L’Ami du Peuple, Hébert’s Père Duchesne — destroyed individual reputations systematically.
The Girondins’ counter-weapons were speeches, decrees, and constitutional procedure. They commissioned the report on the March 10 conspiracy; they voted for the Commission of Twelve to investigate the Commune’s activities; they attempted to discipline Marat through the Revolutionary Tribunal. Each attempt was turned back by the Mountain.
The Character Studies
The Girondins identified four figures as the instruments of Montagnard domination:
Marat — the visible extremist, whose denunciations served as the instrument for destroying individual reputations. Madame Roland’s portrait, drawn from the testimony of a woman imprisoned with her who had visited Marat’s apartment, does not describe a disorganised lunatic but a deliberate operator who extracted personal favours through fear. His acquittal by the Revolutionary Tribunal, Buzot argued, made the Convention permanently subject to factional terror.
Robespierre — the tactician, who rose through the Jacobin Club while Marat was the visible extremist, and moved toward dictatorship once Marat’s assassination removed his cover. Among the Girondins, Louvet was the most explicit enemy of Robespierre, having delivered the formal accusation before the Convention in October 1792 — Je t’accuse, Robespierre! — in which he charged him with conspiring against the republic through his dominance of the Jacobin Club.
Danton — the most complex and contested figure in Girondin memoirs. Madame Roland wrote the most severe judgment: she had warned against placing Danton in the ministry. She describes his repulsive face, his violence of brutal passions half-veiled by an air of joviality, his affectation of frankness. His conduct during the September Massacres is the subject of her most sustained accusation: he was at the Commune’s surveillance committee from which arrest orders were flowing, and at the council table that night when informed of efforts to protect prisoners, he cried out “I don’t give a damn about the prisoners!”
Pache — the Tartuffe of politics, the object of the most sustained anatomisation of betrayal among the memoirs. Roland had recommended him as his own successor at the Interior. As War Minister, Pache destroyed the army’s capacity by purging competent officers. The false simplicity — arriving at seven in the morning with a piece of bread, refusing salary — was a mask for a systematic building of factional power within the ministry.
The Hour of Collapse: 31 May – 2 June 1793
The coup against the Girondins was a three-day operation: 31 May, 1 June, 2 June. The sections of Paris surrounded the Convention each day, the tocsin was rung, the Commune petitioned for the arrest of twenty-two (later thirty-one) deputies. On 2 June the Convention was surrounded by armed National Guards — eighty thousand men by Girondin estimates — and decreed the arrest of its own leading members.
The Girondin reaction was not uniform. Some — like Brissot — were arrested in Paris. Some — like Buzot, Barbaroux, Louvet — escaped to the provinces and attempted to organise resistance. Some — like Vergniaud, Guadet, Gensonné — stayed in Paris and went to prison. Some — like Roland — fled. The central weakness of the Girondins as a political force was evident in the response: they had no organisation for resistance, no armed force of their own, no plan for what to do when the Convention was no longer a free assembly. They were men who believed in the power of speeches, laws, and constitutional procedure against armed insurrection.
After the Proscription
The proscribed Girondins who escaped Paris gathered in Caen, Normandy, under the protection of the departmental administration. There they established an assemblée centrale de résistance à l’oppression and issued a proclamation drafted by Louvet calling on the departments to resist the Convention’s usurpation. A military force was assembled under General Wimpfen but was defeated at Pacy-sur-Eure in July 1793.
Inside the Caen group, tensions ran high. Genuine republicans who wanted to march on Paris sat uneasily alongside men suspected of royalist sympathies or secret intelligences with the enemy. The provincial resistance itself faltered — property-owning republicans unwilling to leave their homes could not sustain the cause. The survivors scattered as the Terror reached each hiding place.
Charlotte Corday came to Caen before Marat’s assassination, ostensibly on family business. She never spoke to any of the fugitive Girondins about her design. If she had consulted them, they later reflected, they would not have directed her toward Marat — whom they knew had at most two days left to live from his disease.
The Trial and Execution
The Girondin deputies who were arrested in Paris were tried by the Revolutionary Tribunal in October 1793, condemned, and guillotined on 31 October 1793 on the Place de la Révolution. The executed were: Brissot, Vergniaud, Gensonné, Ducos, Fonfrède, Lasource, Lehardi, Duprat, Gardien, Duchastel, Mainvielle, Sillery, Valazé (who stabbed himself in the courtroom), Boilleau, Lesterpt-Beauvais, and a number associated with them.
Buzot, Barbaroux, and Pétion escaped the Paris roundup and were discovered dead in a field near Saint-Émilion in June 1794 — shot, or by their own hands. Their bodies were found half-eaten by dogs.
Louvet survived the Terror in hiding, was rehabilitated after Thermidor, and returned to the Convention. He died in 1797 as consul-designate to Palermo. Buzot’s memoirs were found among his papers and published in 1823. Louvet’s were written in a cave in the Jura in April 1794.
