events/10-august-1792.title: 10 August 1792
events/10-august-1792.content:
10 August 1792
I. The Approaching Storm
By the summer of 1792, the French Revolution had arrived at a crisis from which there was no turning back. The Legislative Assembly had been at war with Austria since April, and the war was going badly. The French armies had fled before the advancing Austrians; the émigré princes were gathering on the frontier; and the Duke of Brunswick, commanding the combined armies of Austria and Prussia, stood ready to invade. On the twenty-fifth of July, Brunswick issued his famous Manifesto — a document drafted by French émigrés and approved by the Bourbon princes — which reached Paris on the third of August. Its terms were brutal: any harm done to the royal family would be met with “exemplary and unforgettable vengeance”; the city of Paris would be destroyed if the Tuileries were again violated; the National Guard itself would be shot down as armed civilians if it dared to resist. The Manifesto, which Morris summarised as “Be all against me, for I am against you all; and make a good Resistance, for there is no longer any Hope,” produced the opposite effect from the one intended. Instead of cowing the revolutionaries, it drove men in crowds to enlist. It was the final proof, for those who still needed it, that the King was in league with the enemies of France.
The political temperature in Paris had been rising for months. The King had vetoed the decrees against the refractory priests and the proposed camp of twenty thousand fédérés; the Girondin ministers — Roland, Servan, Clavières — had been dismissed in June; Lafayette had appeared before the Assembly to demand the suppression of the Jacobins, and had been howled down. The sections of Paris, in constant session since the summer began, had voted on the thirtieth of July to petition for the deposition of the King — the déchéance. The fédérés — volunteers from the provinces who had come to Paris for the Federation of the fourteenth of July — remained in the city, armed and restless. Among them were the Marseillais, five hundred men from the southern port, who had marched into Paris singing the war-hymn that would one day bear their name. They bivouacked in the Cordeliers district and drilled openly in the gardens of the Palais-Royal. The court knew what was coming. On the fourth of August, the King and Queen, expecting to be murdered that night, sat up until dawn in the Tuileries, waiting for the blow that did not fall.
II. The Night of the Ninth of August
The day of Thursday the ninth of August was sweltering. Paris was in great agitation. Morris, the American Minister, noted the heat — the same oppressive weather that later in the week would cause a perch caught at six in the morning to be spoiled by dinner-time, so rapid was the state of putrefaction. He went about his business that day: a call on Monciel, a visit to court, a meeting with Constable and Chaumont about a land company, a happy moment with his friend at the Louvre, dinner with the British Ambassador, an evening at Madame d’Albani’s. He returned home near midnight. Paris was in great agitation.
The tocsin began to sound after midnight. It was the signal. From the Cordeliers district, from the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, from the Faubourg Saint-Marceau, the sections rose. Danton, from the Cordeliers, and Robespierre, from the Jacobins, had been concerting with the Commune and the fédérés for weeks. The plan was simple: seize the Hôtel de Ville, replace the legal municipal government with an insurrectionary Commune, and march on the Tuileries. By three in the morning of the tenth, the sections had taken control of the city. The old municipal authorities were arrested or dispersed. The tocsin rang from every church tower in Paris. The drums beat the générale. The streets filled with armed men.
III. The Morning at the Tuileries
At the Tuileries, the royal family had been warned. Mandat, the commander of the National Guard, had stationed what troops he could around the palace — a few battalions of guardsmen, the Swiss regiments, some gentlemen volunteers. But the National Guard was unreliable; many of its men were already in sympathy with the sections. The Marseillais and the fédérés spent the night assembling at the Place de la Bastille and the Place du Carrousel, under the very windows of the palace.
The King had reviewed the National Guard early in the morning. He passed along the ranks in the courtyard of the Tuileries, and the cries that greeted him were not the loyal acclamations of former days but the cold silence of men who had already made their choice. The battalions of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and the Faubourg Saint-Marceau, which had been stationed to defend the palace, defected to the insurgents before the morning was half gone. The guard at the Carrousel opened the gates without a struggle. Mandat was summoned to the Hôtel de Ville by the new Commune, and there he was arrested and murdered — shot dead on the steps of the building he had commanded. The National Guard was left without a leader, and the defence of the palace fell almost entirely to the Swiss.
Inside the palace, the confusion was terrible. Madame Campan, the Queen’s first lady-in-waiting, was not on duty that day, but she did not leave the Queen’s apartment. Two of her sisters and a niece were with her. The King, seeing the defection of the guard, the approach of the mob, and the impossibility of defence, made a decision that would be debated for a century: he would not fight. At the urging of his ministers and of Roederer, the procureur-syndic of the department, he resolved to take his family to the National Assembly and place themselves under the protection of the legislature.
IV. The Flight to the Assembly
The royal family left the Tuileries between seven and eight in the morning. The King, the Queen, the Princess Elisabeth, the Dauphin, and Madame Royale crossed the garden of the Tuileries on foot, guarded by a handful of National Guards, and entered the hall of the Legislative Assembly through the garden door. They were received by the President of the Assembly and placed in the logograph — the reporters’ box, a narrow, stifling enclosure behind the President’s chair, where the stenographers usually sat. The heat was suffocating. There was no food, no change of clothes, nothing but the desperate hope that the Assembly could protect them. Lady Sutherland, the British Ambassador’s wife, sent over some clothes for the little Dauphin, whose son was about the same age. There they sat, the royal family of France, crowded into a box meant for clerks, listening to the debates that would decide their fate.
The King spoke to the Assembly. He said he had come to avoid a great crime, and that he and his family would trust themselves to the representatives of the nation. The Assembly heard him coldly. The deputies of the right sat in silence; the majority, under the pressure of the armed crowd that had gathered outside the hall, leaned towards suspension. Vergniaud rose to speak — the great orator of the Gironde — and pronounced the words that ended the monarchy: the King was suspended from his functions; a National Convention would be summoned to decide the future form of government.
V. The Attack and the Massacre
While the King sat in the Assembly, the Tuileries fell. The insurgents, many thousands strong, poured into the courtyard of the Carrousel and the gardens. The Swiss Guard, about nine hundred men, had been left without orders. Some of their officers had followed the King to the Assembly; others had fled. The Swiss, seeing the crowd surge towards the palace gates, fired. The first volley stopped the advance. But the insurgents, reinforced by the fédérés and by battalions of the National Guard that had gone over to the insurrection, returned the fire from behind the trees of the Tuileries garden and from the windows of the houses on the Carrousel. The fighting was fierce but brief. The Swiss, isolated and outnumbered, sent a messenger to the Assembly to ask for instructions, but no orders came. They began to retreat through the palace, and then the tide turned.
The Swiss Guard laid down their arms. They had been promised safe passage. They were not spared. As Morris noted in his diary that evening: “The Château, undefended but by the Swiss, is carried and the Swiss wherever found are murder’d.” The massacre was systematic and terrible. The Swiss were pursued through the corridors, the salons, the kitchens of the palace. Those who surrendered in the courtyard were shot down. Those who had thrown down their muskets and tried to mix with the crowd were recognised by their uniforms and killed on the spot. Some fled into the gardens and were hunted through the trees. The corpses were stripped, mutilated, and piled in heaps. The palace itself was ransacked: the furniture was smashed, the mirrors shattered, the wine cellars drunk dry. The mob poured through the great apartments, tearing down tapestries, breaking open cabinets, defacing portraits of kings. The papers of the royal household were scattered across the Carrousel. Campan’s house, which stood at the entrance to the court of the Tuileries, was pillaged and partly burned; the Marshal de Villars’ baton, preserved for generations, was thrown onto the pavement and only saved by a servant who recognised its value.
By noon, the palace was a ruin of broken glass and bloody marble. The Swiss dead lay in rows in the courtyard. The Carrousel was strewn with torn clothing, papers, and the debris of a thousand homes. The heat was extreme. Morris noted that some perch alive in the morning were spoiled by dinner — so rapid was the state of putrefaction in that summer heat. Those who had seen the massacre, like Mr Francis, gave accounts so dreadful that they said they would not dare to tell them in America.
VI. The King Suspended
The Assembly met all day under the eyes of the armed crowd that filled the galleries and the approaches to the hall. The deputies of the Gironde — Vergniaud, Gensonné, Guadet — dominated the debates; the Mountain — Robespierre, Danton, Marat — pressed from the tribunes for the abolition of the monarchy itself. The King, in his box, heard himself denounced as a traitor and a tyrant, and could not reply. The Queen, pale and composed, held the Dauphin close and listened in silence.
The decree of suspension was passed in the afternoon. The King was stripped of all his powers. The ministry was replaced: Roland returned to the Interior, Servan to War, Clavières to Finance; Danton, the violent orator of the Cordeliers, took the Ministry of Justice. The King and his family were not allowed to return to the Tuileries; they were sent that evening to the Temple, the old fortress of the Knights Templar in the northern quarter of Paris. The Temple had not been used as a prison for years; it was cold, damp, and unfurnished. But it was secure. And there, in the great tower that had once sheltered the order of soldier-monks, the Bourbon monarchy went to its captivity.
VII. The Aftermath
The insurrection of the tenth of August was the most decisive day of the Revolution since the fall of the Bastille. Where the Bastille had been the destruction of an old symbol, the tenth of August was the destruction of the monarchy itself — not in principle but in fact. The King was no longer the King; he was a prisoner, a hostage, a man awaiting trial.
The Commune of Paris, born in the insurrectionary night of the ninth of August, now ruled the city with an authority that no legal power could challenge. It had armed the sections; it had seized the Hôtel de Ville; it had murdered Mandat; it had forced the suspension of the King. Its leaders — men like Hébert, Chaumette, and the formidable Santerre — were not deputies but militants, and they answered not to the Assembly but to the streets. The Commune demanded a revolutionary tribunal, the arrest of suspects, the confiscation of royalist property. It prepared the September Massacres that would follow within weeks — the slaughter of the prisoners of the Abbaye, the Force, and the Carmes, in which the friends of the court, the Swiss who had not been killed on the tenth, and the priests who had refused the oath would be butchered in the name of revolutionary justice.
The Girondins, who had led the attack on the King and orchestrated the political crisis that made the tenth of August possible, now found themselves the prisoners of forces they could no longer control. Buzot and Louvet, who had been among the fiercest advocates of the déchéance, watched with horror as the Commune seized the authority they had hoped to exercise. The sections, the fédérés, the Jacobin clubs — these were the real powers, and they had no use for the constitutional scruples of the Gironde.
As for the King, he passed his first night in the Temple in a bare room, without a bed, without a servant, without even a change of linen. For the first time in his life, the man who had ruled France locked his own door and slept, if he slept at all, as a prisoner. The monarchy of a thousand years had fallen, and the man who had been its last embodiment lay alone in the darkness of the Temple tower.

Source Material

Gouverneur Morris, A Diary of the French Revolution, Volume II (1790–1793). Morris was the American Minister in Paris; his diary entry for 10 August 1792 records the cannon and musquetry, the fall of the Tuileries, the murder of the Swiss, the King’s suspension, and the stifling heat in the days that followed.
Madame Campan, Mémoires sur la vie privée de Marie-Antoinette (3 vols., 1823). Campan was the Queen’s first lady-in-waiting and present in the Tuileries during the insurrection; her account covers the preparations, the morning of the tenth, the flight to the Assembly, and the destruction of her house on the Carrousel.
François Buzot, Mémoires sur la Révolution française (1823). Buzot, a Girondin deputy, provides the political context of the Girondins’ role in orchestrating the déchéance and the insurrection.
Jean-Baptiste Louvet, Mémoires de Louvet (1823). Louvet, also a Girondin, recounts the political manoeuvring before the tenth of August.
Madame Roland, Mémoires de Madame Roland (1823). Roland, whose husband was Minister of the Interior, gives the governmental perspective on the crisis and the fall of the Girondin ministry.

events/18-brumaire.title: 18 Brumaire
events/18-brumaire.content:
18 Brumaire
The coup of 18–19 Brumaire, Year VIII (9–10 November 1799) overthrew the Directory and replaced it with the Consulate, a provisional executive of three consuls of whom General Bonaparte was the first. The event was the culmination of a conspiracy that had been prepared over several months, driven by the directors’ own weakness and Bonaparte’s calculation that the time had come to seize power.
The Directory’s Final Crisis
By the autumn of 1799 the Directory had exhausted its political credit. A series of military reverses, the renewal of war in Italy and Germany, and the persistent agitation of the neo-Jacobin left had left the executive paralysed. Sieyès, who had been elected a director in the spring of 1799, had concluded from the start that the constitution of Year III was unworkable and that the Directory could not govern. Sieyès began looking for a military sword — a general of sufficient reputation to execute a coup d’état and then retire while Sieyès himself rebuilt the republic on sound principles. He first approached General Joubert, but Joubert was killed at Novi in August 1799. He then considered General Moreau, but Moreau had neither the appetite nor the ambition for such a role. When news reached Paris that Bonaparte had landed at Fréjus on 9 October 1799, returning from the Egyptian campaign, Sieyès recognised his man.
Bonaparte arrived in Paris to immense public enthusiasm. The Directory, already tottering, received him with a forced banquet at the Luxembourg Palace. A coup d’état was already mounted and nearly ready to strike before Bonaparte’s return; Bonaparte seized control of it with skill, threading his way through all the existing intrigues, opposing his military renown to titles founded on birth or long service, winning some men through promises and intimidating others through threats. He alone obtained the direction of the great movement.
The Conspiracy
The conspirators met on 16 Brumaire (7 November) at the house of Lemercier, a former minister. The principal figures included Lucien Bonaparte, who had been elected president of the Council of Five Hundred and was thus the conspiracy’s man inside the legislature; the deputy Chazal; Boulay de la Meurthe; and the financier Collot, among others. Sieyès supplied the constitutional theory; Bonaparte supplied the soldiers.
Bonaparte’s motives were harsher still. He attached himself to Sieyès in order to deceive him, and he deceived him in order not to have to fear him. He saw in his future colleagues nothing but ‘coarse and inert mud’ — a mass without sentiment, ideas, or will. Bonaparte let opinion wander on whose favour the coup would serve, playing for time until the moment was ripe. All uncertainty ceased only when Bonaparte, who until then had been merely the Directory’s general, decided to take everything.
18 Brumaire, Year VIII (9 November 1799)
The plan was deceptively simple: the Council of Ancients would be persuaded that a Jacobin conspiracy threatened the republic and that the government needed to be moved outside Paris to Saint-Cloud for its safety, with Bonaparte placed in command of the troops guarding the legislature. The Directory, deprived of its legal base, would then be swept aside.
On the morning of 18 Brumaire, the Council of Ancients was summoned at an unusual hour. The deputy Cornet delivered an alarmist report of a conspiracy brewing among the Jacobins. The report was a fabrication, but the Ancients, haunted by memories of the Terror, voted the decree of translation to Saint-Cloud. Bonaparte was named commander of the troops responsible for the security of the legislature. He rode to the Tuileries, where a large body of troops had been assembled, and harangued them.
The Directory meanwhile collapsed without resistance. Barras, the most astute of the directors, was approached by Bonaparte’s agents. The negotiation was botched: Barras was offered money but hesitated, and in the end he resigned and retired to his estate. Gohier, the president of the Directory, refused to cooperate and was placed under guard at the Luxembourg Palace. Moulins, the third director, fled. Sieyès and Roger-Ducos, who were in the conspiracy, resigned at the appointed moment. By the end of the day, the Directory had ceased to exist. Bonaparte’s lieutenants were deployed across the city: Moreau commanded at the Luxembourg, Murat stood ready with the grenadiers, Serrurier held Saint-Cloud, and Macdonald kept order at Versailles.
19 Brumaire (10 November 1799)
The second day of the coup was the more dangerous. The two councils reconvened at Saint-Cloud, the Ancients in one hall and the Five Hundred in another. The Five Hundred, many of whom had not been party to the conspiracy, were in an angry and suspicious mood. When Bonaparte entered their hall to address them — a violation of constitutional protocol, since the general was not a deputy — he was met with cries of ‘Down with the dictator!’ and ‘Outlaw him!’ Grenadiers had to extract him from the chamber. The scene reduced Bonaparte to a state of near-collapse; for a moment the coup hung in the balance.
Lucien Bonaparte, as president of the Five Hundred, saved the day. He refused to put the motion to outlaw his brother, and instead harangued the deputies. Lucien accused the deputies who had shouted down Bonaparte of being terrorists and assassins, recalling their previous conspiracies during the Terror. He declared that their reign was over. ‘The French people, the armies, Europe, Africa and Asia contemplate us,’ he cried. ‘If we were weak today, we would be the most cowardly of men.’
Outside, Bonaparte ordered Murat and his grenadiers to clear the hall. The troops marched in with fixed bayonets; the deputies fled through the windows and doors. The hall was evacuated without bloodshed.
That night, a rump session of the Ancients — those who remained or could be rounded up — voted the creation of a provisional consulate. The legislative bodies were adjourned until 1 Ventôse (20 February 1800); a provisional executive council of three members was created; a commission of twenty-five was appointed to revise the constitution; and sixty-four deputies judged hostile to the coup were excluded from their seats. The three provisional consuls were Sieyès, Roger-Ducos, and Bonaparte.
The Constitution of Year VIII
The Constitution of the Year VIII, drafted principally by Sieyès but reshaped by Bonaparte, established the Consulate as the new form of government. Nothing was lacking in the consular constitution to guarantee the liberty of the citizen, the general prosperity, and the consideration of France abroad — except that everything was lacking in the principal agents of authority to make liberty loved and respected. This lack of harmony forced recourse to the spring of fear, which was always fatal to republics.
The Senate, appointed from a list of notables chosen by Bonaparte, displayed an ‘anticipated devotion.’ If the constitution had contained real guarantees, this devotion would have signified nothing but servility without motive or cause. The Chamber of Representatives, the necessary counterweight to executive power, was struck with nullity from its formation. Everything in the new government seemed disposed for the advantage of a single man; the encroachment of powers was foreseen and even provoked. Flattery and obsequiousness descended from the highest ranks, while from the lowest rose the most venal idolatry. All watched for Bonaparte’s passions and invited him to abandon himself without restraint to his ambition.
A striking anecdote captures the character of the new regime: when General Lannes, commanding the consular guard, reproached Bonaparte for trusting only dishonoured men or those whose reputation was ruined, Bonaparte replied, ‘Is it with virtues and honest men that one founds a monarchy?‘
Constant’s Context
Benjamin Constant’s pamphlet De la force du gouvernement actuel (1796), written three years before the coup, provides the intellectual backdrop against which the events of Brumaire must be understood. The pamphlet argued that moderate republicans ought to work with the Directory rather than against it, because the Revolution had created powerful material interests — the purchasers of national lands, the beneficiaries of civil equality, the rising commercial classes — that would rally to any government that defended these gains. The Republic had the first merit of existing, and it rested on interests more solid than the jealousies of faction.
The same pamphlet warned against what it called ‘revolutionary habits’ — the temptation, even among sincere republicans, to treat the constitution as an instrument to be discarded when it became inconvenient. It insisted that the principles of 1789, not merely the material gains of the Revolution, must be defended. A counter-revolution, it argued, would itself be merely a new revolution — a prolongation of instability, not its cure. The Directory’s great weakness was that it governed from a ‘party of sand,’ a central coalition that the slightest wave could divide and drive against either the rock of the right or the rock of the left.
The analysis was aimed at preserving the constitutional republic against royalists on one side and Jacobins on the other. But the logic of the argument — that the Revolution’s material beneficiaries would support any government that protected them — could just as easily serve the architects of Brumaire. The coup of 18 Brumaire was precisely the abandonment of constitutional principle that the pamphlet had feared: a military solution to a political crisis, justified by the same appeals to order, stability, and the defence of the Revolution’s gains that it had deployed for the Directory three years earlier.

events/9-thermidor.title: 9 Thermidor
events/9-thermidor.content:
9 Thermidor
I. The Law of 22 Prairial
By the summer of 1794, the Revolution had turned inward. The foreign armies had been pushed back from the frontiers — the victory of Fleurus in June had secured the Belgian frontier, and the Coalition no longer threatened Paris — but the Terror, far from slackening with the passing of the external danger, had reached a new and terrible intensity. On the twenty-second of Prairial, Year II (the tenth of June, 1794), the Convention, at the insistence of Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety, passed the law that would give its name to the final phase of the revolutionary government.
The Law of 22 Prairial transformed the Revolutionary Tribunal into an engine of condemnation without appeal. It suppressed the preliminary examination of accused persons; it allowed the judges to convict on moral proof — on the inner conviction of the jurors — without the need for material evidence; it denied the accused the assistance of counsel; it reduced the trial itself to a single question: Did the prisoner appear before the Tribunal as an enemy of the people? Those who answered in the affirmative were sentenced to death. There was no other possible verdict.
What followed has been called the Great Terror. In the forty-nine days between the passage of the Law of 22 Prairial and the fall of Robespierre, the Revolutionary Tribunal condemned more than thirteen hundred persons to death — a rate of execution that exceeded anything that had come before. The prisons of Paris were crowded with suspects; the tumbrils rolled daily from the Conciergerie to the Place de la Révolution; the guillotine, which had once been reserved for the great enemies of the Revolution, now fell upon the humblest of citizens — servants who had spoken ill of the Republic, peasants who had evaded the requisitions, old women who had prayed for the King. The blade was never dry.
The deputies of the Convention watched this acceleration with a fear that was personal and immediate. The Law of 22 Prairial had not specified who might be brought before the Tribunal; it had only removed every obstacle to conviction. Any deputy could be denounced; any deputy could be arrested; any deputy could be sent to the guillotine within days of accusation. The Revolutionary Tribunal had already consumed the Hébertists in March, the Dantonists in April; the Committee of Public Safety had purged the Cordeliers, the Indulgents, and all who stood between. There was no reason to suppose that the Convention itself — those deputies who had voted for the execution of the King, who had voted for the proscription of the Girondins, who had given the Committee its powers — would be spared. On the contrary: the more the Terror accelerated, the more the list of the denounced grew, and the more the deputies saw their own names whispered in the corridors of the Tuileries.
II. The Conspiracy
The conspiracy that formed against Robespierre in the weeks before Thermidor was not a conspiracy of principles but of fears. It was a coalition of the Convenient, as Pagès called it — an alliance of men who had nothing in common but their terror of the guillotine. The Mountain had been Robespierre’s instrument; the Terror had been his policy; and those who had served him most faithfully now had the most reason to dread him.
The centre of the plot was Tallien, a deputy who had been sent on mission to Bordeaux and who, having enriched himself there and having married the beautiful Thérésia Cabarrus, had returned to Paris to find that the Committee of Public Safety was preparing his arrest. Tallien had been one of the fiercest Jacobins; he had voted for the death of the King and for the proscription of the Girondins. But he was marked. His mistress had been arrested; his own head was in question. He had nothing to lose.
With Tallien came Barras — the former nobleman, the man of pleasure and violence, who had commanded the army of the South and had returned to the capital to watch the Terror consume its authors. Fréron, who had been sent to Marseilles and had distinguished himself by his brutality, now found that the same violence that had served the Committee might be used against him. Fouché, the former oratorian, the man of cold calculations and unshakeable nerve, had been recalled from Lyon, where he had presided over the fusillades and the noyades in the name of revolutionary justice; Robespierre had denounced him publicly, and Fouché knew that his life depended on the destruction of the man who had made him.
And there was Carnot — the great organiser of victory, the man who had raised the armies of the Republic — who had quarrelled with Robespierre over the conduct of the war, who had watched the Committee’s political domination encroach upon his military authority. The Committee itself, which had once been the solid instrument of the revolutionary government, was now divided: Billaud-Varenne and Collot d’Herbois, who had been responsible for the Terror in Lyon and feared that Robespierre would make them its scapegoats; Saint-Just, who remained loyal to Robespierre to the end; and Barère, who trimmed his sails to every wind.
The conspirators met in secret. They dared not speak openly; Robespierre still commanded the loyalty of the Jacobin Club, the sections of Paris, and the Commune. But they met — in the corridors of the Tuileries, in the houses of the deputies, in the gardens of the Palais-Royal — and they laid their plans. They knew that Robespierre was preparing a speech to the Convention, a speech in which he would denounce his enemies by name. They knew that he was waiting for the right moment. And they knew that they must strike before he did.
III. The Speech of 8 Thermidor
On the eighth of Thermidor — the twenty-sixth of July, 1794 — Robespierre rose in the Convention to deliver the speech that would seal his fate.
He spoke for two hours. It was a long, rambling, terrible speech — not the clear denunciation his friends had expected, but a vague and menacing accusation against unnamed conspirators. Robespierre denounced a plot against the Republic, a conspiracy of the corrupt and the ambitious who sought to destroy the revolutionary government. He spoke of deputies who had enriched themselves, of false patriots who had committed crimes in the name of the Revolution and now sought to turn the public hatred against the Committee. He called for the purification of the Convention, the punishment of the wicked, the defence of virtue against the assaults of vice.
But he would not name names.
The Convention listened in silence — a cold, hostile silence that Robespierre mistook for agreement. He demanded that his enemies be punished; he refused to say who they were. He invoked the Committee of Public Safety; he attacked the Committee of General Security; he called for the reconstruction of both, but would not say which of their members he accused. The deputies sat frozen, each man wondering whether his name was among the denounced, each man waiting for the blow that would fall from a hand he could not see.
When Robespierre finished, there was a long pause. Then Cambon — the financier of the Revolution, the man who had raised the armies and fed the nation — rose to speak. He was a member of the Committee of Public Safety; he had worked with Robespierre for months. Now he turned on him with a fury that shocked the Assembly. “It is time to tell the truth,” Cambon said. “One man alone paralyzes the will of the Convention. That man is Robespierre.”
Others followed. The silence broke into a storm of accusation. Robespierre, pale and trembling, tried to speak again, but his voice was drowned by the cries of the deputies. He had come to the Convention expecting to destroy his enemies; he left it with the knowledge that he had given them the weapon they needed.
That evening, at the Jacobin Club, Robespierre recovered his voice. He read the same speech to the assembled Jacobins, and this time the reception was very different. The Jacobins applauded him; they embraced him; they swore to defend him against the traitors of the Convention. Billaud-Varenne and Collot d’Herbois, who had followed him from the Convention into the Club, were driven from the tribune; they barely escaped the fury of the Jacobins, who would have torn them to pieces. The Club voted to expel all who had spoken against Robespierre; the Commune of Paris prepared to support him.
The lines were drawn. That night, Paris was a city divided against itself, waiting for the morning.
IV. The Ninth of Thermidor
The twenty-seventh of July, 1794 — the ninth of Thermidor, Year II of the Republic — began in confusion. The Convention assembled in the morning with a tension that could be felt in the air. The galleries were packed; the deputies were armed; the streets outside were filled with the patrols of the Commune and the loyal battalions of the revolutionary sections.
Saint-Just rose to speak. He was Robespierre’s closest ally, the most brilliant orator of the Mountain, the man who had written the most terrible decrees of the revolutionary government. He had prepared a speech in defence of Robespierre — a calm, measured, devastating indictment of the conspirators who had plotted against the Incorruptible. He began to read.
He was not allowed to finish.
Tallien interrupted him. The deputy from the Indre-et-Loire, who had been waiting for this moment, who had prepared his own speech, who had nerved himself for the act that would either save his life or end it, rose from his bench and demanded the floor. “I ask the permission of the Assembly to speak a few words,” he said, “and I hope that I shall be allowed to do so.”
Saint-Just hesitated. Tallien began to speak, and his voice was the voice of all the deputies who had trembled through the Great Terror. He had armed himself with a dagger — he brandished it before the Assembly. “I have armed myself with a dagger,” he cried, “to pierce the heart of the new Cromwell if the Convention does not have the courage to decree his accusation!” The words were a signal. The Mountain, which had been Robespierre’s Mountain, broke apart. The deputies rose from their benches; the hall filled with shouting; the President’s bell was drowned by the uproar.
Tallien demanded the arrest of the Robespierre’s creatures — Henriot, the commandant of the National Guard of Paris; Dumas, the President of the Revolutionary Tribunal; the members of the Committee of General Security who had served the Terror. The Convention, caught in the current of accusation, voted the arrests without debate. Then Tallien, seconded by Billaud-Varenne and Collot d’Herbois, turned on Robespierre himself.
“I demand the arrest of Maximilien Robespierre!” Tallien shouted.
The Convention roared its approval. Robespierre tried to speak — tried to mount the tribune, tried to make himself heard above the din. His voice was drowned. He turned to the deputies of the Right, the Plain, the men who had never spoken against him, who had voted as he wished, who had survived by silence. “For the last time,” he cried, “will you hear me?” No one answered. The President, Thuriot, who had been chosen by the conspirators, rang his bell and refused him the floor.
Then the decrees were passed. The Convention ordered the arrest of Maximilien Robespierre, his brother Augustin Robespierre, Louis-Antoine Saint-Just, Georges Couthon, Philippe Le Bas, and François Hanriot. The deputies of the Mountain, who had been Robespierre’s followers, watched in silence as the men who had commanded the Revolution were led from the hall. Robespierre was taken to the Luxembourg prison; Saint-Just to the Écossais; Couthon to the Bourbe; the others to their separate prisons.
V. The Rising of the Commune
But the Convention had not reckoned with the Commune of Paris.
Word of the arrests reached the Hôtel de Ville within hours. The Commune, which had been Robespierre’s most faithful instrument, did not accept the authority of the Convention. It ordered the tocsin to be rung; it ordered the sections to rise; it ordered the prisons to be opened and the arrested deputies to be liberated.
The revolution of the Commune against the Convention began in the afternoon and continued through the night. The sections of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and the Faubourg Saint-Marceau, which had marched on the Tuileries on the tenth of August, rose again. The National Guard of Paris, which had been commanded by Hanriot, answered the call of the Commune. The gates of the Luxembourg were forced; Robespierre was taken from his cell and carried in triumph to the Hôtel de Ville.
But Robespierre, released from prison, hesitated. He had been a prisoner; he had seen the Convention turn against him; he had felt the hand of power slip from his grasp. The Commune urged him to lead the insurrection, to march on the Convention, to crush the conspirators who had arrested him. But Robespierre could not act. He was exhausted; he was uncertain; he had spent his life in the service of the Revolution, and he could not bring himself to attack the Convention that embodied it. He sat in the Hôtel de Ville, waiting, while the hours passed and the night deepened.
The Commune, meanwhile, worked with desperate energy. It issued decrees in Robespierre’s name; it arrested the commissioners of the Convention; it summoned the sections to arms; it prepared the barricades. The tocsin rang from the church towers; the drums beat the générale; the streets of Paris filled with armed men. By nine in the evening, the Hôtel de Ville was a fortress, surrounded by the battalions of the loyal sections, guarded by the gunners of the National Guard. The Commune believed that it held Paris.
VI. The Defection of the Sections
But the Commune had overestimated its power.
The Convention, which had wavered through the afternoon, recovered its nerve. It appointed Barras to command the armed force of the Convention; it declared the Commune outlawed; it sent commissioners to the sections of Paris — not to demand submission, but to argue, to persuade, to remind the citizens of Paris that the Convention was the sovereign power of the nation. And the sections, one by one, began to abandon the Commune.
The National Guard, which had marched to the Hôtel de Ville in the afternoon, began to melt away in the night. The men were tired; they had been under arms since morning; they had no clear orders; they saw the Convention arrayed against the Commune and did not know whom to follow. Barras, who had commanded armies in the field, moved through the streets with the calm authority of a man who had long since passed beyond fear. He spoke to the commanders of the sections; he promised amnesty; he threatened the guillotine. By midnight, the battalions that had surrounded the Hôtel de Ville had begun to disperse.
The Convention decreed the outlawry of Robespierre and his allies. The decree had a single, terrible consequence: any man outlawed by the Convention could be executed on sight, without trial, without appeal. The price of Robespierre’s head was set at the stroke of a pen.
VII. The Second Arrest
At the Hôtel de Ville, the night was passing in confusion. Robespierre sat in the great hall of the municipal building, surrounded by the revolutionary officials of the Commune, waiting for a decision that would not come. He had been urged to march; he had refused. He had been urged to issue a proclamation; he had hesitated. The Commune, which had risen for him, now began to see that he would not lead it.
At two in the morning of the tenth of Thermidor, the forces of the Convention arrived at the Hôtel de Ville. The doors were forced; the guards dispersed; the hall filled with the men of the Convention. Robespierre, hearing the noise, rose from his chair. He knew what was coming.
He tried to take his own life. He had a pistol; he put it to his mouth and pulled the trigger. The shot shattered his jaw but did not kill him. He fell to the ground, covered in blood, his face a ruin of bone and flesh. The soldiers of the Convention found him lying on the floor, moaning, his teeth scattered across the stones.
The others died or were captured. Couthon, whose legs had been paralysed from the waist down by a spinal disease, was thrown from a window by the soldiers; he broke his body on the pavement below and was taken up for execution. Le Bas, the deputy who had been Robespierre’s most faithful disciple, was more successful in his suicide; he shot himself dead in the chamber of the Hôtel de Ville and was not taken alive. The younger Robespierre — Augustin, who had followed his brother to the end — threw himself from a window and survived, broken, to be executed with the others. Hanriot, the commander of the National Guard, was dragged from a sewer where he had tried to hide.
The prisoners were taken to the Conciergerie. Robespierre, his jaw shattered, his face bound in a bloody cloth, lay on a table in the antechamber of the prison, waiting for the morning. He was not given a trial; he was not given a bed; he was not given water. The men who had arrested him did not wish to hear him speak.
VIII. The Tenth of Thermidor
The morning of the tenth of Thermidor was clear and hot. The tumbrils were prepared at the Conciergerie, as they had been prepared every day for months, but this time the prisoners were different. This time, the men who had made the Terror were going to die by the instrument they had perfected.
Robespierre was lifted onto the tumbril. He could not stand; he could not speak; his shattered jaw hung open, bound by a cloth that was soaked through with blood. The crowd that lined the streets did not jeer at him; they did not cheer; they watched in a silence that was more terrible than any cry. Some said that he looked like a corpse already — that the face that had dominated the Revolution, that had spoken from the tribune of the Convention, that had sent thousands to the guillotine, was no longer a face at all but a mask of suffering.
The tumbrils passed through the streets of Paris, along the same route that the condemned had taken every day since the Terror began. The crowd grew as the procession approached the Place de la Révolution. The guillotine stood where it had always stood — at the foot of the statue of Liberty, on the spot where the King had died eighteen months before. The blade was ready.
Robespierre was carried to the scaffold. The executioner tore the bandage from his face; the shattered jaw gaped open; a cry of pain and rage escaped from the man who could no longer speak. The crowd saw the face of the Incorruptible — the face of the man who had sent Danton to death, who had purged the Hébertists, who had made the Law of 22 Prairial — and for a moment, there was silence. Then the blade fell.
The head of Maximilien Robespierre was lifted by the executioner and shown to the people. A great cry rose from the crowd — not the “Vive la République” that had greeted the death of the King, but a cry of relief, of joy, of a nation that had been liberated from a nightmare. The people danced in the streets. The prisons of Paris, which had been filled with suspects, opened their gates. The news spread through France: the Terror was over.
IX. The Thermidorian Reaction
The fall of Robespierre was the end of the Terror, but it was not the end of the Revolution. The Thermidorian Reaction — the period that followed the execution of the Incorruptible — was a slow and chaotic unwinding of the revolutionary government. The Committees of Public Safety and General Security were stripped of their powers; the Revolutionary Tribunal was reformed; the Jacobin Club was closed; the Law of 22 Prairial was repealed. The prisoners of the Terror, who had filled the prisons of France, were released by the thousands. The men who had conspired against Robespierre — Tallien, Barras, Fréron, Fouché — became the masters of the Convention.
But the Reaction had its own violence. The Jacobins were hunted through the streets of Paris; the sections that had supported Robespierre were disarmed; the memory of the Terror was punished in the bodies of those who had served it. The jeunesse dorée — the gilded youth of the Reaction — patrolled the boulevards with clubs and cudgels, beating the Jacobins who dared to show themselves. The White Terror in the provinces surpassed in some places the Red Terror it replaced.
Louvet, who had been proscribed with the Girondins and who returned from hiding after Thermidor, found a city transformed. The men who had denounced him were now the men in power; the men who had sent him into exile were now the men in the prisons. He walked the streets of Paris — the same streets he had walked as a deputy of the Convention, as a proscript, as a fugitive — and he saw the same faces, the same fears, the same shifting allegiances that had marked the Revolution from its beginning. The fall of Robespierre did not bring the Republic that Louvet had dreamed of; it brought only a change of masters.
X. The Meaning of Thermidor
Benjamin Constant, writing two years after the event, gave the Thermidorian coup its most penetrating analysis. The fall of Robespierre, he argued, was not merely the destruction of a tyrant but the demonstration of a fundamental truth about the nature of revolutionary government. The Terror had been based on the principle of arbitrary power — the power of a committee to arrest, to judge, to execute without appeal. That power had been turned against the very men who had wielded it, and the Revolution had discovered, in the most terrible way, that arbitrary power is a weapon that can be used by any hand.
“The government that had claimed the right to strike down all its enemies,” Constant wrote, “had itself been struck down by a faction of its own creation. The men who had proscribed the Girondins, who had sent Danton to the scaffold, who had filled the prisons with suspects, now found themselves the objects of the same justice they had invented. They had built a machine of destruction that could not be controlled; and when they tried to stop it, it devoured them.”
The lesson of Thermidor, for Constant, was that a government founded on force alone carries within itself the seeds of its own destruction. The revolutionary government had no foundation but the will of those who wielded it; and that will could change, could divide, could turn against itself. The Terror had consumed its creators; the Revolution had devoured its own children. And France, exhausted, bleeding, and uncertain, stood at the beginning of a new phase of its history — a phase in which the forms of liberty would be slowly restored, and the substance of power would pass into other hands.
The ninth of Thermidor did not end the Revolution. But it ended the Terror. And in doing so, it ended the Revolution as it had been known — the Revolution of the guillotine, of the Committees, of the Law of Suspects, of the revolutionary tribunals that had judged and condemned without appeal. What followed would be slower, more complex, and in some ways more terrible. But the heart of the Terror had been cut out on the Place de la Révolution, and the man who had personified it lay in the common grave of the executed, his shattered jaw bound in a bloody cloth, his name cursed by the people he had tried to save.

Source Material

Pierre Pagès, Histoire secrète de la Révolution française (6 vols., 1801). Pagès provides the primary narrative of the events of 8–10 Thermidor, Year II: the Law of 22 Prairial, the formation of the conspiracy in the Convention, the speeches of 8 and 9 Thermidor, the arrest of Robespierre, the rising of the Commune, the second arrest at the Hôtel de Ville, the execution, and the Thermidorian Reaction.
Jean-Baptiste Louvet, Mémoires de Louvet (1823). Louvet, a Girondin deputy who had been proscribed and forced into hiding, returned to Paris after Thermidor; his account captures the atmosphere of the days following the fall of Robespierre — the release of prisoners, the joy of the city, the changing of the political guard.
Benjamin Constant, De la force du gouvernement actuel et de la nécessité de s’y rallier (1796). Constant analyzes Thermidor as a theoretical demonstration of the instability of arbitrary government: a revolutionary power founded on force alone must eventually turn against its own agents, proving that no faction can safely wield a power that has no foundation but will.

events/battle-of-austerlitz.title: The Battle of Austerlitz
events/battle-of-austerlitz.content:
The Battle of Austerlitz
The Army from the Sea
On the 27th of August 1805, the emperor gave the order that changed the direction of the war. The Grande Armée, which for two years had been encamped on the heights above Boulogne, watching the white cliffs of England across the grey Channel waters, was to break camp and march east. One hundred and thirty thousand of the most brilliant soldiers of the age — the men who had fought in Italy, in Egypt, in Germany — turned their backs on the sea and began the movement that would carry them, in three months, from the shores of the English Channel to the field of Austerlitz.
The decision was not a choice but a necessity. The invasion of England, the great design that had occupied Napoleon since the rupture of the Peace of Amiens in May 1803, had collapsed at sea. Vice-Admiral Villeneuve, returning from the West Indies with the combined Franco-Spanish fleet, had been intercepted by Calder off Cape Finisterre on 22 July; the action was inconclusive, but Villeneuve had taken refuge in Coruña and then in Cadiz, his will broken. The Toulon fleet that was to have covered the crossing of the Grand Army was scattered and contained. Nelson was returning to his command. The Channel remained closed.
Napoleon understood the meaning of the failure with perfect clarity. “If I am master of the Straits for six hours,” he had said, “I shall be master of the world.” The six hours never came. The navy had failed him, and the invasion was impossible. But the army that could not cross the sea could still march across a continent. Austria and Russia, encouraged by British gold and British diplomacy, had formed the Third Coalition; they believed Napoleon was fixed on the Channel coast, his army tied to its flat-bottomed boats. They were about to learn how quickly an emperor who could not sail could still strike.
The Wheel of the Grande Armée
The movement that followed was one of the most extraordinary in the history of war. The Grande Armée, organized into seven corps under the ablest marshals of the age — Bernadotte, Davout, Soult, Lannes, Ney, Marmont, Augereau — was marched not directly toward Austria but eastward along the Channel coast, then southward through France, crossing the Rhine on a broad front between Strasbourg and Mannheim. The speed was phenomenal: the corps marched separately but converged with the precision of a machine, each commander knowing only his own part but the whole co-ordinated from a single mind.
Napoleon had not waited for his army to assemble before acting. On 25 September, while the Austrian army under General Mack was advancing into Bavaria, the French corps began to cross the Rhine. The plan was Napoleonic in its audacity: instead of advancing directly on the Austrian positions, the Grande Armée would wheel to the south-east, passing north of the Austrian army, crossing the Danube behind it, and cutting its lines of communication with Vienna. The Austrian commander, an able theorist who had never commanded an army in the field, found himself beset by an enemy that seemed to be everywhere at once. On 6 October, the French crossed the Danube at Donauwörth; by the 11th, the Austrian army, which had advanced confidently into Germany, was isolated and surrounded in the fortress of Ulm.
The encirclement of Ulm was a masterpiece of what the nineteenth century would call strategy of annihilation. Mack, with some sixty thousand men, waited for a Russian army that was still marching through Moravia, too far away to help. On 20 October, with his supplies exhausted and his escape routes blocked, Mack surrendered his entire army to Napoleon. Twenty-seven thousand prisoners, sixty guns, and the whole of the Austrian field army in Germany were lost. The soldiers of the Grande Armée had not fought a pitched battle; they had marched the enemy into the ground.
The news reached Napoleon on the same day that Nelson, far away off Cape Trafalgar, was breaking the line of the combined fleet and receiving the mortal shot that would kill him. The two events, separated by a continent and an ocean, were not unrelated. Napoleon’s decision to turn east had been forced upon him by the failure of his naval combinations; but once he had turned, he moved with a speed and decisiveness that made the Third Coalition seem to be fighting in slow motion.
Vienna
The surrender at Ulm left the road to Vienna open. The remnants of the Austrian army and the approaching Russian forces under General Kutuzov retreated eastward, keeping the Danube between themselves and the French. Napoleon advanced without pause: on 13 November, the Grande Armée entered Vienna unopposed. The imperial capital was abandoned by the court, deserted by the government; the emperor Francis had fled to Brünn, into the arms of his Russian allies.
Napoleon established himself at Schönbrunn and for a moment seemed to be master of everything that the Hapsburg monarchy had built over three centuries. But the occupation of Vienna was a strategic complication as much as a triumph. The Grande Armée had marched five hundred miles in two months. Its supply lines were stretched across the breadth of Germany; the harvest of 1805 had been poor, and the army, which had been provisioned for a campaign of weeks, was now entering the winter months far from its magazines. The Russian army, under the overall command of the Tsar Alexander and the immediate direction of Kutuzov, had not been destroyed. It was retreating eastward, drawing the French deeper into the frozen landscape of central Europe, husbanding its strength for a battle on ground of its own choosing.
The allied plan was as old as war itself: trade space for time. The Prussians were arming in the north; the winter was advancing; if the Austrian and Russian armies could hold out without fighting a decisive action, Napoleon would be forced either to retreat or to fight at a disadvantage. The emperor knew this perfectly. He had perhaps a month — six weeks at most — in which to force a battle before the weather and the converging armies of the Coalition would make his position untenable.
This was the argument that Paganel would later make, and Mahan would make it with even greater force: Trafalgar caused Austerlitz. The naval defeat of 21 October did not merely make the invasion of England impossible; it made a safe retreat impossible. The British blockade had cut the French Empire’s maritime commerce; the harvest of 1805 could not feed an army indefinitely. Napoleon could not winter in Vienna; he could not return to France with his work unfinished; he could not wait for the Russian and Austrian armies to double their strength. He had to fight, and he had to fight soon. The battle, when it came, would be imposed by necessity as much as by design.
The Pratzen Heights
The allied army — approximately eighty-five thousand Russians and Austrians under the nominal command of Kutuzov but the effective direction of the Tsar Alexander, who had joined the army in person — took up its position on the Pratzen Heights, a gently sloping plateau that dominated the landscape around the little Moravian town of Austerlitz, some sixty miles north of Vienna. The position was strong: the heights commanded the approach from the west, and the allied army was concentrated on the high ground, with the Austrian contingent on the right and the Russians on the left and centre.
Napoleon’s army, perhaps seventy-three thousand men, arrived before the allied position and — by deliberate design — appeared to be in a state of dangerous weakness. The emperor had marched his corps into positions that suggested he was overextended: the French right, on the Goldbach stream, was held by a thin line of troops; the left, anchored on the Santon hill, was more strongly held but still seemed dangerously stretched. Napoleon was offering a trap, and he relied on the Tsar’s inexperience and the allied eagerness to accept the bait.
He did not rely in vain. The allied war council, dominated by the young Tsar and the Austrian chief of staff Weyrother, against the experienced Kutuzov’s prudent advice, adopted a plan as bold as it was misguided. They would turn the French right, cutting Napoleon’s line of retreat to Vienna, rolling up the army from south to north, and crowding the French against the frozen marshes and lakes that lay at the southern end of the battlefield. To accomplish this, the allied centre would abandon the Pratzen Heights and march south, overwhelming the thin French right wing with a crushing superiority.
It was precisely what Napoleon had hoped for. If the allies abandoned the Pratzen Heights to attack his right, the heights themselves would be exposed. Soult’s corps, concealed from view by the morning mist that rose from the Goldbach valley, was ordered to be ready to take them the moment the allied centre moved away.
The Sun of Austerlitz
The 2nd of December 1805 — the first anniversary of Napoleon’s coronation — dawned cold and foggy. The allied army had marched through the night, executing its great turning movement. At first light, the attack on the French right began in earnest. The village of Telnitz fell; the outnumbered French defenders under Davout — who had marched his corps sixty miles from Vienna in forty-eight hours to reinforce the threatened wing — fought a desperate holding action, falling back from position to position, buying time with the lives of his men.
At approximately eight o’clock, Napoleon rode along the front of the centre. The mist was beginning to clear. Through the thinning fog, Soult’s division commanders could see that the Pratzen Heights, which had been crowded with allied troops the night before, were now emptier. The allied centre had indeed abandoned the plateau to join the attack on the French south.
Napoleon turned to Soult. “How long will it take you to reach the heights?”
“Sire,” Soult replied, “they will be at the summit in twenty minutes, if the enemy does not obstruct us.”
“Then wait a quarter of an hour,” said the emperor.
At nine o’clock, Soult’s corps — twenty thousand men who had been lying in the valley, invisible to the allies behind the fog and the folds of the ground — rose and advanced. The sun, which had been obscured all morning, broke through the mist at the same moment, shining full in the eyes of the allied troops on the heights. It was the famous “sun of Austerlitz” — a thing of legend to the soldiers who remembered it, an omen that convinced the army that destiny was with them.
Soult’s advance rolled up the thin crust of allied troops still holding the Pratzen. The allied centre collapsed within two hours. Kutuzov, unable to persuade the Tsar to react in time, watched the destruction of his army’s centre from the heights as the French poured onto the plateau in irresistible force.
The battle then broke into two halves. On the allied left, the Russian Imperial Guard attacked the French centre north of the Pratzen in a desperate counterattack that came closer to success than any other part of the allied effort that day. The Russian Guard cavalry, splendidly mounted and magnificently brave, broke through the French infantry and threatened Napoleon’s own headquarters. Rapp counter-charged with the Guard cavalry — the famous Mamelukes of the Imperial Guard, the grenadiers à cheval — and a ferocious mêlée developed on the heights. The French Guard eventually held, but only after a bitter struggle that left the Russian Guard shattered.
On the allied right — the southern flank, which had been the scene of the original allied attack — the turn of events transformed the Austrian-Russian effort from an offensive to a desperate retreat. The French right, reinforced by Davout’s hard-marching corps, was no longer merely holding its ground but pressing forward. The allies who had attacked in the morning found themselves attacked in turn, driven southward across the battlefield, their retreat blocked by the frozen lakes — the ponds of Menitz and Satschan.
What happened on the frozen lakes has passed into legend. Thousands of allied soldiers, trying to escape across the ice, found their path blocked. French artillery fired on the ice, which broke under the weight of horses, guns, and men. The official story — that the ice opened and swallowed whole battalions — is almost certainly exaggerated; but the image of the cold, dark waters of the Satschan pond receiving the drowned bodies of the Tsar’s soldiers became one of the fixed memories of the Napoleonic wars. The allied army disintegrated. By four in the afternoon, the battle was over.
The numbers tell part of the story. Fifteen thousand allied dead and wounded; twelve thousand prisoners; a hundred and eighty guns captured. French losses were perhaps eight thousand. But the numbers do not capture the completeness of the victory. The allied army that had marched confidently toward Austerlitz on the morning of 2 December had ceased to exist as a fighting force. The Russians retreated eastward in disorder; the Austrians had no army left in the field. The Third Coalition had been shattered in a single day.
The Treaty of Pressburg
The Tsar Alexander, his army broken, retreated into Poland and refused further operations. The emperor of Austria, Francis II, had no such luxury. His capital was occupied; his army was destroyed; he could not continue the war. On 4 December, he met Napoleon in person at the Spaleny Mill, near the battlefield, and agreed to an armistice. The negotiations that followed were swift; Napoleon dictated the terms.
The Treaty of Pressburg, signed on 26 December 1805, was the most sweeping settlement Napoleon had yet imposed. Austria recognized Napoleon as King of Italy; ceded Venetia, Istria, and Dalmatia to the French kingdom of Italy; surrendered the Tyrol to Bavaria and the Vorarlberg and several Swabian territories to Württemberg; paid an immense indemnity; and acknowledged the complete independence of the sovereigns of Bavaria, Württemberg, and Baden, who were elevated to kingdoms and bound by treaty to Napoleon. Austria was reduced from a great power to a secondary state; it had lost three million subjects and large portions of its revenue and territory.
The Treaty of Pressburg, in Paganel’s judgment, was not a peace but a suspension of arms — like Campo Formio and Lunéville before it. Napoleon treated the treaty as he treated a plan of campaign: he commanded it. The pride of the House of Austria was humiliated, but not destroyed, and Paganel saw in this humiliation the seeds of further wars. “He did not suffer the council,” Paganel wrote, “when he negotiated peace, any more than when he planned or made war.” The consequences were not long in coming.
The Confederation of the Rhine and the End of the Holy Roman Empire
The reorganization of Germany that followed Pressburg was more far-reaching than the territorial settlement with Austria. In July 1806, sixteen German states — Bavaria, Württemberg, Baden, Hesse-Darmstadt, and others — formally withdrew from the Holy Roman Empire and entered into a new Confederation of the Rhine, with Napoleon as its Protector. The Confederation committed its members to provide sixty-three thousand troops to the French Emperor in the event of war; in return, they received territorial gains, sovereign status, and the protection of the French Empire.
The Holy Roman Empire, which had existed in one form or another for a thousand years, was effectively dissolved. In August 1806, the Emperor Francis II — who had also been Holy Roman Emperor Francis II — laid down the imperial crown. The ancient structure that had claimed to be the secular arm of Christendom, that had survived the Reformation, the Thirty Years’ War, and the armies of Louis XIV, was ended by a stroke of Napoleon’s pen.
The Victory That Cost Everything
The victory at Austerlitz was Napoleon’s most brilliant achievement as a commander — the battle that above all others confirmed his claim to genius. The combination of strategic audacity (the march from Boulogne), operational speed (the encirclement at Ulm), tactical deception (the deliberately weakened right wing, the abandonment of the Pratzen), and the perfect timing of the execution created a victory that became the model for everything that followed.
But Paganel — writing from the perspective of a man who had been silenced by the Empire and who now spoke freely from its ruins — saw Austerlitz as the moment when Napoleon’s ambition crossed a threshold from which there was no return. “The battle of Austerlitz,” he wrote, “was decisive against the united powers and against ourselves. It swelled the pride and the ambitious pretensions of Napoleon.” The emperor who had been content to be First Consul of the French Republic was now the master of Europe; the emperor who had crossed the Pratzen Heights that December morning had destroyed the Third Coalition, but he had also destroyed any possibility of moderation in his own soul.
The deeper analysis belongs to Mahan, who saw in the campaign of 1805 the proof of his great thesis about sea power. Trafalgar, fought six weeks before Austerlitz, had made the victory on land possible only by making the victory at sea impossible. Napoleon had not chosen to fight at Austerlitz; he had been driven there by the failure of his maritime design, by the British blockade that choked his supplies, by the harvest crisis that forced him to seek a decision before winter closed the roads. The Grande Armée that marched from Boulogne to the Pratzen was the army that had been meant to conquer England, and it marched east only because Nelson had barred the western passage. Austerlitz was a victory of the first order, but it was a victory won on ground that Napoleon had not chosen, under conditions that he had not desired, against enemies who had forced his hand.
The structure of the European war after Austerlitz reflected this paradox. Napoleon was supreme on land; no continental power could stand against him in the field. But he was confined to the continent. The sea belonged to England; the commerce of the world flowed through English ports; the colonial empires of France and Spain and Holland had been stripped away or blockaded into ruin. The emperor who had conquered Europe could not command the ocean that surrounded it.
In the years that followed, Napoleon would try to break the English hold by economic warfare — the Continental System, the Berlin Decree, the Milan Decree — closing every European port to British goods, attempting to starve the island into submission. It was the strategy of a land power trying to do what it could not do at sea. It would lead him into Spain, into Portugal, into Russia; it would drain the Grande Armée in a hundred small wars and one great catastrophe; it would bring him finally to Waterloo and to Saint Helena.
But all of that was still in the future on the evening of 2 December 1805, when Napoleon rode across the Pratzen Heights under the fading winter sun, past the bodies of fifteen thousand dead and dying men, past the shattered remnants of the Russian Guard, past the guns that had been captured from the emperor of Austria. He was thirty-six years old. He had won the greatest victory of the age. He was already, in the precise sense that Mahan would later define, a prisoner of the sea.
