events/battle-of-copenhagen.title: The Battle of Copenhagen
events/battle-of-copenhagen.content:
The Battle of Copenhagen
The Baltic Expedition
Great Britain, by the spring of 1801, stood alone against all Europe. The Armed Neutrality of the Northern powers—Russia, Sweden, Denmark, and Prussia—had closed the Baltic to British shipping and threatened the supply of naval stores upon which the Royal Navy depended. To break this combination, a fleet of eighteen sail-of-the-line and thirty-five smaller vessels was assembled at Yarmouth on the east coast of England.
The chief command was given to Sir Hyde Parker, a gallant and respectable officer of the old school, but one whose caution was ill-suited to a campaign demanding audacity and speed. As his second-in-command, the government sent Horatio Nelson—the hero of the Nile, the most aggressive and brilliant fighting admiral in the British service. The choice of Parker over Nelson was a mistake that would have been avoided had Lord St. Vincent, who succeeded Earl Spencer as First Lord a few weeks later, been in office when the expedition was planned. Nelson was still among the junior flag-officers, and his conduct in the Mediterranean under the influence of Lady Hamilton had perhaps raised doubts about his fitness for so delicate a command. Whatever the reason, the withholding of the chief command from Nelson weakened the expedition from the start.
The fleet sailed from Yarmouth on the 12th of March, 1801. By the 19th, despite a heavy gale that had scattered the ships, nearly all were collected off the Skaw, the northern point of Jutland at the entrance to the Kattegat. The wind was fair for Copenhagen, and Nelson chafed at delay. “While the negotiation is going on,” he said, “the Dane should see our flag waving every moment he lifted his head.” But Parker sent the envoy forward in a single frigate while the fleet waited.
On the 21st the fleet was off Elsinore. The envoy rejoined them: Denmark had rejected the British terms. The time for negotiation had passed; it only remained to act, and the wind was favourable—an advantage that at any moment might be lost. Nelson immediately addressed a letter to Parker summing up the situation with luminous clarity. “Not a moment should be lost in attacking,” he wrote. “We shall never be so good a match for them as at this moment.” He pointed out that the fleet should have been off Copenhagen when the negotiation failed; then the Danish ships could have been destroyed at once. “Almost the safety, certainly the honor, of England is more entrusted to you than ever yet fell to the lot of any British officer,” he concluded.
The Plan of Attack
Copenhagen lies on the east coast of the island of Zealand, fronting Sweden across the Sound. Before the city, shallow flats extend for half a mile from the shore, and in the Sound itself, little more than a mile out, lies a long shoal called the Middle Ground. Between these two bodies of shallow water runs the King’s Channel, through which heavy ships could sail. At the northern end of this channel, a deep pocket stretches toward the harbour, defended by powerful works rising on piles out of the shoal water—the formidable Three-Crown Batteries. The Danes had moored a line of armed hulks and floating batteries along the inner edge of the King’s Channel, covering the front of the city.
The natural point of attack appeared to be from the north, but Nelson rejected this approach, which he dismissed as “taking the bull by the horns.” Not only was the head of the Danish line exceedingly strong, but the wind that was fair to attack would be foul to return. A disabled ship would have no escape but by running the gauntlet of the entire Danish line. More importantly, so long as the British fleet remained in the Sound without entering the Baltic, the way was left open for the Swedes and Russians to join the Danes. Nelson therefore advised that a sufficiently strong force should attack the southern end of the Danish line, interposing between Copenhagen and the Baltic.
Nelson’s letter of March 24, 1801, was a masterpiece of military reasoning. He concluded with a suggestion worthy of Bonaparte himself: a detachment to Revel to destroy the Russian squadron there. “The measure may be thought bold,” he wrote, “but I am of opinion the boldest are the safest; and our country demands a most vigorous exertion of her force, directed with judgment.” He saw the Northern League as a tree, with Paul of Russia as the trunk and Sweden and Denmark as the branches. “If I can get at the trunk and hew it down, the branches fall of course; but I may lop the branches and yet not be able to fell the tree, and my power must be weaker when its greatest strength is required.”
At Revel lay twelve Russian ships-of-the-line—fully half their Baltic fleet. Their destruction would have paralyzed the naval power of the empire. But Parker was not the man for such a stroke. He adopted Nelson’s plan for the attack on Copenhagen but not the broader strategic conception. Nelson was given twelve ships-of-the-line—two more than he had asked—and the task of destroying the Danish floating defences.
The Sounding of the King’s Deep
The nights of the 30th and 31st of March were employed sounding the King’s Channel. It was perilous work. The pilots were mostly mates of merchantmen trading with the Baltic, and their experience in vessels of three or four hundred tons did not fit them for the charge of heavy battleships. They betrayed throughout a great indecision that would contribute to the principal mishaps of the day.
On the 1st of April the fleet moved up to the north end of the Middle Ground, about four miles from the city. That afternoon, Nelson’s division got under way, passed through the outer channel, and anchored towards sundown off the south-east end of the shoal, two miles from the head of the Danish line. Nelson announced his purpose to attack as soon as the wind served. The night was passed in arranging the order of battle.
The Danish line stretched in a north-west to south-east direction for somewhat over a mile. It was composed of hulks and floating batteries, eighteen to twenty in number, mounting six hundred and twenty-eight guns, of which about three hundred and seventy-five would bear on the engaged side. The southern flank was partly supported by works on shore, but from the intervening shoal water these were too distant for thoroughly efficient fire. It was this southern extremity that Nelson had chosen as his point of assault—the weakest part of the Danish defence, and the one that would interpose his ships between the Danes and their allies in the Baltic.
The Battle of 2 April 1801
The morning of the 2nd of April brought the wind fair from the south-south-east. At eight o’clock the British captains were summoned to the flagship for their final instructions. At half-past nine the signal was made to weigh.
The ships were soon under sail, but the difficulties of pilotage were immediately apparent. The Agamemnon, of sixty-four guns, was unable to weather the point of the Middle Ground and had to anchor out of range, taking no share in the battle. Worse followed: the Bellona and the Russell, seventy-fours both, the fourth and fifth ships in the order of battle, entered the King’s Channel but kept too far to the eastward and ran ashore on the farther side—upon the Middle Ground itself. They were not entirely out of action, but they were beyond the range of efficient gunnery. Nelson’s flagship, the Elephant, passed clear, as did the rest of the heavy ships, but the loss of these three vessels from the line exposed the northern part of the British order to a weight of fire quite disproportioned to its strength. A body of frigates very gallantly undertook to fill the gap.
Thus, from the very beginning, Nelson fought with a third of his force crippled or missing. The battle that followed was not the neat tactical victory he had planned; it was a slogging match, a test of sheer endurance and gunnery against an enemy fighting under the eyes of his own capital.
The battle was at its height by half-past eleven. There was no more manoeuvring—only the simple question of efficient gunnery and endurance. Around two in the afternoon, a great part of the Danish line had ceased to fire, and the flagship Dannebrog was in flames. But the Danish defence was stubborn and resourceful. Throughout the action, fresh crews were frequently sent from the shore to replace the men who had fallen. In several cases, new arrivals reached ships that had already struck their colours and renewed the fight, either through ignorance or indifference. The land batteries fired on British boats attempting to take possession of their prizes.
The Signal and the Blind Eye
It was at this moment that Sir Hyde Parker, watching from the London some four miles to the north, saw the smoke and confusion and drew the worst conclusions. The Agamemnon, Bellona, and Russell were aground; the frigates were taking punishment they were never designed to bear; and the whole British line seemed to be struggling in a trap from which escape would be difficult. Parker raised the signal for recall—Signal No. 39—ordering his ships to discontinue the action.
On the deck of the Elephant, Nelson saw the signal as it rose to the masthead of the commander-in-chief. He understood perfectly what it meant: Parker feared the fleet was being destroyed and wished to withdraw before the losses became catastrophic. Nelson also understood that withdrawal was impossible—his crippled ships could not beat their way out of the King’s Channel against the wind without being raked by the undamaged Crown Batteries. To retreat was to invite destruction. To press the attack was the only hope.
He turned to his flag-captain, Thomas Foley. “You know, Foley,” he said, “I have only one eye. I have a right to be blind sometimes.” Then, raising his telescope to his blind eye, he looked deliberately toward the London and said: “I really do not see the signal.”
Whether he meant the signal was hidden by the smoke or simply chose to ignore it matters little. The gesture has become the emblem of his genius: the deliberate disobedience, the calculated insubordination, the willingness to stake his reputation and his life on a judgment that contradicted the orders of his superior. He ordered his own signal for closer action to be kept flying, and the battle continued.
The Flag of Truce
Nelson seized on the circumstance of the reinforced Danish crews to bring the affair to a conclusion. He wrote a letter addressed “To the brothers of Englishmen, the Danes,” and sent it under a flag of truce to the Crown Prince, who was in the city:
“Lord Nelson has directions to spare Denmark when no longer resisting; but if the firing is continued on the part of Denmark, Lord Nelson will be obliged to set on fire all the floating batteries he has taken, without having the power of saving the brave Danes who have defended them.”
The letter was sent ashore by a British officer who had served in the Russian navy and spoke Danish. The engagement continued until about three o’clock, when the whole line of floating defences south-east of the Crown Batteries had either struck or been destroyed. The Crown Prince demanded the precise purport of the first message. Nelson took a high hand. He had destroyed the part of the enemy’s line he had attacked, but it was now essential to withdraw his crippled ships—and with the existing wind, that could only be done by passing the Crown Batteries, which had been but little injured. He wrote a second letter, politicly ignoring this danger:
“Lord Nelson, with humble duty to His Royal Highness, begs leave to say that he will ever esteem it the greatest victory he ever gained, if this flag of truce may be the happy forerunner of a lasting and happy union between my most gracious Sovereign and His Majesty the King of Denmark.”
Having written the letter, he referred the bearer for definite action to Sir Hyde Parker, four miles off—foreseeing that the long pull there and back would give time for the leading ships, much crippled, to clear the shoals, though their course lay close under the Crown Batteries. Thus the exposed part of the British fleet was successfully withdrawn. Three of the five ships-of-the-line that had borne the heaviest fighting were so damaged that they grounded in the shallows and had to be towed off; one of them, the Monarch, lost her rudder and was forced to steer with sails alone. Desperate measures were required to bring them round the shoals, but by nightfall the squadron had rejoined Parker to the north of the Middle Ground. The fleet was safe.
The Armistice
The result of the battle was to uncover the front of Copenhagen and lay it, with its dockyards and arsenals, open to bombardment. The bomb vessels could now be placed safely in the King’s Channel. Denmark had to choose whether fear of her powerful allies and zeal for neutral claims should lead her to undergo further punishment, or whether the suffering already endured was excuse enough for abandoning the coalition.
Nelson conducted the negotiations himself. He insisted upon an armistice of fourteen weeks, after which hostilities could be resumed on fourteen days’ notice. This would assure Parker complete immunity for his communications and leave Nelson free to act against the Russian fleet—the object he had never lost sight of. During the discussions, the Crown Prince received news that changed everything: the Czar Paul I had been murdered in his palace at St. Petersburg on the night of the 23rd of March—the night after the battle. The Danish government concealed the tidings, but the departure of the soul of the confederacy relieved their worst fears and encouraged them to yield to Nelson’s demands.
The armistice was signed. Denmark’s part in the Armed Neutrality was suspended.
The Aftermath
Among the first measures of the new Czar, Alexander I, was the release of the British seamen imprisoned by his father. On the 12th of April the British ships entered the Baltic—much to the surprise of the Northern powers, who had thought their heavy draught would prevent their passage. Parker anchored in Kioge Bay and there awaited further instructions, but Nelson entirely disapproved of this inactivity. Russia might yield, but she would be more likely to do so if the British fleet lay off Revel.
The British ministry, however, had finally taken the measure of Parker. Four days after news of the victory reached London, orders were issued relieving him and leaving Nelson in command. Taken only a week after a victory, this could scarcely be construed as anything but an implied censure. “They are not Sir Hyde Parker’s real friends who wish for an inquiry,” Nelson wrote. “His friends in the fleet wish everything of this fleet to be forgot, for we all respect and love Sir Hyde; but the dearer his friends, the more uneasy they have been at his idleness, for that is the truth—no criminality.”
Nelson’s first signal upon receiving command was to hoist the boats aboard and prepare to weigh. On the 7th of May the fleet left Kioge Bay, and on the 12th appeared off Revel. But the Russian division had sailed three days before and was now safe under the guns of Cronstadt. The bird was flown. Nelson remained in the Baltic, awaiting the issue of negotiations. Russia meant peace: on the 17th of May the Czar ordered the release of the embargoed British ships. On the 4th of June Great Britain released the Danes and Swedes detained in her ports.
On the 17th of June 1801, a convention was signed at St. Petersburg between Russia and Great Britain, settling the points in dispute. The Armed Neutrality had dissolved.
The Tactical Significance
The Battle of Copenhagen was in many respects Nelson’s most difficult action. Unlike the Nile, where he had struck a fleet at anchor with the advantage of surprise and a clear tactical plan, Copenhagen was a battle fought against a prepared defensive line in waters so treacherous that a third of his attacking force was neutralized before firing a shot. The victory was won not by manoeuvre but by the sheer weight of British gunnery and the iron determination of the man in command.
The action demonstrated the offensive spirit in its most extreme form. Nelson’s refusal to obey Parker’s signal of recall was an act of calculated insubordination that has been debated by naval thinkers ever since. Was it justified? The answer lies in the result: had Nelson obeyed, his crippled ships would have been destroyed in attempting to withdraw, the Danish line would have remained intact, and the Armed Neutrality would have held. By disobeying, he won the battle, broke the Northern League, and secured the Baltic for British commerce.
Yet the campaign was not what Nelson had wished it to be. He had wanted to strike at Revel before Copenhagen, to destroy the Russian fleet at its anchorage and shatter the Northern League at its source. He was overruled by his cautious superior, and the Russian ships escaped destruction. The opportunity never came again. It was the great lost chance of the Baltic campaign—one that Nelson would always regard as the true object of the expedition.
Still, the battle itself stands as a monument to Nelson’s genius. The navigation of the King’s Channel in the face of an armed enemy, the coolness with which he accepted the loss of a third of his force and fought on, the timing and wording of the flag of truce, the deception by which he gained time for his crippled ships to escape—these were not the actions of a mere fire-eater. They were the calculations of a commander who understood that in war, the boldest course is often the safest, and that a successful disobedience is its own justification.

events/battle-of-the-nile.title: The Battle of the Nile
events/battle-of-the-nile.content:
The Battle of the Nile
The Great Pursuit
Throughout the spring and summer of 1798, the Mediterranean had been the theatre of a vast and uncertain chase. On the 19th of May, Admiral Brueys had sailed from Toulon with the greatest armament France had ever assembled: thirteen ships of the line, fourteen frigates, and over four hundred transports, carrying the Army of the East under General Bonaparte. Their destination was Egypt. Their purpose was the conquest of the Orient and the destruction of British power in India.
The British fleet, meanwhile, had scarcely a frigate to its name in those waters. Lord St. Vincent, commanding off Cadiz, had sent his most aggressive subordinate into the Mediterranean with a small squadron of three ships of the line, later reinforced to fourteen. Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson was charged with a mission that seemed almost absurd in its disproportion: to find and destroy the French armada before it could accomplish its design.
What followed was a drama of missed connections that has no parallel in naval history. Nelson reached the neighbourhood of Toulon on the 17th of May, only to be scattered by a gale that dismasted his flagship and nearly drove him onto the Italian coast. While he refitted, Bonaparte slipped past with his entire fleet. Nelson guessed the destination correctly—he reasoned that Malta must be the first objective, Egypt the ultimate one—but he could not prove it, for he had no frigates to scout ahead, no fast vessels to run down the elusive rumours that crossed his path. He was a blind man searching the vastness of the inland sea.
The French seized Malta on the 12th of June, the ancient fortress of the Knights of St. John capitulating after a brief show of force. Bonaparte stayed six days, reorganised the government, confiscated the treasury, and sailed eastward. Nelson, receiving intelligence of the French departure from Malta, pressed on for Egypt. He reached Alexandria on the 28th of June and found no French. Concluding that he had been mistaken—that the French must be bound for Constantinople or the Black Sea—he turned northward in frustration, searching the coasts of Asia Minor and the southern shore of Crete. Two days after his departure, Bonaparte’s fleet arrived off Alexandria. The French army landed on the 1st of July, and within a week Bonaparte had stormed the city and begun his march on Cairo. The French fleet, its troops disembarked, was free to choose its anchorage.
The Dispositions at Aboukir
Admiral François-Paul Brueys d’Aigalliers was a brave officer, but he suffered from a vacillating temperament that the responsibilities of high command only exacerbated. Bonaparte had given him explicit orders: take the fleet into the old harbour of Alexandria if possible; if not, find a defensible anchorage in Aboukir Bay; failing both, make for Corfu. The preservation of the fleet was essential, for the army’s survival in Egypt depended upon it.
Brueys ordered soundings. The old harbour of Alexandria, it was reported on the 18th of July, could indeed accommodate the ships of the line, but the admiral hesitated. The winds were capricious, the passage narrow, and the season advanced. He chose instead the easier alternative: the open roadstead of Aboukir Bay, fifteen miles east of Alexandria.
The Bay of Aboukir stretches from the promontory of the same name to the Rosetta mouth of the Nile, a distance of some eighteen miles. In its western portion, where Brueys moored his fleet, the shore recedes in a long tongue of sand behind which lies the shallow Lake Madieh. North-east from Aboukir Point stretches a line of shoals and rocks, rising at two and a half miles into a small island—since known as Nelson’s Island—and continuing for another mile and a quarter. Behind this four-mile barrier, the fleet found shelter from the prevailing north-west summer wind.
Here Brueys established his line. His thirteen ships of the line were moored in a column running north-west to south-east, their broadsides turned to the sea. The north-western ship—the van, the one most exposed to the wind and to any approaching enemy—was anchored a mile and a half south-east of Aboukir Island, in five fathoms of water. This was the critical error. She should have been moored so close to the shoal that no ship could pass around her. Instead, a gap was left, and the few guns the French had placed on the island were far too light to cover it. The intervals between ships were wide, and the line itself was bent at the rear, but not sufficiently to bring the rear ships into shoal water. The flank that should have been impregnable was open to any captain bold enough to attempt the passage.
Brueys seems to have believed two things that would prove fatal: that no enemy would risk the unknown shoals on the inshore side, and that no attack would be attempted after nightfall. He had anchored his fleet for defence against a conventional approach from the seaward side, and his guns were run out only on that side. The landward guns remained stowed, their ports blocked by the cables that held the ships to their anchors. The assumption was natural, but it was founded on premises that proved disastrously false.
Brueys himself seems to have expected that the attack, if it came, would fall upon his rear. He had written to the minister of marine expressing more fear for that part of his order than for the van. The French fleet had been at anchor for three weeks when, on the 1st of August, the lookout sighted sails on the western horizon. A British squadron of fourteen ships of the line was bearing down upon them under a press of sail.
Nelson’s Resolution
The evening before, Nelson had sent the Alexander and Swiftsure ahead to reconnoitre, expecting to make Alexandria the following day. It was a measure born of necessity—he had no frigates, and the main body could not afford to be caught unprepared. When, at one in the afternoon, the British fleet sighted the French line lying at anchor in Aboukir Bay, Nelson did not hesitate for a moment. There was no council of war, no weighing of risks. The sun was already falling toward the horizon. The waters were unknown—the only chart in the entire British fleet was a rough sketch taken from a captured merchant vessel. The shoals that protected the French position were uncharted. Yet Nelson made the signal to prepare for battle and to anchor by the stern.
It was a decision that ranks among the most audacious in naval history. To attack a fleet at anchor in a defended bay, with night falling and the ground uncharted, was to stake everything on the quality of his captains and the fighting spirit of his crews. Nelson had been thinking of this moment throughout the long weeks of his pursuit. He had discussed the problem with his captains, sounded their views, prepared their minds. Now he trusted them to execute what he could not prescribe from the flagship.
As the British ships rounded Aboukir Island, Nelson hailed Captain Hood of the Zealous and asked whether he thought they were far enough eastward to clear the shoal. Hood replied that he would bear up, sounding as he went, and that the other ships keeping outside him would be safe. Thus the fleet was piloted into action—practical seamanship of the highest order, performed under the eyes of an enemy already opening fire.
The Attack
The leading British ship, the Goliath under Captain Foley, was the first to show what Nelson had intended. Instead of anchoring on the seaward side of the French line—the obvious course, the one the French had prepared for—Foley steered his ship ahead of the French column and crossed the bows of the leading French ship, the Guerrier. He intended to anchor on her inner side, but his anchor hung for a moment, and he brought up instead on the quarter of the second French ship, the Conquérant. Hood, following close in the Zealous, anchored precisely on the bow of the Guerrier.
So the battle began. The French van was caught between two fires: the British ships on its inner flank, firing from the shore side, and the British ships that followed, anchoring on the seaward side. Within five minutes of the first exchange—just as the sun was sinking below the horizon—the foremast of the Guerrier crashed over the side. Three cheers rang across the British line.
The Orion swept wide around the two leading ships, passing between them and the shore, and anchored on the inner side of the fifth French ship, the Peuple Souverain. The Theseus brought up abreast the third, the Spartiate, having passed between the Goliath and Zealous and their antagonists. The Audacious steered between the Guerrier and the Conquérant and anchored on the bow of the latter, already engaged on the quarter by the Goliath. Five British ships were now inside the French line—Goliath, Zealous, Orion, Theseus, and Audacious—doubling on the van. The French had never conceived that ships could pass between their line and the shoals; the landward guns were useless, the crews unable to train their pieces on the enemy that had appeared from the one quarter they had thought secure.
Nelson himself, in the Vanguard, was sixth in the order of battle. He had deliberately allowed the leading ships to pass ahead of him, calculating that by the time his flagship entered the bay the shoals would be well marked and the enemy’s attention fully engaged. He anchored on the seaward side of the third French ship, the Spartiate, already engaged on her inner side by the Theseus. It was a deliberate choice: he could have followed Foley’s example and taken the inner passage, but he anchored outside instead, signalling by his example what he expected of those who came after him. The leading ships doubled the van; the remainder would double the centre.
The French, caught utterly unprepared, fought with desperate valour. Hundreds of their men were ashore fetching water when the British sails appeared; most of them never returned to their ships. Brueys himself, who had clung to the hope that the enemy would not attack at night, faced the catastrophe with a courage that redeemed the hesitations of the previous weeks. His flagship, the Orient, a three-decker of one hundred and twenty guns—the largest vessel in either fleet—became the focal point of the British assault.
The Destruction of the Orient
For half an hour Brueys was a helpless spectator of the destruction of his van, watching from the quarterdeck of the Orient as ship after ship in the leading division was battered into submission. Then the British centre came up, and he had his own battle to fight.
The Bellerophon, a seventy-four, anchored abreast of the Orient and opened fire. The disparity in force was enormous—a seventy-four against a hundred-and-twenty—but the Bellerophon fought with a fury that astonished even her opponents. For three-quarters of an hour she endured the full weight of the French flagship’s broadside, losing her main and mizzen masts. When she could no longer sustain the punishment, her cable was cut and she drifted out of action. As she passed down the French line, her foremast fell, and the successive broadsides of the French rear raked her helpless hull. Out of a ship’s company of six hundred and fifty men, she had lost forty-nine killed and one hundred and forty-eight wounded.
But the Bellerophon had bought time, and with time came reinforcements. The Swiftsure, arriving after dark, anchored on the starboard bow of the Orient and opened fire. The Alexander followed, anchoring on the port quarter of the three-decker, while the fifty-gun Leander placed herself on the port bow of the Franklin, the next French ship ahead of the Orient, and raked both vessels. The French centre was now caught in a concentration of fire as devastating as that which had overwhelmed the van.
The Culloden, under Captain Troubridge—Nelson’s most trusted captain—had been separated from the main body and, attempting to round the shoal in the failing light, ran hard aground on its outer extremity at a quarter before seven. There she stuck, despite all efforts, until two o’clock the next morning, when the battle was already decided. Yet even in disaster she served the fleet: her wreck became a beacon warning the Alexander and Swiftsure clear of the same fate.
At about nine in the evening, flames were seen rising from the stern of the Orient. The cause has never been determined with certainty—paint, tar, the combustibles of a ship cleared for action, a chance spark from the British guns. The fire spread with terrifying speed, and the British, recognizing the danger of proximity to a burning ship, ceased their attack on the flagship and concentrated their efforts on saving themselves.
Brueys himself was spared the sight of his flagship’s end. He had been twice wounded already; at half-past eight, a cannonball carried away his left leg at the thigh. He refused to be taken below. He died calmly on his quarterdeck moments before the fire broke out.
At ten o’clock, the Orient blew up. The explosion was heard miles inland, a thunderclap of such violence that it seemed to shake the very sea. A profound silence fell across the bay, broken only by the crackling of wreckage and the cries of drowning men. Then the battle resumed. Captain Casabianca, commander of the Orient, went down with his ship, and with him his young son—a story that would pass into legend.
The Morning After
Five French ships ahead of the Orient had already surrendered before the explosion. The eighty-gun Franklin struck her flag before midnight. When dawn broke on the 2nd of August, six ships of the French line still flew their colours, but they had drifted far astern in the confusion of the night—their cables cut by shot, their commanders uncertain whether to fight or flee.
The British, repairing their damages through the night, attacked again at first light. Four of the remaining French ships—the Tonnant, Mercure, Heureux, and Timoléon—ran ashore to avoid destruction. The first three hauled down their colours; the fourth was burned by her own officers.
Only two ships of the line escaped: the Guillaume Tell, bearing the flag of Rear-Admiral Villeneuve, and the Généreux. With them fled the frigates Diane and Justice. They slipped away to the south-east as the morning light revealed the scale of the catastrophe, carrying news of the disaster to France.
Of the thirteen French ships of the line that had anchored in Aboukir Bay on the 1st of August, eleven were destroyed or captured. Of the four frigates, one was sunk, one captured, and two escaped with Villeneuve. The French lost some three thousand five hundred men killed, wounded, or drowned, among them their commander-in-chief and three captains. The British loss was two hundred and eighteen killed and six hundred and seventy-eight wounded. Nelson himself was among the casualties: a heavy splinter struck him in the head, and for a time he believed the wound to be mortal. It disabled him for several days. “I think,” he wrote four weeks later, “that if it had pleased God I had not been wounded, not a boat would have escaped.”
The Consequences
The Battle of the Nile was not merely a victory; it was an annihilation. Within the space of a single night, the entire strategic architecture of Bonaparte’s eastern expedition had been swept away. The French fleet, which was to have secured the army’s communications with France and overawed the Ottoman Porte, had ceased to exist. The Mediterranean, which had been a French lake at the beginning of the year, passed utterly into British hands.
For Mahan, writing a century later, the Nile was the most decisive naval battle of the period—the battle that made Waterloo possible. Its strategic consequences radiated across every theatre of the war. The command of the sea, which France had contested since 1793, passed irrevocably to Great Britain, and with it the power to determine where and when the next war would be fought.
The blow struck home in every quarter. The Ottoman Porte, which had been hesitating before the prestige of French arms, declared war on France within weeks of receiving the news of Aboukir. The Second Coalition—Austria, Russia, Naples, and the Porte—which had been slowly forming through the summer of 1798, now crystallized into active hostility. Czar Paul of Russia, already outraged by the French seizure of Malta, eagerly promised troops for the war. Austria, which had been holding back after Campo Formio, signed a convention with Russia on the 10th of August. The conferences at Rastadt were broken off. The war that had seemed to be drawing to a close in 1797 blazed up anew along the whole frontier of Europe.
For the Army of the East, the consequences were immediate and inescapable. The troops had fought the Battle of the Pyramids on the 21st of July and entered Cairo in triumph. They had believed themselves masters of a new empire. When the news of the naval disaster reached them in August, Paganel records that the soldiers gave way to despair. “Here we are,” they cried, “abandoned in this barbarous country, without communication with home, without hope of return.” The entire enterprise, which had seemed so brilliant at its conception, now revealed itself as a vast trap: the army could conquer but it could not leave, it could win battles but it could not communicate with the nation that had sent it.
Bonaparte met the moment with the iron self-control that was the mark of his genius. “We have then laid on us the obligation to do great things,” he told his men. “Seas which we do not command separate us from home; but no seas divide us from Africa and Asia.” The magical influence he exerted over his soldiers restored their courage—but it could not restore their communications, nor bring news from France, nor conjure supplies from the empty desert. Paganel observes that Bonaparte had chosen to sail for Egypt partly to remove himself from the failures of the Directory; the Nile now made that removal permanent, and his army a garrison marooned in a hostile land.
The blockade of Egypt by British squadrons was established immediately and maintained until the final French surrender in 1801. Malta, where Bonaparte had left a garrison of four thousand men, was invested by the combined forces of the British navy and the Maltese insurgents, and held out only until September 1800. The Ionian Islands, which Bonaparte had intended as a base for the eastern empire, fell to a Russo-Turkish squadron in October 1798.
The Battle of the Nile was the most complete naval victory of the age. Lord Howe, asked to comment on the achievement, remarked that it “stood unparalleled and singular in this instance, that every captain distinguished himself.” The judgment was just. The battle was the product not merely of Nelson’s audacity but of the tactical discipline he had instilled in his captains during the long weeks of the pursuit. The combination of doubling the enemy’s line, of passing inside the shoals to bring the French between two fires, of trusting subordinates to act on their own initiative—these were the marks of a new school of naval warfare, one that would find its ultimate expression seven years later at Trafalgar.
For France, the defeat was a wound from which the navy never fully recovered. The Directory, which had counted on the Egyptian expedition to secure its eastern ambitions, saw its entire Mediterranean position collapse in a single night’s fighting. The Army of the East was cut off and stranded, its general reduced to conquering a desert he could not leave, its soldiers condemned to fight battles that decided nothing, for the sea that should have carried them home was held by their enemies. Villeneuve, the fugitive of Aboukir, would carry the memory of that night with him through seven years of command, until at Trafalgar he would face Nelson again—and again be beaten.
The Battle of the Nile did not end the war, but it determined the conditions under which the rest of the war would be fought. The command of the sea had passed decisively to Great Britain, and it would not be challenged again for a generation.

events/egyptian-campaign.title: The Egyptian Campaign
events/egyptian-campaign.content:
The Egyptian Campaign
The Armament of the East
The Treaty of Campo Formio, signed in October 1797, had left France alone in Europe against a single enemy she could not reach: England. The Directory, beset by financial collapse and political faction, needed both a victory and a diversion. Bonaparte, returned from the Italian campaigns with his ambition inflamed and his ambition uneasy in the atmosphere of Paris, needed a new theatre for his genius. Two needs converged in the spring of 1798 upon a single project: the conquest of Egypt.
It was an enterprise that appealed to every element of Bonaparte’s character. The Orient had haunted European imaginations since the Crusades; a French expedition to the Nile would revive the ancient dream of a Mediterranean empire, threaten British India from its western flank, and remove from Paris the most popular general of the Republic at a moment when the Directory found his presence increasingly inconvenient. On the 5th of March 1798, Bonaparte laid before the Directory a detailed memorandum on the dispositions necessary for the seizure of Egypt and Malta. The same day, decrees were issued under cover of a commission on the coast defences of the Mediterranean. The preparations began in earnest.
For three months the ports of Toulon, Marseilles, Genoa, and Civita-Vecchia hummed with extraordinary activity. Thirteen ships of the line, fourteen frigates, and over four hundred transports were assembled—the greatest armament France had ever launched upon the sea. The army numbered some thirty-five thousand men, the finest troops of the Republic, veterans of the Italian campaign, commanded by generals who would give their names to an epoch: Kléber, Desaix, Lannes, Murat, Berthier, Caffarelli, Reynier. But the expedition carried more than soldiers. Bonaparte had insisted on bringing a Commission of Sciences and Arts—over one hundred and sixty savants, mathematicians, engineers, naturalists, chemists, antiquarians, painters, and printers—whose task was to survey, describe, and catalogue the ancient land of Egypt. It was a singular marriage of Mars and Minerva, unprecedented in the history of warfare.
The Treasury was empty; the Directory was borrowing seventeen million francs from the Bernese treasury, seized after the invasion of Switzerland, and draining the other cantons in proportion. Another eighteen million were raised by requisitions. The Swiss Helvetia was plundered, the Papal States occupied, to fund the voyage to the Nile.
The Sailing and the Elusion
On the 19th of May 1798, the great armada weighed anchor from Toulon. The wind was fair, the sea calm, the spectacle immense. As the fleet filed through the narrow exit between the Îles d’Hyères and the coast, Bonaparte addressed his army in the tone that had already become his signature: “Soldiers, you are about to undertake a conquest of which the effects on civilisation and commerce are incalculable. The English nation, which you have already beaten in Italy, awaits you with impatience. The seas which we must cross are infested with their cruisers; but we shall force them to fly before us, or sink in the abyss.”
The British had indeed been watching. On the 2nd of May, the day before Bonaparte left Paris for the coast, Lord St. Vincent off Cadiz had dispatched his most aggressive subordinate into the Mediterranean with three ships of the line, later reinforced to fourteen. Rear-Admiral Sir Horatio Nelson’s orders were to find the French armament and destroy it. He reached the neighbourhood of Toulon on the 17th of May, only to be scattered by a gale that dismasted his flagship. While he refitted, Bonaparte slipped past unseen.
What followed was one of the most remarkable chases in maritime history. Nelson, a blind man in a vast sea, had no frigates—those eyes of the fleet without which a commander gropes in darkness. He guessed correctly that the French were bound for Malta and Egypt, but he could not prove it. He arrived off Alexandria on the 28th of June; finding no French, he turned north in frustration, searching the coasts of Asia Minor. Two days after his departure, Bonaparte’s fleet anchored off the Egyptian coast. On the 1st of July, the French army disembarked near Alexandria.
During the voyage, the French had seized Malta with remarkable ease. The ancient fortress of the Knights of St. John, weakened by internal decay and apathy, capitulated after a brief show of force. Bonaparte stayed six days, reorganised the government, abolished the Order’s privileges, confiscated its treasury, and sailed eastward with the island’s treasure in his holds. The Knights, who had resisted the Ottomans for centuries, had offered the French army hardly a day’s resistance.
The Landing and the Pyramids
When the French army stepped ashore near Alexandria on the 1st of July, it found a country that had not changed substantially since the age of the Ptolemies. Egypt was a province of the Ottoman Empire in name only; in reality, it was ruled by the Mamelukes, a military caste of Circassian and Georgian slave-soldiers who had governed the country for centuries through a system of feudal exploitation that had reduced the native population to poverty and the land to neglect. The Mameluke beys, Murad and Ibrahim, commanded a formidable cavalry that had defeated every Ottoman attempt to reassert imperial authority. They had never faced European infantry.
Bonaparte stormed Alexandria on the 2nd of July, the troops wading ashore through the surf under a hail of musketry. The city fell within hours. The army then began its march across the Delta toward Cairo, a movement of extraordinary hardship through a landscape of heat, dust, and irrigation canals that forced the columns into constant delay and disorder. The Mameluke cavalry harassed the flanks; the Bedouin of the desert intercepted stragglers with a ferocity that the French infantry, accustomed to the formal battles of Europe, found shocking.
On the 21st of July, the French army came in sight of the Pyramids. At the village of Embabeh, on the left bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, the Mameluke army was drawn up in full array: Murad Bey’s horsemen, perhaps twelve thousand strong, the finest cavalry in the East, their sabres gleaming in the morning sun, their horses caparisoned in silk and gold. Behind them lay the Pyramids of Giza, ancient witnesses to a civilisation that had already risen and fallen while Europe was still barbarous.
Bonaparte formed his army into divisional squares, five massive quadrangles of infantry and artillery, with the baggage and the savants in the centre. The Mameluke cavalry charged with the fury that had carried everything before them for centuries. They broke against the French squares like waves against granite. Volley after volley of musketry and canister tore through the horsemen; the squares held, and the Mameluke power was shattered in a single afternoon. The Turks and Mamelukes who had not been killed on the field were driven into the Nile, where hundreds drowned. Cairo submitted the next day; on the 25th of July, Bonaparte entered the city.
The victory had been complete, but the French were not yet masters of Egypt. Murad Bey retreated into Upper Egypt with the remnants of his army; Desaix was despatched in pursuit, a campaign that would occupy him for months through the ruined temples and barren deserts of the upper Nile. Ibrahim Bey fled eastward toward Syria. Bonaparte settled into Cairo, began to organise the administration of the conquered province, and waited for news from his fleet.
The Battle of the Nile
The news, when it came, was the worst that could be imagined.
While Bonaparte had been advancing through the Delta, Admiral Brueys had anchored his squadron in the Bay of Aboukir, fifteen miles east of Alexandria. The anchorage was an open roadstead, sheltered from the prevailing north-west wind by a line of shoals and rocks. Bonaparte had given explicit orders: if the fleet could not enter the old harbour of Alexandria, it must find a defensible position at Aboukir or, failing both, make for Corfu. Brueys, whose temperament was irresolute and whose health was broken, chose the easier alternative. He moored his thirteen ships of the line in a single column, a mile and a half from the shoals, and waited.
He waited for nearly a month. On the 1st of August, the lookout sighted sails. At one in the afternoon, the British fleet of fourteen ships of the line was seen bearing down under full sail. Nelson, who had returned to Egypt after his fruitless search of the Levantine coast, had found the French at last.
The battle that followed was the most complete naval victory of the age. Nelson attacked at once, without hesitation, without a council of war; the sun was already sinking, the shoals were uncharted, but his mind had been running on this moment through the long weeks of the pursuit. He had discussed his plans with his captains; he had prepared them to act on their own initiative. Now he trusted them.
Captain Foley of the Goliath, leading the British line, did something that no French officer had thought possible. Instead of anchoring on the seaward side of the French column—the side that Brueys had prepared for—he steered inside the French line, crossing ahead of the leading ship, and anchored on the inner flank. The Zealous followed; then the Orion, the Theseus, the Audacious. Five British ships were inside the French line, doubling on the van. The French were caught between two fires.
The flag-ship Orient, a three-decker of one hundred and twenty guns, became the focal point of the battle. The Bellerophon, a seventy-four, anchored abreast of her and fought with a fury that astonished both fleets until she was a wreck. The Swiftsure and Alexander arrived in the darkness and completed the concentration on the French centre. At about nine in the evening, the Orient was seen to be on fire. Admiral Brueys, twice wounded already, had a cannonball carry away his left leg at the thigh; he refused to be taken below and died on his quarterdeck moments before the fire broke out. At ten o’clock, the Orient blew up with a detonation that shook the sea and silenced both fleets for a long moment of awe.
By dawn on the 2nd of August, eleven of Brueys’s thirteen ships of the line had been destroyed or captured. Two escaped—the Guillaume Tell and the Généreux—carrying the news to France. The French lost some thirty-five hundred men; the British, under nine hundred. Nelson himself was wounded in the head by a heavy splinter and believed for a time that he was dying.
The strategic consequences were incalculable. In a single night, the entire architecture of Bonaparte’s eastern expedition had been swept away. The Mediterranean passed from French to British control. The Ottoman Porte, which had been hesitating, declared war on France. The Second Coalition—Austria, Russia, Naples, the Porte—crystallised into active hostility. And the Army of the East, which had conquered Egypt, was now marooned in it.
When the news reached Bonaparte, the soldiers gave way to despair. “Here we are,” they cried, “abandoned in this barbarous country.” Their general met the moment with the iron self-control that was the mark of his genius. “We have then laid on us the obligation to do great things,” he told them. “Seas which we do not command separate us from home; but no seas divide us from Africa and Asia. We will found here an empire.”
The Administration of Egypt and the Institute of Cairo
Throughout the autumn of 1798, Bonaparte bent his extraordinary energy to the conquest of Egypt not merely by arms but by organisation. The ancient land, for centuries the private estate of a corrupt military caste, was to be remade in the image of European civilisation. The feudal privileges of the Mamelukes were abolished. A new system of taxation was imposed, the cadastre surveyed, the irrigation canals repaired, the bazaars regulated. The French army imposed order with a severity that the Egyptians, accustomed to the desultory cruelties of Ottoman governance, found novel and oppressive.
On the 22nd of August, Bonaparte founded the Institute of Cairo, modelled on the Institute of France. The savants who had accompanied the expedition—mathematicians like Monge and Fourier, chemists like Berthollet, naturalists like Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, engineers, antiquarians, orientalists—were organised into a learned society that met in the former palace of a Mameluke bey on the shores of the Nile. The Institute undertook the monumental work that would eventually produce the Description de l’Égypte—the most comprehensive survey of an ancient civilisation ever attempted by European science. They measured the temples of Luxor and Karnak, mapped the course of the Nile, catalogued the flora and fauna, studied the customs of the fellahin, and contemplated the riddle of the hieroglyphs. The Rosetta Stone, discovered by a French engineer during the fortification of Fort Saint-Julien in July 1799, would be the most famous fruit of their labours.
Bonaparte attended the meetings of the Institute in civilian dress, participating in the debates on geometry and chemistry with the absorption of a savant. He proposed questions for study: Could the bread of the army be improved by chemical means? Could the Nile floods be regulated by ancient irrigation works? Could Egypt be connected to the Red Sea by a canal through the Isthmus of Suez? The soldiers, who had fought their way through Italy and across the desert, watched with a mixture of bemusement and pride as their general debated the nature of heat with Monge or inspected a collection of scarabs with Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire.
But beneath the intellectual activity, the strategic situation grew steadily worse. In October, an insurrection broke out in Cairo, provoked by a new system of house taxes and by rumours that the Porte had declared war. Bonaparte suppressed it with a ferocity that was carefully calibrated: thirty beheaded in the streets, the heads exposed on the gates of the city, the survivors cowed into submission. The iron grip held, but the underlying hostility of the population was never extinguished.
Desaix, meanwhile, was pursuing Murad Bey through Upper Egypt in a campaign that reads like a prose epic. Through the autumn and winter of 1798, he chased the Mameluke chieftain among the ruins of Thebes and the cataracts of the Nile, fighting actions at Sediman and Samhoud, living off the land, enduring a climate that destroyed his men by disease faster than the enemy could kill them. It was a masterpiece of perseverance, but it drained the French army of resources it could not replace.
The Syrian Campaign
Bonaparte had not abandoned the larger vision that had brought him to Egypt. The destruction of his fleet had not destroyed his ambition. If he could not communicate with France, he could still advance eastward. The road to India ran through Syria, and the road to Syria ran through the desert.
By the end of 1798, he had learned that the Porte, now at war with France, was assembling an army in Syria under the Pasha Djezzar—“the Butcher”—a man whose reputation for cruelty was European legend. A second Turkish army was gathering on the Island of Rhodes, destined to land in Egypt when the summer weather permitted. Bonaparte determined to strike first: to march into Syria, defeat Djezzar’s army before it could take the offensive, seize the ports, and break the pincer before it could close.
On the 5th of February 1799, General Reynier advanced toward the oasis of El Arish, the gateway to Syria through the Sinai desert. The Turks were routed and driven from the oasis; Fort El Arish capitulated on the 20th. The army of thirteen thousand men, stripped of everything that could not be carried on the march, began the crossing of the desert.
They advanced through Gaza, which fell without resistance, and on the 7th of March reached Jaffa. The ancient port, sacred to Christian and Muslim alike, was carried by assault after a short siege. What followed cast a shadow over the campaign that Bonaparte’s apologists would spend the rest of their lives trying to erase. After the surrender of the garrison, by a variety of accounts numbering between two and three thousand men, Bonaparte ordered the prisoners shot—the entire garrison, marched out in parties and executed on the beach. The order was defended on the grounds that the garrison had been paroled after an earlier capitulation and had violated its parole, but the massacre was exceptional even by the standards of an age that did not flinch at severity. The soldiers who carried out the execution were sickened by it.
From Jaffa, the army marched north along the coast toward Acre—Saint-Jean-d’Acre, the ancient fortress that commanded the road to Constantinople. Acre was the hinge of Syria. If it fell, the way to Damascus and Aleppo lay open; the Turkish army could be broken before it could concentrate; the French could raise the population in rebellion against the oppressive rule of Djezzar. If it held, the campaign was lost.
The siege of Acre began on the 17th of March 1799. It would last sixty-two days—a drama of such narrow margins that the outcome seemed to tremble in the balance week after week.
The Siege of Acre
The defence of Acre was organised by a man who had been Bonaparte’s classmate at the military school of Brienne: Colonel Phélippeaux, a French royalist émigré who had escaped from Paris with the assistance of the British captain Sir Sidney Smith. It was one of those symmetrical encounters that history sometimes arranges—two men who had studied mathematics at the same school in France now confronted each other across the walls of a Syrian fortress, one commanding the attack, the other organising the defence.
Smith had arrived off Acre on the 15th of March with his flagship, the Tigre, and another ship of the line, the Theseus. The day before, his squadron had captured the French siege train—heavy artillery that had been sent by sea from Damietta to support the army’s advance. The guns that should have battered the walls of Acre into rubble were now mounted on its ramparts, served by British seamen. It was a stroke of fortune that probably decided the issue.
For two months, the French army flung itself against the fortifications with a desperation that increased as the defenders’ resistance stiffened. The siege was fought at close quarters—the trenches pushed to within yards of the walls, mines and counter-mines criss-crossing the earth beneath the bastions. Phélippeaux, working with feverish energy, repaired the medieval fortifications, connected the houses and garden walls into a second line of defence, and directed the fire of the captured guns with an engineer’s precision. He died at his post in April, but his work survived him.
Bonaparte pressed the assaults with all the skill and ferocity of his Italian campaigns. The attack of the 9th of May came closest to success. The French carried the outer wall and planted their flag on an angle of the tower; for a few hours, it seemed that the city must fall. But Smith, seeing the crisis, manned the boats of his squadron, pulled ashore, and led the British seamen armed with pikes to the breach. The Turkish reinforcements from Rhodes landed in the boats behind them. The fighting raged through the entire day and into the night; at dawn, the French were still outside, and Acre was saved.
The plague had come to the camp at Jaffa. The hospitals were choked with dying men. The army, which had started the campaign thirteen thousand strong, was reduced by killed, wounded, and disease to less than half that number. On the 20th of May, Bonaparte gave the order to retreat.
The withdrawal through the desert was worse than the advance. The plague-stricken were abandoned or, by some accounts that haunted Bonaparte’s reputation, hastened on their way by means that the general’s defenders denied and his enemies insisted upon. The army trudged through the heat of the Syrian summer, carrying its wounded, burning its stores, living on what it could find. On the 2nd of June, it encamped at El Arish, having lost since its departure fifteen hundred killed or dead of disease and more than two thousand wounded. On the 14th of June, the remnants re-entered Cairo.
The Syrian campaign had been a failure. Acre had held; Djezzar’s army had not been broken; the eastern empire that Bonaparte had imagined was as distant as before. But worse news was coming.
The Aboukir Landing and the Return
After the Syrian campaign, the army re-entered Cairo on the 14th of June. For a few weeks, there was breathing space. Then, on the 11th of July, Sir Sidney Smith anchored in Aboukir Bay with a Turkish fleet of thirteen ships of the line and over a hundred transports, carrying an army variously estimated at between ten and thirty thousand men. The blow that Bonaparte had anticipated fell precisely as he had feared.
The Turks landed, stormed the Castle of Aboukir, and entrenched themselves on the peninsula. Bonaparte, who was in Cairo when he learned of the landing, acted with the speed that had made his reputation. He concentrated his forces around Alexandria—Desaix was ordered to evacuate Upper Egypt, every available battalion was drawn to the coast—and on the 25th of July, he attacked.
The Battle of Aboukir was a masterpiece. The French army, outnumbered and exhausted, fell upon the Turkish positions on the same peninsula where Nelson had destroyed the French fleet a year before. The Turks were driven into the sea in a slaughter as complete as any Bonaparte had ever inflicted. Thousands drowned; the Turkish commander-in-chief was taken prisoner. The survivors who escaped were pursued by the French cavalry into the surf.
The victory was total, but it changed nothing. After the battle, flags of truce passed between Bonaparte and Sir Sidney Smith. Through this channel, Bonaparte received English newspapers—the first reliable news from Europe he had seen in months. What he read decided his future.
The news was catastrophic. The armies of the Second Coalition had driven the French out of Italy. The Russian general Suvarov had crossed the Adda, entered Milan, rolled back everything that Bonaparte had won in 1796 and 1797. France itself was threatened. The Directory, which had sent him to Egypt to be rid of him, was crumbling.
Bonaparte took his decision within days. He would return to France. His army—the finest soldiers of the Republic, the men who had followed him across the Alps and through the deserts of Africa—would be left behind under the command of Kléber. The secret was kept so closely that not even the senior generals were informed of the full plan.
On the 22nd of August, Admiral Ganteaume prepared two frigates that had fallen to France from the Venetian fleet. Bonaparte, accompanied by a small party that included Berthier, Lannes, Murat, Monge, and Berthollet, embarked at Alexandria under cover of darkness. Sir Sidney Smith, who had been blockading the port after the Battle of Aboukir, had withdrawn to Cyprus for water on the 9th of August; the window of opportunity was narrow, and Bonaparte sailed through it.
The voyage was long and anxious—forty-two days of constant vigilance against British cruisers. On the 9th of October, the frigates sighted the coast of France. Bonaparte landed at Fréjus, near Cannes, and was received with an enthusiasm that astonished even him. The news of his return spread like wildfire. Within a month, he had overthrown the Directory in the coup of 18 Brumaire and made himself First Consul of the French Republic.
The Army of Egypt: Kléber and Surrender
The army that Bonaparte abandoned in Egypt did not learn of his departure until he was safely at sea. The news produced a fury of indignation that only the iron rectitude of Kléber could have contained. The general to whom Bonaparte had left the command was a man of formidable abilities and a reputation as solid as his frame. He wrote to the French government a letter that fell into British hands and became famous: “I know all the importance of the possession of Egypt… but to do this effectually, a powerful lever is required, and that lever is a Navy. Ours has ceased to exist.”
Kléber recognised what Bonaparte had refused to admit: the Army of the East was trapped. It could neither be reinforced nor evacuated. The only rational course was to negotiate a surrender that would save the soldiers for France. With the countenance of Sir Sidney Smith, who seems to have acted beyond his instructions, Kléber entered into negotiations with the Turkish commander-in-chief. On the 24th of January 1800, the Convention of El Arish was signed: the French army would be allowed to evacuate Egypt and return to France.
The British government, however, repudiated the convention. Lord Keith, commanding in the Mediterranean, received instructions that no evacuation would be permitted unless the French laid down their arms and surrendered as prisoners of war. Smith’s authority to negotiate was disavowed. The convention collapsed.
Kléber resolved to fight. On the 20th of March 1800, he met the Turkish army at Heliopolis—the same battlefield where the ancient Greeks had defeated the Persians twenty centuries before—and inflicted a decisive defeat on the Grand Vizier’s army. The French position in Egypt was temporarily secured. But Kléber was not to enjoy his triumph. On the 14th of June 1800—the same day, as it happened, that Bonaparte won the Battle of Marengo—he was assassinated in Cairo by a Syrian student, a young man named Sulayman al-Halabi, who stabbed him through the heart in the gardens of his palace.
The command passed to General Menou, an incompetent who had converted to Islam, married an Egyptian woman, and lost any realistic sense of the situation. Under his direction, the French army held out for another year—a year of increasing isolation, dwindling supplies, and desperate hopes for a relief that never came. The British landed an army under Sir Ralph Abercromby in March 1801, defeated the French at the Battle of Alexandria, and drove the survivors into a series of fortresses from which they could not escape. One by one, the French positions surrendered. On the 2nd of September 1801, the last French soldiers in Egypt laid down their arms.
They were allowed to return to France with their weapons and their honour—terms far more generous than those that had been offered at El Arish, but by then circumstances had changed. Marengo had been fought and won; the Treaty of Lunéville had made peace on the Continent; the French troops would no longer go to swell the armies of Britain’s allies. The war had moved on, and Egypt had become a side-show.
The Shadow Across the Descent
The Egyptian campaign was the most singular military expedition of the age. It was at once a strategic conception of extraordinary brilliance—the attack on British India through the Middle East—and a catastrophic miscalculation of the fundamental realities of sea power. Bonaparte had defeated every army that opposed him, from the Mamelukes at the Pyramids to the Turks at Aboukir. He had founded an institute, assembled a scientific commission, surveyed the monuments of an ancient civilisation, and laid the foundations of modern Egyptology. But he had not been able to secure the sea.
The campaign’s most enduring legacy was not military but intellectual. The Description de l’Égypte, the massive multi-volume work produced by the savants, opened the ancient civilisation of the Nile to European understanding as it had never been opened before. The Rosetta Stone, discovered in the ruins of a fort, provided the key to the decipherment of hieroglyphs. The Institute of Cairo, though short-lived, established a model for the intersection of scholarship and empire that would shape European relations with the East for generations.
Politically, the campaign transformed Bonaparte’s career. He had left France as a general of the Republic, one among several. He returned as the saviour of the nation, the man who had brought glory to French arms even in defeat, the only leader who could rescue France from the chaos of the Directory. The failures of the Syrian campaign, the abandonment of his army, the loss of the fleet—all were forgotten in the intoxication of his return. Within a month of landing at Fréjus, he was master of France.
For the army he abandoned, the judgment was harsher. Kléber’s letter to the Directory was a damning epitaph for the entire enterprise: “Since that period everything has changed; and peace with the Porte is, in my opinion, the only expedient that holds out to us a method of fairly getting rid of an enterprise no longer capable of attaining the object for which it was undertaken.” The Army of the East, the finest soldiers France had produced, had been locked away in a land they could not leave, to fight battles that decided nothing, for a general who had sailed home to seize a throne.

events/fall-of-the-bastille.title: Fall of the Bastille
events/fall-of-the-bastille.content:
Fall of the Bastille
The fall of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 was the first great insurrection of the French Revolution. The royal fortress and prison in the east of Paris, which was also a symbol of royal authority and a store of arms and powder, was stormed by a crowd that had assembled in the hours after Necker’s dismissal became known. The event was not the result of a long-planned assault; it was the accidental product of three converging pressures: the political crisis at Versailles, the spontaneous insurrection of the Paris crowd, and the failure of the military cordon intended to hold the city.
The Background in the Days Before
Paris in the first fortnight of July 1789 was a city in suspension. The States-General had been in session since May. The National Assembly had declared itself in June. The king had responded by concentrating troops around Paris and Versailles — Swiss regiments, German regiments, the loyal Gardes Françaises — and had dismissed the popular minister Necker on 11 July. The dismissal was the spark.
The news arrived at Jefferson’s house on the evening of 11 July: Necker had been dismissed by a letter delivered by hand — he received it at dinner, proposed a walk to his wife, communicated the news on the road, and departed France that night. The minister Montmorin resigned immediately. Camille Desmoulins mounted a table at the Palais-Royal and called on the people to arm.
12 July: The City Breaks Open
The afternoon and evening of Sunday 12 July saw the first acts of public violence. The city broke open: the armourers’ shops were forced open and their weapons distributed; the armouries of the Invalides and of several hôtels were raided; the Monastery of Saint-Lazare was attacked and its grain distributed — each cart accompanied by a friar to assure the crowd it was legitimate. Wooden barriers around the Palais-Royal and the statue of Louis XV were pulled down or burned.
The green cockade appeared — made from the leaves of trees in the Tuileries gardens, the fashion of the day with which everybody was obliged to comply who meant to walk in peace. Carriages stopped running; the city was on foot. Benjamin Franklin’s portrait was paraded through the streets with black crepe, mourning the old king of France and the new king of America.
The military response on 12 July was ineffective. The Prince de Lambesc, commanding the Royal-Allemand cavalry, charged a crowd in the Tuileries gardens; the Gardes Françaises, the regiments of the line stationed in Paris, refused to fire on the people. The Gardes Françaises joined the crowd: the soldiers who had been the instruments of authority overnight became the leaders of the insurrection. The Baron de Besenval, commanding the troops in the Paris region, found he could not rely on his own regiments.
13 July: Organisation and Arms
By Monday 13 July, the insurrection had taken an organised form. The electors of Paris — the men who had chosen the city’s deputies to the States-General — assembled at the Hôtel de Ville and constituted themselves as a Comité Permanent. They authorised the formation of a civic militia (the future National Guard), called for the creation of a municipal government independent of the traditional city authorities, and sent deputations to the National Assembly at Versailles.
The search for arms intensified. The Hôtel des Invalides was approached; its governor refused to surrender its muskets. The crowd spent the day finding weapons where they could — breaking into the City Hall’s own armouries, taking swords and halberds from private collections, and continuing to raid armourers’ shops.
14 July: The Fortress
The morning of Tuesday 14 July saw the main body of the crowd march on the Hôtel des Invalides. The governor, having no orders from Versailles and seeing the crowd’s size, opened the gates. The insurgents took approximately 28,000–30,000 muskets and several cannon from the cellars. There was no powder: the gunpowder had been moved the night before to the Bastille for safekeeping.
The Bastille was commanded by the Marquis de Launay, the governor. The fortress was garrisoned by about eighty to ninety invalides (veteran soldiers unfit for field service) and thirty Swiss Guards. Its walls were thirty feet high; it had eight towers; the ditch around it was eighty feet wide. Its defensive capacity against artillery was limited — it was not a modern fortress — but against a crowd armed with muskets it was formidable.
The negotiations began in the late morning. A deputation from the Hôtel de Ville approached the Bastille, asking de Launay to receive a garrison of the new civic militia. He agreed to receive them but would not surrender the fortress. The crowd began to enter the outer courtyard. The first shots — fired either by the crowd or by the garrison, the sources disagree — killed several people.
The siege proper lasted about four hours. The crowd had brought cannon captured from the Invalides; the Swiss and invalides fired on them from the towers. The crowd, led by members of the Gardes Françaises who knew how to aim the cannon, fired back. De Launay’s position was hopeless: he had no food for a long siege, no reinforcements were coming, and his garrison was willing to open the gates.
The surrender was negotiated through a note pushed through the wall. De Launay agreed to lay down arms if the garrison’s lives were spared. The drawbridge was let down. The crowd poured into the fortress.
The Killing of de Launay and de Flesselles
The surrender agreement was not honoured. De Launay was seized, beaten, stabbed, and shot on the way to the Hôtel de Ville. The crowd demanded his head; a kitchen boy cut it off with a knife as de Launay lay dying. The head was placed on a pike and carried through the streets. (A counter-version of the episode has a young man named Désilles jumping between de Launay and the crowd to protect him, only to be killed himself — but this detail appears in no other account and may be a conflation.)
Jacques de Flesselles, the prévôt des marchands (the head of the city government), had been suspected of deceiving the crowd about the location of arms during the previous days. On the evening of 14 July, he was shot in the Palais-Royal by a young man named Lallée — “what name, what punishment have they preserved for you?” a contemporary commentator remarked. Flesselles’ head was also placed on a pike. The two heads were carried together through the streets, the first such display of the Revolution.
The King’s Reaction: 15–17 July
The news reached Versailles on the night of 14 July. The Duc de Liancourt, the king’s first gentleman of the bedchamber, woke the king and convinced him to go in person to the National Assembly. The king appeared before the Assembly without escort, announced that he had ordered the troops to withdraw from Paris and Versailles, and was received with an extraordinary ovation.
On 17 July, Louis XVI went to Paris. He was met at the city gates by the new mayor Bailly and the new commander of the National Guard, Lafayette, who presented him with the tricolour cockade — red and blue of the city of Paris, white of the monarchy. The king put it in his hat. The crowd shouted “Vive le Roi.”
Morris, who visited the Bastille on 17 July with Lafayette, thought the day would prove a useful lesson for the rest of the king’s life — “but he is so weak that unless he be kept out of bad Company it is impossible that he should not act wrongly.”
What the Bastille Contained
The Bastille at the time of its fall held only seven prisoners: four men convicted of forgery, two insane men (one English, one French), and the Comte de Solages, imprisoned on his family’s request for a particularly atrocious crime. The discovery that the symbol of royal despotism held so few prisoners — and none of them the political prisoners of the lettre de cachet — became part of the early revolutionary mythology: the Bastille’s evil was symbolic rather than practical, but the symbolism was enough.
The Consequences
The fall of the Bastille had an immediate and durable effect on the Revolution’s direction. The king’s acceptance of the tricolour cockade and his visit to Paris signalled the collapse of the court’s resistance to the early reforms of the National Assembly. The establishment of the Paris Commune and the National Guard gave the insurrection a permanent institutional form. The émigration of the king’s younger brother the Comte d’Artois and of the leading conservatives of the court — the Polignacs, the Prince de Condé — began within days. And the killing of de Launay and de Flesselles established the pattern: the Revolution’s first great victory was also its first public execution.
