events/italian-campaigns.title: The Italian Campaigns 1796-97
events/italian-campaigns.content:
The Italian Campaigns 1796-97
The Army of Italy
In the spring of 1796, the French Army of Italy was a collection of starving, ragged, unpaid battalions huddled along the Ligurian coast. The Directory, which governed France from the Luxembourg Palace, had neglected this army for months. Its soldiers wore tattered uniforms and broken shoes; they had not been paid in bread or coin; the artillery horses were dying of famine in the stables of Nice and Savona. The army’s commander had been the elderly General Schérer, a man of the old school whose talents did not extend to the improvisation of victory from the materials of defeat. Schérer had written despairing letters to Paris — his men could not fight, could not march, could barely exist.
The Directory, preoccupied with the more immediate threat of the Rhine and the internal crises of the Republic, had little attention to spare for the Italian frontier. But the strategic logic of 1796 demanded a decision. The war against Austria had reached a stalemate on the Rhine; the armies of Jourdan and Moreau faced the Archduke Charles across a line of fortresses that neither side could reduce. If the war was to be won, it must be won elsewhere. The Directory resolved to make Italy the decisive theatre.
To command the Army of Italy, the Directory chose a young general of twenty-six whose name was known in Paris only for his role at the siege of Toulon — where he had placed the batteries that forced the British to evacuate the port — and for the suppression of the Vendémiaire insurrection, when his cannon had cleared the streets of the capital. Lazare Carnot, the great organiser of victory who sat in the Directory, recognised something in the young Corsican that others had missed. Bonaparte was appointed commander-in-chief of the Army of Italy on the 2nd of March 1796.
He arrived at Nice on the 26th of March to find an army in ruins. His first act was to reorganise it. The old division structure was broken and recast. New generals were appointed — Augereau, Massena, Serrurier, Joubert — men of the Revolution whose origins were as humble as their ambitions were great. Bonaparte wrote to the Directory that he needed time to train his army; he did not wait for time. Within a fortnight of his arrival, the Army of Italy was in motion.
The Strategy of the Central Position
The problem that faced Bonaparte was a problem of geometry. The allied armies of Piedmont-Sardinia and Austria, commanded respectively by General Colli and the aged Field Marshal Beaulieu, held the passes of the Maritime Alps and the Apennines. They outnumbered the French by nearly two to one. Their positions were connected by the network of valleys that converge at the junction of the Alps and the Apennines. Bonaparte saw that the key to the campaign was not to fight the combined armies but to drive between them — to place himself at the point where the Piedmontese and Austrian armies touched each other, to break that connection, and to defeat each in turn before they could reunite.
This was the strategy of the central position, and it required speed, deception, and a willingness to accept risk that would have horrified a general of the old school. Bonaparte massed his army opposite the point where the two allied armies joined, near the village of Montenotte, on the northern slope of the Apennines above Savona. The Austrian left and the Piedmontese right met at a pass called the Bocchetta. Bonaparte intended to force it.
On the 10th of April, Beaulieu moved first. The Austrian general, mistaking the French concentration for a defensive precaution, advanced against the French left at Voltri with his main body. It was a fatal error. By detaching his main force to the east, Beaulieu left the junction between the Austrian and Piedmontese armies unguarded. Bonaparte struck the next day.
Montenotte, Millesimo, Dego
On the 12th of April, the French divisions under Massena and Augereau attacked the Austrian position at Montenotte. The fighting was savage and close — bayonet work in the narrow valleys, where the slopes rose so steeply that the dead rolled down into the streams. The Austrian general Argenteau, who commanded the Austrian division at the junction, was overwhelmed before he could be reinforced. By nightfall, the French had driven a wedge between the two allied armies. The central position had been seized.
Bonaparte did not pause. On the 13th, Augereau marched west against Millesimo, where the Piedmontese general Provera held a fortified position that commanded the road to Ceva. The fighting at Millesimo was among the most desperate of the campaign. Provera’s garrison, cut off and surrounded, held out for two days in the castle above the village before surrendering. On the 14th, Massena struck the Austrians at Dego, the second hinge of the allied position. The Austrians, shaken by Montenotte, broke and fled eastward toward the Po. In three days, Bonaparte had destroyed the allied junction and separated the Piedmontese from their Austrian allies.
The price of victory was that Bonaparte now had two enemies on his hands. Colli’s Piedmontese army, though isolated, was intact and had taken up a strong defensive position at Ceva, guarding the road to Turin. Beaulieu’s Austrians, though beaten, had withdrawn to Alessandria and could still strike the French flank. Bonaparte chose to pursue Colli first. On the 19th of April, the French forced the position at Ceva; on the 21st, Augereau’s division broke the Piedmontese at Mondovi in a charge that scattered Colli’s army across the Piedmontese plain.
King Victor Amadeus III of Sardinia had staked his crown on the Austrian alliance. With his army destroyed and the French at the gates of Turin, he had no choice but to sue for terms. On the 28th of April, at the village of Cherasco, the Piedmontese signed an armistice that withdrew their kingdom from the war and delivered the fortresses of Coni, Tortona, and Alessandria into French hands. Bonaparte, with characteristic audacity, had dictated terms not merely as a general but as a plenipotentiary of the Republic. The Directory, which had not authorised him to negotiate, was presented with a fait accompli. They accepted it.
The Crossing of the Po and the Bridge at Lodi
The Piedmontese question disposed of, Bonaparte turned east against the Austrians. Beaulieu had taken post along the line of the Po, the great river that divides northern Italy, and had fortified every bridge and crossing from Valenza to Piacenza. The conventional approach would have been to force a crossing at Valenza, where the Austrian defences were strongest. Bonaparte chose instead to feint toward Valenza, drawing Beaulieu’s attention to his left, while his main army marched swiftly east along the south bank of the Po to Piacenza.
On the 7th of May, the French vanguard reached Piacenza and discovered that the Austrian detachment guarding the crossing was dangerously weak. Bonaparte ordered an immediate crossing. By nightfall, the entire French army was across the Po, the boats shuttling ceaselessly in the darkness, while Beaulieu, deceived by the feint at Valenza, remained immobile forty miles to the west.
The Austrians, outflanked and outmanoeuvred, fell back in disorder toward the Adda, the next great river line. Bonaparte pursued with the speed that would become his signature. On the 10th of May, the French caught the Austrian rearguard at the town of Lodi, where the road from Piacenza to Milan crossed the Adda by a long wooden bridge. The Austrian general Sebottendorf had posted twelve thousand men and fourteen guns on the far bank, covering the bridge with artillery fire. The approaches to the bridge were swept by cannon.
What followed became the founding legend of Bonaparte’s army. The French grenadiers formed up under the covering fire of their own artillery. Bonaparte placed himself at the head of the column. At the signal, the grenadiers charged — not marching but running, bent low, the balls of the Austrian cannons tearing gaps through their ranks. The first ranks fell, and the second ranks stepped over them. Bonaparte, on foot among his men, was knocked into the marshy bank by the impact of a passing ball; his staff pulled him out, and he went forward again. The column reached the Austrian end of the bridge, hesitated for a moment under the close-range fire of the Austrian infantry, and then surged forward with the bayonet. The Austrian line broke.
The Battle of Lodi was not a great battle by the numbers — the Austrians lost perhaps two thousand men, the French somewhat fewer — but it was a great event in the history of Bonaparte’s reputation. The men of the Army of Italy had seen their general lead the charge on foot over a bridge swept by case-shot. From that day, they called him simply ‘the Little Corporal,’ and they would follow him anywhere. Bonaparte understood what he had achieved. ‘I saw the future,’ he said later. ‘In that moment, I knew I could become something in the world.‘
Milan and the Siege of Mantua
The army entered Milan on the 15th of May 1796. The Milanese, who had chafed under Austrian rule, received the French as liberators. Bonaparte installed himself in the Palazzo Serbelloni and set about the work of state-building that would run in parallel with his military operations for the next year. The old Austrian administration was swept aside; a provisional government was established; the first steps toward the creation of the Cisalpine Republic were taken. The treasures of Lombardy — its churches, its galleries, its libraries — were systematically inventoried and the choicest works dispatched to Paris.
But before the new order could be consolidated, there was a military problem that demanded solution. The great fortress of Mantua, the strongest in Italy, lay in Austrian hands, garrisoned by the remnants of Beaulieu’s army and commanded by a veteran officer of the Empire. The fortress was built on an island formed by the Mincio River, surrounded by lakes and marshes, approachable only by narrow causeways that were swept by its guns. As long as Mantua held out, Austria had a gate into Italy. Bonaparte resolved to take it.
The siege of Mantua began in earnest in June 1796. The French invested the fortresses on both sides of the Mincio, cutting the land approaches, while a flotilla of flat-bottomed boats patrolled the lakes. The siege works crept forward under the fire of the Austrian guns. Bonaparte, however, had not enough heavy artillery to breach the walls by bombardment alone. He settled in for a blockade, waiting for hunger to do what cannon could not. He would wait seven months.
The First Relief: Wurmser at Castiglione
The Austrian court at Vienna had not abandoned Italy. Throughout the summer of 1796, a new army was assembling in the Tyrol under Field Marshal Wurmser, one of the most experienced commanders of the Imperial service. Wurmser’s plan was to descend from the mountains into the Lombard plain with sixty thousand men, crush the French army before Mantua, and relieve the fortress.
Bonaparte, who had dispersed his forces across Lombardy to live off the land, found himself in a dangerous position when Wurmser’s advance was reported in late July. The Austrian army descended from the Tyrol in three columns: one down the west side of Lake Garda, one down the east side along the Adige valley, and one through the mountains toward the Brenta. Bonaparte faced the prospect of being caught between Wurmser’s army advancing from the north and the Mantua garrison sortieing from the south.
His response was a masterstroke of improvisation. He abandoned the siege of Mantua on the 1st of August, raised the blockade, and concentrated his army in a central position between the three Austrian columns. The artillery train was sent south to safety; the sick and wounded were evacuated. Bonaparte had accepted the loss of the siege works in exchange for the freedom to manoeuvre.
Wurmser entered Mantua in triumph on the 2nd of August, believing the French had been driven off. In fact, he had walked into a trap. Bonaparte had placed himself on the Austrian line of communications, and the three Austrian columns — spread out across the lakes and hills of the Garda region — could not support each other.
The battle of Castiglione, fought on the 5th of August 1796, was Bonaparte’s first great defensive-offensive battle. For four days the armies manoeuvred for position in the rolling hills between Lake Garda and the Mincio. On the morning of the 5th, Bonaparte had his army in place. Massena held the centre at Lonato; Augereau commanded the right at Castiglione; the division of General Guieux, moving along the western shore of Lake Garda, was to strike the Austrian left. Bonaparte’s plan required Guieux’s column to arrive at precisely the right moment — too soon and Wurmser would retreat, too late and the French centre would be crushed.
The timing was perfect. The battle raged through the heat of the Italian August afternoon. The Austrian infantry, the best in Europe, fought with the disciplined courage that had made them the terror of the Turks. But Bonaparte’s divisions moved like interlocking gears. At the critical moment, Guieux’s column appeared on the Austrian flank; Wurmser, his line of retreat threatened, ordered a general withdrawal. The French pursuit was relentless. By nightfall, the Austrian army was streaming north toward the Tyrol, having lost its artillery, its baggage, and twelve thousand men. The siege of Mantua was re-established the next day.
The Second Relief: Bassano and Arcola
Wurmser, however, was not finished. He had retreated into the Tyrol, reorganised his shattered divisions, and received reinforcements from Vienna. In September, he descended again into Italy — this time not from the west of Lake Garda but from the east, through the valleys of the Brenta and the Adige. Bonaparte met him at Bassano on the 8th of September and defeated him again. Wurmser, with the remnants of his army, retreated into Mantua itself, where he became the commander of the very garrison the French were besieging. He had exchanged a field army for a besieged fortress.
The Austrian court sent a third army under Field Marshal Alvinzi, a determined if unimaginative commander, who advanced from the Frioul in November. Alvinzi’s plan was to relieve Mantua by a concentric advance: one column under Davidovich descended the Adige valley from the Tyrol, while Alvinzi himself advanced from the east through the Vicenza plain. The two columns would meet before Mantua and crush the French between them.
Bonaparte, who had spent the autumn reducing the Papal Legations and pacifying the Romagna, raced north to meet the threat. The campaign that followed, in the marshes and canals of the Adige valley in the winter rains, was the most desperate of Bonaparte’s career.
The key to Alvinzi’s position was the village of Arcola, set in the marshes formed by the Alpone River, a tributary of the Adige. The causeways through the marshes were narrow; the Austrian artillery commanded the approaches; the infantry could advance only in columns of two or three men abreast. For three days — the 15th, 16th, and 17th of November — the armies fought for possession of this miserable village in the mud.
The first assault, led by Augereau in person, was driven back by the Austrian fire. Bonaparte ordered a second assault, and a third. He seized a flag and led the grenadiers himself through the marshes, the water up to their waists, the Austrian case-shot tearing the columns apart. His horse was shot from under him; he was knocked into a drainage ditch and nearly drowned in the mud; his staff pulled him out while the bullets chipped the earth around them. The fighting continued through the night, the flares from the burning villages lighting the faces of the dead.
On the third day, Massena, advancing from the left, managed to turn the Austrian flank. A diversionary force from the garrison of Porto-Legnago struck the Austrian rear. Alvinzi, his communications threatened and his army exhausted, ordered the retreat. The battle of Arcola was won, but the French had paid for it in blood. Bonaparte, when he wrote to the Directory, spoke of ‘a battle of giants’ — the phrase of Marshal Trivulzio describing Marignano.
The Third Relief: Rivoli
Alvinzi, however, would try once more. In January 1797, reinforced with fresh troops from the Tyrol, he advanced again toward Mantua with the same plan — a concerted movement by two columns through the Adige valley. The Austrian court had staked everything on this attempt. If Mantua fell, the war in Italy was lost.
This time, the Austrian plan very nearly succeeded. Davidovich’s column seized the heights of Rivoli, a plateau overlooking the Adige north of Verona, and established a fortified position that commanded the valley. Alvinzi’s main army advanced from the east. The French forces, scattered across northern Italy in their winter quarters, had only the two divisions of Joubert and Massena available to meet the threat.
Bonaparte rode through the night from Mantua to Rivoli, arriving on the plateau as the dawn of the 14th of January was breaking. What he saw was not encouraging. Joubert’s division, outnumbered three to one, was holding the edge of the plateau against the Austrian masses. The Austrian columns were visible in the valley below, their campfires still smoking, taking up positions for an assault that would crush Joubert against the cliff.
Bonaparte’s response was the most brilliant tactical improvisation of the campaign. He saw that the Austrian deployment required the columns to approach the plateau by separate ravines, each narrow and dangerous, and that the columns could not support each other while they were climbing. He ordered Joubert to hold the centre at all costs, committed Massena’s division to the left, and sent several battalions of light infantry to scale the cliff on the Austrian right — a movement the Austrians had believed impossible.
The battle of Rivoli, fought on the 14th and 15th of January 1797, was Bonaparte’s masterpiece. The Austrian columns, unable to deploy on the narrow plateau, were fed into the French fire piecemeal. Wave after wave of Austrian infantry climbed the slopes, formed up under the French artillery, and were broken by the bayonet charges of the French line. Massena’s flanking movement — a charge delivered at the double across the plateau, the bayonets glittering in the winter sun — threw the Austrian left into confusion. By nightfall, the Austrian army had ceased to exist as a fighting force. The remnants streamed back toward the Tyrol, leaving fourteen thousand prisoners and fifty guns on the field.
The Fall of Mantua
With Alvinzi’s army destroyed, the fate of Mantua was sealed. Bonaparte returned to the siege lines and delivered Wurmser an ultimatum: surrender or starve. The fortress had been under blockade for seven months; the garrison had eaten the horses, the dogs, the leather of their own harnesses. Typhus was raging in the casements. On the 2nd of February 1797, Wurmser surrendered. The Austrian field marshal, a white-haired veteran of the Seven Years’ War, marched out of the fortress at the head of his garrison — twenty thousand men who had held out longer than any fortress of the age, reduced to skeletons in tattered white uniforms. Bonaparte received him with the courtesy that great commanders owe to great opponents, and sent him to Vienna on parole.
The fall of Mantua ended the Italian campaign in its military phase. In six months, Bonaparte had defeated four Austrian armies, destroyed two of the Empire’s most celebrated commanders, and conquered the richest provinces of Italy.
The Pope, Leoben, and Campo Formio
With Austria prostrate, Bonaparte turned south against the Papal States. Pius VI, who had broken the armistice Bonaparte had imposed after the Faenza campaign in hope of an Austrian resurgence, now found himself defenceless. The French army advanced through the Romagna without opposition. On the 19th of February 1797, the Pope signed the Treaty of Tolentino, surrendering Avignon and the Legations of Bologna, Ferrara, and Ravenna to France, paying thirty million francs in indemnities, and delivering the choicest treasures of the Vatican to the commissioners of the Republic. The temporal power of the papacy, which had stood for a thousand years, was broken at a stroke.
Bonaparte now turned north again. The road to Vienna was open. The Archduke Charles, the most capable Austrian commander, was transferred from the Rhine to the Italian front, but neither his skill nor the reinforcements he brought could stop the French advance. Bonaparte crossed the Tagliamento, defeated the Austrians at Gradisca, took Trieste, and drove through the Norican Alps into the Austrian heartland. By the first week of April 1797, the French vanguard was at Leoben, less than a hundred miles from Vienna. The Austrian court sued for peace.
On the 18th of April, the Preliminaries of Leoben were signed. The terms were generous to Austria — Venice and its territories were ceded to the Emperor in exchange for the Belgian Netherlands and the Austrian recognition of the Cisalpine Republic — but the generosity was Bonaparte’s own calculation. He had exceeded his authority in negotiating terms of peace, as he had exceeded it at Cherasco, but he knew that the Directory, presented with a treaty, would accept it.
The Treaty of Campo Formio, signed on the 17th of October 1797, confirmed the Leoben terms and ended the war between France and Austria. The First Coalition was dissolved. Britain stood alone. Bonaparte returned to Paris in December 1797 to a reception that surpassed any triumph of the ancient world. The streets of the capital were lined with cheering crowds; the Directory received him in the Luxembourg Palace with a ceremony that was half homage, half fear.
The Birth of a Republic
The true significance of the Italian campaigns was not merely military. Bonaparte had not simply conquered Italy; he had remade it. The Cisalpine Republic, created from the conquered territories of Lombardy, the Duchy of Modena, and the Papal Legations, was a French satellite state organised on the model of the Republic — a directory of five members, a legislative council, and a constitution that proclaimed the sovereignty of the people. The old mosaic of duchies and principalities that had divided northern Italy for centuries was swept away. The Republic was a child of the French bayonet, and it would not survive the French defeat, but for the moment it was the most advanced political experiment the Italian peninsula had ever known.
The campaign also created Bonaparte. The young general who had ridden out of Nice in March 1796 had been an unknown appointment, a protégé of Carnot’s in whom no one outside the Directory had much confidence. The general who returned to Paris in December 1797 was the most famous man in Europe. He had given the Republic its greatest victories, its richest provinces, and its most durable peace. The soldiers of the Army of Italy had become his soldiers; the Cisalpine Republic was his creation; the treaties of Tolentino, Leoben, and Campo Formio bore his signature. He had proved himself not merely a great general but a statesman, a diplomat, an administrator of genius. The Directory, which had hoped to use him as an instrument, had created a rival.
Paganel, writing in 1815, looked back on the Italian campaign as the revelation of Bonaparte’s character as much as his military talent. The campaign displayed the qualities that would make him master of Europe: the cold audacity, the precision of calculation, the ability to see a battlefield as a single geometric problem in which the movements of divisions were the lines of a proof. It also displayed the qualities that would destroy him: the insatiable ambition, the contempt for constituted authority, the conviction that he alone could judge the interests of the peoples he conquered. Italy was liberated and conquered, freed and plundered, in the same gesture. It was a pattern that would repeat itself across a continent.
In the history of the French Revolution, the Italian campaigns of 1796-97 occupy a place of unique importance. They saved the Republic from military defeat, destroyed the First Coalition, and created the political conditions for the Directory’s survival. But they also created the man who, two years later, would overthrow the Directory and begin the long march from the Republic to the Empire. The bridge at Lodi was the beginning of everything.
Sources

Fantin-Desodoards, Antoine. Histoire Philosophique de la Révolution de France, depuis la première Assemblée des Notables jusqu’à la paix de 1801, Tome VII. 4th edition. Angers: Mame / Paris: Belin, An IX (1801). The primary narrative source for the Italian campaigns. Covers the appointment of Bonaparte, the Montenotte campaign, Lodi, the siege of Mantua, Castiglione, Bassano, Arcola, Rivoli, the fall of Mantua, the advance on Rome, Leoben, and Campo Formio.
Paganel, Pierre. Histoire de Napoléon Bonaparte, depuis ses premières campagnes jusqu’à son exil à l’isle de Sainte-Hélène. Liège: C. A. Bassompierre, 1815. Provides the moral assessment of the campaign as Bonaparte’s first great achievement and the proof of his genius.
Mahan, Alfred T. The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812, Vol. I. Boston: Little, Brown, 1892. Covers the naval context around Italy, the British evacuation of the Mediterranean (1796), and the strategic setting of the campaign.
Pagès, François. Histoire secrète de la révolution française, Tome III. 2nd edition. Paris: Dentu, An X (1802). Synthetic narrative of the Italian campaigns covering the battles of Montenotte, Lodi, Castiglione, Arcola, and Rivoli.

events/peace-of-amiens.title: The Peace of Amiens
events/peace-of-amiens.content:
The Peace of Amiens
The Collapse of the Second Coalition
By the autumn of 1801, Europe had fought itself to exhaustion. The war of the Second Coalition had begun in 1799 with high hopes: Russia, Austria, England, Turkey, Naples, and Portugal arrayed against a French Republic still reeling from the Directory’s corruption and military reverses. Suwarrow’s Russian armies had swept through northern Italy, Masséna had been besieged in Genoa, and the Republic itself seemed on the verge of collapse. But the tide turned. Masséna’s victory at Zurich saved Switzerland; Bonaparte returned from Egypt and seized power on 18 Brumaire; and in the spring of 1800 he crossed the Great Saint Bernard, fell upon the Austrian rear at Marengo, and shattered the Coalition’s prospects in a single afternoon. Moreau’s victory at Hohenlinden in December completed the work. By February 1801, Austria had signed the Treaty of Lunéville, confirming the French conquests of Campo Formio and extending French dominion to the left bank of the Rhine.
Great Britain alone remained at war. For two years she had sustained the Coalition with subsidies and her own maritime war; now she stood isolated, with no continental ally and the Armed Neutrality of the Northern Powers closing the Baltic to her shipping. The assassination of Tsar Paul I in March 1801 dissolved the Northern League before it could fully form, but it did not remove the underlying strategic problem: Britain had been fighting for eight years, her national debt had reached staggering proportions, and the war party led by William Pitt had given way to the more pacifically inclined ministry of Henry Addington. The country was weary. Pitt’s resignation in February 1801 over Catholic Emancipation had brought to power a government that wanted peace and needed peace.
The preliminaries were signed in London on the first of October, 1801. The very day after the signatures were dry, news reached London of the surrender of Alexandria to British arms — the final expulsion of the French from Egypt. It was believed that Bonaparte had possessed this intelligence at the time of signing but had concealed it, choosing to attribute to France the gracious act of restoring Egypt to the Porte. Whether or not this was true, it set the tone for everything that followed: a peace in which neither party trusted the other, and in which both believed they had been outmanoeuvred.
The Preliminaries of London
The preliminaries established the broad outlines that the definitive treaty would confirm. Great Britain agreed to restore most of her colonial conquests — the Cape of Good Hope to the Batavian Republic, the West Indian islands to France and Holland — retaining only Trinidad, ceded by Spain, and the Dutch possessions in Ceylon. France, for her part, recognised the independence of the Ionian Republic and agreed to evacuate Naples and the Papal States. The island of Malta was to be restored to the Knights of St. John under a guarantee of its independence and neutrality.
To contemporaries, these terms appeared generous to France — excessively so, in the eyes of the British Opposition. Pitt’s supporters had warned that any peace resting on the good faith of Bonaparte was a delusion. But the Addington ministry calculated that the relief of peace, the reduction of taxation, and the restoration of commercial intercourse were worth the sacrifice of conquests that would have been costly to defend in any case. The City of London received the news with jubilation. Illuminations, bonfires, and public subscriptions for the wounded marked the announcement. English tourists began packing their trunks for Paris.
The Negotiations at Amiens
The definitive treaty was to be negotiated at Amiens, a cathedral town in Picardy chosen for its neutrality and its proximity to both Paris and the Channel ports. The British government sent Lord Cornwallis — the same general who had surrendered at Yorktown twenty years earlier, now an elder statesman of unimpeachable integrity — as its plenipotentiary. He arrived in Amiens on the first of December, 1801, and found no one there to meet him.
The delays that followed were deliberate. The French and Dutch envoys trickled in, but the Spanish plenipotentiary failed to appear at all. On various pretexts the negotiations were spun out through the winter. The cause was not French procrastination alone; Cornwallis himself complained bitterly of the tergiversations of his interlocutors. But the chief beneficiary of delay was Bonaparte, who used the months of negotiation to consolidate his position in Europe by actions that had not been contemplated when the preliminaries were signed.
In December 1801, the Cisalpine Republic — whose independence had been guaranteed by the Treaty of Lunéville — adopted a new constitution drawn up under Bonaparte’s personal inspection. Delegates were summoned to Lyon, where the First Consul presided over a consulta that offered him the presidency of the republic. He accepted on the 26th of January, 1802. A few days later the name Cisalpine was changed to Italian, a modification whose aggressive implications were understood in every chancery in Europe. The same man who ruled France now wielded the power of four million Italians.
The news reached London and caused consternation. Many who had supported the peace now clamoured for war. The Addington ministry, however, chose to ignore what had passed so publicly and pressed forward with the negotiations. But by March, patience had expired. A number of ships were ordered into commission, extensive naval preparations begun, and an ultimatum dispatched to Amiens: Cornwallis was instructed to leave in eight days if the terms were not accepted.
Bonaparte had too much at stake on the seas to risk a rupture. The definitive treaty was signed on the 27th of March, 1802 — 6 Germinal, Year X of the French Republic.
The Treaty of Amiens
The treaty did not differ materially from the preliminaries, except in the article of Malta, which was elaborated at length. The Order of the Knights of St. John was to be restored to the island, with the provision that no citizen of either Great Britain or France could thereafter be a member. The neutrality and independence of the Order and the island were proclaimed. The British forces were to evacuate within three months of the exchange of ratifications, upon condition that a Grand Master was on the spot to receive possession and that two thousand Neapolitan troops — sent by the King of Naples, himself a neutral and a weak power — were present as a garrison. The independence of the island was placed under the guarantee of Great Britain, France, Austria, Spain, Russia, and Prussia — whose acquiescence had not been obtained in advance.
These elaborate provisions concealed an essential weakness: the entire structure depended on the active co-operation of powers who had not yet agreed to participate. When the moment came to execute the treaty, this clause would prove the lever by which Great Britain justified retaining Malta long after the stipulated period had elapsed.
Beyond the Maltese question, the treaty provided for the restoration of Porto Ferrajo in Elba (which Britain had held by force of arms), the evacuation of Egypt, and the exchange of prisoners. The cession of Louisiana by Spain to France — known to the British ministry at the time of the preliminaries but publicly unavowed — was not mentioned in the treaty. The boundary of French Guiana obtained from Portugal was pushed back off the Amazon, but no reference was made to the secret treaties by which Bonaparte had already secured commercial advantages from Turkey and territorial gains from Portugal.
The Peace in Europe
The Treaty of Amiens was received in both countries with profound relief. In France, the joy was unbounded. Paganel, writing from the perspective of 1815, observed that the peace was regarded by the French as a triumph wrung from the weakness of the Sea Power — a vindication of Bonaparte’s genius for war and diplomacy. The Legislature was convoked in extraordinary session to ratify the treaties and measures of the government, and the Treaty of Amiens was presented as the crowning work of the First Consul’s statesmanship. For his services, Bonaparte was proposed for a striking mark of public acknowledgment: the Consulate for life, which was approved by plebiscite in August 1802.
Yet even at the moment of celebration, Paganel noted that the public joy was mingled with sad presentiments. The advantages obtained by France at Amiens were regarded by the discerning as forced concessions, dictated by necessity. The contracting parties, in signing the peace, remained in hostile dispositions; and the Consul, more than any other, in a threatening attitude. ‘The Peace of Amiens,’ Paganel wrote, ‘was only a concerted truce between the enemy powers of France.’
For the English, the peace opened Paris to travellers who had not visited the Continent in a decade. The influx of British tourists was one of the most remarked phenomena of the period: they crowded the Palais-Royal, attended the Opéra, climbed the towers of Notre-Dame, and marvelled at the works of art that Bonaparte had plundered from Italy. The painter Benjamin West received permission to visit the Louvre; Charles James Fox, the great Whig statesman, made a celebrated journey to Paris and was received by Bonaparte himself. For fourteen months, the guns were silent and the Channel was open.
The Breakdown
The peace was never allowed to settle. From the moment the treaty was signed, Bonaparte continued the restless political activity that had characterised the negotiation itself. He seemed incapable of treating the peace as final; for him, it was merely a breathing-space in which to consolidate French domination of the Continent.
The first shock came in September 1802, when Bonaparte formally incorporated Piedmont and Elba into France. Piedmont had been organised as a French military department since April 1801, but the decree of annexation changed a de facto condition into a de jure one — a permanent encroachment that menaced Austria’s Italian possessions and destroyed the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Sardinia. No compensation was given to the Sardinian king, and both Great Britain and Russia had sought earnestly to obtain some reparation for him.
Next came Switzerland. In the spring of 1802, Bonaparte had detached the Valais from the Helvetic Confederation and proclaimed it independent, securing the Simplon route into Italy. He then withdrew French troops, leaving the Swiss cantons to settle their own affairs. The opposing parties — Unitarians who favoured the French Revolution and Aristocrats who sought to return to the old constitution — fell into civil conflict. The aristocratic party gained the upper hand. Bonaparte, declaring that he would not ‘deliver the formidable bastions of the Alps to fifteen hundred mercenaries paid by England,’ sent thirty thousand French soldiers under General Ney into Switzerland. All opposition ceased.
The emotion of Europe was profound. The British ministry, which had acquiesced in the annexation of Piedmont in silence, finally spoke. On the 10th of October 1802, the British cabinet dispatched a vigorous remonstrance to Paris and, on the same day, sent a special envoy to the Swiss frontiers with instructions to offer the Swiss pecuniary succour if they would resist. The ministry then took a further step: orders were sent to the West Indies, Dutch Guiana, and the Cape of Good Hope directing that the colonies ordered to be restored should be retained until further instructions.
Bonaparte received the British remonstrance with fury. He dictated instructions to his minister in London that were characterised even by the Bonapartist historian Thiers as ‘truly extraordinary.’ He threatened that if war arose, the coasts of Europe from Hanover to Taranto would be closed to British commerce; that Liguria, Lombardy, Switzerland, and Holland would be converted into French provinces; that Great Britain herself would be invaded by a hundred thousand soldiers. ‘The first consul was but thirty-three,’ he said. ‘He had as yet destroyed only states of the second order. Who knows how long it would take him, if forced thereto, to change again the face of Europe and revive the Empire of the West?’
The crisis over Switzerland passed without immediate rupture — the Swiss had not in fact risen, and the British envoy was recalled — but the damage was irreparable. From that moment, both sides began preparing for war while still nominally at peace. The British ministry recalled its orders to retain the colonies, but the second vessel carrying the countermand might or might not overtake the first. The uncertainty poisoned the atmosphere.
The Question of Malta
Bonaparte, having failed to overawe the British cabinet, now pressed for the evacuation of Malta. The ministry had its own reasons for delay. No Grand Master had yet accepted the sovereignty of the island; Spain, under Bonaparte’s influence, had suppressed the revenues of the Order within her limits; and doubt existed whether the Order’s income would suffice to maintain the island’s defences. More fundamentally, the British public had never reconciled itself to surrendering a position so vital to the control of the Mediterranean and the approaches to India.
The ministry took broader ground. Lord Whitworth, the new British ambassador in Paris, was instructed to affirm Great Britain’s right to interfere in continental affairs whenever her interests required it, and to point out that the annexation of Piedmont, the invasion of Switzerland, and the renunciation of the Grand Duke of Parma had materially altered the conditions since the treaty. These changes, the ministry argued, entitled Great Britain to compensations — of which the retention of Malta was the most obvious.
Bonaparte responded by publishing, on the 30th of January 1803, Colonel Sébastiani’s report on his mission to the Levant. Sébastiani, dispatched the previous September to visit Tripoli, Egypt, Syria, and the Ionian islands, reported that the Eastern peoples revered Bonaparte, that the Ionian islands were ready to declare themselves French at the first opportunity, and — in the passage that caused a storm in London — that ‘six thousand French troops would now suffice to conquer Egypt.’
The publication of this report in the official Moniteur was a deliberate provocation. It was intended to intimidate the British ministry into compliance on Malta; it achieved the opposite. The British government replied that, in view of Sébastiani’s report, the king would not evacuate Malta until substantial security was provided against the purposes therein revealed.
The Rupture
From this point, the slide to war was inexorable. On the 20th of February 1803, Bonaparte sent a message to the Legislature in which he declared that ‘two parties strive for power’ in England — one for peace, one for war — and concluded with the words: ‘England, alone, cannot to-day contend against France.’ The British government responded on the 8th of March by sending a message to Parliament that, in consequence of military preparations in the ports of France and Holland, the king judged it expedient to adopt additional measures of precaution.
The final negotiations were conducted in an atmosphere of mutual ultimatum. Great Britain offered to cede Malta in perpetuity to Britain (Bonaparte replied that he would sooner see the British on the heights of Montmartre), or alternatively to hold the island for ten years as security. Bonaparte refused. On the 12th of May 1803, Lord Whitworth demanded his passports and left Paris.
On the 16th of May, Great Britain declared war against France. The following day, Admiral Cornwallis sailed from Plymouth with ten ships-of-the-line and resumed the watch off Brest. On the 18th, Nelson hoisted his flag on board the Victory at Portsmouth and sailed for the Mediterranean.
The Peace of Amiens had lasted fourteen months.
The Anatomy of Failure
Mahan’s analysis of the failure of Amiens is an anatomy of the fundamental incompatibility between Bonaparte’s ambition and the security of the British state. The peace was conceived, Mahan argues, under a double illusion: that Bonaparte would be content with the territorial arrangements of Lunéville, and that Great Britain could surrender her maritime conquests without receiving in return a stable continental equilibrium.
The first illusion was shattered within weeks of the signature. The second persisted longer but was no less delusive. Mahan observes that the peace was never anything but an ‘armed truce,’ a condition in which both parties maintained large military establishments while pretending to have laid down their arms. The fundamental cause of the rupture was Bonaparte’s conviction that ‘in the existing state of Europe England cannot reasonably make war, alone, against us’ — a conviction he stated openly and acted upon in his interventions in Italy, Switzerland, and Germany.
From the naval perspective, the peace was a disaster for France. Mahan notes that the respite did not restore French sea power; it merely revealed how thoroughly that sea power had been annihilated. The French navy had lost Egypt, Malta, and its best colonial possessions. The expedition to Saint-Domingue — Bonaparte’s grand project to reassert French authority in the Caribbean — was consuming armies whole in the yellow fever epidemic. By the time war resumed, France was no stronger at sea than she had been in 1801, while British naval preparations had been driven forward by the very tensions that preceded the rupture.
Paganel’s analysis, written from the French side in the immediate aftermath of Waterloo, is more sombre. He sees the Peace of Amiens as the apogee of the Consulate — the moment when Bonaparte stood highest in European estimation — and simultaneously as the beginning of the descent. The peace was not genuinely European; it was a bilateral arrangement between two powers that distrusted each other, imposed upon a continent that had not been consulted. ‘The advantages that France obtained by the Treaty of Amiens,’ Paganel writes, ‘were regarded with some reason as forced concessions, dictated by necessity. The contracting parties, in signing the peace, remained in hostile dispositions; and the Consul, more than any other, in a threatening attitude.’
The war that followed was longer, harder, and more terrible than anything that had preceded it. The Peace of Amiens was the last chance for a general settlement in Europe for a generation. It failed not because the terms were inadequate but because the peace rested on no foundation of trust and no balance of power that Bonaparte was willing to respect. In Mahan’s concluding judgment, the rupture demonstrated that a maritime power and a continental power could not coexist in equilibrium so long as one of them was led by a man who ‘would never accept the independence of others as a final condition of the European system.‘

events/september-massacres.title: September Massacres
events/september-massacres.content:
The September Massacres
The September Massacres of 1792 were the slaughter of more than a thousand prisoners in the Parisian prisons between the afternoon of Sunday, 2 September, and the evening of Thursday, 6 September. The killing was organised by the insurrectionary Commune of Paris and the Cordeliers club, carried out by bands of armed volunteers recruited from the sections, and tacitly permitted by the Minister of Justice, Georges Danton. The massacres stand as the first great act of state-sanctioned bloodletting of the Revolution — the passage from the popular insurrection of 10 August to the institutional terror that would follow in 1793.
The Precipice
The fall of the monarchy on 10 August 1792 had left France in an impossible position. The royal family was imprisoned in the Temple. The Legislative Assembly, stripped of executive authority, had named a Provisional Executive Council in which Danton held Justice, Roland the Interior, and Servan the War. The Prussian and Austrian armies, commanded by the Duke of Brunswick, were advancing across the frontier. Verdun, the last fortress on the road to Paris, was under siege and expected to fall within days. The manifesto that Brunswick had issued in July — threatening to deliver Paris to “exemplary and forever memorable vengeance” if the royal family were harmed — had produced the opposite of its intended effect: it had inflamed Parisian opinion and convinced the sections that the city was infested with an internal enemy that would rise in support of the invaders.
The prisons were crowded with the arrestees of the previous weeks. After 10 August, the sections and the Commune’s Committee of Surveillance had carried out waves of arrests against non-juring priests, suspected royalists, Swiss guards captured at the Tuileries, and anyone deemed suspect. The prisons of the Abbaye, the Carmes (the Carmelite convent used as a detention centre), the Conciergerie, La Force, the Châtelet, and Bicêtre held somewhere between 2,600 and 3,000 prisoners.
In the last days of August, a current of talk had begun among the sections — carried first in the Cordeliers district where Danton’s influence was strongest. The enemy was at the gates; the prisoners inside the city must be considered a fifth column; the only sure measure was to eliminate them before they could act. The coming of war news from the frontier — and above all the fall of Verdun — would provide the signal.
2 September: The Signal
The morning of Sunday, 2 September, brought the confirmation that Paris had dreaded: Verdun had fallen, or was about to fall — the reports differed on the day, but the substance was the same. The road to Paris lay open. At the Hôtel de Ville, the Commune ordered the tocsin sounded. The alarm bell of Notre-Dame began to toll. Drums beat the générale through the streets. The sections called their citizens to arms, and the volunteers preparing to march to the frontier gathered in the great squares to receive their marching orders.
It was in this atmosphere — the city braced for invasion, the bells ringing, the drums rolling — that the prisons were opened.
The first attack fell upon the prisoners being transferred from the Hôtel de Ville to the Abbaye prison. A crowd stopped the carriages at the doors of the Abbaye and began the killing. The method was the same across all the prisons: bands of armed men — some in the uniform of the National Guard, others in ordinary dress with sabres, pikes, and axes — entered the prisons, established what they called “popular tribunals” in the courtyards or gatehouses, examined the prisoners one by one, and delivered verdicts of liberty or death. Those condemned were handed to the executioners waiting at the gates, who killed them with sabres, pikes, and axes. The bodies were stripped and piled in the streets or thrown into carts.
At the Abbaye, the first of these “commissions” was improvised. A group of perhaps a hundred to a hundred and fifty men, armed and resolute, took possession of the prison gates. The prisoners were called out one by one. A brief interrogation was conducted — name, profession, the grounds of detention. Those who satisfied the judges of their patriotism were released with a shout of “Vive la Nation!” Those who did not were thrust through the gate to the waiting executioners. The judgments were final; there was no appeal.
Gouverneur Morris, the American Minister to France, was at his house in the Rue de la Planche in the Faubourg Saint-Germain when the news reached him. A servant reported that the people were breaking into the prisons. He could hear the tocsin sounding from the churches. By evening the streets were empty of ordinary traffic; only armed patrols moved through the city. Morris noted in his diary that the city felt as though it were under military occupation — the same city that had been, four days earlier, in a state of revolutionary exaltation, now descended into something darker.
At the Carmes prison, where the non-juring priests had been held since August, the killing began in the afternoon. The Carmelite convent had been converted into a temporary prison after the fall of the monarchy, and held approximately 160 priests — clergy who had refused to swear the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and were therefore considered enemies of the Revolution. A mob of about two hundred men, led by an actor named Collot d’Herbois and a former priest named Jourdan, broke into the convent garden. The priests were dragged out of their cells, lined up against the walls of the cloister, and shot or cut down with sabres. Some tried to climb over the walls; most were caught before they could escape. The killing continued into the night by torchlight. By the end, about 115 priests lay dead in the garden — the “Carmes” massacre became a byword among Catholic Europe for revolutionary cruelty.
The same pattern spread to the other prisons. At the Conciergerie, the old royal prison on the Île de la Cité, the commissioners of the Commune arrived and demanded the keys. The prisoners were brought before a hastily assembled tribunal. The common criminals were released; the political prisoners and the Swiss guards were killed. At La Force prison, where the most distinguished prisoners were held — including the Princesse de Lamballe, the superintendent of the Queen’s household and her closest friend — the killing began in the evening.
Roland’s Protest
Jean-Marie Roland, the Minister of the Interior, was one of the few members of the Provisional Council who attempted to stop the massacres. As minister charged with the general surveillance of public order — though without direct command over the armed force — he had written urgently to the Commune in the person of the mayor, Jérôme Pétion, calling on the municipal authorities to deploy their vigilance. He had addressed himself to the commandant-general, Santerre, requesting him to reinforce the posts guarding the prisons. When he learned that the prisons were directly threatened, he issued a formal requisition calling on the commandant to guard them scrupulously, placing the responsibility for any event on the commandant’s head. To give effect to this measure, he ordered the requisition printed and posted at every street corner — a public appeal to the citizens to watch over the safety of the prisons themselves, since the military commander appeared to neglect his duty.
Roland was not at the Interior Ministry when the crowd arrived there at about five o’clock on the evening of Sunday, 2 September — the same hour the prisons were being invested. Approximately two hundred men appeared in the courtyard, demanding to see the minister and demanding arms. Madame Roland, who was at home, received them. She ordered that ten of them be invited upstairs. They told her they were good citizens about to depart for Verdun but lacked arms. She explained that the Minister of the Interior had never had arms at his disposal; they must apply to the Ministry of War. After a tense exchange, she persuaded them to search the hôtel and satisfy themselves that Roland was not hiding, and directed them to the council meeting at the Ministry of the Marine. They withdrew, taking a domestic servant as a hostage who was released an hour later.
The ministers learned of the massacres only the following morning, Monday, 3 September. Shocked by the abominable crimes, the evident complicity of the Commune, and the impotence of honest men to arrest them, Roland and his wife resolved that the only course left to a minister of honour was to denounce the killings with the greatest possible éclat, to appeal to the Assembly to stop them, to raise the indignation of all honest citizens, and to expose himself, if necessary, to the daggers of the assassins rather than participate by silence in the crime.
Roland wrote his famous letter to the Legislative Assembly on the 3rd of September — a document as celebrated in its way as the letter he had addressed to the king the previous June. The Assembly received it with transports of applause; it ordered the letter printed, distributed, and posted. The Assembly applauded, as weak men applaud, at signs of a courage they cannot themselves imitate but which touches them and awakens some hope.
Later that same day, a former colleague of Roland’s brought to dinner Anacharsis Clootz, the self-styled “orator of the human race.” Clootz defended the massacres as a necessary and salutary measure, reciting commonplaces about the rights of the people, the justice of popular vengeance, and its utility for the happiness of the species. He spoke long and loudly, ate more than anyone, and bored the company. He did not return.
Danton’s Role
Danton, the Minister of Justice, was at the Hôtel de Ville throughout the critical hours, seated in the Committee of Surveillance from which the orders for the multiplied arrests of the previous days had issued. It was there that he had embraced Marat after a feigned quarrel of twenty-four hours. He then went upstairs to Pétion, took him aside, and in his characteristic language — always heightened with vigorous expressions — said: “Do you know what they’ve done? They’ve issued a warrant for Roland’s arrest. Who? That mad Committee. I took the warrant — here it is — we can’t let them act this way. Against a member of the Council!” Pétion took the warrant, read it, smiled, and handed it back. “Let them do it,” he said, “it will produce a good effect.” “A good effect!” replied Danton, examining the mayor curiously. “Oh, I will not suffer that; I will put them in their place.” The warrant was never executed.
The question that follows the reader of these events is whether the two hundred men who appeared at Roland’s hôtel that evening had been sent by the authors of the warrant; whether the failure of their attempt, which introduced delay into the execution of the plan, caused those who had conceived it to hesitate; and whether Danton’s démarche to the mayor was that of a conspirator who wished to test the effect of the blow, or to gain credit for having parried a stroke that had already miscarried.
When the commandant of the prisons, Grandpré — who had spent the morning of 2 September visiting the detenus and had managed to facilitate the release of a considerable number — approached Danton at the council’s exit that evening to speak of what he had seen and of the requisitions that the Minister of the Interior had addressed to the armed force, Danton replied with his bellowing voice and an appropriate gesture: “I don’t give a damn about the prisoners — let them become what they can!” The remark was made in the presence of twenty people, who shuddered to hear a minister of justice speak so.
The Princesse de Lamballe
Of all the victims of the September Massacres, none struck contemporaries with greater horror than the murder of the Princesse de Lamballe. Marie-Thérèse-Louise de Savoie-Carignan, the Princesse de Lamballe, was the superintendent of the Queen’s household and the closest friend Marie-Antoinette had. She had returned from emigration in 1791 to be near the Queen, and after the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August she had been arrested with the other royalists and imprisoned at La Force.
On the afternoon of 3 September, the crowd that had already killed at the Abbaye and the Carmes arrived at La Force. The Princesse was brought before the improvised tribunal in the prison courtyard. She was asked to swear hatred of the king, the queen, and the monarchy. She refused. The tribunal condemned her. She was pushed through the gate and seized by the mob in the street. The killing was prolonged and savage.
Her head was cut off, placed on a pike, and carried through the streets of Paris to the Temple, where the royal family were imprisoned. The mob intended to force the Queen to witness the head of her friend. The guards at the Temple prevented the crowd from entering, but the head was paraded past the windows.
In the Temple that evening, the Queen asked why the noise of the crowd was so great. She was told nothing. But she saw the shadow of the pike move past the window, and she understood — or sensed — what had happened. When the news was confirmed, Marie-Antoinette fainted.
Campan, who wrote the Queen’s story from the testimony of those who were with her in the Temple, recorded that the Queen remained changed from that day forward. The friend who had refused to abandon her, who had chosen imprisonment over safety, was gone, and the Queen’s captivity, already harsh, became a descent into a deeper solitude.
The Third and Fourth Days
The massacres continued on Tuesday, 4 September, and into the following days. By Tuesday the focus had shifted to the remaining prisons: Bicêtre, which held common criminals and the insane as well as political prisoners; the Salpêtrière, the women’s prison; and the more distant prisons of the city. The fury was beginning to exhaust itself, but the Commune did nothing to stop it.
Morris, writing from his house on the outskirts of Paris, recorded the growing tension. The weather was pleasant. Business was suspended. The thoroughfares were no longer safe. The Commission that had been established at the Hôtel de Ville continued to meet, examining papers and directing arrests. On Monday, 3 September — the day of the Princesse de Lamballe’s murder — Morris noted that the prisoners at Versailles had also been killed. “The City of Paris remains in a state of insurrection,” he wrote. “It has named the Ministers, who act in subordination to it. The Commune assumes all powers.”
On Tuesday, 4 September, between two and three in the afternoon, Morris received a note from the Commune informing him that his horses had been stopped and that orders had been given to permit their passage for the future. The assassins were beginning to formalise their procedures.
By Wednesday, 5 September, the killing had begun to subside, though isolated murders continued. Robespierre, speaking at the Jacobins, denounced those who had tried to save the prisoners. The Commune, far from being shamed, defended the massacres as a necessary act of popular justice.
The Aftermath
When the prisons fell silent, the count was appalling. Estimates ranged from 1,100 to 1,600 dead. About half were non-juring priests and royalist political prisoners; the rest were common criminals, including many detained for minor offences and some who were simply in the wrong place. The proportion of priests among the dead was the highest — roughly three-quarters of the non-juring clergy in Paris had been killed.
The Legislative Assembly, which had sat in helpless session throughout the massacres, issued no condemnation. A few deputies protested. Roland’s letter had been printed and applauded, but no deputy proposed to arrest the leaders of the Commune or to send troops to stop the killing. The Assembly, like the city, was paralysed by fear and by the knowledge that the Commune commanded the armed sections.
The Provisional Executive Council was divided. Danton had been at the Hôtel de Ville throughout the three days; he had not lifted a finger to prevent the massacres, and his celebrated dismissal of the prisoners’ fate had been overheard by twenty witnesses. Servan, the Minister of War, sent no troops. Roland alone had acted and had failed; his letter to the Assembly was his only weapon, and it had produced applause and nothing more.
The Girondins — the republican faction that had emerged from the Legislative Assembly and that included Roland, Brissot, Vergniaud, and their allies — broke decisively with the Commune and with Danton after the massacres. The breaking point had been reached; they could no longer pretend to share a common cause with the men who had organised the slaughter. But the break came too late to save them. The Commune and the Montagnards — Robespierre, Marat, Danton — now had the upper hand. The Girondins became the object of the most constant hatred, the most exact surveillance, the most severe rigours. Every act became a crime for them; every accusation became legitimate; every defence was forbidden. Brissot, publicly calumniated by Barère, could not find a single printer in all of France courageous enough to publish the rebuttal he addressed to his calumniator.
The September Massacres left an indelible mark on the Revolution. They demonstrated that the Parisian Commune was willing to exercise a direct and violent sovereignty beyond the control of any constituted authority. They introduced the principle — which the Revolutionary Tribunal of 1793 would later institutionalise — that revolutionary justice could be administered summarily and without appeal. They deepened the division between the Girondins and the Montagnards that would culminate in the proscription of the Girondins in June 1793. And they accustomed Paris to the spectacle of mass killing — a preparation for the Terror that would begin in earnest nine months later.
In the prisons that survived the massacres, the survivors were left with the memory of the days when the tocsin rang and the crowd came. Some of those who had been released by the popular tribunals — able to satisfy the judges of their revolutionary credentials — emerged into a city that had become unrecognisable. The prisons that had been emptied were soon filled again: the Convention, which had replaced the Legislative Assembly on 21 September 1792, passed laws that would fill the Abbaye and the Conciergerie and the Luxembourg with a new generation of prisoners — the Girondins, the Hébertists, the Dantonists — who would be tried by a properly constituted Revolutionary Tribunal and sent to the guillotine, not by pike and sabre, but by the cold machinery of the law.
