events/the-october-days.title: The October Days
events/the-october-days.content:
The October Days
The October Days of 5 and 6 October 1789 were the second great popular insurrection of the French Revolution, and in many respects the more consequential of the two. The storming of the Bastille on 14 July had saved the National Assembly from dissolution and given Paris its armed militia; but the October Days altered the very geography of power. They brought the king, the queen, and the royal family from Versailles to Paris as prisoners of the people. They transferred the National Assembly to the capital. And they ended, in the space of thirty-six hours, the long history of Versailles as the seat of the French monarchy — a seat it had occupied since Louis XIV moved the court there in 1682.
The Bread Shortage and the Banquet
The immediate cause of the October Days was the scarcity of bread in Paris. Throughout September 1789, the grain supply had been irregular, prices had risen, and the bakers’ shops of the capital could not meet demand. Hunger, always the sharpest goad of the Paris crowd, had been aggravated by the political crisis of the summer and by the stagnation of trade that followed the July insurrection. But what turned hunger into insurrection was the news from Versailles of what the people called the orgy of 1 October.
The Flanders Regiment had been ordered to Versailles in mid-September as part of what the court intended as a show of force. The king’s military household, the bodyguards, and the Swiss regiments had long formed the armed core of the court’s security; but the arrival of an additional regiment of the line — regular troops — was interpreted by Paris as a preparation for the dissolution of the National Assembly and a counter-revolutionary stroke. The Comte d’Estaing, commanding the National Guard of Versailles, had received the regiment with all the forms of military honour, and the court resolved to cement the loyalty of the new troops by a gesture of hospitality.
On the evening of 1 October, the bodyguards invited the officers of the Flanders Regiment to a banquet in the great theatre of the château. The hall was decked for a fête. The music of the two regiments played through the meal. At the second service, four toasts were drunk — to the king, the queen, the Dauphin, and the royal family — but the health of the nation was expressly refused. Then the king and queen entered, the queen leading the Dauphin by the hand. She made the tour of the tables, the child in her arms, moving through waves of applause and acclamation. The visit had the appearance of spontaneity; it had been arranged in advance.
The fête dissolved into an orgy. Wine flowed without restraint. The musicians played “O Richard, O mon roi, l’univers t’abandonne” — a song whose perfidious allusion to the king’s abandonment could not, in that moment, have been lost on any hearer — and the march of the howling winds from Iphigénie. The national cockade was trampled. White cockades, the symbol of the monarchy and of resistance to the Revolution, were distributed in the galleries. An officer of d’Estaing’s staff scaled the balcony of the king’s apartment and displayed the white cockade to applause. The banquet was repeated the following night in the riding school, with a greater crowd of guests and circumstances still more offensive to the nation.
The news of these events reached Paris two days later. The effect was explosive. The scarcity of bread, the arrogance of the courtiers who wore the black cockade in the public promenades of Paris as a symbol of the mourning they were preparing to plunge all France into, the insult to the tricolour, the rumour that the king would soon flee to Metz and dissolve the Assembly — all these converged into a single cry: vengeance.
Monday 5 October: The Women March
The morning of Monday 5 October saw the outbreak. Troops of women — the fishwives and market-women of Les Halles, the poorest and most formidable of the Parisian populace — spread through the city like a torrent, crying for bread. A baker was nearly seized and hanged from the street lantern; only the intervention of M. de Gouvion, who threw himself between the man and his pursuers, saved him.
The women gathered before the Hôtel de Ville. Some six or seven thousand of them, by the most moderate estimate, crowded the square. They broke into the municipal building, took what arms they could find, and threatened to burn the whole edifice. At this point a man named Maillard — one of the heroes of the Bastille, known for his composure under fire — imposed himself as their leader. It was Maillard who, seeing that the Hôtel de Ville could not be saved unless the crowd was diverted, proposed to lead the women to Versailles. “While they are walking four leagues,” he said to the authorities, “we can prevent the misfortunes that threaten us.” He persuaded the women to lay down their weapons, telling them they would move the National Assembly far more by appearing as suppliants asking for bread than by presenting themselves as an armed force.
They set out in the rain. A great multitude of armed men had joined them. Companies of volunteers from the Bastille accompanied the march; a troop of the Parisian guard followed with cannon. The tocsin had been ringing all morning; the générale had been beaten; the whole city was in motion.
At Versailles, the National Assembly was debating the king’s response to the constitutional articles. Mirabeau, who had received word of the march before anyone else in the chamber — a circumstance that has never been satisfactorily explained — approached the president, Mounier, and said in a low voice: “Mounier, Paris marches on us. Go to the château; give them this warning. Tell them, if you wish, that you have it from me; I consent. But end this scandalous debate. Time presses; there is not a minute to lose.”
At about three in the afternoon, the women appeared at the entrance of the Avenue de Paris. Maillard was at their head. The bodyguards, three hundred and twenty strong, mounted their horses and formed in squadrons on the Place d’Armes, their backs to the château gates. The Flanders Regiment and the dragoons took up positions. Maillard presented himself at the bar of the National Assembly: “We have come to ask for bread and to demand the punishment of the bodyguards who insulted the national cockade.” At that moment a national cockade was brought to Maillard from the bodyguards; he showed it to the women as a token of peaceable intentions. They cried: “Vive le roi! Vive les gardes-du-corps!”
The president went to the château to lay before the king the picture of the famine that afflicted Paris. But while Maillard was still at the bar of the Assembly, a detachment of women had advanced towards the château to demand bread. The bodyguards moved to bar their way. Lieutenant de Savonnières, sabre in hand, pursued a soldier of the Paris guard whom the women had forced to march at their head. A musket-shot from a citizen-soldier of Versailles shattered Savonnières’ arm and saved the man’s life. This first act of hostility inflamed both sides. Stones were thrown; carbines were fired from the king’s guard; two or three of the women fell. The crowd answered with a volley; two or three bodyguards were thrown from their horses. Three pieces of cannon loaded with grapeshot, brought by the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, were trained on the bodyguards. The match was brought to the touch-hole several times, but the rain had dampened the powder, and voices were heard crying: “Stop. It is not time yet.”
It was the rain and the lack of concert that saved the bodyguards. The women of Paris broke away from the main body of combatants, attacked the Flanders Regiment from the front and took the dragoons in flank. They penetrated the ranks, embraced the soldiers, and made the weapons fall from their hands. The order not to fire, not to irritate the people, was repeated and carried to the bodyguards. They withdrew. The grilles of the château closed behind them.
The Night
The Parisian army, exhausted by the march and the rain, arrived at nightfall. Lafayette, who had been compelled to lead his troops — he paled when the order was given, and cast a sorrowful look over the battalions that surrounded him — took command. The king had accepted the constitutional articles in a pure and simple form. The National Assembly decreed that the king and the Constituent body were inseparable during the current session. Peace seemed to have been restored. Lafayette, assured that all was quiet, took some rest.
But the women and the brigands mingled among them had passed the night in the Assembly hall and in the great guardhouse of the Place d’Armes. They drank; they whipped each other’s rage; they went out at daybreak famished for vengeance and thirsting for blood.
It was about five in the morning of Tuesday 6 October. The day was just breaking. The crowd surged towards the château. The ordinary precautions of security had been forgotten in the confusion of the previous day. The horde penetrated as far as the Cour Royale. The bodyguards seized their arms. A musket-shot from a window of the château, whether by imprudence or blind zeal, struck down a citizen. The crowd, excited by the spectacle, rushed to vengeance with terrible cries directed above all against the queen.
The crowd mounted the great staircase. The bodyguards presented themselves. Miomandre de Sainte-Marie, a bodyguard, descended four steps and was immediately set upon; he managed to disengage himself and rejoin his comrades. The guards fell back, some into the king’s chamber, some into the great hall. The brigands turned towards the queen’s apartment. Tardivet du Repaire, a bodyguard, threw himself before the door to prevent the howling mass from entering. He was assailed and fell under the blows that rained upon him from all sides. A man armed with a pike tried to pierce his heart; he managed to disarm the man and rise again, parrying the bayonet-strokes of a soldier with the very pike. The door of the king’s chamber opened a little, and two of his comrades pulled him inside.
During this time, Miomandre de Sainte-Marie saw a bodyguard of the queen’s antechamber being dragged on the staircase. Terrified only for the princess’s danger, he leaped through the waves of the furious multitude, saw Repaire struggling in the hands of assassins, heard a band of cannibals howling the death-cry. Nothing stopped him. He flew to the queen’s apartment, opened the door: “Madame,” he cried to a woman he perceived at the extremity of the next room, “save the queen; they want her life; I am alone here against two thousand tigers.” He closed the door behind him, and after some minutes of combat was struck down by a pike; another assailant struck him on the head with a musket-butt. He lay senseless and bathed in his blood. The brigands, believing him dead, stripped him and returned to the great hall.
The queen had been asleep. Her women — who had disobeyed her order to go to bed — heard the horrible cries and the gunshots at about half-past four. One of them entered the queen’s chamber and woke her. “Get out of bed, Madame,” she cried; “do not dress; save yourself to the king.” The queen, terrified, threw herself out of bed; a petticoat was passed over her without being tied; her two ladies led her towards the Œil-de-Bœuf. The door of her dressing-cabinet, which communicated with that room, was never locked except on her side. In that terrible moment it was found locked on the other side. They knocked repeatedly; a domestic of the king’s valet de chambre opened it. The queen entered the king’s chamber and did not find him. Alarmed for the queen’s life, he had descended by the staircases and corridors that ran beneath the Œil-de-Bœuf and that led habitually to the queen’s apartment without needing to cross that room. He entered her chamber and found only the bodyguards who had taken refuge there.
The queen, meanwhile, as she crossed the Œil-de-Bœuf, heard threatening voices crying out: “It is a messenger; she must be hanged; we must eat her liver.” A pistol-shot and a musket-shot redoubled her terror. She reached the king at last — he had entered by one door as she entered by another — and threw herself into his arms. Madame de Tourzel, the governess of the royal children, brought the Dauphin and Madame Royale. The family was reunited.
The Parisian National Guard had now arrived in force. The grenadiers mounted to the apartments, and in an instant the brigands were driven out. But a great number of the bodyguards had fallen into their hands. Messieurs Desuttes and de Varicourt, surprised in the first moment of the attack, had been massacred, and their bloody heads carried, each at the end of a pike, from Versailles to Paris. Bands of madmen dragged the surviving prisoners from side to side; some condemned them to the lantern; others summoned an assassin of their band, known as Coupe-Tête, remarkable for his long beard and fierce aspect, his arms naked to the elbow, his hands still bloody from the first executions, brandishing a hatchet and inviting new murders.
Lafayette exerted himself to obtain mercy for the surviving bodyguards. The Paris soldiers placed them under their own banners as under a sacred shield. The bodyguards who had retreated into the interior apartments of the château reappeared suddenly at the windows, raising their hats, displaying the national cockade, and crying: “Vive la nation!” The people answered: “Vive le roi! Vive les gardes-du-corps!” All was reconciliation. The two troops mingled and embraced.
The Balcony and the Return to Paris
The king appeared on the balcony, accompanied by the queen and her children. A voice cried: “The king to Paris!” The people and the army repeated it. Lafayette announced that the monarch consented to the wish of the capital.
Before the departure, there was the moment on the balcony that has become one of the most famous images of the Revolution. The crowd demanded that the queen appear alone. She stepped forward with the Dauphin and Madame Royale. The cry arose: “No children!” Perhaps the faction hoped that some desperate hand would dare to strike her; perhaps they wished to strip her of the protection her children gave her. The queen sent the children back. She advanced alone to the edge of the balcony, her eyes and hands raised to heaven, like a victim offering herself. Lafayette, who had followed her, knelt and kissed her hand. The crowd, which a moment before had been howling for her blood, fell silent, and then broke into acclamations.
The departure from Versailles took place at about one in the afternoon. The cortege was extraordinary beyond any that France had ever seen — part triumphal procession, part funeral march, part saturnalia. The vanguard was composed of a large detachment of the army, trains of artillery, and a great part of the women and the pikemen, some on foot, others in fiacres or hired carriages, others in carts, still others mounted on the cannon. They were followed by fifty to sixty wagons of flour and wheat. A large body of bourgeois cavalry, intermingled with deputies, women, and grenadiers, surrounded the king’s carriage, which moved with the greatest slowness to accommodate itself to the pace of the multitude.
The women who preceded the royal carriage sang allegorical airs, applying their pointed and naive allusions to the king and queen. “We shall not lack bread any more,” they cried; “we bring the baker, the baker’s wife, and the little baker’s boy.” The heads of two massacred bodyguards, those of Desuttes and de Varicourt, were carried on pikes at the head of the procession, preceded by the man called Coupe-Tête, his hair, his garments, his hands dripping with blood, a bloody hatchet on his shoulder. The cortege offered at once the spectacle of a carnage, a civic festival, a saturnalia, and a triumphal march. The king might equally have been taken for a father in the midst of his children, for a victim surrounded by his assassins, or for a dethroned prince paraded in triumph by rebel subjects.
Gouverneur Morris, watching from Paris, recorded what he learned as the news arrived: “Two Heads of the Gardes du Corps are brought to Town.” The queen, he heard from Capellis, escaped the château “in her Shift and Petticoat with her Stockings in her Hand.”
The march was so slow that it was near six o’clock in the evening when the royal family, prisoners of their own people, reached the Hôtel de Ville. Bailly received them. The king spoke with assurance and goodness, saying that he came always with pleasure and confidence into the midst of the inhabitants of his good city of Paris. Bailly repeated the phrase to the representatives of the Commune, but forgot the word “confidence.” The queen recalled it to him immediately and in a loud voice.
The Consequences
The king and queen, their children and Madame Élisabeth, proceeded to the Tuileries Palace. Nothing was prepared to receive them. The palace had been uninhabited for years; it was furnished with what could be found in haste. The royal family was installed in what was, in effect, a gilded prison.
The National Assembly, declaring that it could not remain separated from the king’s person, resolved on 10 October to transfer itself to Paris. The deputies arrived on 19 October and established themselves in the riding school of the Tuileries, the Manège, where they would sit for the next four years. The king’s first act in Paris was his acceptance of the first articles of the constitution and the sanction of the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
The October Days thus accomplished what the fall of the Bastille had not. The king was now in Paris, under the eye of the capital, at the mercy of every popular movement. Versailles, the great palace of the Bourbon monarchy, was abandoned as a royal residence. The court ceased to exist as a distinct political force; the buffer between the king and the Paris crowd had been removed. The monarchy had lost its independence, and the royal family would never again leave the capital alive — except for the doomed flight to Varennes, which itself ended in a forced return to Paris.
The two days of October 1789 were, as Pagès observed, the second revolution within the Revolution. The first, 14 July, had saved the National Assembly and armed the people. The second, 5 and 6 October, had captured the king and placed the Revolution’s ultimate authority — the person of the monarch — in the hands of the capital. From this moment, the Tuileries was a cage, and the Revolution, whatever course it might take, would be enacted under the eyes of the Parisian crowd.

events/the-terror.title: The Terror
events/the-terror.content:
The Terror
The Terror (1793–1794) was both a state system and a social condition: a period in which the revolutionary government in Paris wielded arbitrary power through surveillance, denunciation, and the guillotine, and in which the entire society was shaped by the presence of that power. From the prison cell to the fugitive’s hiding place, from the gambling halls of the Palais-Égalité to the chambers of the Revolutionary Tribunal, the Terror pervaded every level of French life.
The Prisoner’s Experience
In the Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie prisons between August and November 1793, the experience of imprisonment unfolded in ways that revealed the character of the regime. Those arrested faced not merely confinement but a system designed to strip them of every legal protection before delivering them to the guillotine.
The Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie
On 1 June 1793, the day after the coup of 31 May, the first arrests swept through Paris. One of those taken was a woman arrested on the order of Dorat-Cubières — a minor poet who had once tried to ingratiate himself through flattery when her husband was minister, now wielding power over life and liberty. The arrest order bore his signature, a detail that spoke volumes about the kind of men now holding the power of the state. She examined the warrant, found it defective in form, and refused to accompany the commissioners until they returned with a properly executed order.
From the Abbaye prison, letters were sent to the Committee of General Security demanding to know the grounds of detention. No satisfactory answer ever came. After a brief release came rearrest and transfer to Sainte-Pélagie, a prison that held both common criminals and political prisoners. From her cell there, the factional struggle beginning to consume the Montagnards themselves was visible: Robespierre rising against Danton, the Cordeliers and the Jacobins ready to divide. A grand spectacle was preparing for the victims — the tigers were going to tear each other apart.
Daily Life of the Prisoner
Prison life was a matter of confinement punctuated by interrogation and uncertainty. Writing became the prisoner’s primary occupation and only defence: political notices that would become memoirs, portraits of contemporaries, last writings prepared for the day of trial. In twenty-two days of August 1793, roughly three hundred pages were filled. The regime permitted writing materials, but prisoners had no guarantee that their writings would survive — the Abbaye authorities destroyed some of the earlier papers.
Prisoners were held in common rooms or cells depending on their status and the state of overcrowding. Family members were permitted visits when the authorities allowed. Petitions could be sent to the authorities, but petitioning was itself a form of subordination: it acknowledged the legitimacy of a system that had no legal basis for detaining anyone. The letters sent to the Committee of General Security from both prisons illustrated the prisoner’s attempt to use the forms of law against a government that had abandoned them.
The Revolutionary Tribunal
The Revolutionary Tribunal had been created by the Convention in March 1793 after the abortive Montagnard attempt to seize power known as the conspiration du 10 mars. When the Girondins succeeded in nominating honest men to serve as jurors, Marat intervened directly — he cried counter-revolution, threatened to call the people, had the ballot annulled, and imposed his own list. The jurors who sat in judgment were drawn for the most part from those who had participated in the September Massacres.
The encounter with the Tribunal came in November 1793. The proceeding was a formula of judgment from which the victims were systematically prevented from speaking. The trial of the twenty-two Girondin deputies had already shown the pattern: accused of conspiracy against the Republic, they were condemned to death and executed on the same day. A projected defence that one prisoner prepared was never permitted to be delivered.
The Execution of the Girondins
The execution of the twenty-two Girondin deputies — Brissot, Vergniaud, Guadet, Gensonné, and others — took place on 31 October 1793. From prison the reaction was one not of sympathy but of indictment: the twenty-two were condemned not for their principles but for their failure to act. They had temporised with crime, succumbed shamefully without being pitied. Instead of obeying their tyrants and descending from the Assembly like a timid flock, they should have fallen on the monsters to annihilate them rather than receiving their verdict.
Roland’s Own Trial and Death
The Revolutionary Tribunal delivered its judgment on 18 Brumaire, Year II (8 November 1793), sentencing one of its prisoners to death. The judgment, signed by Vice-President Dumas and three judges — Deliège, Denizot, Subleyras — condemned the accused to death, ordered goods confiscated to the Republic, and required the sentence to be executed within twenty-four hours. That same day, in the Place de la Révolution, the condemned woman was executed. Her last reported words, addressed to the statue of Liberty in the square, were: “Oh Liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!”
Jean-Marie Roland, learning of her execution while in hiding near Rouen, died by his own hand with a sword-cane beside him.
The Fugitive’s Experience
For those who escaped the initial arrests, the Terror became a year-long chase across the countryside of France — a period of hiding, flight, and gradual loss of every support that society had once provided.
Buzot on the Run
Proscribed after the coup of 31 May–2 June 1793, one group of fugitives escaped Paris and made their way first to Caen in Normandy, where a federalist resistance had formed under the protection of the Calvados department administration. With them went Pétion, Barbaroux, and Louvet. From Caen they witnessed Charlotte Corday’s departure for Paris — she came ostensibly to beg a favour for relatives, but her real motive was to know the founders of the republic for which she was about to devote herself.
After the federalist military force under General Wimpfen was defeated at Pacy-sur-Eure in July 1793, the fugitive deputies scattered. Some made their way south and west, eventually reaching the Gironde and finding shelter in Saint-Émilion. There a sympathetic republican in the wine country hid them: Pétion occupied one bed, Barbaroux lay on a mattress, and another sat in an old armchair; together they cooked their own meals.
The year in hiding was a period of being “buried alive in this dwelling of death.” A first search of Saint-Émilion found nothing. A second search caught them: Barbaroux shot himself through the head, survived the wound, and was arrested and guillotined. Pétion and another were found dead in a field, their bodies partly consumed by wolves. Whether from self-administered poison, starvation, exposure, or some combination was not established with certainty.
Portraits of Marat, Robespierre, and Danton
Written in two phases (1793 and 1794), the fugitive memoirs of this period included sustained character studies of the three men identified as the principal architects of Montagnard domination.
Marat served as the Mountain’s instrument for destroying individual reputations. His denunciations in the Ami du peuple were systematic and deliberate. His acquittal by the Revolutionary Tribunal after a formal accusation in October 1792 made the Convention permanently subject to factional terror — a moment when the institution proved it could not defend its own members.
Robespierre rose from the Jacobin Club to ascendancy in the Convention through tactical patience: he let Marat remain the visible extremist while consolidating his own position. Only after Marat’s assassination by Charlotte Corday did Robespierre drop his cover and move toward dictatorship.
Danton was assessed through his conduct as Minister of Justice after 10 August 1792, his role in the September Massacres, and his management of the Committee of Public Safety as an instrument of factional power rather than national defence. The final verdict on the two: “Danton and Robespierre are the sole authors of the afflictions that have fallen on France.”
Louvet’s Flight from Caen
The most detailed fugitive narrative of the Terror period was written from a limestone cave in the Jura in April 1794. The author and his wife Lodoïska moved through a series of hiding places as the revolutionary authorities tightened their control.
After Caen’s collapse, the fugitives crossed into Brittany, where the Breton deputies and sympathisers who had formed the core of Wimpfen’s force were gradually drawn off by Parisian emissaries bearing news that their primary assemblies had accepted the new constitution. The growing political isolation of the fugitives became stark: people who had been protected by the Girondins for ten months refused to give them shelter for a single night; friends of twenty years drove them from their doors.
From Brittany the fugitives reached Bordeaux and the surrounding wine country of the Gironde. The Gironde remained longer than other provinces in a state of relative republican independence, but Bordeaux’s submission to the Terror narrowed the window. The decision was made to move further east. Eventually they reached the Jura mountains, where they sheltered in a cave for several months — cold, inadequately fed, writing by whatever light was available. “I throw down notes, and that is all,” one wrote. “I am recording notes that may help me if some day of genuine leisure is given to me — or help someone else, if I do not survive.”
Charlotte Corday and Marat’s Assassination
Charlotte Corday came to Caen before the assassination and met the assembled deputies. She never spoke to any of them a word about her design. If she had consulted them, they would not have directed her toward Marat — they knew he had at most two days left to live from his disease. Her portrait was of a woman proud and gentle, decent and beautiful, with a bearing full of assurance and a gaze tempered by modesty. She was seen the evening before she left for Paris.
Corday left the Caen group for Paris, carried out the assassination in Marat’s apartment on 13 July 1793, and was herself executed four days later.
Return After Thermidor
The fall of Robespierre on 9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794) ended the immediate danger for the fugitives. The return to Paris was compressed in the writings produced during the hiding, not after. What the records show is the first steps of political rehabilitation. The Convention, under Thermidorian pressure, began reversing the proscriptions. One of the fugitives resumed his journalistic and political career, helped found the journal La Sentinelle in its second form, and represented the moderate republican position through the remaining years of the Convention and the early Directory. Not all survived to return.
Social History of the Terror
Beyond the politics of the Convention and the ordeal of the prisoner lay a different world: the social underworld of prostitution, gambling, and erotic life in revolutionary Paris. This world was not separate from the Terror — it was shaped by it, and the machinery of the revolutionary state eventually reached into it.
Prostitution in Paris Under the Terror
The women who had been passionate patriots in 1789 reverted during the Terror to a different role — lovers of love and nothing more. The street prostitution of Paris under the Terror was a fierce and persistent reality: the prostitutes of the streets, the former fishwives and market women, carrying on traditional behaviours under the new regime. Police surveillance reports, contemporary pamphlets, and archival documents from the Archives nationales reconstruct the everyday reality of women who lived by prostitution.
The Palais-Égalité as a Centre of Vice
The Palais-Royal — renamed Palais-Égalité during the Revolution — became the principal centre of organised prostitution, gambling, and erotic entertainment in revolutionary Paris. The gardens functioned as a vast open-air brothel, with women ranging from elegant courtesans (the “nymphs” and “odalisques”) to common prostitutes advertising at the famous price of “four women for five livres.” The Allée des Soupirs (Alley of Sighs) was the most notorious walk.
The Palais-Royal had passed from Cardinal Richelieu’s original construction through its ownership by Philippe-Égalité, the duc d’Orléans, and its transformation into a commercial and entertainment centre. The warning sign placed in the gardens — “Attention! il y a des filles et des filous ou avis à nos frères des départements!” — gave the flavour of the period: an official notice to provincial visitors that the gardens contained both prostitutes and thieves.
Fashion, Gambling, and Erotic Literature
Women’s fashion during the Terror reflected the proximity of pleasure to death. Earrings were designed “à la guillotine” and the “redingotte à la Thessalie” served as practical attire for hurried gentlemen. The Palais-Égalité housed thirty-two gambling houses, which had roots under the monarchy — the queen’s gaming table, the ambassador as croupier — and underwent a revolutionary transformation that included a card game replacing kings and queens with revolutionary titles.
Erotic literature flourished at the Palais-Égalité. Libelles and pamphlets against Marie-Antoinette circulated widely. The police served as what might be called the last refuge of public modesty, and the Revolutionary Tribunal occasionally turned its attention to erotic publishers.
The Case of Madame de Sainte-Amaranthe
The fatal intersection of sexual license with the machinery of the Terror found its central narrative in the story of Madame de Sainte-Amaranthe and her daughter Émilie. Jeanne-Françoise-Louise de Saint-Simon d’Arpajon, daughter of a governor of Besançon, had become a celebrated courtesan of the Revolution whose salon and establishment in the fashionable demimonde connected the worlds of prostitution and high politics. She was caught up in the “foreign conspiracy” investigations of 1794, arrested with her daughter, tried before the Revolutionary Tribunal presided over by Fouquier-Tinville, and executed in the batch (fournée) of 29 Prairial Year II (17 June 1794). Her case illustrated how the Revolutionary Tribunal constructed conspiracy narratives that could sweep up anyone connected to the demimonde.
The Marquis de Sade Under the Revolution
The Marquis de Sade was present in revolutionary Paris, involved in political clubs including the Section des Piques, and imprisoned under the Terror. He narrowly escaped the guillotine. His life during the revolutionary decade — the intersection of sexual deviance, literary production, and political violence — connected his works (Justine, Juliette, Aline et Valcour) to the world he inhabited.
Police Surveillance
Throughout the Terror, the relationship between the revolutionary government and prostitution was ambiguous. The police both regulated and tolerated the trade, with surveillance reports providing the documentary record. Within the Palais de Justice itself during the Terror, sexual scandals abounded: judicial officials, clerks, prisoners, and prostitutes operated within the precincts of the revolutionary courts.
The Theory of the Terror
In 1797, as the Directory struggled to stabilise the Republic, a new doctrine emerged: that the Terror’s violence had saved the Republic and therefore justified its methods. This claim met a sustained refutation on three grounds.
The Terror Did Not Save the Republic
The factual claim that the Terror saved the Republic was false. The Republic was saved by the armies, by geography, and by the incompetence of the coalition — not by the guillotine. The military victories that secured the Republic’s survival were won by generals and soldiers fighting on the frontiers, not by the Revolutionary Tribunal executing prisoners in Paris. The military defence of the Republic must be separated from the internal terror that accompanied it.
The Precedent Destroys Constitutional Government
Even if the Terror had produced beneficial effects, the claim that it was justified set a precedent that systematically destroyed constitutional government. Any emergency could be used to justify any measure. Once the principle was accepted that the state’s survival justifies the destruction of individuals, there was no logical stopping point. The precedent of the Terror taught that safety comes from arbitrary violence, that enemies can be defined by category rather than by individual act, and that the state’s survival justifies any means.
The Corruption of Political Culture
Beyond the factual and structural arguments lay a deeper corruption: the Terror changed French political culture at the level of expectations and habits. It taught citizens to believe that security could be obtained through violence against other citizens. It habituated the political class to governing through emergency powers. A republic that accepts this teaching as even partially valid has undermined the only foundation on which a durable republic can rest: the rule of law, individual rights, and constitutional procedure.
What harmed France most was precisely the impatience to do good — the willingness of well-intentioned men to use arbitrary measures in pursuit of legitimate ends. When honest men used revolutionary means against revolutionary brigands — seizing émigrés’ property, deporting suspects, suspending legal process — they consecrated illegality by making it serve good purposes, and thereby destroyed the only moral argument against illegality: that it always produces harm.
The General Narrative
A six-volume synthetic history of the Revolution, published between 1799 and 1802, presented the Terror from an anti-Jacobin moderate republican perspective — contemptuous of the aristocracy, scathing toward the Jacobins and Robespierre, and broadly favourable to the Directory and Bonaparte as restorers of order.
The Convention and the Establishment of the Terror
The Convention was established in September 1792, abolishing royalty and proclaiming the Republic. Marat and Robespierre stood as the twin architects of the Terror, each with distinct vices. The Convention’s division into factions — Girondins, Montagnards, and the Plain — was the precondition for the Terror, since it was the Mountain’s determination to dominate the Convention by force that made systematic violence necessary.
The Fall of the Girondins and the 31 May Coup
The coup of 31 May 1793 was not a popular revolution but a criminal conspiracy carried out by the armed sections and the Commune with the support of the Orléanist faction. Charlotte Corday’s assassination of Marat was treated sympathetically — she was portrayed as a heroine, her courage and character praised.
The Committee of Public Safety
The Committee of Public Safety — the “decemvirate” — governed France through the Terror. The successive purges of the factions unfolded in sequence: the Hébertists, the Dantonists, and finally Robespierre’s own following. The decrees of accusation against Camille Desmoulins, Hérault de Séchelles, Danton, and the others were enumerated. The executions of Marie-Antoinette and the Duke d’Orléans took their place in the sequence. The magic and ever-powerful words — “patrie, liberté, salut public, conspiration” — were used to impose on the multitude.
Thermidor
On 8–9 Thermidor, Robespierre’s conspiracy came to an end. Tallien’s speech at the Convention triggered the arrest of Robespierre and his followers. The conspirators were executed, including seventy-one members of the Paris Commune. Among the most infamous representatives-on-mission were Lebon at Arras and Carrier at Nantes, whose drownings Carrier himself eventually disavowed.
The Thermidorian Reaction
The period after Thermidor was a reaction against the Terror rather than a clean break. New terrorist gangs or “égorgeurs” emerged, along with royalist youth groups — the Companies of Jesus and of the Sun. Cultural conflicts erupted over revolutionary songs: the Marseillaise and the Réveil du Peuple. The Babeuf conspiracy represented a final Jacobin attempt to revive the Terror, placing it within the broader sequence of revolutionary upheaval that continued through the Directory.
The Terror as Depicted Across the Sources
Taken together, the sources present the Terror as simultaneously a state system and a social condition — a period in which the revolutionary government claimed the right to define, pursue, and destroy its enemies without legal constraint, and a period in which the entire society was shaped by the presence of that power.


















































DimensionSourceKey EvidenceArbitrary governmentRoland, ConstantDetention without charge, warrant defective in form, the Committee of General Security’s refusal to answer legal demands; Constant’s argument that the Terror corrupted the principle of constitutional governmentSurveillanceFleischmannPolice surveillance reports on prostitutes and gamblers at the Palais-Égalité; the secret police apparatus operating throughout ParisDenunciationRoland, BuzotDorat-Cubières signing Roland’s arrest warrant; Marat’s denunciations in the Ami du peuple; the system by which any citizen could denounce any other to the Revolutionary TribunalThe guillotineRoland, PagèsThe daily executions in the Place de la Révolution; the batches (fournées) of 29 Prairial; the execution of the twenty-two Girondins and of Madame Roland herselfThe police stateLouvet, FleischmannThe fugitive’s experience of being hunted across France; the need for false papers and sympathetic intermediaries; the police surveillance of every social activityThe fugitive’s conditionBuzot, LouvetA year in hiding; friends refusing shelter; death by wolf-consumption or self-administered poison in a field near Saint-Émilion; waiting in a Jura caveThe prison systemRolandThe Abbaye, Sainte-Pélagie, the Conciergerie; writing as the prisoner’s only defence; the Revolutionary Tribunal as a formula of judgment from which the victim cannot speakThe social substrateFleischmannThe world of prostitution, gambling, and erotic literature that continued under — and was shaped by — the Terror; the intersection of sexual license with political prosecution
The sources are unanimous that the Terror was not merely a set of institutions — the Revolutionary Tribunal, the Committee of Public Safety, the surveillance committees — but a condition that pervaded every level of French society. The prisoner in her cell, the fugitive in the Jura cave, the prostitute in the Palais-Égalité arcades, and the revolutionary judge in the Palais de Justice all inhabited the same world: a world in which the state could at any moment define any person as an enemy and destroy them, and in which survival depended on invisibility, denunciation of others, or the uncertain protection of factional loyalty.

events/trafalgar-campaign.title: The Trafalgar Campaign
events/trafalgar-campaign.content:
The Trafalgar Campaign
The Trafalgar Campaign (1803–1805) was the culminating naval episode of the Napoleonic Wars, in which the combined fleets of France and Spain were destroyed by the British Mediterranean fleet under Vice-Admiral Horatio Nelson off Cape Trafalgar on 21 October 1805. The campaign forms an indivisible whole with Napoleon’s invasion project: the destruction of the Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar compelled Napoleon to abandon his planned descent upon England and to turn the Grande Armée eastward, producing the victory at Austerlitz two months later. Trafalgar caused Austerlitz — Nelson’s victory at sea determined the course of the war on land.
The Invasion Preparations
After the rupture of the Peace of Amiens in May 1803, Napoleon resolved to strike directly at Great Britain by a cross-Channel invasion. This was not a feint: Napoleon meant to cross, and the preparations were on a scale appropriate to his determination. An army of 130,000 men — the most brilliant soldiery of the age, veterans of Italy, Egypt, and Germany — was encamped along the coast between Étaples and Vimereux, with the principal concentration at Boulogne. By July 1805, the port of Boulogne sheltered over a thousand gunboats and transports, capable of carrying 40,000 men in a single tide. Three subsidiary harbours — Vimereux, Ambleteuse, and Étaples — held another seven hundred vessels, raising the total force to 62,000 soldiers who could be embarked from the four Channel ports, with a further 27,000 in the North Sea ports as a reserve.
The crossing itself presented exceptional difficulties. The flat-bottomed boats were designed to be beached directly on the English coast, so that troops could land without transshipment; they were built to be moved by oars as well as sail, so that a calm or fog might allow them to slip past the British cruisers. Napoleon understood that his gunboats could not fight heavy ships-of-the-line. The flotilla was never intended to force the passage unsupported. Its purpose was to fix British attention on the Channel coast while the real plan — the concentration of the French battle-fleet to cover the crossing — unfolded elsewhere.
The Naval Combination
The key to the invasion was the Toulon fleet. Napoleon’s original design called for the Toulon squadron to evade the British blockade, pick up the Rochefort and Ferrol squadrons en route, and appear off Boulogne with a superior force, holding the Channel long enough — four or five days was the emperor’s phrase — for the army to cross. The choice of admiral was crucial. Napoleon selected Latouche Tréville, his boldest naval commander, and fixed the sailing for January 1804. But Latouche Tréville died in August 1804, and after some hesitation Napoleon chose Vice-Admiral Pierre de Villeneuve — a decision that proved deeply unfortunate. Villeneuve was accomplished, brave, and skilful, but he saw the defects of the French navy with a clarity that sapped his will to take risks. He was incapable of sacrificing his command as a forlorn hope upon which a greater design might follow.
Nelson, meanwhile, commanded the Mediterranean fleet blockading Toulon. The conditions under which Nelson operated were punishing: his ships were poorly equipped and under-manned, the legacy of Lord St. Vincent’s peacetime reforms at the Admiralty. The winter gales of the Gulf of Lyon forced Nelson to keep his fleet at a distance from Toulon, and he was chronically short of frigates to maintain contact with the enemy. Despite these handicaps, Nelson kept the sea for ten consecutive months without a single ship refitting in port. His central problem was the inherent uncertainty of the defence: he could not know whether the Toulon fleet, once it escaped, would steer east for Egypt or west for the Atlantic, and he had to provide against both.
The West Indies Sortie
Villeneuve sailed from Toulon on 30 March 1805 with eleven ships-of-the-line, successfully evading Nelson’s blockade in a north-west gale. Contrary winds delayed Nelson’s pursuit, and by the time he learned of the French departure they had a lead of several weeks. Villeneuve passed through the Straits of Gibraltar, picked up a Spanish squadron at Cadiz, and crossed the Atlantic to Martinique, arriving in mid-May. The West Indies were not the ultimate objective: Napoleon intended the sortie to draw the British squadrons across the Atlantic, clearing the way for a concentration in the Channel.
Nelson pursued with characteristic energy. He guessed correctly that Villeneuve had gone west, crossed the Atlantic in hot chase — outstripping the French, who had a head start — and arrived at Barbados on 4 June, only to find that Villeneuve had already sailed north from Martinique. For two weeks Nelson searched the Caribbean, but Villeneuve had left the West Indies on 9 June, bound for Europe. Nelson’s pursuit, though it failed to bring the enemy to action, was strategically sound: by following Villeneuve he retained the possibility of interception, whereas remaining in the Mediterranean would have surrendered the initiative entirely.
Calder’s Action Off Cape Finisterre
The decisive moment of the campaign prior to Trafalgar occurred on 22 July 1805, when Villeneuve, returning from the West Indies, encountered a British squadron under Vice-Admiral Sir Robert Calder approximately one hundred miles west of Cape Finisterre. This engagement was a lost opportunity — one of the great ‘might-have-beens’ of naval history.
The encounter was precipitated by the alertness of the British Admiralty. A fast brig, the Curieux, had sighted Villeneuve’s fleet returning across the Atlantic and reached Plymouth on 7 July. Lord Barham, the aged First Lord of the Admiralty, acted on the intelligence with remarkable promptness. Within hours of receiving the dispatch, Barham ordered Cornwallis to raise the blockade of Rochefort, sending the five ships there to reinforce Calder off Ferrol, and directed Calder to cruise a hundred miles west of Finisterre with fifteen sail-of-the-line to intercept Villeneuve. The movement was a stroke of generalship comparable to Napoleon’s abandonment of the siege of Mantua in 1796 to throw himself upon the Austrian relief armies.
When the fog lifted on 22 July, Calder found himself facing twenty ships-of-the-line — the Curieux had reported only seventeen. The action that followed was inconclusive. Two Spanish ships were taken, but darkness and fog separated the fleets, and Calder, preoccupied with the safety of his prizes and anxious about the possibility of the Ferrol squadron emerging, declined to renew the engagement the following day. Calder had ‘made to himself a picture’ — that classic error against which Napoleon warned his own generals — and allowed the imagined dangers of the Rochefort and Ferrol squadrons to blind him to the fact that he had the main enemy force before him. Nelson remarked that had Calder found himself alongside the same enemy fleet he would have beaten them soundly even against superior numbers.
The Strategic Reversal
Villeneuve, no more eager than Calder to renew the action, put into Vigo on 28 July and then into Coruña on 1 August, where he received Napoleon’s dispatches. The emperor, who had been at Boulogne awaiting news, learned of the action on 8 August. The failure of the Toulon fleet to appear in the Channel, combined with the damage suffered in Calder’s action and Villeneuve’s evident hesitation, forced Napoleon to confront the collapse of his invasion plan.
This was the hinge of the entire campaign. The Grande Armée, which had been training for the Channel crossing for two years, could not remain indefinitely in its coastal camps. Austria and Russia were forming the Third Coalition, and the strategic situation on the Continent demanded Napoleon’s attention. On 27 August 1805 — the pivotal date — the emperor ordered the army of Boulogne to break camp and march east. The invasion of England was abandoned. The Grande Armée was now to strike at Austria.
The destruction of the combined fleet made the Channel crossing impossible. Napoleon turned east not because he preferred to fight Austria but because the sea was closed to him. The campaign that ended at Austerlitz was thus determined by the naval campaign that ended at Trafalgar.
The Battle of Trafalgar
Villeneuve, after a period of indecision in Cadiz, put to sea on 19 October 1805 with the combined Franco-Spanish fleet of thirty-three ships-of-the-line. Nelson, who had returned to England in August and resumed command of the Mediterranean fleet at the end of September, was waiting off Cadiz with twenty-seven ships. The ensuing battle was the consummation of Nelson’s tactical thought.
Nelson’s plan was a departure from the conventional line-of-battle tactics that had governed fleet engagements for a century. Instead of forming his fleet in a single line parallel to the enemy and exchanging fire at long range, Nelson divided his force into two columns and drove them perpendicularly at the Franco-Spanish line, cutting it in two places. The idea was to concentrate overwhelming force on the enemy’s rear while leaving the van unable to turn back to support it. The risk was that the leading ships of each column would have to endure a concentrated fire from the enemy line for a prolonged period without being able to reply effectively.
The battle was fought on 21 October 1805, approximately fourteen miles off Cape Trafalgar. Nelson’s column, in the Victory, broke through the allied line astern of Villeneuve’s flagship Bucentaure; Collingwood’s lee column penetrated the rear. The engagement that followed was a confused melee in which the superior British gunnery and ship-handling proved decisive. By the end of the afternoon, nineteen Franco-Spanish ships had been captured or destroyed; the remainder were scattered. Nelson himself was shot by a marksman from the rigging of the Redoutable and died at four-thirty in the afternoon, having learned that the battle was won.
A violent storm followed the battle. The British fleet, with its shattered prizes in tow, was caught by a gale that raged for several days. Many of the captured ships were wrecked on the Spanish coast or had to be scuttled; only four of the nineteen prizes ever reached a British port. The storm cost the British much of the material fruits of the victory, but it could not undo the strategic result: the combined fleet had ceased to exist as a fighting force.
Strategic Consequences
The destruction of the Franco-Spanish fleet gave Great Britain command of the seas for the remainder of the Napoleonic Wars — command that was never again seriously challenged. Napoleon could still build ships, but he could not assemble a fleet capable of meeting the British in a general action. The naval war became a war of attrition and commerce raiding, a contest in which sea power, though less dramatically exercised than at Trafalgar, steadily drained the resources of the French Empire.
The more far-reaching consequence is that Trafalgar caused Austerlitz. The point is not merely chronological — that Trafalgar was fought on 21 October and Austerlitz on 2 December 1805 — but causal. By defeating Villeneuve, Nelson made the invasion of England impossible, and Napoleon was therefore compelled to turn his army against the only enemy he could reach: Austria and Russia. The campaign that culminated at Austerlitz was a strategic diversion forced upon Napoleon by the failure of his maritime design. The emperor had not chosen to fight the Third Coalition on the Danube; he had been driven to it because the sea had been closed to him. The Grande Armée that marched from Boulogne to Ulm and Austerlitz was the army that had been meant to conquer England, and it marched east only because Nelson had barred the way to the west.
Napoleon continued to hold the initiative on land, and Austerlitz was a victory of the first order. But the decisive defeat of the war had already been inflicted — not at Austerlitz, but at Trafalgar. Nelson’s victory did not end the war, but it established the condition under which all subsequent campaigns were fought: British command of the sea, and French confinement to the Continent.
Sources
