sources-map.title: Sources Map
sources-map.content:
Sources Map
This page provides a guided overview of every source page in the wiki — 22 source pages covering 27 distinct works (counting multi-volume and multi-title collections). They are grouped by type to help you navigate the material efficiently. Each entry describes the author’s perspective, the date range covered, and the key events the source illuminates.

Memoirs & Eyewitness Accounts
The memoirists are the wiki’s most vivid windows into the Revolution. Most wrote in extremis — from prison, in hiding, or looking back at lives upended — which gives their testimony an intensity no later historian can match. The Girondin cluster (Roland, Buzot, Louvet) covers the same events from different angles and can be read as a single overlapping testimony.
Madame Roland — Mémoires
roland-memoires-vol1-1823 and roland-memoires-vol2-1823
Date range: Childhood (1754) to November 1793
Madame Roland, the intellectual centre of the Girondin circle, wrote these memoirs in the Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie prisons between August and November 1793, knowing she would face the Revolutionary Tribunal. Volume I is autobiographical — her childhood, convent education, the reading of Plutarch and Rousseau, her marriage, and her husband’s first ministry. Volume II is political: the second Roland ministry, both imprisonments, devastatingly sharp portraits of every major figure (Robespierre, Danton, Brissot, Buzot), and the trial documents. Her perspective is Girondin, republican, fiercely anti-Montagnard. She writes with the moral clarity of someone with nothing left to lose. The two volumes together are the single most important primary source for the Girondin experience of the Terror.
Buzot — Mémoires sur la Révolution Française
buzot-memoires-revolution-1823
Date range: c. 1789 – June 1794
François-Nicolas-Léonard Buzot (1760–1794), Girondin deputy for Eure and the man Madame Roland loved, wrote these memoirs while proscribed and in hiding after the coup of 31 May – 2 June 1793. He hid for nearly a year at Saint-Émilion before being found dead in a field. The memoirs cover the Convention, the factional struggle with the Mountain, the proscription, and his flight through Normandy and Brittany. He includes portraits of Marat, Robespierre, Danton, and Pache, and a sustained refutation of the charge that the Girondins were federalists. His perspective is Girondin, defensive, embittered — a testament written by a man who knew he was already condemned.
Louvet de Couvray — Mémoires
louvet-memoires-1823
Date range: October 1792 – July 1794
Jean-Baptiste Louvet de Couvray, Girondin deputy and author of the novel Les Amours du chevalier de Faublas, wrote these memoirs in April 1794 from a cave in the Jura, expecting to die. He survived and returned to the Convention after Thermidor. The memoirs are deliberately unpolished — “I throw down notes, and that is all,” he says. They cover the May–June 1793 coup, the Girondin resistance at Caen, Charlotte Corday’s mission to Paris, and his extraordinary clandestine flight across France. He is the author of the famous “Je t’accuse, Robespierre!” speech of 29 October 1792. His perspective is Girondin, dramatic, fugitive. The rawness is the value — this is not retrospective literary memoir but a record written under mortal danger.
Madame Campan — Mémoires sur la vie privée de Marie-Antoinette
campan-memoires-marie-antoinette-3vols-1823
Date range: c. 1770 – August 1792
Jeanne Louise Henriette Campan was première femme de chambre to Queen Marie-Antoinette. Her three-volume memoir is the most intimate royalist source in the wiki. Volume I covers the court of Louis XV and the early years of Louis XVI’s reign. Volume II runs from the Diamond Necklace Affair through the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August 1792. Volume III collects historical anecdotes and correspondence. She writes from inside the royal household, with access to the queen’s private conversations and emotions. Her perspective is royalist, loyalist, court-insider — but she is not uncritical of the queen or the court, and her testimony on the October Days and 10 August is indispensable.
Gouverneur Morris — A Diary of the French Revolution
morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789 and morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793
Date range: March 1789 – January 1793
Gouverneur Morris — American statesman, drafter of the U.S. Constitution, and United States Minister to France from 1792 — kept a diary beginning March 1789 that forms the most sustained foreign eyewitness account of the French Revolution in English. Volume I covers the States-General, the fall of the Bastille, the October Days, and Morris’s informal diplomatic mission to London. Volume II covers the Constitution of 1791, the Legislative Assembly, the Flight to Varennes, the storming of the Tuileries on 10 August, and the September Massacres. Morris was privately a royalist sympathiser (he secretly organised a 5,000-louis fund for the king) and publicly a cold-eyed analyst. His perspective is American constitutionalist, aristocratic, skeptical of revolutionary idealism. He provides the best outside view of the Revolution’s political mechanics.
Marmontel — Mémoires d’un père
marmontel-memoires-3vols-1804
Date range: 1723 – c. 1795
Jean-François Marmontel (1723–1799) was a leading philosophe, contributor to the Encyclopédie, and Secrétaire Perpétuel of the Académie Française. His posthumous memoirs (20 books across 3 volumes) cover his entire life. The first two volumes deal with the ancien régime — his provincial origins, literary career, the salons, his academic life. The third volume (Books XII–XX) covers the Revolution from the pre-1787 crisis through the Terror, written by a man who lost nearly everything in the revolutionary crisis. His perspective is moderate-constitutionalist, Enlightenment liberal, anti-Jacobin. He writes from inside the pre-revolutionary intellectual establishment, watching it be destroyed by the forces it helped unleash.
Baron de Besenval — Mémoires
besenval-memoires-4vols-1805
Date range: c. 1735 – July 1789
Pierre-Victor, baron de Besenval (1721–1791), was a Swiss-born lieutenant-general of the royal armies and intimate of the French court under Louis XV and Louis XVI. His four-volume posthumous memoir is structured as a series of topical articles rather than a continuous narrative. The volumes cover his Swiss origins, the Seven Years’ War, court intrigues under the Choiseul and Maupeau ministries, and — crucially — his own command of the troops around Paris during the July 1789 crisis. He was the senior royal commander on the ground when the Bastille fell, and was subsequently arrested and tried as a scapegoat. His perspective is royalist, military, courtier — from the inside of the Bourbon military establishment at the moment of its catastrophic failure.
Ernest Daudet — Three Works on the Counter-Revolution
police-chouans-consulat-empire-daudet-1895, conspirations-royalistes-midi-daudet-1881, and histoire-emigration-daudet-1908
Date ranges: 1790–1793, 1800–1815, and 1789–1814 respectively
Ernest Daudet (1837–1921), elder brother of Alphonse Daudet, was a professional historian who specialised in the diplomatic and political history of the Counter-Revolution. The three works form a trilogy covering the royalist resistance across the entire Revolutionary and Napoleonic period.


conspirations-royalistes-midi-daudet-1881 covers the early royalist conspiracies in southern France (1790–1793): the Camp de Jalès, the Saillans conspiracy, the Charrier uprising, set against the Catholic–Protestant conflict in the Gard and Ardèche. Perspective: archival historian, sympathetic to royalist subjects but methodologically rigorous.


police-chouans-consulat-empire-daudet-1895 covers Chouan resistance under Napoleon (1800–1815): the Clément de Ris kidnapping, the murder of Audrein, English spy networks in Bordeaux and Jersey. Perspective: police-and-conspiracy historian, drawing on official records.


histoire-emigration-daudet-1908 is Daudet’s synthetic masterpiece on the Bourbon emigration as a whole (1789–1814): Coblentz, Quiberon, the Fructidor deportations, the courts in exile at Hamm, Verona, Mitau, and Warsaw. He draws on French, Russian, Austrian, English, and Prussian archives, including the papers of the duc de Blacas and unpublished correspondence of Louis XVIII. Perspective: scholarly, royalist-leaning, but archivally exhaustive — the definitive secondary work on the emigration.


Hector Fleischmann — Les Filles Publiques sous la Terreur
filles-publiques-fleischmann-1908
Date range: 1793–1794
Hector Fleischmann (1882–1914) was a French historian who specialised in the social and sexual history of the Terror. This work examines the world of prostitution in Paris during the Terror, drawing extensively on police surveillance reports, archival documents, and contemporary pamphlets. It covers the Palais-Royal brothel culture, the Sainte-Amaranthe case, the Marquis de Sade, gambling, and erotic literature. Fleischmann’s perspective is social historian of the “underbelly,” deliberately sensational in subject but documentary in method. He refuses to generalise from the exceptional behaviour of prostitutes to conclusions about French society as a whole. This is the wiki’s primary source for the histoire des mentalités approach to the Terror.

Historical Works
These are secondary accounts written during or shortly after the Revolution, blending narrative history with the political commitments of their authors. They are themselves primary documents of how the Revolution was understood by its contemporaries and near-contemporaries.
Alfred Thayer Mahan — The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire
mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol1 and mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2
Date range: 1783–1812
Rear Admiral Alfred Thayer Mahan’s two-volume work (1892) applies his famous sea-power thesis to the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. Volume I covers 1783–1801 (the destruction of the French navy, the Nile, Cape St. Vincent, the Irish expeditions); Volume II covers the Second Coalition through Trafalgar, the Continental System, and Napoleon’s Russian invasion (Copenhagen, Amiens, the commerce war). Mahan’s argument is that Britain’s ultimate victory was determined less by Wellington’s armies than by the Royal Navy’s control of the seas — and that this control was the product of sustained national commitment to maritime strength. His perspective is American naval historian, strategic analyst, Anglo-Atlanticist. He writes to draw lessons for American naval policy.
François Pagès — Histoire secrète de la révolution française
pages-histoire-secrete-revolution-6vols-1801
Date range: Merovingian origins to Marengo (June 1800)
François Pagès (1745–1802) produced this ambitious six-volume synthetic history between 1799 and 1802 (second edition, revised just before his death). The title “secret history” signals his aim to reveal the hidden intrigues and conspiracies behind public events. He opens with a compressed constitutional history from the Merovingians through Louis XV (arguing that the estates-general were an ancient institution suppressed by absolutism), then covers the Revolution month by month through the Estates-General, the Bastille, the October Days, Varennes, the Convention, the Terror, Thermidor, the Directory, Bonaparte’s Italian and Egyptian campaigns, 18 Brumaire, and Marengo. His perspective is anti-Jacobin, moderate republican, pro-Bonaparte-as-restorer-of-order. He is scathing about Robespierre and Marat, admiring of Bonaparte, and deeply suspicious of both aristocratic reaction and popular extremism. The work includes embedded documents — letters, treaty texts, official reports — and lengthy character portraits of every major figure.
Fantin-Desodoards — Histoire Philosophique de la Révolution de France
fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-vol7-1801
Date range: 1796 – September 1797 (Volume VII)
Antoine Fantin-Desodoards (1738–1820) wrote a multi-volume synthetic history of the Revolution as it was still unfolding. Volume VII (4th edition, 1801) covers the Italian campaign of 1796–97 (Castiglione, Arcola, Rivoli, Mantua), the Babeuf Conspiracy, Moreau’s retreat, the Irish expedition, and the Fructidor coup of September 1797. His “philosophical” method means he pauses regularly to assess causes, moralise on consequences, and reflect on the relationship between constitutional forms and political reality. His perspective is moderately conservative republican — critical of the Terror, respectful of the Directory, suspicious of both Jacobin extremism and royalist reaction, and admiring of Bonaparte’s military genius.
Pierre Paganel — Histoire de Napoléon Bonaparte
paganel-histoire-napoleon-1815
Date range: Egyptian expedition (1798) to Saint Helena (1815)
Pierre Paganel, a former member of the legislature and former secretary-general of the Ministry of Foreign Relations, wrote this political and moral history of Napoleon’s career in the weeks immediately after Waterloo. The book is itself a primary document: Paganel had published a historical essay in 1810; Napoleon read it, was offended by the words “souveraineté du peuple” and “représentation nationale,” and ordered the edition seized. The preface frames everything that follows as a judgment delivered by a man who was silenced under the regime and now speaks freely. His perspective is liberal republican, anti-imperial, freshly liberated from censorship. He covers Napoleon’s career from Egypt through the Consulate, the Empire, the Russian campaign, the fall, and the Hundred Days, with the moral arc of a man watching a republic become a tyranny.
Brissot — À ses Commettans
brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793
Date range: August 1792 – May 1793
Jacques-Pierre Brissot de Warville, the leading Girondin journalist and politician, wrote the texts collected in this volume between August 1792 and May 1793 — just before his arrest, condemnation, and execution on 31 October 1793. The volume (published in London as a document of an enemy of Britain) contains four texts: a declaration to foreign powers on the king’s suspension, two reports on British hostility and the case for declaring war, and the May 1793 address to his constituents on anarchist domination of the Convention. Brissot’s perspective is Girondin, war-party, anti-Montagnard — arguing that the Republic can only be saved by crushing the anarchist faction within. The London publisher’s framing (“Faction Brissotine”) makes the English reception as interesting as the text itself.

Statistical & Reference Works
These are not narrative histories but systematic surveys — the bones of the revolutionary state, laid out in numbers and names.
Herbin de Halle et al. — Statistique Générale et Particulière de la France
herbin-statistique-france-1803
Date range: Circa 1803 (Consulate)
Volume VII of a collaborative statistical survey of France and its colonies, published in the year after the Treaty of Amiens. The volume covers exclusively the French colonial empire — Saint-Domingue, Guadeloupe, Martinique, Louisiana, Africa, and the Indies — with contributions from several named authors: Peuchet on commerce and colonies, Sonnini on climate and geography, Delalauze on agriculture, Gorsse on mineral productions, and Herbin on topography and population. The perspective is Consular-state statistical, encyclopaedic, practical — a snapshot of French imperial ambitions at their momentary post-Amiens peak, before the disaster of Saint-Domingue and the renewal of war with Britain.
Testu — Almanach Impérial, 1808
testu-almanach-imperial-1808
Date range: 1808 (single year)
The official annual directory of the French Empire for the leap year 1808, presented to the Emperor and King. Published by Testu, the Emperor’s own printer, it lists every named office-holder in the imperial state — ministers, councillors of state, prefects, generals, judges, university functionaries, diplomatic corps, and decorations — with their ranks, addresses, and appointments. The perspective is imperial-state self-description, administrative, official. It represents the Empire’s organisation at its most confident and complete, after Austerlitz and Tilsit but before the Spanish catastrophe and the Russian campaign.

Contemporary Political Analysis
Benjamin Constant — De la force du gouvernement actuel; Des réactions politiques; Des effets de la terreur
constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796
Date range: 1796–1797 (written under the Directory)
Benjamin Constant’s three pamphlets — his first sustained political writings — constitute the founding texts of French liberal political thought. De la force du gouvernement actuel (1796) argues for rallying to the Directory as the only viable Republic. Des réactions politiques (1797) and Des effets de la terreur (1797) respond to the Thermidorian and royalist backlash. Together they address the central problem of post-Terror politics: how to stabilise a republic without collapsing into either renewed Jacobinism or royalist reaction. Constant’s perspective is liberal, republican, constitutionalist — the first systematic attempt to found a French liberalism on the experience of revolutionary failure.

How to Use This Map

For the Girondin experience, read the Roland, Buzot, Louvet, and Brissot cluster together — they cover the same events (the 31 May coup, the proscription, the federalist revolt) from different personal angles.
For the court and royalist perspective, read Campan, Besenval, and Marmontel alongside Morris’s external commentary.
For military strategy, Mahan (naval) and Paganel (Napoleonic) complement each other; Pagès and Fantin provide contemporary campaign narratives.
For the Counter-Revolution, Daudet’s three works form the most complete archival survey available in the wiki.
For the social history of the Terror, Fleischmann is the only source that systematically examines non-political life under revolutionary government.
For institutional and quantitative data, Herbin and Testu provide the numbers and names that the narrative sources lack.
For political theory, Constant’s pamphlets are the wiki’s only dedicated liberal-theoretical source.

Note: This map covers all 22 source pages currently in the wiki. Additional works referenced in the project — including Sir Archibald Alison’s History of Europe, Pierre Pagès (no relation to François) — appear as citations within existing sources rather than as separate wiki pages.

sources/besenval-memoires-4vols-1805.title: Pierre-Victor, baron de Besenval — Mémoires de M. le baron de Besenval, 4 vols. (c. 1805)
sources/besenval-memoires-4vols-1805.content:
Pierre-Victor, baron de Besenval (1721–1791), Mémoires de M. le baron de Besenval, lieutenant-général des armées du roi, sous Louis XV et Louis XVI, grand’croix de l’ordre de Saint-Louis, gouverneur des ville et château de Haguenau, 4 vols. Paris: F. Buisson (posthumous, c. 1805). Extracted raw text from University of California (UCAL) digitised copies. Vol. 1 (Tome I, UCAL b3343817) approximately 402 pages, 374 KB; Vol. 2 (Tome II, UCAL b3343818) approximately 388 pages, 370 KB; Vol. 3 (Tome III, UCAL b3343820) approximately 452 pages, 434 KB; Vol. 4 (Tome IV, UCAL b3343819) approximately 436 pages, 420 KB. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]
Besenval was a Swiss-born soldier and courtier who served as Lieutenant-General of the royal armies under Louis XV and Louis XVI. Born in Soleure to a patrician family of Savoyard origin, he entered the régiment des Gardes as a cadet at age nine, served in the campaigns of 1735 and 1748 (Bohemia), and rose to become a key figure at the French court, deeply involved in military administration and court politics. He was also the author of various literary works and a member of the literary academy formed by officers at Drévenich during the 1757 campaign. His memoirs were published posthumously under the editorship of his testamentary executor, A. J. de Ségur. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]
The memoirs cover the period from approximately 1735 through July 1789 — Besenval died in 1791, so the narrative breaks off at the outset of the Revolution, but his account of the July 1789 crisis (as the commander responsible for the troops around Paris) is of exceptional value. The work is structured not as a continuous chronological narrative but as a series of separate articles or mémoires on specific subjects, persons, and events — a format typical of the genre. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]
Volume Structure
Volume 1 (Tome I) — Switzerland, Prussia, the Seven Years’ War, Court Life under Louis XV
The first volume opens with A. J. de Ségur’s Avertissement (as executor of Besenval’s will) and a Notice sur M. le baron de Besenval providing biographical context, then proceeds to the memoir articles:


Des Suisses, et du changement de leur constitution militaire en France, en 1764 — Besenval, himself Swiss-born and a colonel of the Swiss Guards, writes on the Swiss military constitution in France and the reforms of 1764. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Anecdote singulière de la Suisse — A remarkable anecdote from Switzerland. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Du Roi de Prusse — Observations on Frederick the Great, his character and military methods. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Anecdote du Roi de Prusse — Particular anecdote concerning Frederick. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Anecdote sur la Campagne de 1744 — Besenval’s own experience in the campaign of 1744 during the War of the Austrian Succession. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Bataille d’Hastenbeck, et ce qui l’a précédée; Réflexions sur la conduite de M. de Maillebois; Caractères de quelques Généraux — The Battle of Hastenbeck (26 July 1757) and the campaign of 1757 in Germany during the Seven Years’ War, with character sketches of the French generals. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Bataille de Fillinghauzen; ce qui l’a précédée; Caractères de quelques Généraux — The Battle of Villinghausen (15–16 July 1761) and preceding events, with further general character sketches. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Further articles cover court anecdotes, the comte de Frise, Montesquieu at Venice, the maréchal de Richelieu, the Jansenist-Jesuit controversies, and:

Principes de la haine des Jésuites contre M. de Choiseul — The Jesuits’ hostility to the duc de Choiseul, leading up to the expulsion of the Society from France. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]

Volume 2 (Tome II) — Political Intrigues, the Choiseul Disgrace, Louis XV’s Death, the Early Reign of Louis XVI
The second volume is entirely concerned with court politics and ministerial intrigues:


Intrigue de M. de Lavaugayon contre M. le duc de Choiseul, en 1760 — The earliest of the cabals against Choiseul, led by Lavaugayon. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Dernière intrigue qui détermina la disgrâce du duc de Choiseul; détails sur l’abbé de la Ville — The final intrigue that brought down Choiseul in 1770, with particulars on the abbé de La Ville. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Comment le duc de Choiseul perdit la charge de colonel-général des Suisses, et les suites de cet événement — Choiseul’s loss of the colonel-generalcy of the Swiss regiments — a matter directly affecting Besenval’s own military career. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Anecdotes sur le renvoi des Jésuites — The expulsion of the Jesuits from France (1762–1764). ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Mort du Roi Louis XV — The death of Louis XV (10 May 1774), including details of the smallpox that killed him and the court’s reaction. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Exil du duc d’Aiguillon — The exile of the duc d’Aiguillon, Louis XV’s last foreign minister, following the accession of Louis XVI. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Anecdote du chancelier de Maupeou, et du président de Lamoignon — The chancelier Maupeou’s coup against the parlements (1771) and the role of président de Lamoignon. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Caractère du chancelier — A character portrait of Maupeou. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Des Parlemens — Besenval’s reflections on the parlements as institutions. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Anecdote de Louis XV; réflexions sur M. Necker — A Louis XV anecdote and reflexions on Necker, his character and financial administration. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Origine et fortune de M. de Vergennes, Ministre — The rise of the comte de Vergennes, Louis XVI’s foreign minister. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Mort du chevalier de Muy, ministre de la Guerre; nomination de M. de Saint-Germain à sa place; d’autres Événemens; Caractères de quelques Gens de la Cour — The death of the chevalier de Muy, Saint-Germain’s appointment as Minister of War, and sketches of various court figures. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Comment madame de Guémené perdit la place de Gouvernante des Enfans de France, et comment la duchesse de Polignac lui succéda — The change of gouvernante of the Children of France, from the princesse de Guémené to the duchesse de Polignac — a key event in court politics under Louis XVI. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Combat de M. le comte d’Artois et de M. le duc de Bourbon — The duel between the comte d’Artois (the future Charles X) and the duc de Bourbon, a celebrated court affair. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Comment M. de Castries et M. de Ségur sont parvenus au Ministère — How the maréchal de Castries (Marine) and the maréchal de Ségur (Guerre) attained their ministerial positions — Besenval was intimately involved in the latter’s appointment. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


Volume 3 (Tome III) — Justice Reform, the Parlement Crisis, Cardinal Rohan, the Calonne Ministry, the Assembly of Notables, the Pre-Revolution, and the July Days of 1789
This is the most important volume for the French Revolution wiki. It covers the political crisis of 1786–1789, culminating in Besenval’s personal role as commander of the troops around Paris during the July 1789 uprising.


De M. de Lamoignon, président à mortier au Parlement de Paris; et de la réforme des abus de la Justice dans ce Parlement — Besenval’s extensive account of his friend Lamoignon, his project for judicial reform, and the struggle between the crown and the parlements. Includes the Mémoire sur la Réforme de la Justice and its subsidiary proposals: reform of judicial instruction, reform of judges’ remuneration, reform of clerks, reform of the greffes, and the King’s formal response. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Comité de Finances — The financial committee and the state of the royal treasury. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


De la Société des Rois — Reflections on the nature of monarchy and princely society. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Procès du Cardinal de Rohan — The trial of Cardinal de Rohan (1785–1786) for his role in the Diamond Necklace affair. Besenval, a well-placed courtier, provides inside details on this scandal that fatally weakened the monarchy’s prestige. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Lettre du baron de Besenval au maréchal de Ségur, ministre de la Guerre, en date du 6 novembre 1786 — Official correspondence on military matters. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Lettre du baron de Besenval au comte de Ségur, ministre plénipotentiaire du Roi auprès de l’Impératrice de Russie, en date du 6 mars 1787. Assemblée des Notables. Comment M. de Lamoignon est parvenu à être garde-des-sceaux, et M. de Brienne, archevêque de Toulouse, à la tête des finances — A crucial section covering the Assembly of Notables (1787), Lamoignon’s appointment as Keeper of the Seals, and Brienne’s rise to head the finances. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Réflexions sur le Plan de M. de Calonne, et sur son exécution — Besenval’s critique of Calonne’s financial plan presented to the Assembly of Notables. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


La Hollande abandonnée. Le comte de Brienne, ministre de la Guerre, et M. de la Luzerne, de la Marine. Conseil de guerre établi. La guerre évitée. — The Dutch crisis of 1787, the Patriot uprising, Prussian intervention, and France’s failure to intervene due to financial exhaustion. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Édit d’un emprunt, et d’un autre pour accorder le droit de Citoyen aux Protestans, portés par le Roi au Parlement. Celui de l’emprunt enregistré par ordre exprès — The struggle over the edict for a new loan and the edict granting civil rights to Protestants (the Edict of Tolerance, 1787–1788). ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Portrait de M. le duc d’Orléans. Exil de ce prince et des conseillers Freteau et l’abbé Sabatier de Cabre — A character portrait of the duc d’Orléans (Philippe-Égalité) and the exile of the duc and two conseillers following their protests during the séance royale. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


L’archevêque de Toulouse troque son archevêché contre celui de Sens — Brienne’s exchange of the archbishopric of Toulouse for that of Sens. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Further sections on the Brienne ministry, the May Edicts (8 May 1788), the abolition of the parlements, the establishment of the Cour plénière, provincial resistance in Brittany and Dauphiné, the financial collapse, Brienne’s resignation, the recall of Necker, and the second Assembly of Notables (November 1788). ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Complot dirigé par Laclos et le comte de Mirabeau, en faveur du duc d’Orléans — The conspiracy of Laclos (author of Les Liaisons dangereuses) and Mirabeau on behalf of the duc d’Orléans during the pre-revolutionary crisis. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Ce qui m’est arrivé à la Révolution de 1789 — Besenval’s personal account of the revolutionary crisis. As lieutenant-general commanding the troops concentrated around Paris (the “camp of the Champ de Mars” and the troops at Saint-Denis, the Bastille, etc.), he was at the centre of the military response to the July 1789 uprising. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


12, 13 et 14 juillet 1789. Ma prison et mon Procès — The most important section for the wiki. Besenval’s detailed day-by-day account of the July Days — the dismissal of Necker, the military preparations, the fall of the Bastille, and his own arrest and prosecution. He was made a scapegoat for the government’s failure to suppress the insurrection, arrested at Provins while attempting to flee, and brought back to Paris for trial before the Châtelet. His account of his imprisonment in Brie-Comte-Robert and his trial is a unique source on the immediate aftermath of 14 July from the perspective of the defeated royal command. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Volume 4 (Tome IV) — Mélanges Littéraires et Philosophiques
The fourth volume is entirely different in character — it contains Besenval’s literary and philosophical works, not his memoirs proper. The editor’s Avertissement explains that the volume originated in a literary academy formed by officers at Drévenich during the 1757 campaign, where each member contributed prose or verse. The volume opens with a letter from Crébillon fils reviewing Besenval’s manuscript. Contents:

Le Spleen — A prose piece on melancholy. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Idées politiques et militaires — Political and military reflections. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Les Amans soldats — A tale of soldier-lovers. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Féerie — A fairy tale. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Socrate et Gassendi — A philosophical dialogue. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Alonzo — A story. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Cœlia — A story. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Réflexions sur la Comédie — Reflections on comedy. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
L’Hermite — The Hermit, a tale. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Réflexions sur le Ton — Reflections on tone in society. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Histoire des Revenans — A ghost story. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Pensées détachées — Detached thoughts and maxims. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Nouvelle espagnole — A Spanish novella. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Du Chagrin — On sorrow. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Anecdote bretonne — A Breton anecdote. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Première Scène d’une Comédie — First scene of a comedy. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Aventure et Conversation de M. le Baron de Besenval avec une dame de Wesel — Besenval’s own encounter and conversation with a lady of Wesel. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Opinion des Turcs sur les femmes — Turkish opinions on women. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Disgrâce de madame des Ursins, et ce qui l’a occasionnée — Historical account of the disgrace of the princesse des Ursins (18th century Spanish court). ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
De la Douleur — On pain, physical and moral. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Traduction d’un ouvrage chinois sur les jardins — Translation of a Chinese work on gardens. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Épître à Damon — Verse epistle. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Épître au comte de F* — Verse epistle. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
À l’abbé Allaire, mon précepteur, en lui envoyant une collection d’auteurs latins — Verse to his former tutor. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]
Sur la mort du comte de Frise, neveu du maréchal de Saxe — On the death of the comte de Frise. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]

Revolution-Related Coverage Guide
Volume 3 is the principal revolution source. The following sections are of particular interest:


Procès du Cardinal de Rohan (Tome III, art. 4) — The Diamond Necklace affair, which fatally undermined the moral authority of the monarchy and is widely considered a proximate cause of the pre-revolutionary crisis. Besenval’s court connections give him access to details unavailable to the press. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Lettres to Ségur; Assemblée des Notables; Calonne’s Plan (Tome III, arts. 5–7) — Besenval’s correspondence provides documentary evidence of the military and financial situation in 1786–87, and his critique of Calonne reflects the views of the court military establishment. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


The Brienne Ministry and the Parlement Crisis (Tome III, arts. 8–12) — The entire pre-revolutionary crisis of 1787–88, including the exile of the Parlement, the May Edicts, the Cour plénière, the provincial revolts, and the collapse of the Brienne ministry. Besenval was a close friend of Lamoignon and has unique insight into the government’s internal deliberations. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Portrait of the duc d’Orléans (Tome III, art. 10) — Besenval’s unflattering character sketch of Philippe-Égalité, written by a military courtier who despised Orléans’s ambitions. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


The Laclos-Mirabeau-Orléans Conspiracy (Tome III, art. 13) — Besenval’s account of the plot to place the duc d’Orléans on the throne or in the regency, a conspiracy theory widely held in royalist and moderate circles but documented here by a participant-observer. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


The July Days: Besenval’s Command, Arrest, and Trial (Tome III, arts. 14–15) — These are the most valuable pages in the entire work for the wiki. Besenval was the officer commanding the royal troops stationed around Paris. His account of 12–14 July 1789 — the decision not to use force against the Parisian insurrection, his loss of control over the troops, his flight, and his arrest — is the senior royal commander’s own version of events. The trial narrative also contains testimony from witnesses and documents that survive nowhere else. This is a rare source from the defeated royalist military side, complementing the popular/national assembly narratives that dominate other sources. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


Quality
OCRed text from University of California library scans. The French text preserves late 18th-century orthography (e.g., “événemens,” “foible,” “paroît”). The OCR quality is variable — some pages have significant scan artifacts (especially in Tome IV, where the Greek and decorative typefaces cause frequent misreads). The text is serviceable for keyword search but requires care for verbatim quotation. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]
Value to the Wiki
Besenval’s memoirs are valuable as:


A court insider’s view of the Louis XV and Louis XVI administrations — As a colonel of the Swiss Guards, lieutenant-general, and frequent at Versailles, Besenval had direct access to ministers (Choiseul, Maupeou, Ségur, Castries, Lamoignon), to court factions (the Choiseul circle, the Polignac set, the Maurepas party), and to the royal family itself. No other source in the wiki covers the court politics of 1760–1789 from this angle in such detail. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol2.txt]


A military commander’s account of the July 1789 crisis — Besenval was the man on the ground, responsible for the very troops that were supposed to suppress the Paris insurrection. His account of 12–14 July is the closest thing we have to the official royal military report on the fall of the Bastille, written by the commander who failed to hold Paris. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


A unique perspective on the Parlement-Monarchy struggle — As Lamoignon’s intimate friend, Besenval documents the internal debates of the government during the 1787–88 crisis from a position of trust. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol3.txt]


A Swiss officer’s perspective on French institutions — Besenval’s Swiss origins and his role as colonel of the Swiss Guards give him a distinctive angle on the French military constitution, the Swiss regiments, and the relationship between foreign troops and the French crown. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol1.txt]


Literary mélanges (Volume 4) — While less directly useful for the revolution wiki, Tome IV shows Besenval as a man of letters and provides the philosophical and literary context for his memoir judgments. It also includes Crébillon fils’s editorial criticism of Besenval’s writing style, which sheds light on the literary culture of the 18th-century military aristocracy. ^[source: raw/besenval-memoires-vol4.txt]

sources/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.title: Brissot — À ses Commettans, précédé d'autres pièces (written 1792–1793, pub. London 1794)
sources/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.content:
J.-P. Brissot de Warville, À ses Commettans, sur la Situation de la Convention Nationale, sur l’Influence des Anarchistes, & les Maux qu’elle a Causés, sur la Nécessité d’Anéantir cette Influence pour Sauver la République; Précédé d’autres Pièces intéressantes de Brissot. Paris: Imprimerie de P. Provost; reprinted London: R. Edwards, No. 142 Bond-Street, & T. Spilsbury & Sons, Snow-hill, 1794. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 9,320 lines and 397 KB, from a New York Public Library copy (Gordon Lester Ford Collection, presented by his sons Worthington Chauncey Ford and Paul Leicester Ford). Brissot (1754–1793) was the leading Girondin journalist and politician, editor of the Patriote Français, deputy for Eure-et-Loir, one of the leading advocates for declaring war on Austria and later on Britain. He was arrested after the coup of May 31–June 2, 1793, condemned by the Revolutionary Tribunal, and guillotined on October 31, 1793. The texts in this volume were written between August 1792 and May 22, 1793. ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Contents at a Glance
This volume is a London reprint, produced for English readers, of four separate Brissot texts that circulated widely in France and were subsequently reprinted abroad. The publisher’s preface (Avertissement) explains: “The Address of Brissot to his constituents, which has made so much noise on the Continent, having also excited much curiosity in our Country, it was judged proper to reprint it here, and to precede it with some of the Decrees of the Brissotine Faction concerning the Government of Great Britain.” The framing — “Faction Brissotine” — signals that the London publishers are not sympathetic to Brissot; they are printing his texts as documents of an enemy of Britain, available for English readers to judge.
The text is in 18th-century French typography with long-s characters throughout (the character ſ is rendered in the OCR as “f,” making standard words appear in altered form: “fes” = ses, “eft” = est, “fufpenfion” = suspension, “puiffances” = puissances). The texts are readable with standard French literacy and awareness of this convention.
The four texts are printed in the order in which Brissot composed them: the post-August 10 declaration to foreign powers; the January 1793 report on British policy; the February 1793 report calling for war declaration; and the May 1793 address to his constituents. Together they form a continuous record of Girondin foreign and domestic policy positions from the fall of the monarchy through the eve of the Girondin overthrow. ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Full Contents Map
Text I — Projet de Déclaration de l’Assemblée Nationale aux Puissances Étrangères (post-August 10, 1792)
Drafted by Brissot and printed by order of the National Assembly. This is the Assembly’s formal statement to neutral foreign powers — particularly those that had recalled their ambassadors or suspended relations following Louis XVI’s suspension on August 10 — explaining the legal and constitutional basis of what had been done.
The case against the king. The declaration opens by summarizing the grounds for Louis XVI’s suspension: he had consistently surrounded himself with men who detested the Revolution; when patriots entered his council he expelled them; he formed a guard on counter-revolutionary principles; he paid his former body-guards (suppressed by decree) who were in open rebellion; he worked to destroy the popular societies, to undermine the National Assembly, to provoke conflict between the people and the National Guard, to discredit the assignats, to facilitate the entry of émigrés — “and the king followed and encouraged all these projects with criminal constancy.” The proof had been found in the registers of the civil list expenditures and in other authentic documents. He had used the money the nation gave him to maintain royal splendor to “crush the nation and stifle liberty” — to pay the assassins of the people who had raised him to the throne.
The legal argument. The Assembly had searched the constitution for the means to arrest the course of these betrayals, examining whether the king had fallen into the cases that pronounce abdication of the crown, when the insurrection of August 10 anticipated the decision. The declaration argues that the Assembly’s response — suspension of the king pending Convention judgment — was itself constitutionally grounded: the suspension power exists in the constitution for cases of absence, and by necessary analogy for cases of incapacity or when public safety imperiously demands it. The Convention is being called not as a revolutionary act but as an appeal to national sovereignty: “only it can, through new organs, pronounce between the two powers.”
The argument to neutral powers. Foreign governments that have recalled their ambassadors or suspended relations on grounds of the king’s suspension are, the declaration argues, contradicting themselves: they had recognized the French constitution, which contains the people’s inalienable right to change their government; to break relations on grounds of the suspension is to interfere in France’s internal government, the very thing they declared they would not do. The king under the French constitution “is only the first of the public functionaries, only the organ of the nation with foreign powers: a simple citizen if considered in himself.” Relations with France are formed for the nation, not for the king. The declaration notes the irony of Britain: France had not interfered when Britain’s “Glorious Revolution” changed its government and dynasty; how can Britain now adopt the principles it then combatted? ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Text II — Rapport fait au nom du Comité de Défense Générale sur les Dispositions du Gouvernement Britannique envers la France, & sur les Mesures à prendre (January 12, 1793)
Delivered by Brissot to the Convention on January 12, 1793, printed by order of the Convention.
Britain’s response to August 10. The report traces the deterioration of Franco-British relations from their pre-August 10 equilibrium. Before the suspension of the king, Britain had maintained exact neutrality in the Franco-Austrian/Prussian war — profiting commercially from staying out, and consolidating its ministry through commercial prosperity. “This neutrality was maintained until the immortal day of August 10.” After the suspension, Britain recalled its ambassador Lord Gower on August 17, citing the futile pretext that his letters of credence were only for a king, as if new credentials could not simply have been issued. Brissot reads this as interference in French internal affairs under cover of a principle of non-interference that Britain simultaneously professed.
The diplomatic sequence, August–January. After the French victories at Jemappes and Spires, and the conquest of Savoy and Brabant, British ministers concluded that this new Republic, “which was making its debut in such a brilliant manner amid the greatest difficulties, which at its dawn was crushing the best armies commanded by the ablest generals,” might consolidate itself and carry the flame of revolution across Europe. A negotiation was established in October–November 1792; at that point the British ministry did not even complain about the opening of the Scheldt.
The deterioration. The report then details how British policy hardened through November–December 1792: the Scheldt decree, the November 19 decree of fraternity to peoples wishing to recover their liberty, and above all the impending trial and execution of Louis XVI together produced a change in British public posture. Britain now demanded that France explain its intentions; France responded with dignity and moderation; Britain found reasons to escalate each time France conceded.
The three grievances and the draft decree. Brissot presents three French demands: (1) execution of Article 4 of the 1786 commercial treaty, which would allow French citizens to travel and reside in England without the humiliating restrictions imposed by a January act of Parliament; (2) free export of grain and provisions from Britain for French purchasers; (3) clarification of what the recent British armaments are directed at. If satisfaction is not given on all three points, the Republic reserves the right to take the measures that its interest and security require. A draft decree to this effect is printed with the report. ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Text III — Rapport sur les Hostilités du Roi d’Angleterre et du Stadhouder des Provinces-Unies, et sur la Nécessité de Déclarer que la République Françoise est en Guerre avec Eux (February 1, 1793)
Presented to the Convention on February 1, 1793, by Brissot in the name of the Committee of General Defense, printed by order of the Convention.
Britain wants war. The opening declaration: “The court of England wants war: Citizens, you can no longer doubt it.” Three acts prove it: the expulsion of the French ambassador within eight days, the public mourning displayed for Louis XVI, and the request to Parliament for a considerable addition of land and sea forces following news of the execution. To expel France’s representative and arm at the news of “the death of the traitor” is to say to Europe and the universe: “France condemned Louis, and I absolve him; she condemned him as a traitor, and I hold him innocent; I see in France only rebels and sacrilegists; France wants neither king nor royalty, and I wish to avenge the king and restore royalty. I wish to join the coalition of kings leagued to support the cause of all thrones.”
The Stadtholder. The report covers simultaneous Dutch hostility: the Stadtholder, acting in concert with the British court, has taken measures hostile to France in the United Provinces. The Republic cannot maintain French commerce and interests in Holland under these conditions.
The argument for declaring war. Brissot argues that France did not seek this war; it had used every means to preserve peace with England. But peace is no longer possible once England has chosen to treat the French Republic as an illegitimate rebel against monarchy. The Convention is asked to formally declare that the Republic is at war with the King of England and the Stadtholder. The execution of Louis XVI — which Brissot characterizes throughout as the just condemnation of a traitor — is the immediate occasion for British belligerence, but the deeper cause is that no tyrant can forgive France its liberty. ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Text IV — J. P. Brissot, Député du Département d’Eure et Loire, À ses Commettans, sur la Situation de la Convention Nationale, sur l’Influence des Anarchistes, & les Maux qu’elle a Causés, sur la Nécessité d’Anéantir cette Influence pour Sauver la République (May 22, 1793)
Dated Paris, May 22, 1793 — nine days before the Montagnard coup that would proscribe Brissot and the other leading Girondins. This is the text for which the volume is principally named: Brissot’s address to his constituents in Eure-et-Loir, his political reckoning with what has gone wrong in the Convention, and his call to the nation to judge between the two parties.
The “Avis aux Lecteurs” preface. Brissot opens with a preface in which he acknowledges that “complete truth has never been told since the beginning of the Revolution” because people feared that saying it would harm the cause of liberty, discourage the people, and obstruct affairs. This circumspection was appropriate when nations save themselves through a few men or a few bodies; it is fatal when only the nation itself can save itself. “To conceal from it its situation is to encourage its lethargy; it can only be brought to make great efforts, to direct them well, when it is well enlightened about that situation.” He acknowledges he may be thought too severe toward certain individuals and bodies. “I have been truthful, and I had to be.”
The three propositions. The main text is organized around three demonstrations:

That a party of anarchists has dominated and still dominates almost all deliberations of the Convention and operations of the Executive Council.
That this party has been and still is the sole cause of all the ills, both internal and external, afflicting France.
That the Republic can only be saved by taking rigorous measures to wrest the nation’s representatives from the despotism of this faction.

The definition of anarchy. Before presenting the evidence, Brissot insists on defining his terms: “Laws without execution, constituted authorities without force and debased, crime unpunished, property attacked, the security of individuals violated, the morals of the People corrupted; neither constitution, nor government, nor justice: these are the traits of anarchy.” He warns against the abuse of words — the “political charlatans” who confuse anarchism with patriotism.
Brissot’s own principles. He describes what he believed on arriving at the Convention: since the monarchy was annihilated and the Republic established, since all powers were in the hands of the people or its representatives, the patriots had to change their conduct in accordance with the changed situation. The insurrectional movement had to cease — where there is no tyranny to overthrow, there should be no force in insurrection; where one is only building, one needs only order and reason. He acknowledges that after three years of revolution it was difficult to calm the people’s movements immediately; a people coming out of slavery “is a child, and it is natural that it sometimes breaks even its own work, that it rises against the authorities created by itself.” But if these movements — “which throw society into frightful convulsions” — were prolonged too long, the people would tear itself apart, believing it was only breaking its instruments. It would soon regret the lethargic calm of its first slavery, if not given a republican calm in its place: “the people wants to be happy… happiness is not in the eternal repetition of violent convulsions; if brigands live by seditions, the people lives by repose.”
The indictment of the “anarchist party.” The body of the Adresse presents Brissot’s account of how the anarchist party — centered on the Paris Commune, Marat, Robespierre, and their allies in the Mountain — has systematically used insurrectionary pressure to dominate the Convention, prevented constitutional government from functioning, prolonged the war through military incompetence and political interference, and brought France to the brink of dissolution. He argues that every major catastrophe of the Convention period can be traced to this faction’s actions: the September Massacres, the policy toward the generals, the management of the war, the financial disorder.
The appeal to constituents and to the nation. The address closes with a direct appeal: “It is time that our fellow-citizens, that foreign peoples, judge between us and our adversaries; it is time to see which men have wanted to save the Republic, and which men have wanted to lose it. The evil is at its height; mystery would be only a dangerous palliative.” He asks his constituents to read, to judge, and to act — to use their civic authority to demand that the Convention be freed from the faction that oppresses it. ^[source: raw/brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793.txt]
Coverage Guide


The Girondin case against Louis XVI, August 1792 — Text I gives the fullest Girondin constitutional argument for why the king’s suspension was not a coup but a constitutionally grounded act: the evidence of betrayal from the civil list accounts, the legal analogy to the suspension power, the appeal to national sovereignty through a Convention. Cross-reference roland-memoires-vol2-1823 for a parallel Girondin reading of the same events.


The argument for war with Britain, January–February 1793 — Texts II and III document the diplomatic sequence from August 10 through the declaration of war: Britain’s recall of Lord Gower, the failed November negotiations, the expulsion of the French ambassador after Louis XVI’s execution, and Brissot’s case that Britain had chosen war to avenge the king and restore monarchy across Europe. For the British naval side of the war that followed, cross-reference mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol1.


Girondin self-description of the Convention’s internal conflict — Text IV is the most complete Girondin account of the Convention period before May 31, written from inside the conflict. Brissot’s three propositions (anarchist party dominates the Convention; anarchist party is sole cause of all troubles; only rigorous measures can save the Republic) are the Girondin reading of the situation that louvet-memoires-1823 describes from the fugitive’s perspective after June 2, and that roland-memoires-vol2-1823 describes from prison.


Definition and critique of revolutionary anarchism — Brissot’s careful definition of anarchism (laws without execution, authorities without force, crime unpunished, property attacked, individual security violated, morals corrupted) is one of the clearest contemporary definitions of what the Girondins meant by the term they applied to the Mountain.


The Girondin theory of post-revolutionary order — Brissot’s account of his own political principles — that once the monarchy fell, insurrection should cease and order and reason replace it; that prolonged popular convulsions destroy the revolution that produces them — is a statement of Girondin republican theory as distinct from Montagnard theory.


The execution of Louis XVI and its international consequences — Texts II and III track in detail how the execution transformed Britain from neutrality to belligerence, and give the Girondin argument that France was the victim of British aggression rather than its initiator.


Quality
NYPL copy (Gordon Lester Ford Collection), OCR from a 1794 London print. The text is printed in 18th-century French typography throughout, with the long-s character (ſ) rendered as “f” in the OCR. This affects the readability of every word containing “s” — “ses” appears as “fes,” “est” as “eft,” “suspension” as “fufpenfion,” “puissances” as “puiffances,” etc. With knowledge of this convention, the texts are fully comprehensible. The print quality of the original appears good; the OCR has handled the long-s consistently rather than randomly. Page numbers appear in parentheses, section headers are preserved. The four texts are separated by clear title pages. Total length approximately 9,320 lines / 397 KB.

sources/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.title: Buzot — Mémoires sur la Révolution Française (written 1793–1794, pub. 1823)
sources/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.content:
François-Nicolas-Léonard Buzot, Mémoires sur la Révolution Française.
Paris: Béchet Aîné, 1823. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 16,280 lines and 776 KB, from a Harvard/Widener Library copy.
Buzot (1760–1794) was a Girondin deputy to the National Convention from Eure, one of the closest colleagues of Jean-Marie Roland and the man Madame Roland loved. He was proscribed after the coup of May 31–June 2, 1793, fled through Normandy and Brittany, and hid for nearly a year at Saint-Émilion before being found dead in a field in June 1794.
His memoirs were written in hiding (1793–1794) and published posthumously in 1823, edited by Joseph Guadet, who added a biographical notice, a historical essay on the Girondins, and editorial footnotes. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
The memoirs are direct and unpolished — written without the leisure to revise, addressed to posterity and to his constituents. Buzot writes in two phases: the 1793 memoirs, analytical, dissecting Montagnard domination of the Convention and its means; and the 1794 memoirs, more personal, written in the most desperate months of his flight — his last wishes, his judgment on what constitution France needed, and his final assessments of Robespierre, Saint-Just, Barrère, and Danton. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]

Full Contents Map
Mémoires — Première Partie (written 1793)
Chapter I — Disposition of minds; the true causes of Girondin proscription.
Buzot opens by examining the political atmosphere in the Convention’s early months. He identifies the “true causes” of the proscription: not the public charges (royalism, federalism, counter-revolution, corruption by foreign gold), but the Girondin insistence on order, legality, and constitutional procedure at a moment when the Mountain’s power depended on maintaining popular agitation. He writes: since the monarchy had been annihilated, the insurrectional movement had to cease; where there is no tyranny to overthrow there should be no force in insurrection; where one is only building, one needs order and reason.
Chapter II — Examination of the charges against the Girondins.
Buzot takes each accusation in turn. Were they counter-revolutionaries? He traces the Girondin record from the States-General through the Convention. Were they agents of foreign powers? He challenges accusers to produce evidence, then turns the charge: “the anarchists who accuse others of theft to divert attention from their own — corrupt the French people to conceal their own corruption — render your accounts, render account of your scandalous fortunes, brigands! I wait for you there.” Were they royalists? He notes most Girondins voted for the king’s death, himself included. Were they federalists? He finds this the most absurd charge — the Girondins never proposed dissolving the Republic into independent parts. The word “federalism” had been deployed to stigmatize any resistance to Parisian sectional power. He quotes Charron on the credulity of the people: “In 1791, they were told: Brissot, Pétion, and Buzot are republicans, good to hang; and everywhere the people repeated that they were republicans and would have hanged them willingly. Today they are told: Brissot, Pétion, Buzot and their friends are royalists who must be chased, pursued, put to death; and the people repeat that they are royalists, and chase them, pursue them, kill them. The people in all cases did its job, even in assassinating us.” ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Chapter III — Means used to change public opinion against the Girondins.
Buzot examines how the Mountain managed popular opinion: through the press, the sections, and deliberate misrepresentation of the federalist resistance after May 31 — casting republican resistance to an illegal coup as royalist counter-revolution. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Mémoires — Deuxième Partie (written 1793)
Chapter I — Means used to dominate the people.
The Jacobin Club as a parallel power structure outside constitutional institutions. Buzot describes how the affiliated clubs in the departments let the Mountain mobilize public opinion against the Convention itself. He also describes the radical women’s sections that provided street pressure at key moments.
Chapter II — Means used to dominate the Convention: portraits of Marat, Robespierre, Danton, and Cambon.
The most mined section of Buzot’s memoirs — sustained character studies of the four men he identifies as principal instruments of Montagnard domination.
Marat: Buzot gives Madame Roland’s portrait of Marat (physical repulsiveness and moral monstrousness) before adding his own assessment: a man whose denunciations served as the Mountain’s instrument for destroying individual reputations; whose “acquittal” by the Revolutionary Tribunal (after Louvet’s accusation) made the Convention permanently subject to factional terror.
Robespierre: Buzot traces Robespierre’s rise from the Jacobin Club through the Convention, his tactical patience while Marat was the visible extremist, his move toward dictatorship once Marat’s assassination removed his cover.
Danton: Described through his conduct as Minister of Justice after August 10, his role in the September Massacres, his management of the Committee of Public Safety as an instrument of factional power rather than national defense. Buzot writes: “Danton and Robespierre are the sole authors of the afflictions that have fallen on France.”
Cambon: The Convention’s finance man — “an honest scoundrel who, always speaking of economizing the people’s funds, knew only how to economize his own.” Cambon’s power over the assignats, his management of financial decisions without accountability, his fury at contradiction: “his ignorance was so bold that one did not even dare reproach him with it.” ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Chapter III — Means used to dominate the ministry: Roland, Garat, Pache.
Buzot traces how the Mountain worked to discredit and destroy each minister. Roland is described with the “rigid virtues of the finest ages of the Roman Republic.” Garat he calls a man of letters who flattered each faction in turn as each rose — “with much wit, incapable of all good; without soul, without energy, without character.” Pache is the most detailed portrait: Buzot recounts how he recommended Pache for the War Ministry on Roland’s advice, and then Pache’s systematic betrayal — his false simplicity (arriving at the ministry at seven in the morning with a piece of bread in his pocket, refusing salary and title), and his destruction of the army’s capacity: “all those without morals and without credentials as without capacity were sure to be welcomed” if they affected extreme Jacobinism; armies lacked everything; generals’ campaign plans were undermined. Buzot calls Pache and Garat “names of horror, execrable memory! how many regrets, how many remorse they cause me! It is to you that I partly owe your sudden elevation, and I am well punished for it.” ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Chapter IV — Conduct of the anarchists toward the army and departments; Conclusion.
Montagnard representatives-on-mission used their powers to purge capable officers and convert military appointments into instruments of factional control. The conclusion surveys France’s state at the time of writing: the Republic nominally established, the constitution not yet applied, the arbitrary power of the Paris sections replacing constitutional government. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Mémoires — Année 1794
Written when Buzot had been a year in hiding and the situation in France had worsened.
Chapter I — Response to the charge they did not prevent the state’s ills.
Buzot answers the implicit accusation that the Girondins should have done more. He gives the honest answer: the cowardice of the departments after May 31 left the fugitive deputies isolated; the federalist resistance in Calvados and the Gironde was real but insufficient; the departments that rose were outmaneuvered, intimidated, and then submitted. France’s current state is the consequence.
Chapter II — What constitution France needed; anecdotes on Robespierre, Barrère, Saint-Just, Danton.
Buzot examines the constitutional question from hiding. He distinguishes his actual position (departments should have equal weight; no city should dictate to the whole Republic) from the “federalism” caricature. He examines the Directory constitution of 1795, correctly anticipating its defects before it existed. The anecdotes on surviving Montagnard leaders give his final assessments: Robespierre’s ascendancy, Barrère’s servility, Saint-Just’s fanaticism, Danton’s corruption.
Chapter III — Who can judge us; trial of Brissot and friends; last wishes.
His account of the Revolutionary Tribunal’s trial of Brissot and the other proscribed Girondins — conducted by judges who were instruments of the faction that had overthrown them. His last wishes: addressed to posterity, to his constituents. He ends on Rousseau’s line: “One who falls asleep in the bosom of a father is not anxious about the waking.” ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Morceaux Détachés — Fragments from Buzot’s Manuscripts
Scattered passages from Buzot’s papers, published posthumously:


Anecdotes on Valazé, Lacaze, and Brissot — Personal recollections of three Girondin colleagues: Valazé’s suicide at the bar of the Revolutionary Tribunal when his verdict was announced; Lacaze’s conduct in hiding; Brissot’s character and final period.


Anecdotes on Dubois-Crancé and Collot-d’Herbois — Two of the most notorious Montagnard representatives-on-mission, both implicated in the massacres at Lyon.


New developments on federalism — Additional arguments distinguishing the Girondin position from the federalism charge.


Trial of Danton; new judgment on Robespierre, Saint-Just, and Barrère — Written after news of Danton’s trial reached the fugitives, Buzot revises some of his earlier judgments in light of the factional devourings unfolding in Paris. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]


Première and Seconde Lettres de Buzot à ses Commettans (January 11 and 21, 1793)
Two formal letters to his constituents in Eure-et-Loir, written at the height of the Louis XVI trial debates. The first gives his account of the Convention’s political situation; the second covers the question of the king’s judgment — he voted for death with appeal to the primary assemblies for confirmation. His full speech on this question, preserved in the Pièces Justificatives, argues: the Convention has the power to judge; it should pronounce death; but it should also call the departments to confirm, both to exercise national sovereignty and to give the judgment greater legitimacy than a Paris-dominated Convention alone could confer. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Précis des Évènements qui ont eu lieu à Évreux après le 31 mai
An account of what happened in Buzot’s home department (Eure) after the coup: the initial resistance to the coerced Convention decrees, the arrival of armed forces from Calvados and Brittany under Puissaye, the brief alignment with the federalist resistance, and the rapid collapse when military defeat at Brécourt made clear the resistance could not be sustained. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Notice sur les Derniers Jours des Députés Réfugiés dans le Département de la Gironde
The most harrowing section of the volume: an account of the fugitive deputies’ last months at Saint-Émilion.
The fugitives — Buzot, Pétion, Barbaroux, Salles, and others — made their way to the Gironde after Caen’s resistance collapsed, sheltered by sympathetic republicans in the wine country. At Saint-Émilion they were “buried alive in this dwelling of death”: the man who sheltered them later described exactly which men slept where — Pétion occupied this bed, Barbaroux lay on a mattress there, Buzot sat in the old armchair, together they cooked their meals in that corner.
A first search of Saint-Émilion found no one. A second caught them: Barbaroux shot himself through the head — he survived the wound but was arrested and guillotined. Pétion and Buzot were found dead in a field, their bodies partly consumed by wolves. Whether from self-administered poison, starvation, exposure, or some combination is not established with certainty. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]
Pièces Justificatives
Supporting documents:


Buzot’s speech on the trial of Louis XVI — his full statement of position: Louis is guilty, the Convention should judge him, the death penalty is deserved, the appeal to the primary assemblies should confirm. He argues methodically against both acquittal and immediate execution without appeal.


His account of his own conduct on May 31 — a minute-by-minute account of the coup: how he learned of the planned arrest lists the night before, how he went at dawn to warn Grangeneuve, how he held his position in the Convention through the morning’s violence, how he escaped.


Documents relating to the petition of May 31 and the mechanics of the coup — the addresses to the Convention from the sections, the armed encirclement, the debate inside. ^[source: raw/buzot-memoires-revolution-1823.txt]



Coverage Guide


Girondin self-portrait from the inside — Buzot’s memoirs are written from the position of a man present at every key moment, giving the Girondin reading without diplomatic filter. His account of the Convention’s internal politics complements roland-memoires-vol2-1823, louvet-memoires-1823, and brissot-a-ses-commettans-1793 from the same perspective.


Portraits of Marat, Robespierre, Danton, Cambon — Chapter II of Part II gives Buzot’s character studies of the four key Montagnard figures. Cross-reference with roland-memoires-vol2-1823 and louvet-memoires-1823.


The Roland ministry: Garat and Pache — The detailed portraits in Chapter III, including Buzot’s personal remorse at having recommended both men. Cross-reference roland-memoires-vol2-1823 for Roland’s side.


Buzot’s vote on Louis XVI — His two letters to his constituents and full speech in the Pièces Justificatives give the complete Girondin constitutional argument for death with appeal to the people.


The federalism charge — Buzot’s most extended refutation of the “federalist” label occurs across Chapters II and III of Part I and Chapter II of the 1794 memoirs.


The last days at Saint-Émilion — The Notice sur les Derniers Jours is the primary narrative for the fugitive deputies’ concealment and deaths. Cross-referenced in louvet-memoires-1823.


Évreux and the federalist resistance — The Précis des Évènements à Évreux gives the only detailed account of the resistance in Buzot’s home department, its collapse, and submission.



Quality
Harvard/Widener Library copy, OCR from the 1823 Béchet Aîné Paris edition. Clean 19th-century French prose throughout. The 1823 edition includes a biographical notice and historical essay by editor Joseph Guadet, who also added scholarly footnotes providing counter-evidence, cross-references to other published memoirs, and occasional qualifications to Buzot’s claims. Proper names are reliable throughout. Total length approximately 16,280 lines / 776 KB.
