sources/campan-memoires-marie-antoinette.title: Campan — Mémoires sur la vie privée de Marie-Antoinette, 3 vols. (1823)
sources/campan-memoires-marie-antoinette.content:
Campan — Mémoires sur la vie privée de Marie-Antoinette (3 vols., 1823)
Author: Jeanne Louise Henriette Campan (1752–1822), lectrice de Mesdames, première femme de chambre de la reine Marie-Antoinette
Full title: Mémoires sur la vie privée de Marie-Antoinette, reine de France et de Navarre ; suivis de Souvenirs et anecdotes historiques sur les règnes de Louis XIV, de Louis XV et de Louis XVI
Publication: Baudouin frères, Paris, 1823. Deuxième édition. 3 volumes.
Raw text: wiki/raw/campan-marie-antoinette-vol1.txt (12,069 lines), campan-marie-antoinette-vol2.txt (10,972 lines), campan-marie-antoinette-vol3.txt (8,681 lines)

Structure
Tome 1 — Mémoires (Chapitres I–XI)
Notice sur la vie de Madame Campan — Biographical notice by the editors recounting Campan’s life: born 1752, daughter of a clerk in the foreign ministry, appointed reader to Louis XV’s daughters at age 15, then première femme de chambre to Marie-Antoinette. Her son died before her.
Avant-propos de l’auteur — Campan explains her motivation: to record the inner life of the princess she served, to defend her reputation against calumny, and to preserve facts for posterity.
Chapitre I. — Cour de Louis XV. — Goût du roi pour la chasse. — Son caractère. — Il s’habitue à ne plus rougir de ses mœurs. — Mesdames, ses filles. — Portrait de madame Adélaïde.
Chapitre II. — Naissance de Marie-Antoinette marquée par un désastre mémorable. — Vers le milieu du dix-huitième siècle, les cabinets de l’Europe travaillent à détruire la puissance de la maison d’Autriche. — La France s’en mêle. — Mariages des archiduchesses avec le Dauphin de France.
Chapitre III. — Arrivée de l’archiduchesse en France. — Madame de Noailles, sa dame d’honneur. — Sa première entrevue avec Louis XV. — Comparaison du cérémonial de la cour d’Autriche avec les usages de la cour de France.
Chapitre IV. — Maladie de Louis XV. — Tableau de la cour. — Renvoi de madame Du Barry. — Vénus anadyomène. — Mot de madame Du Barry. — Abolition de l’ancienne étiquette. — Sacre du roi. — Fête de la reine. — Conduite de Louis XVI.
Chapitre V. — Révision des papiers de Louis XV par Louis XVI. — Homme au masque de fer. — L’académie des sciences. — Esprit du règne de Louis XV.
Chapitre VI. — Hiver rigoureux. — Courses en traîneaux blâmées des Parisiens. — Liaison de la reine avec la princesse de Lamballe. — La reine obtient la place de la surintendance pour la princesse. — Son amitié pour la duchesse de Polignac.
Chapitre VII. — Le duc de Choiseul reparaît à la cour. — La reine ne peut obtenir sa grâce. — Exil du duc d’Aiguillon.
Chapitre VIII. — Voyage de Joseph II en France. — Son caractère. — Ses paroles. — Sa conduite. — Il donne à la reine de sages conseils.
Chapitre IX. — Paroles que la reine adresse à la princesse qui vient de naître. — Soins de la reine pour ses enfans.
Chapitre X. — Voyage du comte et de la comtesse du Nord en France. — Leur réception à la cour. — Portrait du comte du Nord.
Chapitre XI. — La reine mécontente de la nomination de M. de Calonne. — Million qui lui est offert par le roi pour ses dépenses. — Elle refuse.
Éclaircissemens historiques — Recueillis et mis en ordre. (Pièces justificatives.)
Éclaircissemens historiques et pièces officielles. — (Additional documentation, including documents on the marriage and the diamond necklace affair.)

Tome 2 — Mémoires (Chapitres XII–XXI + Conclusion)
Chapitre XII. — Affaire du collier. — Détails sur le joaillier Bœhmer. — Parure de diamans destinée à madame Du Barry. — On prend des arrangemens avec le cardinal de Rohan. — Sa criminelle imprudence.
Chapitre XIII. — Nomination de l’archevêque de Sens au ministère : joie qu’éprouve l’abbé de Vermond. — Plans de M. de Calonne pour le rétablissement des finances. — Convocation des notables. — Suites funestes de cette mesure.
Chapitre XIV. — Serment du Jeu-de-Paume. — Insurrection du 14 juillet. — Le roi se rend à l’Assemblée nationale. — Visite du roi à Paris. — La Famille royale aux Tuileries.
Chapitre XV. — Création de la garde nationale. — Anecdote à ce sujet. — Départ de Monsieur. — Brigandages dans les provinces. — Les poissardes à Versailles. — Le 5 et 6 octobre 1789.
Chapitre XVI. — Affaire de Favras. — Son procès et sa mort. — On présente imprudemment un verre d’eau à la reine. — Projet de départ pour la cour. — Fête de la Fédération en 1790.
Chapitre XVII. — Première fédération. — Tentatives d’assassinat contre la reine. — Autre fédération. — Retour de l’évêque d’Autun.
Chapitre XVIII. — Préparatifs du voyage de Varennes. — Par qui la reine est observée et trahie. — On arrête la famille royale à Varennes. — Détails donnés par la reine sur cette douloureuse époque.
Chapitre XIX. — Acceptation de la constitution. — Avis de Barnave et de ses amis partagé par la reine. — Mariage de Madame avec M. de St. Priest. — Retour de M. de Jarnac, député extraordinaire à Saint-Domingue.
Chapitre XX. — Nouveau libelle de la femme Lamotte. — On propose à la reine de lui faire offrir une pension. — Son refus. — Sages conseils de Barnave. — Dernière fête donnée aux Tuileries. — Prise des Tuileries.
Chapitre XXI. — Relations de madame Campan avec M. Bertrand de Molleville pour le salut de la famille royale. — Dévouement du maire de Versailles. — Page qui sauve le portrait de la reine. — La reine menace de se montrer au peuple.
Conclusion. — Pétion refuse à madame Campan la permission de s’enfermer au Temple avec la reine. — Elle excite les soupçons de Robespierre. — Visites domiciliaires. — Madame Campan ouvre le porte-feuille qu’elle a reçu du roi. — Papiers qu’il renfermait avec les sceaux de l’État. — Correspondance secrète de Mirabeau avec la cour. — Elle est détruite ainsi que les autres papiers. — Seule pièce conservée. — Elle est remise à M. de Malesherbes au moment du procès de l’infortuné Louis XVI. — Fin des Mémoires.
Éclaircissemens historiques — Recueillis et mis en ordre.
Éclaircissemens historiques et pièces officielles. — (Documents and supporting materials.)

Tome 3 — Souvenirs et anecdotes historiques + Lettres de deux jeunes amies
Avis de l’éditeur — Introductory note framing the three sets of material that follow.
Avant-propos de l’auteur — Campan explains that she writes for her family, collecting facts about the interior life of the princess she served. Written in retirement, drawing on memory and notes.
Anecdotes du règne de Louis XIV — Traditions and recollections of the Sun King’s court, passed down through courtiers and servants who had served under Louis XIV.
Anecdotes du règne de Louis XV — Reminiscences of the reign Campan herself witnessed in her youth as lectrice de Mesdames, with observations on court life, mœurs, and personalities.
Anecdotes relatives à Marie Leckzinska — Stories concerning the pious queen of Louis XV, illustrating her character, her domestic life, and her relations with the court.
Anecdotes sur le règne de Louis XVI, sur ce prince et sur Marie-Antoinette — Additional stories about the king and queen not included in the main memoirs, including personal details and character sketches.
Anecdotes diverses — Miscellaneous recollections, including remarks on various notable figures and events from the ancien régime through the Revolution.
Quelques notes sur ma conduite auprès de la reine — Campan’s personal defence of her conduct during the Revolution, addressing accusations and suspicions from émigrés about her loyalty.
Avis des libraires-éditeurs — Notice introducing the following work, describing the origin of the Lettres de deux jeunes amies as a product of Campan’s experience as headmistress of the Maison d’Écouen, founded by Napoleon.
Lettres de deux jeunes amies, sur la maison d’Écouen — A didactic epistolary novel, set at the Écouen school for girls (a Napoleonic educational institution). Two young friends exchange letters about their studies, daily life, and moral development under Campan’s direction. Provides insights into women’s education under the Empire.
Éclaircissemens historiques et pièces officielles. — (Supplementary documents and references for the anecdotes and letters.)

Notes

Campan’s perspective is unique: she was present in the inner circle of the royal family from the 1770s through the Revolution. Her account of the October Days (5–6 October 1789), the flight to Varennes, and the August 10 attack are first-hand.
The memoirs were written in retirement after Campan left France, drawing on notes and memory. They are defensive in tone regarding her own conduct but generally favourable to the queen, whose side she takes on the diamond necklace affair.
The third volume’s Anecdotes are more loosely structured than the main memoirs, collecting observations from various sources, some second-hand.
The Lettres de deux jeunes amies is a separate pedagogical work appended to the third edition, reflecting Campan’s later career as headmistress of the imperial school at Écouen (Napoleon appointed her in 1807).
Chapter subtitles above are from Campan’s own table of contents and chapter headings.
Key chapters for the Revolution: Ch. XIV (July 1789), Ch. XV (October Days), Ch. XVIII (Varennes), Ch. XX (August 10), Conclusion (destruction of the Mirabeau correspondence).

sources/conspirations-royalistes-midi-da.title: Histoire des conspirations royalistes du Midi sous la Révolution (1790-1793)
sources/conspirations-royalistes-midi-da.content:
Histoire des conspirations royalistes du Midi sous la Révolution (1790-1793)
Ernest Daudet’s 1881 study of royalist conspiracies in the Midi (southern France) during the Revolution, drawn from contemporary publications, official documents, and unpublished sources. Covers the three assemblies of the Camp de Jalès, the Saillans conspiracy, and the Charrier uprising, set against the background of sectarian conflict between Catholics and Protestants in the Gard, Ardèche, and Lozère.
Contents
INTRODUCTION
Sets the scene in the Midi: the recrudescence of religious antagonism after 1789, with Protestants embracing revolutionary ideas and Catholics rallying to the defence of throne and altar. Describes the structural tensions in Nîmes — Protestant commercial dominance, Catholic municipal power, unequal distribution of arms in the National Guard — that made the region a tinderbox.
LIVRE PREMIER: Le Camp de Jalès
I. La bagarre à Nîmes. The outbreak of violence in Nîmes on 13 June 1790. Protestant National Guards massacre Catholics in the streets; houses are pillaged and destroyed, with hundreds killed and the Catholic quarter devastated. The breakdown of municipal authority and the flight of Catholic notables. The event polarises the region and drives royalists toward organised conspiracy.
II. La première assemblée de Jalès. The first royalist gathering in the plain of Jalès (Ardèche), ostensibly a “federal” meeting of National Guards but in reality a counter-revolutionary assembly. Composition of the gathering: nobles, clergy, Catholic peasants. The role of the chevalier de Bussy and the comte de Saillans. The assembly disperses without action due to lack of arms and division among its leaders.
III. Préparatifs de combat. Royalist efforts to arm and organise in the aftermath of Nîmes. Recruitment among Catholic peasants; the search for foreign support. Correspondence with the princes in exile. The formation of a coordinated plan for a general uprising across the Midi.
IV. Un échec. The first attempt at a royalist rising falters. Government surveillance, the arrest of key agents, and the reluctance of the peasantry to commit to open rebellion. The dispersal of the first camp and the temporary retreat of the conspirators.
LIVRE SECOND: La Conspiration de Saillans
I. Coblentz en 1792. The émigré court at Coblentz and its plans for the invasion of France. The comte de Saillans presents his scheme for a rising in the Midi to the princes and receives their authorisation. Daudet draws on unpublished correspondence to reconstruct the émigré perspective on the southern campaign.
II. Entreprises avortées. A series of failed royalist initiatives in the provinces surrounding the Midi: attempts to raise the Vivarais, the Gévaudan, and the Comtat Venaissin. Each collapse due to insufficient coordination, government repression, or the hesitation of local royalists.
III. Un émigré en France. The secret return of the comte de Saillans to France in disguise. His itinerary, his contacts, and his efforts to reunite the dispersed royalist networks. Daudet traces his movements through the Lozère and Ardèche.
IV. L’action. The second assembly of the Camp de Jalès in July 1792. Saillans takes command and issues a manifesto calling for the restoration of the monarchy. Military operations: the capture of Banne, skirmishes with republican forces, the siege of Joyeuse. The internal divisions within the camp — tension between Saillans and local royalists, between nobles and priests, between moderates and intransigents.
V. L’envers d’une conspiration. The collapse of the second camp. Government forces converge on Jalès; Saillans is defeated and flees. Daudet examines the causes of failure: lack of popular support, poor discipline, the betrayal of confidences, and the effectiveness of republican intelligence. The aftermath: repression, arrests, and the execution of captured conspirators.
LIVRE TROISIÈME: “L’Infâme” Charrier
I. Les projets d’un royaliste. The figure of Charrier, a former priest turned counter-revolutionary organiser in the Lozère. His vision of a “sacred battalion” for the king; his correspondence with the princes and with the British. Daudet presents Charrier as a fanatic whose schemes outran his resources.
II. Émeutes et combats. Charrier’s rising in the winter of 1792-1793. The capture of Mende, the march on Marvejols, the attempt to coordinate with the Lyonnais federalists. Daudet narrates the campaign day by day, drawing on trial records and official reports.
III. La fin d’une émeute. The defeat of Charrier’s forces by the republican army under General Carteaux. Charrier’s flight, capture, and execution. Daudet’s assessment: the Charrier episode as the last serious royalist conspiracy in the Midi before the Terror, and its significance for understanding the regional dynamics of the counter-revolution.
PIÈCES JUSTIFICATIVES
Three sets of supporting documents:

I. Correspondence of the comte de Saillans, including his letters to the princes and to local royalist committees.
II. Official reports and interrogations relating to the Camp de Jalès.
III. Documents concerning Charrier: his correspondence, the decree of accusation against him, and excerpts from his trial.

sources/constant-de-la-force-gouvernemen.title: Benjamin Constant — De la force du gouvernement actuel; Des réactions politiques; Des effets de la terreur (1796–1797)
sources/constant-de-la-force-gouvernemen.content:
Benjamin Constant, De la force du gouvernement actuel de la France et de la nécessité de s’y rallier (1796); Des réactions politiques (1797); Des effets de la terreur (1797). Collected in: Paris: Flammarion (Champs), 2013. The extracted text runs to approximately 752 lines of clean prose from a high-quality epub, with a modern editorial preface. These three pamphlets — Constant’s first sustained political writings — were written during the Directory and constitute the founding texts of French liberal political thought. The source is the epub only; the accompanying PDF is a scan of the 1796 original with 18th-century long-s typography and unreadable OCR. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Constant (1767–1830) wrote these three texts between 1796 and 1797, during the Directory — the post-Thermidorian regime that governed France between the fall of Robespierre and Napoleon’s coup of 18 Brumaire. They are polemical pamphlets, not academic treatises: each responds to a specific political moment and a specific set of opponents. Together they constitute the first systematic liberal engagement with the problem of how to stabilize a republic that has survived a revolution and a terror without collapsing into either renewed Jacobinism or royalist reaction.
The modern editor’s preface (Flammarion, 2013) frames all three texts as Constant arguing on two fronts simultaneously: defending the social order produced by the Revolution against those who want to undo it, while also defending the constitutional principles of 1789 against those who would use emergency power to consolidate the post-Thermidorian state. This double position — neither reactionary nor revolutionary, neither royalist nor Jacobin — is the structural position of French liberalism as Constant defines it in these texts.
Full Contents Map
Modern Preface (Flammarion, 2013)
The editor situates the three pamphlets in the intellectual history of French liberalism. He notes the recent recovery of the major 19th-century French liberal thinkers — Constant, Guizot, Tocqueville — after a long period of neglect. The specific interest of the Directory-period texts is that they show Constant’s doctrine in statu nascendi: the liberal synthesis is not yet fully formed, and can be seen under construction in real political conditions. The central tension the editor identifies: the world produced by democratic revolution claims both the autonomy of private interests and civil society, and (through popular sovereignty) the transcendence of political power over those interests. Constant’s career-long project is to resolve this tension; these texts are its earliest version. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]

Text I — De la force du gouvernement actuel de la France et de la nécessité de s’y rallier (1796)
Opening argument. The pamphlet begins with a stark political frame: “The present moment is one of the most important of the Revolution. Order and liberty are on one side; anarchy and despotism on the other. Few instants remain to declare oneself; one must hasten to set aside memories and hatreds, or tomorrow these hatreds will be replaced by useless regrets, these memories by bitter remorse.” Moderate republicans who continue to attack the Directory on principled grounds are, Constant argues, making the perfect the enemy of the possible — and in doing so, are objectively serving the forces of either renewed terror or royalist restoration. The pamphlet is an argument for rallying. Constant addresses this specifically to men of genuine republican conviction — not to opportunists or turncoats — and his argument is precisely that it is the most honorable republicans who are causing the most damage by their scrupulous, persistent, and ultimately futile harassment of the government. “These men are, on the contrary, not only useless but essentially dangerous in revolutions and in nascent governments.”
Chapter I — Des hommes qui ont attaqué la Convention — Constant opens with a sociological portrait of the critics he is addressing: scrupulous, vain, honest men of talent who attack governments with a “fleuret” (fencing foil) when a “poignard” (dagger) would be the only proportionate instrument, and who mistake sharpness for efficacy. In established governments, such men perform a useful irritant function; in revolutionary transitions, they are dangerous — not because they threaten the government, but because they force it toward defensive harshness, confirm the most violent faction’s claims that moderation is weakness, and prevent the consolidation of constitutional norms. Their characteristic error is treating their own defeat as evidence that the goal itself has been lost, wanting to “bring things back” rather than follow where things have gone. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter II — De la force que les circonstances actuelles donnent au Gouvernement — An assessment of the Directory’s actual structural position. Constant argues it is stronger than its critics assume: the Revolution has created interests (in land, in contracts, in careers, in the new property order) that are now widespread and have no stake in a royalist restoration. These interests, not ideology, are the government’s real base. Any restoration would require dispossessing millions of people who acquired biens nationaux, who hold Republic-issued contracts, who have built careers under the new order. This socio-economic argument for stability is one of Constant’s most original moves: he grounds the republic not in abstract principle but in the material interests of a new class of proprietors. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter III — Des maux actuels de la France — An honest accounting of what is wrong: economic disorder, assignat collapse, administrative dysfunction, moral exhaustion after years of upheaval. Constant does not deny these; he argues they are real but not fatal, and that they are the consequences of past excesses, not of the current government’s incompetence. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter IV — Des ressentiments et des maux irréparables — On the psychology of revolutionary resentment. Constant addresses those who have suffered genuine injustice under the Terror and cannot forgive. He acknowledges their right to their feelings, but argues that resentments based on irreparable wrongs (the dead cannot be restored, the years of imprisonment cannot be returned) produce political demands that can only be satisfied by new injustices. The logic of revenge is self-defeating in a republic because it requires the same arbitrary power it claims to oppose. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter V — Du rétablissement de la terreur — The chapter that most directly names the danger Constant is trying to prevent. He argues that continued pressure on the Directory, by making constitutional government appear weak, creates the conditions for a return of emergency power — either Jacobin or military. The Terror did not arise from virtue perverted; it arose from the belief that virtuous ends justified arbitrary means. Any political discourse that normalizes that belief, however pure its intentions, prepares the ground for the next Terror. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter VI — Des objections tirées de l’expérience, contre la possibilité d’une République dans un grand État — Constant addresses the Montesquieu-derived objection that republics cannot function in large states (a standard argument used by those who believed France’s size made monarchy inevitable). He rejects it: the objection confuses ancient direct democracy with modern representative government. Representative republic is a different form, compatible with large territory and population. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter VII — Des avantages du Gouvernement Républicain — A positive argument for republican government: its advantages over monarchy in incentivizing civic participation, distributing power, providing legal equality, and allowing peaceful change of leadership. Constant is careful to distinguish republican government (rule by law, separation of powers, representative institutions) from democratic excess (unlimited popular sovereignty, the logic of the Terror). ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter VIII — Conclusion — Constant turns from addressing the government’s critics to addressing the government itself, and the writers who defend it. His warning to the Directory: the greatest danger to it is not its external enemies but its own “habitudes révolutionnaires” — the continued use of arbitrary expedients even in service of legitimate ends. “What did France the most harm, the harm most difficult to repair, was precisely the impatience to do good.” Robespierre killed, but he did not seduce. The opinion he crushed was not led astray. By contrast, when honest Thermidorian men used revolutionary means against revolutionary brigands — seizing émigrés’ property, deporting suspects, suspending legal process in the name of emergency — they consecrated illegality by making it serve good purposes, thereby destroying the only moral argument against illegality: that it always produces harm. The Directory must break with arbitrary habit and commit to constitutional law. Not because it is weaker than its opponents — constitutionalism is not weakness — but because “it is by praising men that one pushes them toward the good; it is by showing oneself convinced that they cannot refuse honest actions that one forces them to those actions.” The chapter ends with Constant’s most quoted aphorism: “Heaven has given to crime itself a kind of modesty, which dares not belie the virtues attributed to it and which serves it as a conscience.” ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]

Text II — Des réactions politiques (1797)
A longer and more systematic essay, organized around the concept of political reaction — the tendency in revolutionary periods for violence to cycle through successive parties, each claiming to restore order and each producing a new form of disorder.
Chapter I — Des différents genres de Réactions — Constant distinguishes types of reaction: reactions against men (revenge, purge, prosecution of individuals associated with a prior regime) and reactions against ideas (censorship, prosecution of opinion, attempts to suppress doctrines associated with the Terror). Both are dangerous but in different ways and require different responses. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter II — Des devoirs du Gouvernement dans les Réactions contre les hommes — On how governments should handle demands for prosecution and punishment of Terrorists after Thermidor. Constant is not an abolitionist: he accepts that real crimes require real punishment. But he insists on procedural regularity — law, courts, evidence, individual accountability — against the logic of collective guilt. To punish men by category (former Jacobins, former deputies who voted for the king’s death) rather than by individual criminal act is to reproduce the Terror’s own logic. Governments that yield to reactive popular demand for exemplary mass punishment validate the precedent that safety of the state justifies arbitrary punishment. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter III — Des devoirs du Gouvernement dans les Réactions contre les idées — On censorship and intellectual reaction. Constant’s position is firm: governments should not suppress ideas, even dangerous ones. Suppression of ideas is always counterproductive — it martyrs, it concentrates, it drives underground — and it requires precisely the arbitrary police power that a constitutional republic must not permit. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapters IV–VI — Des devoirs des écrivains; De la conduite des écrivains actuels — Extended criticism of the writers (journalists, pamphleteers) who are defending the Thermidorian reaction by arguing that arbitrary measures against former Terrorists are acceptable because the Terrorists themselves were arbitrary. Constant’s argument: writers who adopt this position destroy the principled foundation of constitutional liberalism. They cannot simultaneously argue that rule of law is the alternative to Jacobinism and that extra-legal measures against Jacobins are justified. The inconsistency corrupts both the argument and the practice. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter VII — Des ressources qui restent aux amis de la Liberté et des lumières — What remains available to genuine liberals after all compromises are rejected. Constant’s answer: the patient construction of institutions, education of opinion, and defense of individual rights case by case. Not a heroic answer, but an honest one: the alternative to constitutional patience is revolutionary violence, and revolutionary violence always destroys what it intends to build. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapter VIII — Des principes — The longest and most abstract chapter: a defense of principled over expedient politics. Constant’s core argument: systems based on pure expediency (doing whatever works in the moment) are inherently unstable because they have no fixed point of reference. Systems based on principles provide “des calculs politiques rapprochés des sciences exactes par leur précision, des bases inébranlables pour les institutions générales, une garantie positive pour les droits individuels.” He explicitly compares constitutional law to mathematics: both derive reliable conclusions from fixed premises, and both are worthless if the premises are abandoned whenever the conclusions are inconvenient. This is the earliest statement of what becomes the central Constant doctrine: arbitrary power is wrong in principle, not merely in excess. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Chapters IX–X — De l’arbitraire; Récapitulation — On arbitrary government as a category: not just cruelty or excess, but any exercise of power without fixed legal basis. Constant argues that arbitrary government corrupts even those who benefit from it, because it makes all relationships — between citizen and state, between individuals — dependent on favor rather than right. The Récapitulation draws together all threads: constitutional republic, rule of law, individual rights, and the rejection of emergency power as a permanent governing mode. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]

Text III — Des effets de la terreur (1797)
A shorter essay, added to the second edition of Des réactions politiques in response to a doctrine Constant identifies as newly spreading: that the Terror had beneficial effects — that its violence, by routing out traitors and saving the Republic at its moment of maximum external danger, justified its methods.
Constant’s refutation has two parts. First, the factual claim is false: the Terror did not save the Republic. The Republic was saved by the armies, by geography, and by the incompetence of the coalition — not by the guillotine. Second, and more important, even if the Terror had beneficial military effects, the claim that it was justified sets a precedent that destroys constitutional government: any emergency can be used to justify any measure, and once that principle is accepted, there is no logical stopping point.
The deeper argument: the Terror corrupted French political culture at the level of expectations and habits. It taught that safety could come from arbitrary violence; that enemies could be defined by category; that the state’s survival justified individual destruction. A republic that accepts this teaching as even partially valid has undermined the only foundation on which a durable republic can rest. ^[source: raw/constant-de-la-force-gouvernement-1796.txt]
Coverage Guide


Political theory of the Directory period — Constant’s three texts are the wiki’s primary source for liberal political thought in the post-Thermidorian moment. They are not retrospective analysis but live engagement: written in 1796–97, arguing about what should happen right now.


Defense of the Directory’s constitutional path — De la force is the clearest argument in the wiki for why moderate republicans should work with the Directory rather than attacking it. The socio-economic argument (new property interests created by the Revolution) is particularly useful.


Analysis of Thermidorian reaction — Des réactions politiques is the most sophisticated analysis of the Thermidor-to-Directory transition in the wiki: the political psychology of revenge, the duties of government and writers, the danger of using arbitrary means against arbitrary men.


Critique of the Terror’s defenders — Des effets de la terreur directly addresses post-Terror apologetics: was the Terror justified by its outcomes? Constant’s answer is one of the founding documents of anti-utilitarian liberalism.


Constant’s founding liberal argument — The Chapter VIII of Des réactions (“Des principes”) is the earliest systematic statement of Constant’s constitutional liberalism: rule of law as inviolable principle, not expedient tool; individual rights as fixed guarantees, not revocable concessions. This is the intellectual foundation of everything Constant wrote later.


The problem of arbitrary government — Chapter IX of Des réactions (“De l’arbitraire”) defines arbitrary government as a category — not excess of severity but absence of legal foundation — in a way that cuts across left/right political lines. Useful for any wiki page discussing the Directory, the Consulate, or the early Empire’s constitutional arrangements.


Quality
Flammarion Champs epub (2013), clean modern typeset text. The epub is fully readable with no OCR issues. The modern editorial preface and critical apparatus are clearly distinguished from Constant’s original texts. Footnotes by the modern editor appear in a separate notes file (EP033); Constant’s own notes appear inline. The PDF companion file (a scan of the 1796 original) is not used as the source: its 18th-century long-s typography produces garbled OCR throughout. The epub is the correct text to mine.

sources/fantin-histoire-philosophique-re.title: Fantin-Desodoards — Histoire Philosophique de la Révolution de France, Vol. VII (1801)
sources/fantin-histoire-philosophique-re.content:
Antoine Fantin-Desodoards, Histoire Philosophique de la Révolution de France, depuis la première Assemblée des Notables jusqu’à la paix de 1801, Tome VII. 4th edition. Angers: Mame père et fils / Paris: Belin, An IX (1801). The extracted raw text runs to approximately 16,830 lines and 645 KB, from a University of Michigan copy. Fantin-Desodoards (1738–1820) was a French citizen writing a multi-volume synthetic history of the whole Revolution as it was still unfolding; by the fourth edition he could extend the narrative to the Peace of Lunéville (1801). Volume VII covers Books XX, XXI, and XXII, spanning approximately 1796 to September 1797 (the Fructidor coup). ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Fantin-Desodoards writes as an informed, moderately conservative republican — critical of the Terror, respectful of the Directory’s institutions, suspicious of both Jacobin extremism and royalist reaction, and deeply admiring of the military genius displayed in the Italian campaign. His “philosophical” history means he pauses regularly to assess causes, to moralize on consequences, and to reflect on the relationship between constitutional forms and political reality. He cites classical precedents, draws comparisons between French institutions and ancient republics, and quotes from documents (dispatches, proclamations, letters) at length.
Volume VII covers one of the most consequential years of the Revolution: the Italian campaign of 1796–97, in which Bonaparte conquered Lombardy, forced Austria to seek terms, and reorganized northern Italy around a cluster of new republican states. Simultaneously it covers the Directory’s dangerous domestic politics — the Babeuf conspiracy of Floréal Year IV (spring 1796), the federalist and royalist threats, and the crisis of 18 Fructidor Year V (September 4, 1797), when the Directory used army force to purge the two councils of royalist-leaning deputies. By the end of the volume, Austria has accepted the preliminaries of Léoben, the Treaty of Campo Formio is approaching, and France has prevailed on the continent while Britain remains at war.
Full Contents Map
Book XX — The Italian Campaign, 1796 (First Phase)


Ch. I: Rhine armistice breaks; state of the armies — The armistice between Austria and France on the Rhine breaks down; strategic situation of Moreau’s army (Rhine-Moselle) and Jourdan’s (Sambre-Meuse) facing the Archduke. Fantin notes that the French could have accelerated the Italian campaign’s results by sending Rhine forces to reinforce Bonaparte, but political and geographic constraints prevented it. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. II: Pichegru resigns; Moreau takes command; Austrians abandon the Palatinate — Pichegru’s disgrace and departure (his secret royalist contacts were already suspected). Moreau assumes command of the Rhine-Moselle army and pursues the Austrian withdrawal east of the Rhine. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. III: Moreau crosses the Rhine — The Rhine crossing by Jourdan’s and Moreau’s armies in early summer 1796. Coordination problems between the two commands. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. IV: Capture of Fort Kehl — The storming of the Austrian bridgehead at Kehl on the Rhine. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. V: Battle of Rhinchel; capture of Fribourg and Frankfurt — Desaix’s division advances; Frankfurt is occupied. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. VI: The French advance to the Rhaetian Alps — The deepest French penetration into southern Germany in this campaign. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. VII: Field Marshal Wurmser enters Italy; revolt of Lugo — The Austrian relief of Mantua under Wurmser begins; the rebellion at Lugo in the Romagna against French requisitions is suppressed. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. VIII–IX: Battle of Castiglione — The first great defensive-offensive battle of the Italian campaign: Bonaparte abandons the siege of Mantua to mass against Wurmser’s relieving columns, defeats them at Castiglione (August 5, 1796), and re-establishes the siege. Fantin gives the battle in considerable tactical detail, including the strategic situation before and the aftermath — Austrian flags sent to the Directory, the relief of Mantua reversed. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XI: Organization of the Trentino principality — Bonaparte’s administrative reorganization of Trento after its occupation. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XII: Austrians in the Frioul; Battle of Bassano — A second Austrian attempt to relieve Mantua, this time through the Brenta valley; defeated at Bassano (September 8, 1796). ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XIII: Wurmser retreats into Mantua — Wurmser’s battered army takes refuge inside Mantua, which the French then besiege again. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XIV: Italian reactions to Austrian defeats — The political impact of French victories on the Italian populations: Milan, Bologna, Ferrara oscillating between hope and fear; the occupying French requiring requisitions that alienate support the ideology of liberation had generated. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XV: The Pope breaks the armistice — Pope Pius VI, emboldened by a temporary Austrian resurgence, breaks the armistice Bonaparte had imposed after the Faenza campaign. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVI: Modena and Reggio raise the flag of liberty — Republican movements in the Este duchies, anticipating the later Cispadane Republic. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVII: The British take Porto-Ferraio in Elba — The British seizure of the principal port of Elba (which Fantin notes Bonaparte had intended as a forward naval base to threaten British commerce through Livorno). ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVIII–XX: Corsica — Pasquale Paoli’s power in Corsica; George III assumes the title “King of Corsica” under the Anglo-Corsican union; insurrections against the British; Corsica’s return to the French Republic. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Book XXI — Consolidation and Internal Crisis, 1796–1797


Ch. I (opening): Interior of France, Year IV — A panoramic survey of France’s internal condition in the months before Fructidor: economic hardship, assignat inflation, the political atmosphere in Paris, the Directory’s uncertain authority, the competing factions within and outside the constitutional framework. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. II: France-Spain and France-Genoa alliances — The Treaty of San Ildefonso (August 1796) bringing Spain into the war against Britain; the treaty with the Genoese republic, which ties Genoa’s commercial and political fate to France. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. III: Vacillations in public opinion — Fantin’s analysis of why France, feared by all neighboring states, could not yet secure a peace that would allow it to consolidate. He identifies the Directory’s internal divisions and the competing factional pressures as the primary obstacle. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. IV: Parties dividing France since the constitutional regime — A systematic analysis of the political factions: royalists, Jacobins, moderate republicans, and the new electoral class emerging from the Year III constitution. Fantin argues that the factions’ irreconcilability made stable government structurally impossible without periodic coercive interventions. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. V: Reflections on French constitutional regime vs. ancient republics — A philosophical digression: Fantin compares the Directory constitution to the republics of Greece and Rome, arguing that the French system lacked the civic traditions and moral education that made ancient republicanism functional. A representative passage of his “philosophical” method. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. VI–XI: The Babeuf Conspiracy (Conjuration de Floréal) — The most detailed section in Volume VII devoted to domestic politics. Fantin covers the conspiracy in six chapters of escalating specificity.
Ch. VI — Context and the conspiracy’s origins. Fantin opens with a reflection on opinion publique as a political force: “one must have studied it, in the midst of revolutionary convulsions, in the sections of Paris, or at the bar of the National Convention — always unjust in its impatience, but almost always in good faith in its aims — the abusive power of institutions it reprobated, trampling laws it had demanded; arbitrary and mysterious power, it always has a laudable goal and almost always overshoots it.” The conspiracy emerged from the Jacobin rump that had survived Thermidor and Vendémiaire: men who found all regular government intolerable once they had grown accustomed to power through anarchy, “like those whirlwinds of wind that, in a violent fire, constantly rekindle the devouring flames that generous hands strive to extinguish.” Babeuf himself, Fantin notes, was “only the obscure and secondary agent of a faction of whose secrets he perhaps himself knew only a part.” ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]
Ch. VII — Organization of the conspiracy. The operational structure was elaborate: a directoire secret de salut public directing the movement, with agents in each of Paris’s twelve arrondissements. These agents reported on food stores, arms depots, workshops, workers’ numbers and opinions; compiled lists of well-off patriots who could house provincial militants; organized subscription to fund the insurrection; provided lists of police spies to be neutralized or enlisted; and organized teams of groupeurs — men who circulated daily in the Tuileries gardens and other gathering-places reading aloud the most recent numbers of patriot journals to crowds. The design was for everything to be activated simultaneously on 22 Floréal Year IV. Drouet — the postmaster famous for recognizing Louis XVI at Varennes — was chosen as the conspiracy’s public face, “very suitable, by his enthusiasm and his ignorance, to the role of Seïde they had destined for him.” ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]
Ch. VIII — Babeuf’s letter to Bodson. Fantin quotes at length from a letter found at Babeuf’s address and included in the minister of police’s published collection. In it Babeuf defends the Robespierre Terror as correct in principle: “I think that government was the one best suited to make a revolution succeed… I do not think, as you do, that they committed great crimes and killed good republicans.” He argues that Robespierre could justifiably have said: “Let us suppress these tiresome nuisances and their good intentions — my opinion is that he did well. The salvation of twenty-five million men must not be weighed against consideration for a few equivocal individuals. A regenerator must see on a grand scale; his duty is to mow down everything that hinders him, everything that obstructs his passage, everything that can retard his arrival at the goal — scoundrels, idiots, the presumptuous alike, it is all the same; too bad for them, why were they in the way?” Babeuf adds that invoking Robespierre is tactically essential: “to revive Robespierre is to revive all the energetic patriots of the republic, and with them the people, who long listened to and followed only them.” Fantin quotes this letter at such length precisely because it is the most explicit surviving statement of the conspiracy’s ideology. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]
Ch. IX — Arrest of the conspirators. The conspiracy’s plan was to assassinate “a part of the deputies, the entire Directory, the ministers, and all members of the constituted authorities of Paris,” then proclaim a new regime. An informer in the conspiracy’s inner circle revealed the plan to the Directory, which arrested the leading figures before the date of action. Fantin is careful to note the distinction between those who were genuinely committed communists and those who were simply disaffected Jacobins riding the conspiracy for factional reasons — the distinction becomes important at the trial.
Ch. XI — Trial at Vendôme. The conspirators were sent before a specially constituted high court at Vendôme rather than the ordinary courts, to prevent the political circus that a Paris jury might have produced. Babeuf and Darthé were condemned to death; others were deported. Fantin’s treatment is hostile to the conspiracy’s program but scrupulous about procedure — he regards the Vendôme court as a legitimate extraordinary jurisdiction rather than a new form of Terror, and is at pains to distinguish the Directory’s management of the trial from the Jacobin show-trials of 1793. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XII: Second Fructidor conspiracy — A further royalist-Jacobin agitation following the Babeuf trial; suppressed before reaching the scale of Floréal. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XIII–XIV: French enter Bavaria; Jourdan retreats; Battle of Neresheim/Battle of Teming — The Archduke Charles maneuvers against Jourdan on the Danube; Jourdan is badly beaten and forced to retreat hastily to the Rhine, threatening Moreau’s flanks. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XV: Moreau’s retreat; Battle of Biberach — Fantin presents Moreau’s strategic retreat from deep in southern Germany as one of the campaign’s great military achievements: an orderly withdrawal over immense distances under constant pressure, described admiringly as rivaling the classic retreats of military history. Biberach is a rearguard victory during the withdrawal. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVI: The Irish descent (1796) — The French expedition to Ireland under Hoche: the fleet’s departure from Brest, the storm that scattered the fleet at Bantry Bay and prevented a landing. Fantin covers the strategic rationale (opening a second front against Britain using Irish republican sentiment) and the operational failure caused by weather and poor fleet cohesion. Cross-reference with mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol1 for the British naval perspective on this operation. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVII–XVIII: Siege of Kehl; fall of Kehl — The Austrians besiege and eventually retake the bridgehead of Kehl on the Rhine that the French had captured in 1796. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XIX–XX: Alvinzi commands in Italy; Battle of Arcola — Field Marshal Alvinzi makes his second attempt to relieve Mantua through the Brenta and Adige valleys. At Arcola (November 15–17, 1796), the French face a village fortified by nature at the center of marshes and deep canals lined with artillery. Fantin traces the three-day battle in close tactical detail. On day one: Augereau seizes a flag and charges the bridge at Arcola himself — forced back; Bonaparte commands from the front of Augereau’s division and leads grenadiers at the same bridge at thirty paces when murderous Austrian fire breaks the column, and Bonaparte himself is knocked into a marsh from which his staff struggles to retrieve him under fire. A flanking column under General Guieux crosses the Adige two miles downstream, enters Arcola from the rear at midnight, and withdraws with hundreds of prisoners and four guns. Day two: equally fierce, equally indecisive. Day three: Massena presses from the left, Augereau from the front, a diversion from Porto-Legnago’s garrison hits the Austrian rear — Alvinzi abandons the field and retreats on Vicenza. Fantin compares the four-day engagement, by the marshal Trivulzio’s phrase, to Marignano as “a battle of giants.” ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XXI: Alvinzi retreats; Italian republics formed — Alvinzi withdraws; Mantua remains besieged. The political map of northern Italy begins to reshape around French-sponsored republics. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XXII: Alvinzi returns; Battle of Rivoli — The fourth Austrian attempt, again under Alvinzi: the battle of Rivoli (January 14, 1797), Napoleon’s most complete Italian victory. The Austrian force is destroyed; the way to Vienna is open. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Book XXII — The Peace Settlement, 1797; 18 Fructidor


Ch. I: Pope resumes war; French in the Romagna — With Austria collapsing, Pope Pius VI’s gamble on an Austrian resurgence fails; French forces under Victor advance into the Romagna. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. II: Mantua surrenders — The capitulation of Mantua (February 2, 1797) after a six-month siege: Field Marshal Wurmser surrenders with his garrison. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. III: The Duchy of Urbino; negotiations with the Pope — The French occupy Urbino and the Papal legations; negotiations begin at the Hotel d’Espagne. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. IV: Peace with the Pope; Archduke Charles takes Italian command — The Treaty of Tolentino (February 19, 1797) strips the Pope of the Legations, Avignon, and cash and art; the Archduke Charles — the most capable Austrian commander, who had defeated Jourdan — is transferred to the Italian theatre. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. V–IX: The drive toward Vienna — Bonaparte crosses the Tagliamento, defeats the Austrians at Gradisca, takes Trieste, drives through the Norican Alps to Klagenfurt in the Austrian heartland. Bonaparte’s proclamation from Klagenfurt and his famous letter to the Archduke (offering peace while advancing) are quoted. The French reach Leoben, less than 100 miles from Vienna, and the Austrian court sues for terms. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. X: Bonaparte’s position amid the Alps — Fantin assesses the strategic risk Bonaparte accepted by advancing so deep while his communications were precarious and the Italian rear was potentially unstable. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XI: Armistice between Bonaparte and Archduke — The cease-fire that preceded Léoben. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XII–XIII: Sambre-Meuse and Rhine-Moselle cross the Rhine — Simultaneous Rhine crossing operations in support of Bonaparte’s advance: Hoche’s victory at Neuwied, the Rhine-Moselle army recaptures Fort Kehl. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XIV: Preliminaries of Léoben — The preliminary peace treaty signed April 18, 1797, between France and Austria, ending the Italian campaign’s military phase. Fantin gives the terms and the background of the secret articles (which ceded Venice to Austria in exchange for the Belgian Netherlands — a transaction not publicly disclosed). ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XV: Reflections on war — A philosophical chapter on the miseries and waste of war, unusually direct given that Fantin has been narrating a string of French victories. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Ch. XVI–XXVII: 18 Fructidor and the Genoese crisis — The final section covers the Fructidor coup in detail alongside simultaneous events in Genoa. The Genoese crisis: the Genoese republic’s ambivalent posture toward France, French pressure, popular insurrection in Genoa against the oligarchy, the installation of a new government friendly to France. The Fructidor 18 (September 4, 1797) coup: the Directory, facing a royalist-leaning majority in the two councils after the elections of Year V, uses General Augereau (sent by Bonaparte from Italy with troops) to arrest or deport two Directors and 53 deputies. The journals are shut; the royalist press is suppressed. Fantin gives the full sequence: the Directory’s intelligence about royalist contacts with the Bourbon pretender (the Duverne de Presles revelations), the Directory’s session of 10 Fructidor, the coup itself, the permanent session of the surviving councils, the deportation law, the adresses to the French people. He is critical but not simplistic — he accepts that a genuine royalist threat existed while questioning whether the Directory’s methods were constitutional. ^[source: raw/fantin-histoire-philosophique-revolution-1801.txt]


Coverage Guide


Bonaparte’s Italian campaign, 1796–97 — This is the wiki’s most detailed narrative source for the operational campaigns: Castiglione, Bassano, Arcola, Rivoli, the drive to Leoben. Fantin gives tactical detail, strategic context, and political consequences for each battle. For the naval and strategic context from the British side, cross-reference mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol1.


The Babeuf conspiracy — Chapters VI–XI of Book XXI give the fullest account of the Conspiracy of Equals in the wiki: ideology, organization, Babeuf’s letter, the Vendôme trial.


Moreau’s retreat — Book XXI Chapter XV. One of the great operational feats of the campaign, treated admiringly by Fantin as a model of controlled withdrawal under pressure.


The Irish expedition of 1796 — Book XXI Chapter XVI, French side. Cross-reference mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol1 Chapter XI for the British/naval view of the same operation.


Fructidor 18 (1797) — Book XXII, final chapters. A detailed account of the Directory’s constitutional coup against the royalist-leaning councils: the intelligence, the preparation, the operation, and the deportation law.


Italian political reorganization — The formation of French-sponsored Italian republics (Cispadane, anticipations of Cisalpine) is traced through Books XX–XXII as a running theme alongside the military narrative.


The Peace of Tolentino — Book XXII Chapter IV. The treaty that stripped the Pope of the Legations and effectively ended Papal temporal power in central Italy for this period.


The Preliminaries of Léoben — Book XXII Chapter XIV. The end of the first Austrian war; the secret articles pointing toward the Treaty of Campo Formio are identified.


Quality
University of Michigan copy, OCR from an Angers/Paris 1801 print. The text is 18th-century French administrative and historical prose: long, complex sentences, frequent classical allusions, chapter headings that summarize contents in the manner of the period. Running page headers (“RÉVOLUTION / DE FRANCE” alternating) are picked up by the OCR. Chapter numbers are sometimes misread by the OCR (Roman numerals — “CHAPITRE XI” vs “CHAPITRE XII” vs “CHAPITRE XII I”). Quotations from official documents (proclamations, letters, Directory resolutions) are readable. Battle sequences with place names are generally accurate though accent marks are inconsistent. Medium difficulty for French readers; high difficulty for readers unfamiliar with the period’s geographic and institutional vocabulary.

sources/filles-publiques-fleischmann-190.title: Hector Fleischmann — Les Filles Publiques sous la Terreur (pub. 1908)
sources/filles-publiques-fleischmann-190.content:
Hector Fleischmann, Les Filles Publiques sous la Terreur: d’après les rapports de la police secrète, des documents nouveaux et des pièces inédites tirées des Archives nationales. Paris: Albert Méricant, Éditeur, 1908. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 10,499 lines and 419 KB, from a Princeton University Library copy (Gustave Bord Collection).
Hector Fleischmann (1882–1914) was a French historian and journalist who specialized in the social and sexual history of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic periods. He published extensively on the “darker side” of the Revolution — women, prostitution, pornography, the mechanisms of the Terror, the psychology of its principal actors. His works under the series title “Les Dessous de la Terreur” (“The Underbelly of the Terror”) were deliberately provocative, aiming to expose the aspects of revolutionary society that conventional historiography had ignored or suppressed. Other works in the series include Les Femmes et la Terreur, Anecdotes secrètes de la Terreur, and planned but unfinished studies including an Apologie de Maximilien de Robespierre and a Réhabilitation de Fouquier-Tinville.
This work examines the world of prostitution and public sexuality in Paris during the Terror (1793–1794). Fleischmann draws extensively on police surveillance reports, archival records from the Archives nationales, contemporary pamphlets and newspapers, and other primary sources to reconstruct the lives of prostitutes and courtesans (“filles publiques”) under the revolutionary regime. The author’s stated methodology — elaborated in the Avant-Propos — distinguishes between two possible approaches: drawing general conclusions from particular events (following the method of Taine and Michelet) or presenting archival documents as particular facts, as scenes from daily life. He deliberately chose the latter, refusing to generalize from the exceptional behavior of prostitutes to conclusions about French society as a whole. The work is dedicated to Xavier Roux. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]
Contents at a Glance
The work is organized into three Livres and one Appendice, each examining a different dimension of prostitution during the Terror. The Avant-Propos explains the author’s rationale: while much had been written about the political role of women in the Revolution (Mme Roland, Olympe de Gouges, Charlotte Corday), virtually nothing had been written about the everyday social reality of the thousands of women who lived by prostitution. Fleischmann argues that these women’s lives are as worthy of study as those of the revolutionary heroines, and that their fate — many were guillotined for trivial offenses — reveals something important about the revolutionary society that executed them. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]
Full Contents Map
Avant-Propos (Preface)
Fleischmann explains the rationale for the work: the gap in revolutionary historiography concerning prostitution; the author’s choice of the factual/documentary method over the generalizing/analytical method; the argument that the lives of prostitutes and courtesans are as worthy of study as those of the revolutionary heroines. He draws on an epigraph from Michelet (“la multiplication des filles, l’énervation de l’homme était un vrai fléau”) and engages with arguments from Taine, the Goncourt brothers, Mercier de Compiègne, and Bonaparte’s youthful writings on gallantry. The preface is notable for its claim that “C’est une sœur de Mme Roland, que la prostituée menée à l’échafaud pour avoir crié, étant ivre: Vive le Roi!” — a deliberately provocative framing that equates the fates of the virtuous revolutionary heroine and the degraded public woman. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]
Livre Premier — La Vénus des Carrefours
An overview of the world of street prostitution and public women in Paris during the Terror.


I. Les citoyennes “férosses”. — The opening chapter establishes the paradoxical situation: the women who had been passionate patriots in 1789 reverted to their true role during the Terror — “amoureuses de l’amour, et uniquement.” The chapter covers the “fierce” (férosses) prostitutes of the streets; the peculiar story of the gendarme of the Revolutionary Tribunal; the Longchamp promenades of 1793; the “great conspiracy of women at the Salpêtrière”; the campaigns for repopulation and free union; and the repression of prostitution under the Old Regime as context for the revolutionary period. Draws on Restif de la Bretonne’s Le Pornographe and other reform proposals.


II. Les ci-devant poissardes. — The former fishwives and market women of Paris; their transformation under the Revolution; their political roles; the persistence of their traditional behaviors and language.


III. Inconvénients de l’égalité. — The comic and tragic consequences of revolutionary egalitarianism applied to sexual relations; the role of pipe-smoking in outrages against the “beau sexe”; a new method of reprimanding guilty actors; “procureuses, satyres et fruits verts.”


IV. Le citoyen “Alphonse.” — Male pimps and procurers under the Terror; the police category of “individus qui paraissent déterminés”; a nocturnal adventure at the Hôtel de Bourgogne; thieves operating around the guillotine; proposals for radical measures against prostitution.


V. Court chapitre consacré aux agréments nocturnes. — A brief chapter on the nocturnal pleasures and dangers of Revolutionary Paris. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]


Livre II — Le Palais-Égalité ou le Jardin des Plaisirs
An extended study of the Palais-Royal (renamed Palais-Égalité during the Revolution) as the principal center of organized prostitution, gambling, and erotic entertainment in revolutionary Paris.


I. Du grand cardinal au prince régicide: Palais, cirque, boutique, club. — The history of the Palais-Royal from Cardinal Richelieu’s original construction through its ownership by the duc d’Orléans (Philippe-Égalité); its transformation into a commercial and entertainment center; the “manifestation du roquet travesti” (a satirical incident involving a dressed-up dog); the atmosphere on July 14, 1790; the warning sign “Attention! il y a des filles et des filous ou avis à nos frères des départements!”


II. Le jardin-lupanar: Nymphes, odalisques et dames du monde; quatre femmes pour cinq livres! — The Palais-Royal gardens as a vast open-air brothel; the range of women — from elegant courtesans (“nymphes,” “odalisques”) to common prostitutes; the famous price of “four women for five livres”; from Sodom to Cythera; the Allée des Soupirs (Alley of Sighs); police raids; the political dimension of prostitution.


III. Les modes féminines au Palais-Égalité. — Women’s fashion and its relationship to prostitution; the prospectus of the citizen Lisfrand, a fashion merchant; the “redingotte à la Thessalie” as practical attire for hurried gentlemen; earrings “à la guillotine”; the elegances of the Terror.


IV. Le jeu sous la Monarchie: Les trente-deux maisons de jeu du Palais-Égalité. — Gambling at the Palais-Royal; the history of gambling under the monarchy; the queen’s gaming table; the ambassador as croupier; the Knights of Saint-Louis; the thirty-two gambling houses of the Palais-Égalité; the police agent Monti, enemy of gambling; “Avez-vous du pouvoir exécutif de pique?” — the revolutionary card game.


V. La littérature érotique au Palais-Égalité. — Erotic and pornographic literature available at the Palais-Royal; the role of the police as the “last refuge of public modesty”; the poet Florian; the libelles and pamphlets against Marie-Antoinette; the Revolutionary Tribunal’s treatment of erotic publishers.


VI. La “Science de la gueule” suivant Montaigne: Les traiteurs à la mode. — The restaurants and eating-houses of the Palais-Égalité; Méot, Beauvilliers, Very, Venua; the last dinner of a regicide; a terrorist’s menu; the “science of the gullet” as Montaigne defined it. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]


Livre III — De la Luxure à la Guillotine
The fatal intersection of sexual license with the machinery of the Terror — how prostitutes and courtesans were caught up in the revolutionary judicial system.


I. Une courtisane de la Révolution; le 50 et ses habitués; la suave Émilie; un mari qui aime les actrices; une épouse qui aime les chanteurs; la conspiration de l’étranger; Fouquier-Tinville et les dames de Sainte-Amaranthe; la fournée du 29 prairial; au cimetière Sainte-Marguerite. — The central narrative of the book: the story of Madame de Sainte-Amaranthe and her daughter Émilie, a celebrated courtesan of the Revolution. Fleischmann traces her career from her origins (Jeanne-Françoise-Louise de Saint-Simon d’Arpajon, daughter of a governor of Besançon) through her marriage, her salon, her establishment in the fashionable demimonde, her involvement in the “foreign conspiracy” investigations of 1794, her arrest with her daughter, the trial before the Revolutionary Tribunal presided by Fouquier-Tinville, and her execution with her daughter in the “batch” (fournée) of 29 Prairial Year II (June 17, 1794). The chapter connects the world of prostitution with the world of counter-revolutionary conspiracy as constructed by the revolutionary tribunals.


II. Un professeur de débauche: M. le marquis de Sade; le roman de la femme dépecée vivante; l’aventure de la maison close de Marseille; satyrographomanie, érotomanie ou folie?; les prisons du marquis de Sade; sous la Terreur; de Justine à Juliette; la morale de l’auteur d’Aline et Valcour; la fin du divin marquis. — An extended study of the Marquis de Sade (1740–1814) during the revolutionary period. Fleischmann covers Sade’s presence in revolutionary Paris, his involvement in the political clubs (Section des Piques), his imprisonment under the Terror, his narrow escape from the guillotine, and the relationship between his literary works (Justine, Juliette, Aline et Valcour) and his own life. The chapter treats Sade as a case study in the intersection of sexual deviance, literary production, and political violence. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]


Appendice — Les Scandales au Palais de Justice sous la Terreur
A supplementary chapter on the sexual scandals that occurred within the Palais de Justice itself during the Terror, involving judicial officials, clerks, prisoners, and prostitutes who operated within the precincts of the revolutionary courts. This appendix draws on police reports and archival documents from the Archives nationales. ^[source: raw/filles-publiques-terreur-1908.txt]
Coverage Guide


The geography of prostitution in revolutionary Paris — The work provides a detailed street-level map of where and how prostitution operated in Paris during the Terror: the Palais-Royal gardens, the streets around the Tuileries, the arcades, the public promenades. Fleischmann’s reconstruction draws heavily on police surveillance reports.


The Palais-Royal as a microcosm of revolutionary society — Livre II is the most extensive portion of the work and treats the Palais-Royal not merely as a location for vice but as a complete social system: gambling, dining, fashion, literature, and politics all intersected there. The chapters on gambling (IV) and erotic literature (V) are useful for understanding the broader culture of the Palais-Égalité.


Prostitution and the revolutionary state — Throughout the work, Fleischmann documents the ambiguous relationship between the revolutionary government and prostitution: the police both regulated and tolerated it; the revolutionary tribunals occasionally prosecuted prostitutes for political offenses while leaving the trade broadly unregulated; the state’s concern with “public morality” coexisted with the practical toleration of vice as an economic necessity.


The case of Madame de Sainte-Amaranthe — The most sustained narrative in the book, this case study shows how a woman of the demimonde could be drawn into the machinery of the Terror — accused of involvement in a foreign conspiracy, tried by Fouquier-Tinville, and executed alongside her daughter. The case is valuable for understanding how the Revolutionary Tribunal constructed conspiracy narratives.


The Marquis de Sade under the Revolution — Fleischmann’s treatment of Sade during the revolutionary period is one of the earliest sustained analyses of this subject. It covers Sade’s political activities, his imprisonment, and the relationship between his life and his literary production during the 1790s.


Methodological approach — The Avant-Propos is a significant statement of historiographical method: Fleischmann’s explicit rejection of the generalizing approach (Taine, Michelet) in favor of a documentary, particularist approach has implications beyond the subject matter. He argues that the sexual behavior of a minority cannot be generalized into conclusions about an entire society.


Quality
The OCR quality is moderate. The original printed text includes frequent page headers, decorative separators, and footnotes that the OCR has handled inconsistently. The text exhibits some OCR noise — horizontal dashes, irregular spacing, and occasional misread characters. The page numbers are preserved in the margins. The text is in French throughout, with extensive footnoted references to archival sources (Archives nationales, series F7 and others), contemporary printed works, and secondary scholarship. Total length approximately 10,499 lines / 419 KB.
Fleischmann’s work belongs to the “history from below” tradition of French historiography, though with a deliberate sensationalist edge. The book is both a documentary study and a work of provocation — Fleischmann’s framing of prostitutes as “sisters of Madame Roland” and his planned “Apologie de Maximilien de Robespierre” and “Réhabilitation de Fouquier-Tinville” signal his intention to challenge conventional judgments. The work should be read as a social history with a strong polemical orientation, drawing on genuine archival research but shaped by the author’s provocative agenda.
