sources/herbin-statistique-france-1803.title: Herbin de Halle et al. — Statistique Générale et Particulière de la France, Vol. VII (1803)
sources/herbin-statistique-france-1803.content:
P. E. Herbin de Halle et al., Statistique Générale et Particulière de la France et de ses Colonies, Tome VII. Paris: F. Buisson, An XII (1803). The extracted raw text runs to approximately 26,220 lines and 1.14 MB of OCR from a Princeton University Library copy. This is Volume VII of a collaborative statistical survey of France, with atlas, produced by a team of specialists. Volume VII covers exclusively the French colonial empire and an agricultural appendix, published in the year after the Treaty of Amiens (1802) momentarily restored French possessions abroad and made a comprehensive colonial account both possible and politically timely. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Contents at a Glance
The Statistique Générale is a planned, systematic survey rather than a narrative. Volume VII brings together contributions from several named authors — Peuchet handled commerce and colonies; Sonnini handled climate, geography, and natural history; Delalauze handled agriculture; Gorsse handled mineral productions; and Herbin himself handled topography, population, rivers, canals, administrative divisions, routes, commerce, and navigation. The atlas that accompanied the full work contained nineteen tables and nine colored maps of France, its internal navigation, and its colonies across the four parts of the world, engraved by Tardieu after Poirson.
The volume treats the French colonial empire as it stood at the Consulate — at what Herbin presents as a moment of recovery. The preface traces the losses of 1713 (Treaty of Utrecht), 1763, and the Revolutionary wars, then notes how the Treaty of Amiens of 1802 restored to France its possessions, restoring her to a position from which she might again rival the other European powers in colonial commerce. The volume then proceeds colony by colony, section by section, with statistical tables of products, trade, population, and administration embedded throughout.
The structure is three major colonial sections followed by an appendix on French agricultural vegetable productions — the appendix placed here because the volume of material forced it out of its original position in Volume I.
Full Contents Map
Preliminary: Treaty Context and Colonial Government


Historical overview of French colonial losses and recoveries — From the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) through the Peace of 1763, through the partial recovery at the 1783 treaty, through the Amiens settlement of 1802: each treaty’s specific effect on the colonial empire is traced. The 1783 treaty restored Senegal, Gorée, Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, and French Indian possessions; Amiens restored everything taken during the Revolutionary wars. This framing positions the statistical survey as a document of imperial restoration rather than of contraction. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Colonial government under the Consulate — The administrative apparatus established by the consular arrêté of 6 Prairial an X (1802), described through the Martinique, Sainte-Lucie, and Tabago model: three magistrates govern each colony — a captain-general (military command, defense, passports, fortification), a colonial prefect (civil administration, agriculture, commerce), and a grand judge (justice). The captain-general holds immediate command of land and sea forces, the national guard, and the gendarmerie; he has exclusive charge of the colony’s interior and exterior defense; he provides provisionally for all military appointments and posts through to the rank of battalion or squadron commander, proposing higher replacements to the minister; he determines and arrests each year, with the colonial prefect, the works to be done for fortifications and roads. The authorities of colonial prefect and grand judge over civil, commercial, and judicial matters are similarly itemized. All communicate with each other through defined protocols and report to the minister of the navy and colonies in Paris. This governmental model is presented before the colony-by-colony survey because it was applied — with local variations — across the entire French American colonial empire as of 1802. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Section I — French Colonies and Possessions in America


Commercial regime of French American colonies — The arrêté of 3 Thermidor an X regulating colonial trade: which goods can be brought in and out, on what terms. Tables give the customs duty tariffs on colonial French products and on foreign colonial products entering France; lists of the colonial produce subject to these duties. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Saint-Domingue — The most extensive single entry in the volume, treating the island that was France’s most valuable colonial possession before the Revolution. The geographic description covers general situation, size, climate, and natural resources. The departmental organization of the French (western) part is detailed through five departments: Département du Sud (covering the southern peninsula, including Jacmel and Les Cayes, sugar and coffee country); Département de l’Ouest (Port-au-Prince and the Cul-de-Sac plain, the richest sugar district of the world); Département du Nord (Le Cap, the colony’s commercial capital and finest harbor, indigo and sugar); Département de Samaná (the northeastern peninsula and bay, important for its harbor); Département de l’Inganne (the interior districts). Each department receives a topographic description, principal towns, port facilities, and note of its principal agricultural products. A table gives the state of exports from the French part in 1788 — the last full pre-revolutionary year — providing the baseline against which the post-revolutionary collapse can be measured: sugar, coffee, cotton, indigo, cacao, and hides in the quantities that had made Saint-Domingue the single most productive colonial territory in the Atlantic world. The Spanish part of the island is then described, covering its interior commerce (cattle, tobacco, hides, mahogany) and noting the fundamentally different character of the Spanish colony (ranching and subsistence agriculture rather than plantation monoculture). The article’s presence in a volume dedicated to the Consulate reflects the ongoing French military effort to reassert sovereignty under Leclerc — an effort that would fail completely within two years of publication. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


La Martinique — Brief statistical description of Martinique: situation, extent, principal towns, agricultural products, commercial value. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


La Guadeloupe — Extended treatment with full geographic description: the island’s two parts (Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre), the channel separating them, the dependent islands. Agricultural products and commerce covered. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Sainte-Lucie — Statistical description of Sainte-Lucie, returned to France by the Treaty of Amiens. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Tabago (Tobago) — Statistical description, similarly restored by Amiens. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Marie-Galante — Brief description of this dependency of Guadeloupe. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


La Désirade — Brief description. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Les Saintes — Brief description of this island group. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Saint-Martin — Brief description of the French part of this shared island. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Saint-Pierre et Miquelon — Description of these fishing islands off Newfoundland, restored in 1783, with their fisheries rights and their dependence on the Newfoundland and northern waters fishing economy. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Cayenne et Guiane Française — Extended geographic description of French Guiana: coastline, rivers, interior territory, indigenous peoples, agricultural potential, European settlements. Commerce and administration covered. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Louisiane (Louisiana) — Description of Louisiana as a French possession, with its geography, the Mississippi basin, the city of New Orleans, its population, and its commerce. This entry was written before the Louisiana Purchase (the sale to the United States occurred in April 1803, the same year as publication), so it reflects the state of French Louisiana in the immediate post-Amiens moment. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Section II — French Possessions in Africa


Slave trade merchandise table (1789) — A table listing the types and values of merchandise used in the slave trade at the African coast in 1789 — the last year before the Revolution disrupted the trade — and a note on the price of a captive of choice in that year. The merchandise listed includes textiles (Indian cottons and European woolens in specified lengths and colors, each type valued for different coastal markets), alcohol (brandy and rum in specific quantities), firearms and powder, iron bars, copper basins, tobacco, and assorted trade goods. The price of a prime captive is given in a unit of account combining the merchandise types. This table is the volume’s most direct statistical statement of the French slave trade before the Revolutionary abolition of 1794 (which the Consulate had effectively reversed for the colonies, though this is not stated explicitly in the volume). ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


French establishments on the western coast of Africa — Survey of each post in geographic order from north to south:

Arguin — The island off the Mauritanian coast, France’s oldest African trading post, described for its history and its current subordinate status to Senegal. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Sénégal — The principal West African establishment, centered on the island of Saint-Louis at the mouth of the Senegal River. Herbin describes the island’s fort, the mixed population of French officers and merchants, African and métis habitants and signares, and the commerce: gum arabic from the interior (the dominant commodity, used in French textile printing), slaves and captives (still the foundation of the trade’s profitability), gold dust, ivory, and hides. The river posts up-river — Podor (trade and communication with the middle Senegal valley) and Galam (the furthest French penetration, at the junction of the Falémé, with access to Bambara gold country) — are described separately with their trade volumes. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Gorée — The island off the Cape Verde peninsula, described for its strategic position (the finest natural harbor in West Africa south of Morocco), its history of repeated Anglo-French seizure and restitution, its population (French garrison, African grumetes, liberated slaves, and the mixed-race signare merchant class), and its importance as a slave-trade entrepôt and revictualing station. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Gambia — The French trading presence on the Gambia River, described for its secondary status relative to British competition in the same river system. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Barbarie (Barbary Coast) — Brief notes on the North African littoral in relation to French commercial and diplomatic interests, including the treaty relations with the Barbary states that protected French shipping from corsairs. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]



Section III — French Establishments in the Indies


Eastern coast of Africa — Description of French interest and trading presence along the Mozambique Channel coast. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Cape of Good Hope, Mozambique, Madagascar — Brief notes on these way-stations and their relation to French Indian Ocean navigation. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Île de la Réunion (ci-devant Bourbon) — Description of the island: physical geography, climate, agriculture (coffee, spices, sugar), population, and administration under the Consulate’s new colonial government (captain-general, colonial prefect, commissaire de justice). ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Île de France (Mauritius) — Extended description: situation, extent, the capital Port-Louis, harbor, commerce, population (European, African, Indian), agricultural products (sugar, coffee, spices), and importance as the hub of French Indian Ocean operations. The government of the Île de France is described alongside that of Réunion since the two islands were administered together under a shared captain-general and colonial prefect. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Île Rodrigue — Brief description of this smaller Indian Ocean island dependency. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Îles Seychelles et Praslin — Description of the Seychelles archipelago as a French possession. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Diego Garcia — Brief description of this atoll in the Chagos group. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Coromandel Coast establishments — Survey of French trading posts on the eastern Indian coast:

Pondichéry — The principal French establishment in India: its geography, fortifications, European town and Indian town (White Town and Black Town), population, commerce, the period of British occupation and the condition of the settlement at restoration. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Karikal — The secondary Coromandel establishment south of Pondichéry, with its dependent magans (rural districts). ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]
Chandernagor — The French factory on the Hooghly River near Calcutta, its special position within Bengal, and its commerce. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]



Malabar Coast establishments — Survey of French posts on the southwestern Indian coast:

Mahé — The French settlement on the Malabar Coast, its commerce, and its condition after British occupation and restoration. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]



Appendix — Vegetable Productions of France
This appendix was displaced from its intended location in Volume I by the volume of material. It covers the major categories of French agricultural vegetable production in statistical detail:


Grains — Wheat (froment), rye, barley, oats: volumes, regional distribution, and price tables. The centrepiece is a table giving the mean annual price of a setier of wheat (240 livres weight, equivalent to 117.6 kg) at the Rosoy market near Paris from 1643 to 1788 — 145 years of pre-Revolutionary prices, the longest continuous price series in the wiki’s source collection. The series shows the secular price trends, harvest failures (the sharp spikes of 1693–94 and 1709 visible as mortality crises in the historical literature), and the gradual rise through the 18th century to the pre-Revolutionary peak. Supplementing this long series are: mean myriagramme prices of wheat by department for Year IX (1800–01) and Year X (1801–02), allowing comparison across the Republic’s 98 departments; a month-by-month series for Year X showing seasonal price variation; a departmental series for the Aude from Prairial Year VIII through Prairial Year IX; a table of grain exports through Dunkirk; and Halles de Paris price means for Years VIII and X. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Major industrial crops — Flax and hemp (linen textile and naval cordage supply — critical for wartime France, both as domestic textile and as naval rigging material); colza, navettes, and poppies (oil crops for lighting, cooking, and textile finishing); maize and buckwheat (subsistence crops in southern and western departments); madder (garance — the principal red dye, concentrated in Avignon and the Comtat Venaissin, essential for military uniforms); saffron, weld (gaude — yellow dye), and woad (pastel — the traditional blue dye largely supplanted by indigo from the colonies); anise and coriander (pharmaceutical and food flavoring); tobacco (production by department, given that tobacco was a state monopoly with controlled cultivation zones); hops (with coverage of the beer economy in northern and eastern departments where viticulture was impossible). Each crop is treated with production geography, regional specialization, and commercial uses. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Vegetables as garden and fodder plants — Forage and kitchen garden vegetables treated more briefly, closing the agricultural appendix. ^[source: raw/herbin-statistique-france-1803.txt]


Coverage Guide


French colonial empire at the Consulate — The Statistique is the most systematic source for the French colonial world as reconstituted after Amiens: what France held, where, under what administrative arrangement, and what commercial value each possession was expected to generate. It records the colonial empire at the precise moment before Louisiana was sold and before Saint-Domingue was definitively lost.


Saint-Domingue before and after the Revolution — The 1788 export figures and the departmental description give the pre-Revolutionary baseline; the article’s structure reveals how France still conceived of the colony in administrative terms even as Haitian independence was being fought out.


Louisiana — The article on Louisiana as a French possession, written and published in 1803 before the sale, is a document of what France expected to recover and what it then yielded.


West African slave trade — The 1789 merchandise table and price of a captive entry are the volume’s most direct statement of the French slave trade before abolition. The descriptions of Gorée, Sénégal, and Gambia provide geographic and commercial context.


French Indian Ocean empire — Réunion, Île de France, Rodrigue, Seychelles, Diego Garcia: the full French presence in the Indian Ocean is described in the Consulate period, when these islands served as the support network for French naval and commercial operations in Asian waters.


French India — Pondichéry, Karikal, Chandernagor, Mahé: the restored Coromandel and Malabar establishments, their geography, and their condition after the Revolutionary war’s interruptions.


French agricultural prices (grain, 1643–1802) — The appendix’s long wheat-price series at Rosoy near Paris runs from 1643 to 1788 and is supplemented by Consulate-era departmental tables. This is one of the few places in the wiki’s source collection with pre-Revolutionary price data over a long run.


Colonial administrative structures under the Consulate — The captain-general / colonial prefect / grand judge triad, with its specific competencies, is laid out in the preliminary government section before the colony-by-colony survey begins.


Quality
Princeton University Library OCR from a scanned copy. The text is approximately 1.14 MB of mixed prose and tabular material. Prose sections are readable with the usual OCR artifacts (word splits, garbled proper names). The statistical tables — customs tariffs, commodity prices, export values — have suffered significant column-collapse in the OCR: figures are often detached from their labels or run together. The geographic descriptions are more reliably extracted than the numerical tables. For any precise price or volume figure, verification against the page images is necessary. Place names in Africa and India are spelled according to 1803 French conventions and may require matching against later standardized forms.

sources/histoire-emigration-daudet-1908.title: Ernest Daudet — Histoire de l'Émigration pendant la Révolution Française (pub. 1905–1908)
sources/histoire-emigration-daudet-1908.content:
Ernest Daudet, Histoire de l’Émigration pendant la Révolution Française: d’après les précédentes publications de l’auteur et de nouveaux documents inédits. Paris: Ancienne Librairie Germer Baillière et Cie., Félix Alcan, Éditeur, 1905–1908. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 9,284 lines and 3.2 MB, from a library copy bearing the Princeton University Library stamp.
Ernest Daudet (1837–1921) was a French historian, journalist, and novelist, the elder brother of Alphonse Daudet. He specialized in diplomatic and political history of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic periods, publishing extensively on the Bourbon emigration, Franco-Russian relations, and the Counter-Revolution. This work is his synthetic masterpiece: as he explains in the Avertissement, it draws on and recasts his earlier studies — Les Bourbons et la Russie, Les Émigrés et la Seconde Coalition, Coblentz — adding extensive new material from previously unavailable archival sources, particularly the papers of the duc de Blacas (Louis XVIII’s minister and confidant). The work covers the entire history of the emigration from July 1789 through the Restoration of 1814, drawing on French, Russian, Austrian, English, and Prussian archives as well as unpublished correspondence of Louis XVIII, the comte d’Artois, the comte d’Avaray, and Joseph de Maistre. ^[source: raw/histoire-emigration-1908.txt]
Contents at a Glance
The work is organized into 15 Livres covering the emigration from its origins through the Restoration. The author states in the preface that his goal was to produce a “tableau complet de la politique des émigrés” — a complete picture of émigré politics — and that “quel que soit l’effort des historiens qui tenteront après moi de faire revivre les mêmes personnages et de raconter les mêmes événements, ils ne trouveront que de rares épis à glaner dans mon sillon.” This confident claim is supported by the extraordinary range of archival sources on which the work rests. The material is treated as straight narrative history rather than as memoir or contemporary analysis. The text includes 107 numbered footnote annotations, many of which reproduce entire documents — letters from Louis XVIII, the comte d’Avaray, Joseph de Maistre, the duchesse d’Orléans, Mme Moreau, and others. ^[source: raw/histoire-emigration-1908.txt]
Full Contents Map
Livre Premier — Les Premières Étapes (1789–1791)
Covers the beginning of the emigration from the fall of the Bastille. The comte d’Artois flees Paris on the night of July 16–17, 1789, followed by Condé, Bourbon, Enghien, and the court nobility. The émigrés gather at Turin under the protection of the king of Sardinia. The early chapters cover the arrival at Turin, the growing dissensions among the émigré factions, and the political agitation that develops around the princes’ court-in-exile.

I. Les Débuts de l’Émigration — The flight of Artois and the first wave of émigrés after July 14, 1789; the court’s reaction; the spread of emigration across Europe.
II. L’Arrivée à Turin — The establishment of the émigré court at Turin under the protection of the king of Sardinia; the roles of the comte d’Artois, the prince de Condé, and their entourages; Calonne’s arrival and his influence.
III. Les Dissentiments et les Conflits — Internal divisions among the émigrés: conflicts between Artois and Condé, between the nobility and the clergy, between moderates and intransigents.
IV. L’Agitation à Turin — Political intrigues at Turin; relations with the king of Sardinia; the question of armed intervention; the role of the court of Vienna.
VII. Sur la Route de Coblentz — The shift of the émigré center from Turin to Coblentz on the Rhine, closer to the Austrian and Prussian courts; the departure of Artois and Condé for Germany.

Livre Second — Coblentz (1791)
The émigrés establish their principal center at Coblentz on the Rhine, under the joint protection of the Elector of Trier and the Holy Roman Emperor. Daudet describes the diplomatic efforts of the princes to coordinate a coalition of European powers against revolutionary France.

I. La Diplomatie des Princes — The princes’ efforts to build a European coalition; the mission of Fersen to Vienna; Calonne’s negotiations in London; Leopold II’s reluctance; the shifting Austrian position.
III. Une Cour d’Exilés — Life at the émigré court in Coblentz: the composition of the court, daily routines, rivalries, and the growing gap between the princes’ illusions and reality.
IV. Autour de la Constitution de 1791 — The émigré reaction to the Constitutional Monarchy; their refusal to accept the Constitution; their campaign to discredit Louis XVI’s acceptance of it.
V. La France Menacée — The escalating war of words between the émigrés and the revolutionary government; the Legislative Assembly’s decrees against the émigrés.
VI. L’Émigration en 1792 — The growth of the emigration as the Revolution radicalizes; the émigré military preparations; the formation of the Army of the Princes.
VII. Missions Multipliées — Émigré diplomatic missions to European courts; efforts to win support from Russia, Sweden, Spain, and the German states.

Livre Troisième — La Campagne de 1792
The military campaign of the Duke of Brunswick’s allied army and the émigré forces against revolutionary France. Covers the period from the declaration of war (April 1792) through the French victory at Valmy and the retreat.

I. À l’Approche de la Guerre — The allied preparations; the Brunswick Manifesto; émigré hopes and plans.
III. Les Derniers Jours de Coblentz — The collapse of Coblentz as an émigré center after Valmy; the dissolution of the Army of the Princes; the dispersion of the émigrés.
IV. La Retraite de Brunswick — The allied retreat after Valmy; the émigré despair; the beginning of the long exile.

Livre Quatrième — Hamm et Vérone (1792–1795)
After the collapse of Coblentz, the comte de Provence (the future Louis XVIII) settles first at Hamm in Westphalia and then at Verona on Venetian territory. He proclaims himself Regent after Louis XVI’s execution and then King after the death of Louis XVII.

I. La Régence de Monsieur — The comte de Provence proclaims himself Regent of France after Louis XVI’s execution (January 21, 1793); his establishment at Hamm; his diplomatic correspondence.
II. Le Comte d’Artois à Saint-Pétersbourg — Artois’s mission to the court of Catherine the Great; Russian policy toward the émigrés.
V. Monsieur Devient Roi — The death of Louis XVII in the Temple (June 1795); the comte de Provence proclaims himself King Louis XVIII; the shift in his diplomatic and political position.

Livre Cinquième — Quiberon (1795)
The disastrous British-supported landing of émigré forces at Quiberon Bay in Brittany (June–July 1795). Daudet covers the planning, the landing, the hopes of the Breton Chouans, the military operations, and the catastrophic defeat and execution of the émigré prisoners.

I. Préparatifs Défectueux — The planning of the Quiberon expedition: British support under Pitt’s government, the Puisaye leadership, the role of the émigré military.
II. Émigrés et Chouans — The landing at Quiberon; the junction with the Chouan forces; the military operations under Hoche’s republican counter-offensive.
V. Le Roi Expulsé de Vérone — The French Directory’s diplomatic pressure forces the Venetian Republic to expel Louis XVIII from Verona; his expulsion and its consequences.

Livre Sixième — Blanckenberg (1795–1797)
Louis XVIII establishes his court at Blanckenberg in the Duchy of Brunswick. Daudet covers the king’s efforts to reorganize the royalist movement and the growing internal conflicts within the émigré community.

I. Le Comte de Saint-Priest à Saint-Pétersbourg — Saint-Priest’s mission to the Russian court; the shifting policy of Paul I.
II. Louis XVIII à l’Armée de Condé — The king’s relations with the Condé army, the last organized émigré military force.
IV. Saint-Priest, Premier Ministre — The brief ministry of Saint-Priest in the émigré government; the conflicts between the king’s ministers.

Livre Septième — Les Émigrés et le XVIII Fructidor (1797)
The coup of 18 Fructidor Year V (September 4, 1797) and its devastating effects on the royalist cause in both France and the emigration. The royalist party had made significant gains in the 1797 elections; the Directory’s coup annulled these gains, purged royalist deputies, and reignited the persecution of émigrés.

I. Regard en Arrière — Retrospective on the state of the royalist movement between 1795 and 1797.
II. Le Parti Royaliste en 1796–1797 — The growth of royalist sentiment in France; the Clichy club; the elections of Year V; the royalist revival.
IV. Le Plan des Agents de Paris — The royalist agents’ plans for a peaceful restoration; their negotiations with the Directors.
V. La Catastrophe du 31 Janvier 1797 — The abortive royalist coup attempt and the republican response; the prelude to Fructidor.
IX. Les Débuts d’une Intrigue — New intrigues within the émigré leadership.
X. Le Lendemain de Fructidor — Aftermath of the coup; the proscription of royalists; the hardening of the Directory’s anti-émigré policy.

Livre Huitième — Louis XVIII et Madame Royale (1795–1799)
The negotiations between Louis XVIII and his niece Marie-Thérèse-Charlotte (Madame Royale, daughter of Louis XVI), who was released from the Temple in December 1795 and exchanged for French prisoners in Austria. Daudet covers the protracted negotiations over her marriage, her arrival at the émigré court, and the tensions surrounding her position.

I. La Délivrance — The release of Madame Royale from the Temple; the negotiations for her exchange.
II. Le Consentement de Madame Royale — Her agreement to join her uncle’s court; the political significance of her arrival.
III. L’Abbé Edgeworth à Blanckenberg — The arrival of the abbé Edgeworth de Firmont (Louis XVI’s confessor) at Blanckenberg; his role in the émigré court.
V. Dissentiments Passagers — Friction between Madame Royale and the émigré court; her independent position.
VI. Le Roi Chassé de Blanckenberg — Prussian diplomatic pressure forces Louis XVIII to leave Blanckenberg.
VII. En Route pour Mitau — The king’s journey to Mitau in Courland (now Jelgava, Latvia), under the protection of Tsar Paul I of Russia.

Livre Neuvième — Agitations et Intrigues (1797–1799)
The émigré court at Mitau; the intense political intrigues within the royalist leadership as the Directory’s power weakens and the prospect of a second coalition against France takes shape.

I. Le Roi à Mitau — The establishment of the émigré court at Mitau; Paul I’s patronage; the conditions of exile in Courland.
III. Fauche-Borel à Londres — The Swiss royalist agent Fauche-Borel’s missions to London; his role in émigré intelligence and diplomacy.
IV. Les Lettres Patentes — Louis XVIII’s Letters Patent of 1798–1799; his political program for a restoration.
VI. Dumouriez Royaliste — The former revolutionary general Dumouriez, now a royalist agent; his schemes and proposals.
VII. La Seconde Coalition — The formation of the Second Coalition (Russia, Austria, Britain, Naples, Ottoman Empire) against France; émigré hopes for a restoration through allied victory.

Livre Dixième — À la Veille et au Lendemain du Dix-Huit Brumaire (1799–1800)
The coup of 18 Brumaire Year VIII (November 9–10, 1799) and the establishment of the Consulate under Bonaparte. Daudet covers the émigré response to Brumaire, the initial confusion, and the first tentative contacts between Louis XVIII and Bonaparte.

I. Le Roi et son Neveu — Louis XVIII and the duc d’Angoulême (son of Artois); the question of the royal succession.
II. De la Coupe aux Lèvres — The émigré hopes raised by the Second Coalition’s early victories; the disappointment as Bonaparte defeats the coalition.
III. Les Préparatifs — Émigré military preparations for a landing in France; coordination with the Chouans.
IV. Le Mariage — The marriage of the duc d’Angoulême and Madame Royale; its political significance.
V. Nouvel Essai de Recours à Bonaparte — Louis XVIII’s famous letter to Bonaparte (February 1800), proposing a restoration in exchange for Bonaparte’s support; Bonaparte’s cold reply.
VII. Les Plans de Dumouriez et de Willot — Dumouriez’s and General Willot’s plans for a restoration through military action.
VIII. Le Conseil Royal et sa Mission — The reorganization of the royal council; missions to European courts.
IX. Autour de Bonaparte — Émigré efforts to sound out Bonaparte’s intentions; the shifting political situation.
X. Les Dessous d’une Négociation — The secret negotiations between the royalists and Bonaparte; their failure.

Livre Onzième — La Cour de Mitau en 1800
Daily life and politics at the Mitau court during the year 1800, as the émigré leadership struggles with internal divisions and the growing power of Bonaparte.

I. L’Église et la Royauté — Church-state relations within the émigré community; the question of ecclesiastical authority in exile.
II. Les Divisions de l’Épiscopat — Conflicts among the exiled French bishops; their competing claims to authority.
III. La Rentrée des Évêques — The gradual return of bishops to France under the Consulate’s tolerance.
IV. Les Préliminaires du Concordat — The negotiations leading to the Concordat of 1801; the émigré reaction to Bonaparte’s religious policy.
V. Les Princes d’Orléans en Angleterre — The Orléans branch of the royal family in English exile; their separate position.
VI. Réconciliés — Attempts at reconciliation between the various émigré factions.
VII. Les Dissentiments Entre le Roi et son Frère — The growing rift between Louis XVIII and the comte d’Artois over policy and authority.
VIII. Aggravation des Conflits — The escalation of the king-brother conflict.
IX. Querelles Apaisées — Temporary resolution of some conflicts.
X. Négociations en Vue d’un Mariage — Marriage negotiations for the duc de Berry.
XI. Misères de Prince — The material and psychological hardships of the exiled princes.
XII. Le Duc de Berry et les Bourbons de Naples — The duc de Berry’s relations with the Neapolitan Bourbons.

Livre Douzième — Louis XVIII et Paul Ier (1799–1801)
The relationship between Louis XVIII and Tsar Paul I of Russia, who had granted the émigré court asylum at Mitau. Daudet covers the warm initial reception, the tsar’s erratic policy shifts, and the deterioration of the relationship as Paul moves toward rapprochement with Bonaparte.

I. L’Abbé Edgeworth et le Comte de Caraman à Saint-Pétersbourg — The missions of Edgeworth and Caraman to the Russian court.
II. Le Voyage du Général Dumouriez — Dumouriez’s journey to Russia; his efforts to influence Paul I.
III. Bonaparte et Paul Ier — The diplomatic rapprochement between Bonaparte’s Consulate and Paul I.
IV. Fin du Rôle de Dumouricz — The end of Dumouriez’s political career as a royalist agent.
V. L’Expédition de Willot — Willot’s projected expedition to France.
VIII. Le Roi Chassé de Mitau — Paul I’s abrupt order expelling Louis XVIII from Mitau (January 1801); the collapse of the Russian patronage.

Livre Treizième — Varsovie (1801–1804)
After his expulsion from Russia, Louis XVIII settles in Warsaw, then under Prussian control. The period covers the Peace of Amiens, the brief respite for émigrés who could return to France, and the hardening of Bonaparte’s regime after the assassination attempt of 1803 and the execution of the duc d’Enghien in 1804.
Livre Quatorzième — Avant et Après l’Entrevue de Calmar (1804–1807)
The new international situation after the formation of the Third Coalition; Louis XVIII’s journey to Sweden and the famous interview at Calmar with King Gustav IV Adolf; the failure of the coalition and the Austerlitz campaign; the Treaty of Tilsit and the Franco-Russian alliance, which destroys émigré hopes for a restoration through Russian power.
Livre Quinzième — Les Dernières Années de l’Émigration (1807–1814)
The final years of the emigration as Bonaparte’s empire reaches its height and then collapses. Louis XVIII’s wanderings through Sweden, Prussia, and finally England; the émigré community in London; the Russian campaign of 1812 and the destruction of the Grande Armée; the formation of the Sixth Coalition; the allied invasion of France; the abdication of Napoleon; the restoration of Louis XVIII. ^[source: raw/histoire-emigration-1908.txt]
Coverage Guide


The origins of the emigration, 1789–1791 — Livre Premier gives the most detailed single account of how and why the emigration began, who left first, the choice of Turin, and the role of the king of Sardinia. The emphasis is on the nobility and the princes’ immediate circle rather than on the lesser nobility or clergy who emigrated later. Cross-reference paganel-histoire-napoleon-1815 for the republican perspective on the same events.


Coblentz and the Army of the Princes, 1791–1792 — Livre Second provides a comprehensive account of the émigré political and diplomatic establishment on the Rhine. Daudet draws heavily on diplomatic correspondence to reconstruct the princes’ negotiations with Leopold II, Frederick William II, Catherine the Great, and Gustav III of Sweden. The portrait of Calonne as an endlessly optimistic but ultimately deluded advisor is a recurring thread.


The military campaigns, 1792–1793 — Livre Troisième covers the Brunswick campaign and the émigré military participation. The focus is less on the military operations themselves than on the émigré political leadership’s strategic illusions and the diplomatic context that produced them.


Louis XVIII’s court in exile, 1793–1807 — Livres Quatrième, Sixième, Huitième, Neuvième, Onzième, Douzième, and Treizième provide a continuous narrative of Louis XVIII’s successive residences: Hamm, Verona, Blanckenberg, Mitau, and Warsaw. Daudet’s access to the Blacas papers gives these sections unusual depth — he reproduces extensive correspondence between the king, his ministers, and his agents across Europe. The treatment of the king’s character is generally sympathetic but not uncritical: Daudet presents him as a genuine politician whose natural moderation was warped by exile, by the intransigence of his brother Artois, and by the relentless pressure of circumstances.


Quiberon, 1795 — Livre Cinquième covers the Quiberon expedition in detail, from the planning stages through the landing, the military campaign, and the execution of the prisoners. Daudet’s account is notable for its clear-eyed assessment of the planning failures, the political conflicts between Puisaye and the other émigré leaders, and the British government’s ambiguous commitment to the enterprise.


18 Fructidor Year V (1797) and its consequences — Livre Septième covers the royalist revival in France, the elections of Year V, the coup of 18 Fructidor, and its devastating effect on both the émigrés and the internal royalist party. This is one of the most detailed sections of the work, reflecting Daudet’s extensive use of police and diplomatic archives.


The émigrés and Bonaparte, 1799–1814 — Livres Dixième, Quatorzième, and Quinzième cover the complex relationship between the émigrés and Bonaparte: from Louis XVIII’s letter offering reconciliation, through the Cold War of the Consulate and Empire periods, to the final restoration in 1814. The treatment of the Concordat negotiations (Livre Onzième, chapters III–IV) from the émigré perspective is particularly useful.


Émigré internal politics — Throughout the work, Daudet emphasizes the émigrés’ political divisions: between Artois and Provence/Louis XVIII, between the military faction (Condé) and the diplomatic faction (the king’s ministers), between the intransigents who refused any compromise with revolutionary France and the moderates who sought accommodation. This internal political history is one of the work’s principal contributions.


Quality
The OCR quality is generally good, with clear section headers and well-preserved French text. The text was produced from a printed edition with careful typography — footnotes are numbered and the note markers in the text are preserved. There are approximately 107 numbered notes, some of which run to considerable length as they reproduce entire documents. The OCR has handled diacritical marks and special characters well. Total length approximately 9,284 lines / 3.2 MB.
The work dates from the early 20th century (first published 1905–1908) and reflects the historiographical conventions of its time: narrative-driven, diplomatically focused, with a generally sympathetic but not uncritical view of the Bourbon monarchy. Daudet’s archival research is extraordinary for its breadth; his access to the Blacas papers — the private archive of Louis XVIII’s most trusted minister — gives the work a documentary depth unusual for royalist historiography. The tone is consistently professed as impartial (“Je me suis efforcé d’être indulgent et impartial”), though the work is clearly oriented toward a readership sympathetic to the monarchy. The treatment of the revolutionary government and its leaders is factual rather than polemical.

sources/louvet-memoires-1823.title: Louvet de Couvray — Mémoires (written 1794, pub. 1823)
sources/louvet-memoires-1823.content:
Jean-Baptiste Louvet de Couvray, Mémoires, in Collection des Mémoires relatifs à la Révolution Française. Paris: Baudouin Frères, 1823. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 14,010 lines and 674 KB, from a Harvard/Widener Library copy. Louvet (1760–1797) was a Girondin deputy to the National Convention, best known for his speech of October 29, 1792, in which he formally accused Robespierre before the Convention (“Je t’accuse, Robespierre!”). After the Montagnard coup of May 31–June 2, 1793 proscribed the leading Girondins, Louvet went into hiding; he wrote these memoirs in April 1794 from a cave in the Jura, expecting to die. He survived, returned to the Convention after Thermidor, and died in 1797 as French consul-designate to Palermo. Published posthumously as part of the Baudouin Frères series of revolutionary memoirs. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Louvet’s Mémoires are explicitly unpolished — he says so himself in his prefatory note, written from hiding on 19 April 1794: “I throw down notes, and that is all. Do not expect either stylistic concision or abundance of detail. Truly, I am writing neither history nor what is called memoirs. I am recording notes that may help me, if some day of genuine leisure is given to me — or help someone else, if I do not survive.” The rawness is part of their value. This is not a text composed for literary effect after the fact; it is a record written under mortal danger by someone who did not know he would survive.
The Mémoires cover two intertwined things: the political history of the Girondin faction from the perspective of one of its most combative members, and the personal narrative of Louvet’s flight, concealment, and eventual return. The political sections give the Girondin reading of the May 31–June 2 coup, the responsibility of Robespierre and the Mountain, the federalist resistance in Caen and Bordeaux, and the fate of various colleagues. The personal narrative — hiding in Caen, escaping to Brittany, crossing to Bordeaux, taking refuge in the Gironde, making his way to the Jura, waiting in a cave — is among the more vivid fugitive accounts of the Terror period.
The volume also includes a biographical Notice on Louvet by the Baudouin editors, and a crucial related text: his “Lettre à la Convention,” written from hiding, in which he addresses the survivors of the Convention still under Montagnard control and argues for his own rehabilitation and for the victims of the June 2 coup.
Cross-reference: Madame Roland’s Mémoires (Volume II in this wiki) include a portrait of Louvet; he appears in her Portraits as “courageous and vivacious, with political limitations.” The two texts illuminate each other from complementary Girondin positions.
Full Contents Map
Editors’ Avertissement and Notice on Louvet’s Life
The Baudouin Frères editors explain the series: the Collection des Mémoires relatifs à la Révolution Française is organized around the principle of reproducing primary documents without alteration — not even removing passages that are objectionable, since accuracy matters more than editorial comfort. They had faced criticism for including a Maratist pamphlet comparing Marat to Christ; they defend it as evidence of the “monstrous absurdity” of the period, not endorsement.
The Notice biographique on Louvet’s life gives the basic facts: born 1760, author of the novel Faublas (one of the most popular erotic novels of the 1780s), journalist, elected to the Legislative Assembly and then the National Convention representing the Loiret, Girondin activist. His wife Lodoïska (the model for the heroine of Faublas) managed a bookshop in Paris under the Terror while he was in hiding. He died in 1797 aged thirty-seven, named but not yet installed as consul at Palermo. His manuscripts — poetry and correspondence — were destroyed during the Terror. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Prefatory Documents: The Manifesto of Caen
Before the main narrative, Louvet reproduces and defends the Proclamation de l’assemblée centrale de résistance à l’oppression (the so-called “Manifeste de Wimpfen”), drafted by him at Caen in June 1793 and adopted by the Girondin deputies who had gathered there. The document called on departments to resist the Convention’s coup as a usurpation, and to rally republican forces to restore the rightful deputies. He was charged with it (as a federalist manifesto); he defends it as a purely republican document aimed at the Montagnard usurpers, not at the Convention or the Republic as institutions.
He also prints his response to Lindet’s report accusing the Girondins, and references Faure’s report with its sixty-three signatures — a key documentary set for the Girondin-Montagnard conflict. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Author’s Avertissement (from the Jura, April 19, 1794)
The prefatory note from hiding. Louvet explains the conditions under which he is writing — cave in the Jura, in hiding for nearly a year, time limited, materials sparse. He dedicates the text to the memory of Madame Roland, quoting an extract from her defense manuscripts: “Liberty! it is for proud souls who despise death and know when to give it; it is not for those corrupt men who, rising from the bed of debauchery or from the mud of misery, rush to bathe in the blood streaming from scaffolds.” He introduces this as the only preface worthy of his notes. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Quelques Notices pour l’Histoire, et le Récit de mes Périls depuis le 31 mai
The main body of the text — the “Some Historical Notes and Account of My Perils since May 31” — is the combined political history and personal narrative. The opening section describes Louvet before the Revolution: living in the country near Paris, composing the novels that would become Faublas, with a small income (eight hundred francs a year “made me live”), and deeply in love with Lodoïska — a woman married off to a wealthy man when she was sixteen, who returned six years later and became his companion and eventually wife. The Revolution interrupted his literary plans and pulled him toward political journalism. He records writing his first political pamphlet, Paris justifié, in response to Mounier’s attack on the October Days, and entering the Jacobins in the club’s earliest months — “only admitted with the credentials of true civism and some talent.” He became the editor of the Sentinelle and the author of the famous Robespierre accusation. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
The March 10 conspiracy and Marat’s tribunal. Before the June 2 coup proper, Louvet narrates the conspiration du 10 mars — a Montagnard attempt to seize power prematurely, which he had exposed in a pamphlet he describes as his “political testament.” He documents the creation of the Revolutionary Tribunal and how Marat intervened to force through his own jury list when the Girondins succeeded in nominating honest men: “he cried counter-revolution, threatened to call the people, had the ballot annulled, imposed his list.” The jurés were “for the most part massacreurs de septembre.” At this point Louvet prints a key anecdote: when Pache read the petition of the “twenty-two” to the Convention, Boyer-Fonfrède took the floor and said, roughly, “as for me, I regret not to be among those on whom the municipality of Paris today calls daggers” — and nearly the whole Assembly rose spontaneously, crying “All! all!” This moment of Convention solidarity was real; it did not prevent May 31. A Bordelais recently released from Austrian captivity had told Guadet that the Austrian general staff was confident twenty-two heads would fall in the Convention — and when Pache presented the petition naming precisely twenty-two, the coincidence seemed to Louvet proof of Montagnard collusion with Austria. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Political prelude: the May 31–June 2 coup. Louvet is categorical: May 31 was not a popular revolution but a criminal conspiracy. The Convention was held prisoner by armed sections and the Commune; its decrees were extorted at gunpoint; the republic was effectively overthrown. He documents his own near-arrest and flight: “I say this to the friends of liberty, if any remain.” His account of the weeks immediately after the coup is not triumphalist about the Girondins — he is honest that many were passive, many fled too quickly, many had been politically cautious when courage was needed. But his verdict on the coup itself is unequivocal: “these crimes were not those of the republic! They never permitted us to establish it! It was to debase it, to make it hateful, to destroy it forever, that they constantly mixed its name with their cruel turpitudes.” ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Caen and the federalist resistance. Louvet was among the proscribed deputies who gathered in Caen under the Norman department administration’s protection. He drafted the Proclamation de l’assemblée centrale de résistance à l’oppression (the Manifesto of Caen) — he emphasizes that it was a collective document, approved by the assembled deputies, not his alone. The military force assembled under General Wimpfen attempted to march on Paris but was defeated at Pacy-sur-Eure in July 1793. Louvet is honest about why the federalist resistance failed: property-owning republicans in the provinces were fundamentally unwilling to leave their homes; they sent “hired men” whose loyalty could be bought against them; while “the ardent, audacious Mountain, inured to crime, drew the sword against the fatherland” and its Parisian emissaries arrived in the provinces offering provincial compliance the name of patriotism. “The most formerly proud cities began to fall before two or three Jacobins.”
The internal tensions of Caen are documented: genuine republicans who wanted to march on Paris; men who had their own reasons for not wanting a Montagnard victory but who were suspected of royalist sympathies; the impossibility of maintaining a disciplined political identity when the common enemy was pressing from outside and suspicion was corroding from within. Wimpfen himself was suspected of secret intelligences with the enemy — Louvet raises but does not resolve the question. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Charlotte Corday. The most celebrated passage in the Mémoires outside the political narrative. Corday came to Caen before the assassination, Louvet says, ostensibly to beg a favor for some of her relatives — but her real motive “was doubtless to know some of the founders of this republic for which she was about to devote herself; and perhaps she was also glad that one day her features would be vivid in their memory.” He declares: “I affirm that she never said to any of us a word about her design.” He adds the crucial detail: if she had consulted them, they would not have directed her toward Marat — they knew he had at most two days left to live from his disease. “Let us humble ourselves before the decrees of Providence; it wished that Robespierre and his accomplices live long enough to destroy each other, long enough for it to be well proven to the French nation… that some were traitorous royalists, and the other the most ambitious of tyrants.”
His portrait of Corday is among the most intensely felt passages in the text: “proud and gentle, decent and beautiful, as she always appeared to us; her bearing had that dignity full of assurance, and her gaze that fire tempered by modesty.” He had seen her the evening before she left for Paris. He is explicit that her act was just; he does not claim to have approved its direction. The footnote by the editors notes Adam Lux — the deputy from Mainz who wrote a public apology defending Corday as greater than Brutus, was imprisoned, and went to the guillotine saying “I am going to die for Charlotte Corday.” Louvet also notes an unnamed young man who asked to be imprisoned in Corday’s place; the Cordeliers granted him part of his request. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
The failure of federalism and the broader Terror. Louvet provides a sweeping indictment of the Terror’s provincial manifestations: Collot-d’Herbois and Ronsin deliberating for hours at Lyon about which method of mass execution would be most solemn — mitraillade or sword — while the crowd applauded; Lebon at Arras forcing a wife to stand under the guillotine dripping with her husband’s blood. “Why did it require nothing less than this experience for me to be convinced of this unfortunate truth, that… men must be slaves, since men are wicked, or cringe before the wicked?” He pulls back from this despair in the next paragraph: “among so much depravity, it is consoling to declare that even in France there still exist some beings worthy of liberty. We found them above all among individuals of that sex reputed frivolous and timid. Women prodigued us the most touching attentions and all those courageous succors that generous compassion never refuses to unmerited misfortune.” ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Escape to Brittany. After Caen, the Breton deputies and sympathizers who had formed the core of Wimpfen’s force were worked on by emissaries: their primary assemblies had accepted the new constitution, they were told; to continue fighting was now to constitute a faction. The Bretons — “naturally very brave” — were drawn off. Louvet’s account of the flight through Brittany emphasizes the political unreliability of the countryside: people who had been protected by the Girondins for ten months refused to give them shelter for a single night, or opened their doors only to close them when they heard footsteps on the road. “Friends ferocious through pusillanimity would refuse to recognize their friend… friends of twenty years would drive you from their door, repulse you to the foot of the scaffold!” ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Bordeaux and the Gironde. Louvet and several other fugitives reached Bordeaux and its surrounding wine-country. The Gironde region — from which the Girondin party took its name and many of its leading figures — remained longer than other provinces in a state of relative republican independence. The title of the chapter’s section from Saint-Emilion’s grottos (given in the opening dateline) is significant: Louvet was writing some of his notes from hiding in the wine-cellar caves of that town, where several proscribed deputies sheltered together. Bordeaux’s submission to the Terror narrowed the window, and the decision was made to move further, toward the Jura. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
The Jura and the cave. The dateline of the Avertissement — “From the grottos of the Jura, April 19, 1794” — gives the physical setting: a limestone cave in the Jura mountains, where Louvet and Lodoïska sheltered for several months. Cold, inadequate food, isolation, the sound of distant wind. He is writing by whatever light is available, at speed, knowing he may not live. “I throw down notes, and that is all… I am recording notes that may help me if some day of genuine leisure is given to me — or help someone else, if I do not survive.” The psychological portrait of this period is stark: a man who had been a journalist, novelist, political orator, and Convention deputy is now invisible, cold, waiting. His one solid political act from the cave is the Lettre à la Convention — the demand that the surviving Convention recognize the June 2 coup for what it was. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Return after Thermidor. The fall of Robespierre on 9 Thermidor Year II (July 27, 1794) ended the immediate mortal danger. Louvet’s account of the return to Paris is relatively compressed compared to the flight narrative — the Mémoires were written during the hiding, not the return. What he records is the first steps of political rehabilitation: the Convention under Thermidorian pressure began reversing the proscriptions, and the surviving Girondins returned to their seats. Louvet resumed his journalistic and political career, was among the founders of the journal La Sentinelle in its second form, and represented the moderate republican position through the remaining years of the Convention and the early Directory. He died in 1797, named as consul to Palermo, before he could take up the post. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Lettre à la Convention
A formal political address from hiding, directed at the surviving deputies of the Convention still under Montagnard control. Louvet argues for the return of the proscribed deputies, defends the Girondin record against specific charges, and calls on the Convention to recognize that the June 2 coup had violated every constitutional principle the Republic claimed to uphold. The letter is a political document, not a personal appeal; it is written in the register of constitutional argument. It ends with a demand that those responsible for the proscriptions be held accountable. ^[source: raw/louvet-memoires-1795.txt]
Coverage Guide


The Girondin coup of May 31–June 2, 1793 — Louvet’s account is the most detailed in the wiki for the coup itself from the Girondin side: who was where, what was said in the Convention, how the sections and the Commune operated, who resisted and who capitulated. Cross-reference with roland-memoires-vol2-1823 for the complementary Girondin account.


The federalist resistance at Caen — The only source in the wiki describing from the inside the Caen assembly’s organization, the drafting of the Manifesto, the military failure at Pacy-sur-Eure, and the political tensions within the federalist camp about royalism vs. republicanism.


Charlotte Corday and Marat’s assassination — Treated obliquely but memorably: Corday came from the same Norman milieu as the Caen resisters; Louvet’s disavowal combined with his evident sympathy for the act’s justice is historically significant.


The mechanics of clandestine survival during the Terror — The flight narrative is one of the more complete accounts of how proscribed republicans actually survived: false papers, sympathetic intermediaries, regional networks, the geography of resistance (Brittany, the Gironde, the Jura). Cross-reference with roland-memoires-vol2-1823 for the complementary experience of a prisoner rather than a fugitive.


Robespierre accusation (1792) — Referenced throughout: the famous speech of October 29, 1792 (“Je t’accuse, Robespierre!”) is the defining act of Louvet’s political identity and the origin of the Montagnard vendetta against him.


Thermidorian rehabilitation — The return to the Convention after Thermidor, and the beginning of the reversal of Girondin proscriptions.


Louvet as portrayed by Roland — The Portraits section of roland-memoires-vol2-1823 gives Roland’s character sketch of Louvet, written at roughly the same time. The two texts are complementary primary accounts of the same circles.


Quality
Harvard/Widener Library copy, OCR from a Baudouin Frères 1823 print. The text is cleaner than the Fantin (shorter sentences, more direct prose style); Louvet was a professional writer and the text’s roughness is intentional rather than editorial. Editors’ footnotes are numerous and marked as “(Note des éditeurs)” — they supply context and correct or qualify Louvet’s claims where they had documentary evidence. These notes are generally useful and readable in the OCR. The editors’ avertissement and the Notice biographique are in the same print run and fully legible. Running headers are simple and do not interfere with the prose extraction.
