sources/mahan-sea-power-french-revolutio.title: Mahan — The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, Vol. I (1892)
sources/mahan-sea-power-french-revolutio.content:
Rear Admiral Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812, Volume I. Published 1892. The epub text runs to approximately 870 KB across eleven chapters and a notes section. This is the sequel to Mahan’s famous The Influence of Sea Power upon History, 1660–1783 (1890), and carries the same thesis — that control of the sea is the decisive factor in the outcome of great conflicts — forward through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. This volume covers 1783 to approximately 1801; the preface states the full work’s terminus is 1812 (Napoleon’s Russian invasion). Mahan wrote the work in his capacity as lecturer on Naval History and Naval Tactics at the United States Naval War College. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Mahan’s argument in this volume is that Britain’s ultimate victory over Napoleonic France was determined less by Wellington’s armies than by the Royal Navy’s control of the seas — and that this control was not accidental but the product of sustained national commitment to maritime strength, professional officer corps, and strategic coherence, against a French navy systematically destroyed by the Revolution’s institutional ignorance and class warfare before it ever fought the British.
The book works on two levels simultaneously. At the strategic level, Mahan traces how British sea power shaped every major theatre of the war: blockading France’s Atlantic ports, contesting the West Indies, dominating the Mediterranean, defeating the Egyptian expedition, and strangling French colonial commerce. At the institutional level, he provides a devastating anatomy of how the Revolution — through mutiny, the emigration and execution of trained officers, politically driven reorganizations, and the simple failure to understand that seamanship is a specialized professional skill — reduced a fine navy inherited from Louis XVI to a rabble incapable of fighting. The contrast with the British navy — itself flawed, burdened by press-gangs, low pay, and endemic supply shortages, but sustained by professional tradition and a trained officer corps — runs through every chapter.
The volume ends in 1801 with the French navy effectively destroyed as a fighting force capable of independent action, the British in control of the Mediterranean, Malta and Egypt lost by France, and the second coalition formed and dissolved. Volume II (not in this epub) covers the period through 1812.
Full Contents Map
Preface (October 1892)
Mahan explains that the work grew from his Naval War College lectures, as a sequel to his 1890 sea power study. He states its purpose: not merely to write naval history, but to demonstrate the influence of maritime force on the political and military results of one of history’s greatest struggles. The work’s terminal date is 1812 — Napoleon’s Russian invasion — marked simultaneously by the outbreak of the Anglo-American War, which Mahan intends as a future separate study. The preface identifies his central argument: that “statesmanship directing arms” required sea power to be effective, and that nations unprepared on the sea paid for it regardless of their armies. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter I — Introductory: Outline of Events in Europe, 1783–1793
The longest chapter in the book, covering the decade between the Peace of Versailles (1783) and the outbreak of war with Britain (1793). Mahan argues this decade was not stagnation but the formation of the conditions that made the great war inevitable and shaped its outcome.
The chapter traces four overlapping processes:
British recovery under Pitt. Britain emerged from the American war humiliated and debt-laden, but under William Pitt the Younger — who Mahan regards as a peace genius rather than a war minister — rapidly rebuilt its commercial and financial base. Exports and imports grew over fifty percent between 1784 and 1792. The 1786 commercial treaty with France temporarily eased tensions. Pitt’s political position gave him unusual unity of command: king, people, and Commons behind a single leader through the critical years when opinion was hardening. Mahan reads this concentration of executive power as a structural advantage for Britain throughout the coming war.
France’s financial and political collapse. Against Britain’s recovery, France’s finances were hopeless under existing social conditions. The rapid succession of ministers, the king’s weak character, and the conflict of orders and opinions led through the Assembly of Notables (1787) and the States-General (1789) to revolution. France was simultaneously “moneyless and leaderless.”
The Eastern Question and Russian expansion. Mahan devotes considerable space to Russia’s expansion southward (Black Sea, conquest of Oczakow) and northward (domination of the Baltic), and to the Austrian emperor Joseph II’s scheme to open the Scheldt to Antwerp. He treats these not as peripheral distractions but as the structural backdrop against which British strategic thinking was being remade. Britain’s traditional alliance with Russia was eroding as Russia’s reach toward the Mediterranean threatened British interests in the Levant. Mahan shows Pitt’s ministry quietly frustrating Russia’s attempts to use British ports and British-chartered ships for Baltic fleet movements, and the parliamentary debate of 1791 — in which Fox and Burke opposed armed pressure on Russia, while Pitt’s majority fell — as evidence of how slowly British opinion was adjusting to the Eastern threat. His point: the Levant, Egypt, and the Eastern Mediterranean were already recognized strategic prizes before Napoleon made them theatres of war; Nelson’s battles there were not surprises but the fulfilment of a strategic logic twenty years in formation.
The revolution and the road to war. The chapter then follows the French Revolution’s course from 1789 to February 1793: the Bastille, the royal family’s forced return to Paris, the flight to Varennes, the September Massacres, the battle of Valmy, the National Convention, the opening of the Scheldt, the decree of November 19 offering “fraternity and assistance to all peoples wishing to recover their liberty,” and the execution of Louis XVI. Each step is read for its effect on British opinion and on the practical grounds for war. The Scheldt decree in particular — cutting the knot that Joseph II had been unable to untie — directly threatened British sea power by opening the great port of Antwerp to French warship access. The execution of the king brought matters to a head. Britain declared diplomatic relations severed; France declared war on Britain and Holland on 1 February 1793. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter II — The Condition of the Navies in 1793, and Especially of the French Navy
The analytical heart of the book and its most original chapter. Before following the military narrative, Mahan stops to explain why the sea war went the way it did, using the French navy’s institutional destruction as a case study in the consequences of applying ideological thinking to a profession it does not understand.
The argument from professional specialism. Mahan insists that seamanship, fleet gunnery, and squadron manoeuvre are highly specialized skills that cannot be acquired by enthusiasm, patriotism, or years of time in a merchant vessel alone. The gun at sea is inseparable from the ship that carries it; the ship is a moving battery requiring precise combined handling; the fleet is an organism that must act from common training and common tradition. To ignore these requirements and treat naval command as interchangeable with civic virtue was not revolutionary boldness — it was ignorance with fatal consequences.
The destruction of the officer corps. The pre-revolutionary French navy of Louis XVI was, Mahan argues, genuinely excellent in material and officer quality — the navy of Suffren, De Grasse, and D’Albert de Rions. Mahan traces in detail how it was destroyed:


Mutiny from below. Starting with the Toulon riots of 1789, where De Rions — described by Suffren as the finest officer in the navy — was dragged through the streets by a mob, beaten, and imprisoned, while the National Assembly declared there was no one to blame. Similar incidents followed at Brest, Rochefort, Cherbourg, and in the West Indies colonies. Officers could not enforce discipline because the civil authorities would not support them.


Emigration. By July 1791, more than three-quarters of the old officer corps had left the service. Mahan attributes this less to royalist sentiment than to the utter subversion of discipline, which destroyed the professional pride and self-respect without which military service is meaningless.


Misguided reorganization. The Constituent Assembly’s naval reorganization of April 1790 blurred the boundary between naval and merchant service, gave merchant captains almost interchangeable status with naval officers, and provided so few inducements to full naval career commitment that a commercial boom could have stripped the fleet of its best men. Mahan is precise: the requirement for the lieutenancy allowed a man to split his professional years between merchant and naval service until age forty, by which time the formative period of military habit had been lost.


Convention-era purges. The Legislative Assembly and Convention lowered qualifications repeatedly. The decree of October 7, 1793 required all officers to be posted for public denunciation — seamen and citizens invited to send written accusations — with the decision reached by majority vote of a popular assembly including all seamen of the district. Promotion was filled by popular nomination from similar bodies. Admiral Villaret Joyeuse — himself a transitional figure who had entered from the auxiliary navy — quotes the results: not the most skilled and patriotic officers were promoted, but the most intriguing and the most fluent in patriotic phraseology.


The Terror. D’Estaing, D’Orléans (admiral of France), Kersaint, and Grimouard were guillotined. The greatest admirals of the previous war — D’Orvilliers, De Grasse, Guichen, Suffren — had already died before the Terror could reach them.


Ideological destruction of the gunner corps. The ten thousand trained seamen-gunners maintained since 1763 were abolished in 1794 on the motion of Jean Bon Saint-André, the Revolution’s naval commissioner, on the grounds that it was aristocratic for any class of men to have exclusive right to fight at sea. The effect on gunnery accuracy was immediate and documented: Mahan gives several comparative engagement statistics showing French ships consistently suffering several times the casualties they inflicted on equivalent British opponents in one-on-one actions.


Material conditions. Parallel to the personnel disaster, the ships themselves deteriorated: no spare spars or rigging, no stores, scurvy among crews who were within sight of the French coast, men going to sea without change of clothing. Pay was fifteen months in arrears by 1801. The condition of ships sent on critical missions — the 1796 Irish expedition, the 1798 Egyptian expedition with condemned ships and guns that could not bear their proper batteries — is documented from French admirals’ own reports.
The British navy by contrast. The Royal Navy had its own problems: pay unchanged since Charles II, brutal press-gang, harsh variable discipline, chronic stores shortages on foreign station. Mahan documents the British mutinies of the mid-1790s in detail, noting their disciplined and reasonable character by comparison with French mutiny — seamen maintaining military forms, demanding fair complaints, stopping short of hanged officers when the admiral took responsibility. The British navy’s strength lay in its continuous professional tradition, its officer corps trained in the previous war (the lists of 1793 show names who had fought under Keppel, Rodney, and Howe now commanding alongside those who would serve under Hood, Jervis, Nelson, and Collingwood), and its institutional memory of supply management: a reserve-stores system adopted in 1783 and tested in the mobilizations of 1790 and 1791 allowed Britain to double its ships-of-the-line in commission within weeks of the 1793 declaration.
The allied navies. Spain had 76 ships-of-the-line on paper; in practice its officers were incompetent, its crews press-ganged from streets and jails, its administration decayed. Nelson’s letters from Cadiz in 1793 document this in the bluntest terms (“they cannot make men”). Holland’s ships were mostly too shallow for line-of-battle and in poor material condition. Portugal and Naples provided useful early support in the Mediterranean but were neutralized as French armies advanced. Napoleon himself, Mahan argues, never understood why his navy failed — repeatedly attributing it to lack of courage rather than to the irreplaceable professional destruction his own revolution had wrought. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter III — The General Political and Strategic Conditions, and the Events of 1793
Mahan opens with the strategic map at the moment general war begins. France is surrounded on all land frontiers — Austria, Prussia, Spain, Sardinia, Piedmont — except the Swiss mountain border, and faces Britain at sea. But the coalition is not a unified instrument: Austria and Prussia are rivals for German preponderance, they had each been France’s ally within living memory, they distrust each other’s military intentions, and they were “unable from mutual distrust and their military traditions to act in concert.” The revolutionary armies could not be dispersed by a coalition that could not cooperate; the Committee of Public Safety, brutal as it was, produced unity of command that the allies lacked. Mahan’s strategic thesis for the chapter: the same levée en masse that raised France’s land armies could not raise a navy, and could not repair the officer corps; therefore Britain’s task was clear — hold the sea, sustain the allies financially, and wait for the French navy’s structural weakness to tell.
Toulon (1793) is this chapter’s operational centerpiece. The royalist faction within the city handed the port and its fleet to Admiral Hood. The British occupied it from August to December, holding thirty French ships-of-the-line. The French recapture — directed by a young artillery officer named Bonaparte, whose battery placement on the heights made Hood’s continued occupation of the harbor impossible — is analyzed as a strategic loss disproportionate to the tactical effort: ten thousand troops evacuated or captured, a French fleet burned or taken, and one of France’s two major Mediterranean bases lost for the duration. Mahan reads Toulon as proof that land armies driven by revolutionary energy could recover what naval weakness could not prevent the enemy from seizing — but that the naval consequences (a drastically reduced battle fleet, further degradation of trained seamen) would be permanent. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter IV — The West Indies, 1793–1810
Mahan covers the entire Caribbean theatre in one chapter spanning seventeen years — a deliberate structural choice that emphasizes the theatre’s unity as a strategic problem. The West Indies were the prize colonial economy: Saint-Domingue, Martinique, Guadeloupe together produced the commerce that financed French Atlantic naval operations. British strategy was straightforward — seize the islands, cut off French colonial revenue — and it largely succeeded for Martinique and several smaller islands by early 1794. But Guadeloupe was recaptured almost immediately by a French force under the commissioner Victor Hugues, who armed the slave population under the banner of the Republic and conducted a guerrilla war the British could not suppress. Saint-Domingue became a catastrophe for both sides: the Haitian Revolution, the death of Toussaint Louverture in a French prison, the eventual destruction of the expeditionary army sent by Bonaparte in 1801-02 — Mahan reads this entire sequence as a demonstration that sea power could seize islands but not govern them against a determined population in a lethal climate. Yellow fever killed more British soldiers than French arms. By 1810 Britain had most of the French Caribbean islands but the strategic utility of the Caribbean theatre had been exhausted by the disease and the distance. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter V — The Naval Campaign of May 1794, and the Battle of the First of June
The first major fleet engagement of the war is set up by Mahan as a strategic paradox. France needed grain desperately; a convoy from America was approaching; Villaret Joyeuse’s fleet had to cover it. Howe’s Channel fleet had to intercept. The outcome was a French tactical defeat (six ships of the line captured or sunk, Howe breaking the French line in the classic manner) combined with a French strategic success (the grain convoy got through). Mahan uses this duality to make his sharpest point about the difference between British and French naval cultures: the British fought to destroy the enemy fleet; the French fought to accomplish an objective and were willing to sacrifice the fleet to do so. The disproportion of casualties — the standard ratio of British versus French killed and wounded in a period engagement showing French gunnery consistently inferior — is documented against the specific ships engaged. The professional composition of Villaret Joyeuse’s officer corps at this date (from Chapter II: the commander-in-chief had been a lieutenant in 1791, his two flag-officers a lieutenant and a sub-lieutenant, most captains merchant officers or boatswains) is presented as the structural explanation for why the tactical outcome was foregone. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter VI — The Year 1794 in the Atlantic and on the Continent
The 1794 Atlantic campaign’s centerpiece is not a battle but an administrative disaster: the Brest fleet sent out in December by the Committee of Public Safety’s order on a mid-winter Bay of Biscay cruise, with ships badly equipped, crews in rags without changes of clothing, and no clear operational objective. The fleet’s condition — documented from French admirals’ own letters — illustrates the supply failure that Chapter II described theoretically. On land, 1794 was a year of French strategic recovery: the armies reconquering Belgium, Austria retreating from the Netherlands, Prussia beginning to negotiate a separate peace. Britain’s political and financial role as the coalition’s sustainer was becoming clear: without British subsidies, none of the continental powers could maintain their war effort. Mahan traces how Britain’s dominance at sea, which prevented France from taxing its colonies or reaching its American credit, was the direct enabler of British financial capacity to sustain the land war through others. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter VII — The Year 1795 in the Atlantic and on the Continent
1795 marks the effective end of the First Coalition as a continental force. Spain makes peace with France (Treaty of Basel, July); Prussia follows; Holland is converted by French armies into the Batavian Republic, switching from British ally to French satellite. The Dutch fleet’s fate becomes one of naval history’s more improbable incidents: frozen in the Texel in January 1795, it is captured by a French hussar regiment riding across the ice — a cavalry charge against ships-of-the-line. Britain loses a substantial allied naval contingent and gains instead a new potential enemy fleet. The Battle of Île de Groix (June 1795) — another French squadron engagement against superior British force — produces the same pattern as the First of June: French losses disproportionate to British, gunnery statistics again showing the structural inferiority documented in Chapter II. Mahan notes that at this engagement five French ships under the fire of three British for several hours inflicted thirteen casualties on the enemy; a few days later three French ships struck with six hundred seventy killed and wounded. By the end of 1795 Britain stands effectively alone against France on the continent, with Austria still technically at war but increasingly isolated. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter VIII — The Mediterranean and Italy, 1793–1797; Cape St. Vincent
The Mediterranean theatre from 1793 to 1797 is a single sustained argument: that the ability to maintain a naval presence in the Mediterranean — sustaining Austro-Sardinian operations, threatening French coastal communications, providing a base for British political leverage in Italy — could not survive the French army’s success on land. When Bonaparte’s Italian campaign began cutting off Austrian forces in 1796, the British position at Corsica and in the central Mediterranean became untenable; Lord Jervis withdrew the fleet from the Mediterranean entirely. The chapter then narrates the return. Spain’s entry as a French ally in 1796 placed a large (if poor-quality, per Chapter II) Spanish fleet in Jervis’s path. At Cape St. Vincent (February 14, 1797), Jervis with fifteen ships-of-the-line confronted twenty-seven Spanish. The tactical core of the engagement is Nelson’s unauthorized break from the British line: seeing the Spanish van about to escape the engagement entirely, Nelson wore his ship out of formation and placed it across the Spanish course, compelling hand-to-hand fighting between his single ship and the Spanish van until other British ships could come up. Mahan uses this action as a demonstration of everything the French navy lacked: the professional initiative, the willingness to accept personal responsibility for a deviation from orders, the ship-handling capacity to execute the maneuver under fire. Jervis’s famous remark — “I do not care, Sir William, how many ships there are, for I am sure of one of them” — Mahan cites as the expression of British naval culture at its most concentrated. Austria, defeated at Campo Formio in October 1797, dissolves the First Coalition. Britain stands alone. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter IX — The Mediterranean, 1797–1798; the Egyptian Expedition; the Battle of the Nile
Britain returns to the Mediterranean after Cape St. Vincent, and Nelson’s Mediterranean command begins. The Egyptian expedition is analyzed as the most ambitious French strategic stroke of the entire war and the clearest demonstration of why sea power determined its outcome. Bonaparte’s plan — seize Egypt, threaten India through the overland route, cut British commerce in the East — was coherent at the level of grand strategy. Its weakness was operational: the fleet sailed almost without spare rigging or stores, three of thirteen ships-of-the-line were not fit for sea, and the entire operation depended on avoiding Nelson’s fleet long enough to land the army. Nelson twice misguessed the expedition’s destination — once at Alexandria, finding it empty, then ranging east — before returning to find the French fleet anchored in Aboukir Bay. The Battle of the Nile (August 1, 1798) is Mahan’s strategic set-piece. Nelson attacked without waiting for tactical formation, sending ships inside the French line as well as outside — exploiting the fact that Brueys, anchoring in shoal water to protect his shoreward side, had not cleared his guns on that side or given his crews enough room to run them out. Thirteen of seventeen French ships-of-the-line were taken or destroyed; Brueys himself was killed. The consequence Mahan emphasizes: with the fleet gone, the army in Egypt was cut off absolutely from France, Malta fell to Britain, and the powers of Eastern Europe — Austria, Russia, the Ottoman Empire — could join a Second Coalition knowing British sea power would sustain them. The Nile is, in Mahan’s account, the battle that made Waterloo possible. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter X — The Mediterranean, 1799–1801; Syria; Admiral Bruix; Bonaparte Returns
Napoleon’s Syrian expedition and the siege of Acre (March–May 1799) are analyzed as a demonstration of sea power’s leverage at the tactical level. The British naval squadron under Sidney Smith did two decisive things: it supplied the Acre garrison with naval artillery (without which the town could not have held), and it intercepted the French siege train at sea — the heavy guns without which Napoleon could not breach Acre’s walls. Napoleon had the army but not the means; Smith had the means. The siege failed; plague was ravaging the French force; Napoleon retreated to Egypt. Mahan compares this to the Nile’s strategic logic: the army that sea power cannot supply cannot operate, regardless of its tactical quality.
Admiral Bruix’s incursion of the Brest fleet into the Mediterranean in 1799 receives extended analysis as the one genuine strategic opportunity France had to recover its Mediterranean position — and the clearest example of French naval command failure. Bruix entered the Mediterranean with twenty-five ships-of-the-line, evading the watching British squadrons. He could have joined the Spanish fleet, reinforced Egypt, and threatened the British position at multiple points simultaneously. He declined battle repeatedly, accomplished nothing, and returned to Brest. Mahan is dry but conclusive: the fleet was in the Mediterranean; the moment existed; the professional capacity and the command nerve to use it did not. Napoleon’s return to France — slipping through British-controlled waters in a fast frigate — is noted as a personal exception that required individual luck and speed, not a replicable naval operation. Malta falls to Britain; the French army in Egypt surrenders to combined British-Ottoman-naval pressure. The Second Coalition collapses from Austrian defeat on land, but the Mediterranean is British. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Chapter XI — The Atlantic, 1796–1801; the Brest Blockades; the Irish Expeditions
The Atlantic chapters return to the period covered by Chapters VI–VII, now tracing the Brest blockade and the French attempts on Ireland in the same years. Both expeditions — 1796 (Hoche’s fifteen thousand troops scattered at Bantry Bay by storm) and 1798 (Humbert’s landing in Connaught with about a thousand men, briefly victorious at Castlebar, quickly surrounded and defeated, Wolfe Tone captured at sea in the follow-up squadron) — are presented as strategic logic that could only be executed with naval quality France did not possess. The design was sound: Ireland was genuinely restive; a French army landing in force would have drawn British forces away from the Channel and the continent; if it survived long enough for a rising to develop, it could have changed the war’s character. What failed was execution.
The 1796 expedition — the most serious in scale — scattered at Bantry Bay because French seamanship in a North Atlantic winter gale was unequal to maintaining formation and landing in difficult conditions. Mahan contrasts this with British fleet operations in the same winter conditions and argues the difference was entirely the professional destruction documented in Chapter II. The Brest blockade is analyzed in its two forms: close blockade (maintaining a constant watching force off the port mouth, with its risks of lee shores and winter weather) and open-sea or distant blockade (watching from a position that could intercept a sortie without risking the watching ships on the coast). Mahan traces the strategic consequence of each approach for what the French could and could not attempt, and notes that British commanders alternated between the two as weather and strategic urgency dictated — but that whichever form was used, the practical result was the same: French expeditionary forces could not reliably concentrate, embark, and sail before British reaction closed the window. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution.txt]
Coverage Guide


Sea power thesis applied to the French Revolutionary Wars — This is the wiki’s primary source for the Mahanian argument: that naval supremacy, not land armies, determined the war’s outcome. The Preface and Chapters I, II, and IX are the densest passages for the theoretical argument.


Destruction of the French navy, 1789–1794 — Chapter II is the single most detailed account in the wiki’s sources of how the Revolution destroyed French naval capacity: mutiny, emigration, ideological reorganization, gunner corps abolition, and supply collapse. Cross-reference with paganel-histoire-napoleon-1815 for the political context and with almanach-imperial-1808 for the 1808 personnel structure that partially replaced it.


European diplomatic background, 1783–1793 — Chapter I covers the Scheldt question, Russian expansion toward the Black Sea and Baltic, the Eastern Question, the path to the First Coalition, and British strategic repositioning more thoroughly than any other source in the wiki. Particularly strong on how the Levant and Egypt were already recognized strategic prizes before Napoleon acted on them.


Battle of the First of June (1794) — Chapter V. The first great fleet action of the war, analysed tactically and strategically.


Battle of Cape St. Vincent (1797) — Chapter VIII. Jervis and Nelson’s defeat of the Spanish fleet; Nelson’s independent tactical decision analysed.


The Egyptian Expedition and Battle of the Nile (1798) — Chapter IX. The strategic logic of the Egyptian venture, Nelson’s Nile campaign, and the Second Coalition’s formation.


The Irish expeditions (1796, 1798) — Chapter XI. France’s attempts to use Ireland as a strategic lever against Britain; their failure attributed to Brest blockade and French seamanship limits.


West Indies theatre — Chapter IV. The colonial war in the Caribbean: British captures, French recaptures, Saint-Domingue, yellow fever. Cross-reference with herbin-statistique-france-1803 for the colonial economy at stake.


Comparative navy quality — British, French, Spanish, Dutch — Chapter II’s closing sections assess all four navies. Nelson’s letters about the Spanish fleet at Cadiz are quoted extensively.


Brest blockade strategy — Chapter XI. The mechanics of Atlantic blockade: close versus open-sea watching, weather constraints, effect on French operational planning.


Quality
Clean prose from an epub of professional quality. Mahan’s text is heavily footnoted — numbered citations appear inline in the OCR as {1}, {2}, etc. — and the notes section is a separate HTML file. The prose is 19th-century formal English: dense, precise, and well-organised. No significant OCR degradation; this is among the most readable sources in the wiki. Mahan is an American naval officer writing in 1892, not a Frenchman writing in 1815 like Paganel; his perspective is Anglo-American strategic analysis rather than French political judgment. Both are valuable but different lenses.

sources/mahan-sea-power-french-revolutio.title: Mahan — The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, Vol. II (1892)
sources/mahan-sea-power-french-revolutio.content:
Rear Admiral Alfred Thayer Mahan, The Influence of Sea Power upon the French Revolution and Empire, 1793–1812, Volume II. Published 1892. This volume continues Mahan’s great thesis from Volume I (which covered 1783–1801) through the remainder of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, from the Second Coalition through Trafalgar, the Continental System, and Napoleon’s Russian invasion. The text runs to approximately 2 MB across eight chapters (XII–XIX) plus footnotes and an index.
Volume II covers the period from roughly 1798 to 1812. The two great set-pieces are the Battle of Copenhagen (1801) and the Trafalgar campaign (1805), but the volume’s analytical weight falls equally on the economic warfare that dominated the later years — the Berlin and Milan Decrees, the British Orders in Council, and the attempt by both belligerents to strangle each other through commerce. The final chapter (XIX) is Mahan’s comprehensive summary of the function of sea power in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, drawing together the threads of both volumes into a single argument about British naval policy, national strategy, and the structural sources of Britain’s victory. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Volume II opens with France in crisis under the Directory and the Second Coalition pressing on all frontiers; Bonaparte’s coup of Brumaire and the subsequent Italian campaign shatter the Coalition, but his attempt to isolate Britain through the Armed Neutrality of 1800 is broken by Nelson at Copenhagen. The Peace of Amiens (1802–1803) provides a brief interlude, then war resumes with Napoleon preparing the invasion of England and assembling the great flotilla at Boulogne. The Trafalgar campaign — the only great naval campaign ever planned by Napoleon — occupies two chapters and ends with the destruction of the Franco-Spanish fleet and the permanent frustration of any invasion attempt. The final three chapters turn to the economic war: the commerce raiding that preceded the Berlin Decree, the Continental System in full operation (1806–1812), and the conclusive summary of sea power’s role in the war’s outcome.
Full Contents Map
Chapter XII — Events on the Continent, 1798–1800. Disorders of France under the Directory. Disastrous War of the Second Coalition. Establishment of the Consulate. Bonaparte overthrows Austria and frames against Great Britain the Armed Neutrality of 1800. Peace of Lunéville with Austria.
The longest chapter in the volume, covering the period from Bonaparte’s Syrian campaign through the establishment of the Consulate. Mahan opens with the collapse of the Neapolitan campaign (November 1798) — a premature blow instigated by Nelson after the Nile — and traces the building of the Second Coalition: Russia, Austria, England, Turkey, Naples, Portugal, and the Two Sicilies united against France. The Coalition’s early successes are real but uncoordinated: Suwarrow’s Russian army sweeps through northern Italy, the French are driven from the peninsula, and Austria presses into Switzerland. But the Coalition’s fatal weakness, Mahan argues, was the same as the First’s — powers with divergent aims acting in mutual distrust. Russia’s withdrawal after Suwarrow’s disagreements with the Austrian council leaves the Coalition crippled; Bonaparte’s return from Egypt and the coup of 18 Brumaire (November 1799) give France a unified command just as the Coalition loses its coherence. The chapter follows Bonaparte’s Italian campaign of 1800 — the crossing of the Saint Bernard, the battle of Marengo (June 14), and Moreau’s concurrent victory at Hohenlinden — which shatters Austria. The Peace of Lunéville (February 1801) removes Austria from the war, leaving Britain isolated. At the same moment, Bonaparte is constructing the Armed Neutrality of 1800: Russia, Sweden, Denmark, and Prussia combined against British maritime rights, closing the Baltic to British shipping and challenging the right of search. Mahan presents this as Bonaparte’s most coherent attempt to counter British sea power through political combination rather than naval action. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XIII — Events of 1801. British Expedition to the Baltic—Battle of Copenhagen—Bonaparte’s futile attempts to contest control of the Sea—His Continental Policy—Preliminaries of Peace with Great Britain, October, 1801—Influence of Sea Power so far upon the Course of the Revolution.
The chapter’s centerpiece is the Battle of Copenhagen (April 2, 1801), narrated with the tactical precision characteristic of Mahan’s battle pieces. The British government, with Britain isolated after Lunéville and the Baltic closed, assembles a fleet of eighteen sail-of-the-line at Yarmouth under Sir Hyde Parker, with Nelson as second-in-command. Mahan traces the diplomatic negotiations with Denmark that precede the battle — the British demands, the Danish refusal, the decision to force the Sound. The tactical challenge of Copenhagen is presented as one of the most difficult of the age: the Danish fleet anchored in a shoal-strewn channel, protected by shore batteries, the Trekroner fortress, and a line of hulks and floating batteries. Nelson’s decision to run the channel from the south, his careful sounding operations aboard a hired pilot-boat the night before, Parker’s signal of recall, and Nelson’s legendary act (turning his telescope to his blind eye, saying “I really do not see the signal”) are all recounted. Mahan’s strategic point is classic: the Armed Neutrality, which had seemed to Bonaparte a brilliant diplomatic counter to British sea power, was broken in a single morning because it rested on paper — on conventions between sovereigns — while British sea power rested on ships, men, and a professional navy that could act at distance. The Danish fleet was destroyed, the Coalition dissolved, and the Baltic reopened. Mahan then traces the preliminaries of peace: the evacuation of Egypt (the French army in Egypt surrenders in September 1801), the resignation of Pitt, the negotiation with the new Addington ministry, and the signature of the Preliminaries of London (October 1, 1801). He closes with a short assessment of sea power’s influence to this point in the war, noting that at every critical juncture — the Nile, the Second Coalition, the Armed Neutrality — British naval action had determined the outcome of political combinations that seemed overwhelming on land. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XIV — Outline of Events from the Signature of the Preliminaries to the Rupture of the Peace of Amiens. October, 1801–May, 1803.
The Peace of Amiens (March 1802) was the longest interval of peace between Britain and France in the entire war — fourteen months. Mahan’s chapter is an anatomy of why it failed. The preliminaries had seemed to settle the main outlines: Britain would restore most colonial conquests (except Trinidad and Ceylon), France would leave Naples and the Papal States, and Malta would be returned to the Knights of St. John under a guarantee of independence. But almost immediately, Mahan shows, Bonaparte violated the spirit of the treaty: French troops remained in the Batavian Republic, French influence expanded in Italy (the Cisalpine Republic was transformed into the Italian Republic with Bonaparte as president), and Piedmont was annexed outright. Bonaparte’s interventions in Switzerland (the Act of Mediation, 1803) further alarmed Britain. Mahan reads these not as random aggressions but as a consistent pattern: Bonaparte was using the peace to consolidate French domination of the Continent, and he never intended the treaty as a final settlement. Britain’s response was belated and divided: the Addington ministry was accused of weakness, Pitt criticized the peace from opposition, and public opinion swung from relief to fear as Bonaparte’s intentions became clear. By early 1803 the breach was irreparable; Britain declared war on May 18, 1803. The chapter closes with Mahan’s assessment that the Peace of Amiens was never a real peace — it was an armed truce in which both sides prepared for the next round, and the only question was which side would be readier when it came. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XV — The Trafalgar Campaign to the Spanish Declaration of War. May, 1803–December, 1804. Preparations for the Invasion of England. The Great Flotilla. Napoleon’s Military and Naval Combinations and British Naval Strategy. Essential Unity of Napoleon’s Purpose. Causes of Spanish War.
The opening of the military narrative after the resumption of war, and the first of two Trafalgar campaign chapters. Napoleon’s grand design is presented: an invasion of England, the decisive stroke that would end British sea power at its source. The preparations at Boulogne are described in detail — the flotilla of hundreds of flat-bottomed barges, the Camp de Boulogne with 150,000 men encamped and training, the press of shipping in the Channel ports. But Mahan’s analytical purpose is to show that Napoleon understood the invasion could not succeed without at least temporary naval control of the Channel, and that he therefore framed the most elaborate naval combination ever attempted: a series of sorties by squadrons from Toulon, Rochefort, Brest, and the Spanish ports, designed to draw the British fleet into the West Indies, then double back and concentrate in the Channel for a brief window of superiority.
The chapter traces the early attempts at this plan. Missiessy escapes from Rochefort in January 1804 and reaches Martinique; Villeneuve sails from Toulon but is forced back by weather. Napoleon’s pressure on Spain — whose treasure fleets from America Britain had intercepted — forces Spain toward war despite her reluctance. The Spanish declaration of war (December 1804) brings the French-Spanish alliance into force, giving Napoleon a combined fleet that matches the British in numbers. Mahan devotes considerable space to the British defensive strategy: the close blockade of Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, and Ferrol; the strain this placed on British ships, crews, and supplies; the constant need to guess which sortie was the real one. The chapter closes with the strategic situation at the end of 1804: Napoleon’s plan intact but not yet executed, the British holding their breath, and Nelson returning to command of the Mediterranean station after a brief rest. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XVI — The Trafalgar Campaign—Concluded. Successive Modifications of Napoleon’s Plan. Narrative of Naval Movements. Final Failure of Napoleon’s Naval Combinations. War with Austria, and Battle of Austerlitz. Battle of Trafalgar. Vital Change Imposed Upon Napoleon’s Policy by the Result of the Naval Campaign.
The climax of the volume and one of the finest sustained passages in Mahan’s entire oeuvre — a combined narrative of the Trafalgar campaign, the Ulm-Austerlitz campaign, and their interaction. Mahan treats them as one campaign fought on two elements: Napoleon on land, the Royal Navy at sea, each trying to achieve a decisive concentration before the enemy could react.
The narrative is intricate. Villeneuve escapes from Toulon in March 1805, eludes Nelson (who is guarding the Strait of Gibraltar), reaches the West Indies, and joins the Ferrol squadron. Nelson pursues across the Atlantic — Mahan emphasizes that Nelson guessed the destination and went straight, while Villeneuve’s orders were to avoid action. Once in the West Indies, Villeneuve misses Nelson by days; the French fleet finds no strategic opportunity (the British islands take warning, colonial operations stall) and Villeneuve, against Napoleon’s explicit orders, returns to Europe rather than waiting. He is sighted off Cape Finisterre on July 22 by Calder’s squadron; the action is indecisive (two Spanish ships taken, Churchillian weather obscures the rest), and Villeneuve puts into Ferrol and then Cadiz rather than proceeding to Brest as ordered. Napoleon, waiting at Boulogne with his army and flotilla ready, hears that the combined fleet has gone to Cadiz instead of Brest. In a rage — Mahan quotes Napoleon’s letter to Decrès: “What a navy! What an admiral!” — he abandons the invasion of England, turns the Army of England eastward, and marches against Austria.
The land campaign is summarised: Ulm (October 1805), where Mack’s Austrian army is surrounded and captured before it can join the Russians; Austerlitz (December 2, 1805), where Napoleon destroys the combined Austro-Russian army in one of his greatest battles. But at sea, on October 21, 1805, off Cape Trafalgar, Nelson falls upon the combined Franco-Spanish fleet of thirty-three ships-of-the-line with his twenty-seven. Mahan’s account of the battle is tactical and analytical: the British approach in two columns, the break in the allied line, the yardarm-to-yardarm engagement, Nelson’s wound and death, the capture or destruction of nineteen enemy ships without the loss of a single British vessel. The strategic consequence is not that Britain gains control of the sea — it already had that — but that Napoleon’s naval arm is broken for the rest of the war. The Emperor would never again be able to assemble a fleet that could challenge the Royal Navy in a line-of-battle engagement. Mahan’s closing argument is that Trafalgar imposed a vital change on Napoleon’s policy: unable to fight Britain at sea, he turned to the economic warfare of the Continental System — the attempt to starve Britain by closing every European port to her trade. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XVII — The Warfare against Commerce during the French Revolution and Empire, to the Berlin Decree. 1793–1806.
A turning point in the volume’s structure. Mahan steps back from narrative to analysis, tracing the development of commerce raiding as a weapon against British trade from the opening of the war in 1793 through the eve of the Berlin Decree in 1806. The chapter covers the privateering system of the French Republic, the convoy system adopted by the British, the legal and diplomatic disputes over neutral rights, and the escalating measures of both sides. Mahan argues that commerce warfare was the one area where French naval weakness did not tell: a single privateer or small squadron could do disproportionate damage to British shipping, and the French government consistently overestimated the effect. He provides statistical evidence of British shipping losses year by year, showing that while losses were real and painful, they never approached the levels that would force Britain to sue for peace. The British merchant marine, with its enormous tonnage and global reach, absorbed losses that would have shattered any smaller trading nation. The chapter also covers the British reaction — Orders in Council, the blockade decrees, the tightening of the convoy system — and the steady expansion of the definition of contraband. By 1806, Mahan shows, both belligerents had moved far beyond the Law of Nations as it had been understood in 1793: the war was consuming the legal order as surely as it consumed men and treasure. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XVIII — The Warfare against Commerce, 1806–1812. The Berlin and Milan Decrees of Napoleon, 1806 and 1807. The British Orders in Council, 1807–1809. Analysis of the Policy of these Measures of the two Belligerents. Outline of Contemporary Leading Events.
The Continental System in full operation. Mahan opens with Napoleon’s Berlin Decree (November 21, 1806), issued from the Prussian capital after Jena: the British Isles declared in a state of blockade, all commerce and correspondence with Britain forbidden, all British subjects in French-controlled territory declared prisoners of war, all British goods and merchandise declared lawful prize. The Decree was not, Mahan argues, a military measure in any ordinary sense — it was economic war, an attempt to destroy British commerce by closing the entire European continent to its trade.
The chapter traces the system’s enforcement and its evasion. Napoleon demands that every state under his control or influence adopt the Decree; the British retaliate with the Orders in Council (1807, 1809), blockading any port that excluded British goods and requiring neutral vessels to call at British ports for inspection. Mahan analyzes the effect on European economies: ports rotting idle, colonial goods vanishing from markets, smuggling becoming a universal industry, and the resentment of European populations growing against the system that was impoverishing them to serve French strategic ends. The Portuguese royal family’s flight to Brazil under British escort (November 1807) is a set-piece illustrating the interaction of naval power and continental politics: the British could not save Portugal on land, but they could preserve the Portuguese crown and empire across the Atlantic. Napoleon’s attempt to close the entire Baltic by seizing the Danish fleet (the second Copenhagen expedition, 1807 — Canning’s preemptive strike that carried off the Danish fleet before Napoleon could take it) is narrated as a parallel to Nelson’s 1801 operation.
The chapter closes with the expansion of the system into Russia — the Tilsit agreement (July 1807) in which Alexander I accepted the Continental System — and the first cracks in the structure: the Peninsular War (1808), the Austrian revival (1809), the growing tension between Napoleon and the Tsar over the blockade’s enforcement. Mahan’s treatment is analytical rather than narrative: he uses the events as evidence for the proposition that economic warfare, however devastating to neutrals and civilians, cannot by itself defeat a nation with command of the sea and access to world markets. The Continental System inflicted serious hardship on Britain but did not bring her to terms; it simultaneously created the conditions for Napoleon’s eventual downfall by alienating the populations and rulers he needed to keep the system closed. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Chapter XIX — Summary—The Function of Sea Power and the Policy of Great Britain in the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.
The concluding chapter of the entire two-volume work, and Mahan’s final statement of his thesis. He opens with Britain’s unpreparedness in 1792 — Pitt’s small navy estimates, the expectation of peace, the complete absence of any plan for the war that was coming — and traces the development of British strategy through the twenty-three-year struggle. The chapter is not a narrative but an argument, organised around the question: what did sea power actually contribute to the defeat of Revolutionary and Napoleonic France?
Mahan identifies seven functions of British sea power in the war:


Strategic mobility. Sea power allowed Britain to shift military force from one theatre to another faster than any continental power could march: troops landed in the West Indies, the Mediterranean, Portugal, Holland, and the Peninsula, at times of Britain’s choosing.


Economic pressure on France. British control of the sea cut France off from its colonial revenues, destroyed its overseas trade, and forced the French treasury to rely on continental exactions and plunder — a method that worked in the short term but exhausted the territories subjected to it.


Sustaining the coalitions. British subsidies — made possible by a thriving commerce protected by the navy — kept the Austrian, Russian, and Prussian armies in the field. Without British gold, Mahan argues, no continental coalition could have sustained war against France for more than a single campaign.


The blockade of French naval ports. The continuous watching of Brest, Toulon, Rochefort, and later Cadiz prevented the French fleet from concentrating, exercising, or intervening decisively in any theatre. Mahan emphasizes that the blockades were not passive but aggressive: they forced the French to sea at disadvantage, or kept them in port where they could not influence events.


Direct naval action. The Nile (1798), Copenhagen (1801), and Trafalgar (1805) were the three great fleet actions of the war. Each destroyed an enemy fleet and each had immediate strategic consequences: the Nile formed the Second Coalition, Copenhagen broke the Armed Neutrality, Trafalgar made the invasion of England impossible forever.


Protection of British commerce. The convoy system preserved the flow of trade that underlay British credit, taxation, and subsidy capacity. Mahan provides comparative loss statistics to show that while commerce raiding hurt, it never approached the level needed to force Britain’s surrender.


The Peninsular War as the culminating demonstration. The British army in Portugal and Spain under Wellington was supplied, reinforced, and sustained entirely by sea. The French could not turn the British flank because they could not control the sea; they could not starve the British army because it was fed by sea; they could not invade England because the navy stood in the way. The Peninsular War, in Mahan’s reading, was the final demonstration of what sea power meant: not a weapon of conquest but the condition that made endurance possible.


Mahan closes with a comparative assessment of Pitt’s war policy. Pitt’s great achievement, he argues, was not any single strategic decision but the steady refusal to treat sea power as an end in itself. Pitt understood that the navy’s function was to enable a comprehensive strategy in which British commercial strength, coalition diplomacy, and limited continental intervention worked together. The moments when British policy faltered — the Peace of Amiens, the costly West Indian expeditions, the hesitation over the Baltic in 1800 — were moments when this comprehensive view was lost. The final victory, Mahan concludes, belonged not to any single battle but to the twenty-three-year application of sea power as an instrument of national policy, sustained through changing ministries, fluctuating popular support, and the immense strain of the longest war in modern European history. ^[source: raw/mahan-sea-power-french-revolution-vol2.txt]
Coverage Guide


Battle of Copenhagen (1801) — Chapter XIII. The destruction of the Danish fleet and the breaking of the Armed Neutrality. Essential for understanding the Baltic theatre and the second of Mahan’s three great fleet actions.


The Trafalgar campaign — Chapters XV and XVI. The most extended naval narrative in the volume: Napoleon’s invasion plan, the great flotilla at Boulogne, the transatlantic chase, Villeneuve’s indecision, Calder’s action, and the Battle of Trafalgar itself. Cross-reference with standard naval histories for additional tactical detail.


Battle of Austerlitz and the Ulm campaign (1805) — Chapter XVI (integrated into the Trafalgar narrative). Mahan shows the interaction of the naval and land campaigns in 1805 as a single strategic event: Trafalgar made the Ulm-Austerlitz campaign possible because Napoleon abandoned the invasion of England.


The Peace of Amiens (1802–1803) — Chapter XIV. Mahan’s analysis of why the peace failed: Bonaparte’s consistent expansionism, British rearmament, and the structural impossibility of a durable settlement while Napoleon dominated the continent.


The Armed Neutrality of 1800 — Chapters XII–XIII. The diplomatic combination against British maritime rights and its destruction at Copenhagen.


Commerce raiding and the Economic War — Chapters XVII and XVIII. The longest treatment in either volume of the guerre de course, the Continental System, the Berlin and Milan Decrees, and the British Orders in Council. Chapter XVIII covers the period 1806–1812 in detail.


Mahan’s final synthesis — Chapter XIX. The only extended summary of sea power’s role across the entire 1793–1812 period. The seven-function framework is the most concise statement of Mahan’s argument in either volume.


Bonaparte’s rise and the Consulate — Chapter XII. The coup of 18 Brumaire, Marengo, Hohenlinden, and the Peace of Lunéville — the consolidation of Bonaparte’s power. Mahan reads these events through the lens of their naval and strategic implications.


Comparative navy quality — Throughout, but especially Chapters XIII (Baltic navies at Copenhagen) and XV (the condition of the Franco-Spanish fleet before Trafalgar). Mahan continues the argument from Vol. I, Chapter II about the institutional superiority of the British officer corps.


Quality
Clean text extracted from an epub of professional quality. Mahan’s text is heavily footnoted — most chapters contain several hundred numbered citations — and a substantial footnotes section is appended. The prose is 19th-century formal English: dense, precise, and argumentative. This volume contains Mahan’s most famous single sentence (“England expects that every man will do his duty”), his most quoted anecdote (Nelson’s blind eye at Copenhagen), and his most sustained analytical passage (Chapter XIX’s summary). No significant OCR degradation. Mahan is an American naval officer writing in 1892, not a Frenchman writing in 1815; his perspective is Anglo-American strategic analysis rather than French political judgment. Both volumes together form one of the foundation texts of modern naval theory.

sources/marmontel-memoires-3vols-1804.title: Jean-François Marmontel — Mémoires d'un père pour servir à l'instruction de ses enfans, 3 vols. (1804)
sources/marmontel-memoires-3vols-1804.content:
Jean-François Marmontel, Mémoires d’un père pour servir à l’instruction de ses enfans, 3 vols. Paris: 1804 (posthumous). Extracted raw text from Project Gutenberg ebooks: Vol. 1 (EBook #27773) approximately 2,887 lines and 517 KB; Vol. 2 (EBook #27807) approximately 2,806 lines and 584 KB; Vol. 3 (EBook #27808) approximately 2,887 lines and 574 KB. Marmontel (1723–1799) was a French writer, poet, philosophe, and academician — a leading literary figure of the Enlightenment generation. He was a contributor to the Encyclopédie, historiographer of France, and from 1783 secrétaire perpétuel of the Académie française. His memoirs, written in retirement during the Revolution, cover his entire life from childhood in Bort-les-Orgues (Bas-Limousin) through his Paris literary career under the ancien régime and his direct experience of the French Revolution, ending with his retreat to Abbeville in 1795. Books XII–XX (Volume 3) constitute a moderate-constitutionalist eyewitness account of the Revolution from its pre-1787 origins through the Terror, written by a man who had lived at the centre of the intellectual and institutional life of pre-revolutionary France and lost nearly everything in the revolutionary crisis. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Volumes and Book Structure
The complete memoirs run to 20 books across three volumes. The first two volumes (Books I–XI) cover Marmontel’s life under the ancien régime — his provincial origins, literary career, the salons, his role at the Mercure de France, and his academic life. The third volume (Books XII–XX) covers the Revolution and its aftermath.
Volume 1 — Books I–IV: Provincial Origins and Entry into Paris
Book I — Childhood and Education
But de l’auteur en écrivant ses Mémoires.—Description de Bort et de ses environs.—Souvenirs d’enfance.—Première éducation.—Défaut de mémoire.—Portrait de la mère de Marmontel et des autres membres de la famille.—Entrée au collège. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book II — Preceptor and Seminary
Séjour de Marmontel à Saint-Bonnet, et au château de Linars, comme précepteur.—Retraite au séminaire de Limoges.—Entretiens littéraires de Marmontel avec les directeurs du séminaire.—Présentation à l’évêque (Coetlosquet).—Plaisanteries et chansons de l’auteur contre les Anglais. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book III — Voltaire and First Literary Success
Première visite à Voltaire et conseils de celui-ci.—Premier logement et premières ressources.—Vauvenargues.—Bauvin.—L’Observateur littéraire.—Prix à l’Académie française.—Grande pénurie.—Procédé délicat de Voltaire.—Marmontel présenté à tous les gens de lettres de Paris. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book IV — Literary Life, Madame de Tencin, and the Marshal de Saxe
Liaison de Marmontel et de Mlle Marie Verrière.—Colère du maréchal de Saxe.—Double rupture.—Mariage de La Popelinière.—Son train de maison à Passy.—Lecture d’Aristomène chez Mme de Tencin.—Découverte de la cheminée secrète de Mme de Tencin.—Son salon. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Volume 2 — Books V–IX: Career, Salons, and Literary Work
Book V — Royal Service and Court Life
Entrée en fonctions de l’auteur auprès de M. de Marigny.—Qualités et défauts de celui-ci.—Vie de Marmontel à Versailles, à Marly, à Fontainebleau, à Compiègne.—Nouvelles liaisons; l’abbé de La Ville, Dubois, premier commis de la guerre.—Projets de l’abbé de La Ville pour la réunion des protestants.—Mesures adoptées par le gouvernement à ce sujet. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book VI — The Mercure de France and Madame Geoffrin’s Salon
Changements et progrès apportés à la composition du Mercure; collaborateurs recrutés par Marmontel: Malfilâtre, Colardeau, Thomas, J.-D. Le Roy, C.-N. Cochin.—Gallet et Panard.—Portrait de Mme Geoffrin.—Principaux habitués de son salon: d’Alembert, Mlle de Lespinasse, l’abbé Morellet, Diderot, l’abbé de La Porte, le comte de Creutz, etc.—Caractère de d’Alembert. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book VII — Reflections and Travels
Réflexions de Marmontel sur son passé à cette date et sur ses projets d’avenir.—Sa situation et celle de sa famille.—Voyage en compagnie de Gaulard.—Séjour à Bordeaux.—Mésaventures de Le Franc de Pompignan.—Arrêts à Toulouse, à Montpellier, à Nîmes, à Marseille. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book VIII — Diderot, Rousseau, and the Philosophe Circle
Récit fait par Diderot à Marmontel des origines de sa rupture avec Rousseau.—Relations de Jean-Jacques avec le baron d’Holbach et avec Hume.—Séjour de Marmontel à Saumur, près de sa soeur et de son beau-frère.—Visite au comte d’Argenson, retiré dans sa terre des Ormes.—Son salon. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book IX — Grétry and Musical Theatre
Séjours à Ménars.—Séjour à Maisons.—Le comte de Creutz présente Grétry à Marmontel.—Le Huron, Lucile, Sylvain, l’Ami de la maison, Zémire et Azor. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Volume 3 — Books X–XX: Marriage, Académie, and the Revolution
Book X — Marriage and Domestic Life
Mort de Mme Odde et de ses enfants.—Inquiétudes de Marmontel sur son propre avenir.—Mme et Mlle de Montigny, soeur et nièce de MM. Morellet.—Prédiction de l’abbé Maury à Marmontel.—Projets de bonheur.—Mariage de l’auteur et de Mlle de Montigny.—Naissance du premier enfant.—Vie de famille. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XI — Secrétaire Perpétuel of the Académie Française
Élection de Marmontel comme secrétaire perpétuel de l’Académie française.—Concert de M. de La Borde.—Réunion des amis de l’auteur à sa maison de campagne.—Mort d’un troisième enfant.—Pénélope, opéra.—Le Dormeur éveillé. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XII — Causes of the Revolution; Louis XVI and the Ministries
Coup d’oeil sur les causes de la Révolution.—Portrait de Louis XVI.—Rentrée en grâce du comte de Maurepas; son passé, ses vues, sa politique, ses principes.—Renvoi de Terray.—Vues de Turgot, son successeur.—Émeute de 1775.—Renvoi de Turgot, remplacé par Necker.—Renvoi et rappel de Necker. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XIII — Brienne, the Parlement, and the Pre-Revolution
Portrait de Brienne.—Ses luttes contre le Parlement au sujet des édits sur le timbre et sur l’impôt territorial.—Lit de justice.—Exil du Parlement à Troyes.—Continuation de la lutte.—Séance royale.—Mouvement d’opinion en faveur de la réunion des Etats généraux.—Exil du duc d’Orléans à Villers-Cotterets.—Lit de justice (8 mai 1788).—Examen du nouveau système judiciaire.—Résistance des Etats de Bretagne et de Dauphiné.—Ressources désastreuses imaginées par Brienne.—Sa démission.—Situation déplorable du Trésor et de l’agriculture.—Impopularité et suicide de Lamoignon.—Projets de Necker.—Seconde convocation des notables (3 novembre 1788).—Opinion de six bureaux touchant le mode de représentation du tiers aux Etats généraux.—Conseil d’État du 27 décembre 1788.—Choix de Versailles pour lieu de réunion des États.—Ce que voulait Necker et ce qui aurait pu arriver. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XIV — The Estates-General and the Electoral Assemblies
Marmontel membre de l’assemblée primaire du district des Feuillants et de l’assemblée électorale.—Rôle de Duport.—Influence des avocats, dans ces réunions préliminaires.—Target élu président de l’assemblée électorale aux Feuillants.—Choix des électeurs.—Élection du duc d’Orléans.—Rapports de Marmontel avec La Fayette et Sieyès.—Première fermentation à Paris.—Menaces d’Agnès de Lorme.—Frayeur et fermeté de l’assemblée électorale.—Ouverture solennelle des États généraux (5 mai 1789)—Discours de Necker.—Le tiers se refuse à la vérification des pouvoirs par chambre. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XV — The Third Estate and the Tennis Court Oath
Contestation entre le tiers et les deux autres ordres au sujet du mode de délibération et de la vérification des pouvoirs.—Arrêté pris le 10 juin par le tiers touchant cette vérification.—Autre arrêté (17 juin) spécifiant que le tiers s’érige en Assemblée nationale.—Arrêt du roi (23 juin).—La noblesse protesté.—Vote du clergé en faveur de la réunion des ordres.—Réunion des trois ordres.—Séance royale du 22 juin; rétablissement des trois ordres dans leurs premières délibérations.—Serment du Jeu de Paume.—Proposition de Necker au conseil.—Rappel de Necker; renvoi des ministres. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XVI — The July Crisis and the Fall of the Bastille
Imprévoyance de la cour.—Adresse au roi (rédigée par Mirabeau).—Réponse du roi.—Du droit de veto.—Renvoi des ministres.—Agitation dans Paris.—Charge du prince de Lambesc.—L’agitation redouble; on court aux armes.—Promesse imprudente du prévôt des marchands, Flesselles.—L’arsenal des Invalides est envahi.—Distribution d’armes par les électeurs au Palais royal.—Le tocsin sonne; on se porte en foule à la Bastille.—Élie et Hulin à la tête de la colonne.—De Launey capitule et ouvre les portes.—Massacre de De Launey et de ses gardes.—Massacre de Flesselles. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XVII — The Bastille’s Fall: Élie’s Eyewitness Account
Attaque et reddition de la Bastille.—Récit d’Élie, l’un des vainqueurs, recueilli par Marmontel.—Massacre de de Launey, de ses principaux officiers et de Flesselles.—Motion du baron de Marguerittes à l’Assemblée nationale.—Discussion.—Adresse au roi.—Le peuple de Paris veut avoir le roi dans ses murs.—Fermeté de l’Assemblée.—Scène à la séance du 14 au 15 juillet.—Le roi se rend à l’Assemblée.—Le roi répond à la députation de l’Assemblée sur le voeu du peuple de Paris.—Choix de La Fayette comme commandant de la milice parisienne.—Nomination de Bailly à la mairie de Paris.—Délibération sur le sort des fugitifs. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XVIII — The October Days and the Revolutionary Government
Discussion de la prérogative royale touchant la nomination des ministres.—Meurtre de Foulon et de Bertier.—Massacres commis en province.—Retour de Necker et arrêté d’amnistie qu’il obtient des électeurs de Paris.—Improbation de la cour.—Projet d’éloigner le roi orage de Versailles; fêtes données aux gardes du corps.—Scènes d’orgie.—Les 5 et 6 octobre.—Marche des femmes à Versailles.—Envahissement du château.—Meurtre des gardes du corps.—La famille royale ramenée à Paris.—Suite des journées d’octobre.—Vues sur la translation du siège du gouvernement.—Marmontel quitte la ville. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XIX — The Terror and Marmontel’s Retirement
Commencement de la Terreur.—Maladie et mort de Charpentier, précepteur des enfants de Marmontel.—Dom Honorat.—Retour à Abbeville; réflexions de l’auteur sur sa situation actuelle.—Gravité croissante des événements publics.—Lois des suspects.—Procès et jugement du roi.—Proscription des Girondins.—Attentat de Charlotte Corday contre Marat.—Mort des principaux Girondins.—Suppression des académies; la pétition des artistes; l’abbé Morellet.—Décrets contre les ex-nobles et ex-prêtres.—Émotion à la nouvelle de la mort de la reine.—Défense de la religion; combat de Valeurs, de M. d’Anquetil, de l’abbé de La Bletterie; lettres de M. de Beauvais sur la situation de l’Église de France. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Book XX — Retrospect and Last Works
Les événemens dont je viens de rappeler le souvenir ont tellement occupé ma pensée qu’à travers tant de calamités publiques je me suis presque oublié moi-même.—Retour de Marmontel sur lui-même.—Nouveaux Contes moraux.—Cours de grammaire, de logique, de métaphysique et de morale, rédigés pour ses enfants.—Rédaction des présents Mémoires.—Aveu de l’auteur à ce sujet. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Notes and Alphabetical Index — The third volume concludes with editorial notes to the text and an alphabetical index of persons, places, and subjects mentioned across all three volumes. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]
Revolution-Related Coverage Guide
Books XII through XX (all in Volume 3) constitute Marmontel’s account of the Revolution. His perspective is that of a constitutional monarchist and moderate philosophe — a man of letters who had been at the centre of the Académie française, the Encyclopédie circle, and the salon society of the ancien régime, who watched the monarchy collapse, survived the Terror, and wrote his memoirs in retirement. The following sections are of particular interest to the wiki:


Book XII: Causes of the Revolution — Marmontel’s analysis of the structural causes: the character of Louis XVI, the weakness of the ministries, the fiscal crisis, and the political miscalculations of the court. His portrait of the king is one of the most extended by a contemporary moderate. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XIII: The Brienne Ministry and the Pre-Revolution — The most detailed section on the 1787–88 pre-revolutionary crisis: the struggle between Brienne and the Parlement over the stamp tax and land tax, the lit de justice, the exile of the Parlement to Troyes, the séance royale, the resistance of the Breton and Dauphiné estates, Brienne’s resignation, the suicide of Lamoignon, Necker’s return, and the Second Assembly of Notables. Marmontel, as a member of the Académie and a client of the salons, had access to the political elite of this period. This is an insider’s view of the mechanism of government collapse. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XIV: The Electoral Assemblies of 1789 — This is one of the most valuable sections of the memoirs for the wiki: Marmontel was himself a member of the primary assembly of the Feuillants district and of the electoral assembly. He describes the electoral meetings, the role of Duport, the election of Target as president, the growing influence of the avocats, and the election of the duc d’Orléans. He also records his own relations with Lafayette and Sieyès during this period. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XV: The Estates-General and the Tennis Court Oath — The constitutional struggle between the orders, the Third Estate’s self-proclamation as the National Assembly, the séance royale of 23 June, the Tennis Court Oath, and Necker’s recall and dismissal. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XVI–XVII: The Fall of the Bastille — Books XVI gives the narrative of the July crisis: Lambesc’s charge, the seizure of arms from the Invalides, the storming of the Bastille, and the massacres of de Launey, Flesselles, and the Bastille garrison. Book XVII contains the remarkable eyewitness account of Élie, one of the “vainqueurs de la Bastille,” which Marmontel collected directly from him. Élie’s récit is one of the few surviving participant narratives of the Bastille’s fall from the insurgent side, embedded within a moderate memoirist’s frame. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XVIII: The October Days — The events of 5–6 October 1789: the women’s march to Versailles, the invasion of the château, the murder of the gardes du corps, and the forced return of the royal family to Paris. Marmontel records these events from Paris. He also describes the murder of Foulon and Bertier. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XIX: The Terror — The Terror seen from the perspective of a constitutional monarchist academician in hiding or retirement: the law of suspects, the trial and execution of the king, the proscription of the Girondins, Charlotte Corday and Marat, the suppression of the académies (which Marmontel felt with particular force as secrétaire perpétuel), the decrees against ex-nobles and ex-priests, and the death of the queen. Marmontel writes as a man whose entire social and institutional world was systematically dismantled. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Book XX: Retrospect — Marmontel’s final reflections and his account of his literary work in retirement: the Nouveaux Contes moraux, the educational courses in grammar, logic, metaphysics, and morality that he wrote for his children, and the composition of these memoirs themselves. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol3.txt]


Quality
Project Gutenberg ebooks produced from images generously made available by the Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF/Gallica). French text, 18th-century orthography and typography preserved (e.g., “foible” for “faible,” “événemens” for “événements”). Marmontel’s prose is clear, classical, and measured in the academic style — one of the most readable of the French memoirists of this period, far less digressive than Buzot or Paganel. The PG editions are cleanly transcribed with page notes. Medium difficulty for French readers; low difficulty for those used to 18th-century French prose. ^[source: raw/marmontel-memoires-vol1.txt]
Value to the Wiki
Marmontel’s memoirs are one of the most valuable moderate-constitutionalist sources in the wiki’s collection. He writes as:

An institutional insider of the ancien régime (Académie française, Mercure de France, the salons)
A participant in the 1789 electoral assemblies, giving a rare ground-level view of how the Paris electoral machinery worked
A collector of participant testimony (e.g., Élie’s Bastille narrative)
A victim of the Terror (he was proscribed, his academic world was destroyed) but without the Girondin partisan intensity of Buzot or Roland
An elder of the Enlightenment generation (born 1723, friend of Voltaire, d’Alembert, Diderot), writing a synoptic view of his entire life across both the ancien régime and the Revolution

The memoirs are especially valuable for the pre-1789 period (Books XII–XIII) where they cover the Brienne ministry and the collapse of the royal administration — a period less well covered by other memoir sources in the wiki, which tend to begin with the Estates-General.
