sources/morris-diary-french-revolution-v.title: Gouverneur Morris — A Diary of the French Revolution, Volume I (March 1789 – September 1790)
sources/morris-diary-french-revolution-v.content:
Gouverneur Morris, A Diary of the French Revolution, Volume I. Edited by Beatrix Cary Davenport. Boston: Houghton Mifflin / The Riverside Press, 1939. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 27,590 lines and 1.53 MB, from a University of Michigan library copy (Bequest of Arthur Lyon Cross). Morris (1752–1816) was an American statesman and lawyer, drafter of much of the final text of the United States Constitution, who arrived in Paris in February 1789 on a private commercial mission and remained through 1794 — first as a private citizen, then as United States Minister to France. Volume I covers March 1, 1789 through late September 1790, spanning the States-General, the fall of the Bastille, the October Days, and Morris’s informal diplomatic mission to London. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Morris bought a blank-book bound in apple-green vellum at a shop called À l’Espérance, rue Neuve des Petits Champs, and made his first diary entry on March 1, 1789. He was in Paris on commercial business for Robert Morris (a leading American merchant-financier, no relation): to settle the tobacco contract with the French Farmers-General, to extract payment from the reluctant Farm, and to attempt to raise loans from Parisian and Dutch bankers for the Delaware ironworks at Trenton — all of this amid a political crisis he had not anticipated and could not ignore. The business negotiations run continuously through the diary, interleaved with observations on the Revolution happening around him.
Morris moves in the highest social and political circles. He dines at Versailles, visits the salons of the great ladies of the ancien régime, attends the National Assembly debates, and converses regularly with Jefferson (American Minister), Lafayette (commander of the National Guard), Talleyrand (then Bishop of Autun), Montmorin (Foreign Minister), Necker, and the leading constitutional politicians of both the aristocratic and the reforming parties. He is received at court. He is consulted by Lafayette on constitutional design; he advises against giving the legislature too much power and the executive too little; he predicts the constitution that emerges will fail because it lacks adequate executive authority.
The diary is written in Morris’s characteristic style: terse, precise about times and names, economical with political judgment, ironic about human weakness, and laconic about violence. He records the great events of 1789 — the States-General, the Tennis Court Oath, the fall of the Bastille, the October march to Versailles — not as theatrical spectacles but as data about a political process he is observing with skeptical attention. The editor Beatrix Cary Davenport has woven extensive editorial notes throughout, bracketed in square brackets, providing biographical sketches of individuals mentioned, linking diary entries to the broader historical literature, and occasionally supplying context from letters Morris wrote at the same time.
Format and Edition
The Davenport edition is not a verbatim transcript of the diary but a shaped literary production: the editor selects, brackets editorial commentary, provides thematic section headings in the running text (printed in the original as chapter-like titles such as “First Impressions,” “Sightseeing in the Bastille,” “Augean Stable of Versailles”), and supplies the letters Morris wrote during the same period when the diary is thin or has gaps. The diary entries themselves begin with the day — “Monday 20” — followed by continuous prose; no paragraph breaks between sentences, all records of time, weather, business, and politics in the same breath. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Full Contents Map
Prefatory Material


Introduction by the editor — Beatrix Cary Davenport provides a biographical introduction covering Morris’s background: born at Morrisania manor in New York, half-brother of Lewis Morris who signed the Declaration of Independence, educated at King’s College (Columbia), admitted to the bar at nineteen, member of the New York Provincial Congress, drafter of the New York Constitution of 1777, contributor to the Federalist arguments around the Constitution. His clubfoot — he lost a leg below the knee in a carriage accident in 1780 — was a permanent feature of his Paris life, and the irony of a physically distinctive American aristocrat moving through the most radical event in modern European history is present throughout. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]


Preliminary letters — Before the diary proper, Davenport includes Morris’s letters to Franklin (from Paris, February 23, 1789, reporting on French interest in Franklin’s health and reputation), and the exchange between Morris and Washington (November–February 1788–89) in which Washington commissions a watch and provides introductory letters, and Morris promises to execute the commission and requests credentials. The Washington–Morris letters are remarkable: Washington writes with dry humor about the Chinese pigs he is sending as a gift; Morris responds with advice about the likelihood of Washington being compelled to accept the presidency (“I hope the choice will not fall upon me and, in the second, if it should and if I can with any degree of propriety decline, I shall certainly contrive to get rid of the acceptance”). ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]


Part I — Fall of the Bastille (1 March to 31 July 1789)
States-General (March–May 1789). Morris’s first diary entries describe a Paris paralyzed between the pressure of events and the inertia of pleasure-seeking: “Paris is if possible a worse place for Business than Virginia. Every Body here has his Country Seat and comes to Town to do Business once in three or four Days and then works not to finish but to get Rid of Work that he may again get out of Town. Indeed Pleasure is the great Business.” He attends sessions at Versailles, delivers introductory letters, begins negotiations with Le Couteulx and the tobacco contractors, and observes the political atmosphere as the States-General opens in May.
He meets Lafayette — whose character becomes a running subject of the diary. Morris’s assessment, delivered across many entries: Lafayette’s ambition is of the vain rather than the proud kind; “he is the Lover of Freedom from Ambition, of which there are two Kinds, the one born of Pride, the other of Vanity and his partakes most of the latter.” He commands the National Guard, has marched the king through the streets, could have kept him prisoner — and yet claims to want to return to private life. Morris finds this both self-deception and attempt to deceive others.
He meets Madame de Flahaut at a dinner at the Comte d’Angivillier’s in Versailles: “She speaks English and is a pleasing Woman. If I might judge from Appearances, not a sworn Enemy to Intrigue.” (The editor’s footnote here provides a full portrait of Adèle de Flahaut — she has rooms in the Louvre, is the mother of Talleyrand’s son, and will become a novelist celebrated by Sainte-Beuve.) Their relationship becomes a central social thread of the diary, her apartment in the Louvre a fixed point in Morris’s Paris life. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
National Assembly (June 1789). Morris records the political events of June with the same compressed notation he gives his business meetings: “This Day the Majority of the Clergy and a Minority of the Noblesse have joined the Tiers. The National Assembly, or whatever else they may now choose to call themselves, have agreed on a Deputation to the King.” He notes Necker’s influence on finance debates, attends to the position of the various parties, and dispatches letters to Robert Morris in Philadelphia while continuing to press Le Couteulx and Le Normand on the tobacco settlement.
He converses with Lafayette and other constitutional politicians about executive power. His consistent advice is that the Assembly is making a structural error by failing to give the executive sufficient authority: “a constitution of a single Assembly without a Senate and without a real executive will fail.” He discusses the constitutional options with Mirabeau and with the Bishop of Autun (Talleyrand), noting that Talleyrand has not the right kind of head for a ministry — too visionary in his ideas — a judgment the Marquis de La Luzerne corroborates. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Necker’s dismissal and the Bastille (12–14 July 1789). The entries for July 12–14 capture Paris moving from agitation to insurrection. On July 12, Morris is visiting Jefferson when word arrives that Necker has been dismissed by letter delivered by hand — he received it at dinner, proposed a walk to his wife, communicated the news on the road, and departed France that night. Montmorin resigned immediately. Morris records the city breaking open: armorers’ shops forced, armories raided, the Monastery of Saint-Lazare attacked and its grain distributed — each cart accompanied by a friar. He is turned back by guards in the Place Louis Quinze. He goes to his club, where a gentleman just arrived from Versailles reports on the new ministry. He puts a green cockade in his hat — “the fashion of the Day which every Body is obliged to comply with who means to march in Peace” — and walks to the Palais-Royal because no carriages are moving: “I apprehend nothing from the Populace.”
On July 14, he reports the fall of the Bastille indirectly through the mood of the city and what people say at dinner. On July 17, Lafayette takes him to the Hôtel de Ville and gives him a passport to visit the Bastille. Morris describes proposing to a painter that instead of his current subject (Love escaped from his cage) he should paint the storming of the Bastille — specifically, a guardsman who, having seized the gate and unable to pull it down, cried to his companions to pull on his legs, and held while a dozen pulled him like a rope, racking himself, until the gate came down: “To represent him drawn out of Joint with his Head turned round, encouraging them to draw still harder, must I think have a fine Effect.” The Bishop of Autun (Talleyrand), who is present, agrees entirely. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Lafayette and the new order (July–August 1789). Morris visits Lafayette at the Hôtel de Ville and finds him exhausted by “a Variety of Attentions.” He tells Morris he has had the utmost power his heart could wish, has commanded absolutely a hundred thousand men, has marched his sovereign through the streets as he pleased, prescribed the degree of applause the king should receive, and could have kept him prisoner — “and is grown tired of it.” Morris does not believe the desire for private life is sincere. He suggests to Lafayette a plan for the Gardes Françaises — incorporating them into the City Guard with high pay. He records that the king confirmed Bailly as mayor, received the cockade of the city (red and blue), and only after putting it in his hat received the general shouts of Vive le Roi! — “This Day I think will prove a useful Lesson to him for the Rest of his Life, but he is so weak that unless he be kept out of bad Company it is impossible that he should not act wrongly.” ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Part II — London and Loyalists (1 August to 10 September 1789)
Morris departs for London on business — the tobacco negotiations require him to work with English bankers and creditors of Robert Morris — and the diary continues from England. He visits the Penn family (John Penn and his circle, English-born proprietors of Pennsylvania who had refused independence and were living on expectations), calls on bankers and merchants with letters of introduction, dines at the French Ambassador’s. He observes the English political scene during the early weeks of the Revolution’s English reception and comments on Necker’s departure from France and the new ministry. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Part III — Versailles Comes to Paris (11 September 1789 to 16 February 1790)
Morris returns to Paris in mid-September and resumes his daily round — business meetings with Le Couteulx and Le Normand, visits to Madame de Flahaut at the Louvre, attendance at the National Assembly debates, dinners with the diplomatic corps and the reforming nobility. This section covers the October Days and their aftermath.
The October Days (5–6 October 1789). The women’s march to Versailles and the forced return of the royal family to Paris is covered through what Morris hears and observes from Paris, not from Versailles where the events occurred. He notes the meaning of the transfer: the court at Versailles had been a buffer between the king and the Paris mob; Paris and the Tuileries place the king directly in the city’s hands. His entries in the following days record the changed atmosphere.
Conversations with the King (autumn 1789). Through intermediaries — principally the Abbé Bertrand and Madame de Flahaut — Morris is drawn into advising the royal household on the constitutional situation. He is consulted on the form of the king’s address to the Assembly, and he prepares drafts or revisions. He records that the king’s speech will contain “partly mine and partly other Materials.” He gives advice through channels he does not always name explicitly, including through the Comte de La Marck (a Belgian who had stayed in the king’s confidence since Marie-Antoinette’s arrival in France).
Mirabeau. The diary records meetings with Mirabeau — “one of those extraordinary Characters which Nature sometimes produces” — who moves between the constitutional politicians and the court, attempting to broker a settlement that would give the executive real authority while satisfying the Assembly. Morris respects his intelligence while noting his personal corruption and vanity. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Constitutional advice. Morris’s consistent position through all conversations — with Lafayette, with Montmorin, with the king’s advisers — is that the Constitution being drafted gives the legislature too much and the executive too little. He draws on the American experience: “I preach incessantly Respect for the Constitution under which we live and for that which is forming here.” He argues that a single assembly without a senate and without genuine executive power will produce anarchy — a prediction the diary treats as confirmed by events visible in each week’s entries. He does not trust the enthusiasm for natural rights as a foundation for stable government: “Like the cut of a Coat and the Form of a Constitution. Like the English, they want what they know not.” ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Part IV — Antwerp and Amsterdam (17 February to 26 March 1790)
Morris travels to Antwerp and Amsterdam to pursue the financial negotiations for Robert Morris’s account — trying to raise loans from Dutch bankers, settling the tobacco accounts with French agents in the Low Countries, and meeting with the banking houses of Van Staphorst and others. The diary continues with the same mixture of financial negotiation and political observation, now applied to the Dutch and Belgian political situation. He notes the impact of the French Revolution on banking confidence across northern Europe. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Part V — Informal Mission to England (27 March to 24 September 1790)
Washington, through Secretary of State Jefferson, asks Morris to undertake a confidential probe of British intentions regarding the commercial treaty between the two countries and the posts still held by Britain on American territory in violation of the 1783 peace treaty. Morris conducts this inquiry in London — meeting with the Duke of Leeds and other British ministers — while continuing to manage Robert Morris’s commercial affairs. The diary in this section covers the London diplomatic world, English political society, news from France, and the business of the informal mission. Morris’s mission produces no formal result; the British are not ready to negotiate. He reports to Jefferson and returns to France at the end of September 1790. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]
Key Figures as Morris Records Them


Lafayette — Described across many entries. Morris respects his military record and his commitment to liberty but finds him politically naive, vain rather than proud in his ambition, and unwilling to make the hard choices that constitutional stability required. He admires that Lafayette could have detained the king prisoner and chose not to. He doubts the sincerity of Lafayette’s desire for private life.


Talleyrand (Bishop of Autun) — A regular presence at Madame de Flahaut’s Louvre salon. Morris describes him as having ideas too visionary for administrative office, not the right kind of head for a ministry. The diary records their conversations on constitutional design, finance, and the colonial question. Talleyrand in this period is the ex-bishop turned administrator of the Department of Paris.


Jefferson — Morris visits Jefferson regularly at the American Legation. Their relationship is cordial but not close politically — Jefferson more sympathetic to the Revolution than Morris. Morris uses Jefferson’s letter-of-introduction network and consults him on French commercial law. Jefferson recommended a watchmaker who turned out to be a rogue; Morris found a better one.


Necker — Morris observes Necker’s position as finance minister — respected for his competence, undermined by his own fame and the political dynamics around him. Necker’s dismissal on July 12, 1789 is recorded through what Jefferson tells Morris: the letter delivered by hand, the walk, the secret departure.


Mirabeau — Encountered at dinners and in the Assembly. Morris records his physical presence, his eloquence, his corruption, and his attempts to broker a constitutional settlement that would preserve the monarchy’s effective power.


Madame de Flahaut — Her apartment in the Louvre is a fixed social coordinate for Morris throughout Volume I. She is described as speaking excellent English, having “chestnut hair curled under its powder” and “charmant face with the wittiest eyes in the world” (the editor’s note quotes Vigée-Le Brun’s portrait). She is Talleyrand’s intellectual companion and the mother of his acknowledged son; she is working on the novel Adèle de Sénanges during the same period the diary covers. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol1-1789-1790.txt]


Coverage Guide


The States-General and National Assembly, March–June 1789 — Morris observes the States-General from Paris and Versailles throughout the spring: the political maneuvering, the constitutional debate, the transformation into the National Assembly. His entries give the atmosphere of these weeks from the inside of the reforming and diplomatic circles.


The fall of the Bastille, July 1789 — Recorded through Morris’s direct experience: the green cockade in his hat, the city’s tumult, Necker’s dismissal as Morris heard it from Jefferson, his own walking through the streets on July 12–13 (no carriages moving), the post-Bastille political reconfiguration. He visits the Bastille after Lafayette provides a passport.


Lafayette’s character and the National Guard — One of the most sustained character studies in the volume. Morris’s assessments of Lafayette’s strengths and weaknesses run through every visit. He is the American observer who knew Lafayette best during this period and was most willing to be candid.


Constitutional advice to the court — The diary records Morris’s position as an informal constitutional adviser to the royal household through 1789–90. He drafted or revised texts for the king’s speeches. His consistent argument (single assembly without senate and without executive power will fail) is the organizing political opinion of the volume.


Talleyrand in the early Revolution — The diary records Talleyrand as a regular interlocutor before he became famous. The early assessments — “not the right kind of head” for a ministry — and the evolution of his position (from Bishop of Autun to administrator of Paris) are tracked across the entries.


Business negotiations in revolutionary Paris — The tobacco contract with the Farmers-General, the loans for the Delaware ironworks, the Dutch banking negotiations, the Paris credit markets — all are detailed through the diary’s business entries. These give a ground-level view of how American commercial interests in France operated while the Revolution was happening.


The London diplomatic probe, 1790 — Morris’s informal mission to sound British intentions on the commercial treaty and the frontier posts is documented through his meetings with the Duke of Leeds and other ministers. This is an early instance of American executive diplomatic practice.


Quality
University of Michigan library copy (Bequest of Arthur Lyon Cross), OCR from the 1939 Houghton Mifflin Riverside Press edition. The edition itself is a substantial editorial production: the diary text is clean, readable 1930s print quality, with editorial bracketed notes throughout. OCR is reliable; Morris’s abbreviations (M! for Monsieur, Mad! for Madame, Mess! for Messieurs) are consistent. French passages in the original are preserved and legible. Running headers give the month and a thematic phrase for each spread. The most challenging sections for OCR are the footnotes, which are keyed to superscript numbers in the text — these are generally readable but occasionally fragmented.

sources/morris-diary-french-revolution-v.title: Gouverneur Morris — A Diary of the French Revolution, Volume II (November 1790 – January 1793)
sources/morris-diary-french-revolution-v.content:
Gouverneur Morris, A Diary of the French Revolution, Volume II. Edited by Beatrix Cary Davenport. Boston: Houghton Mifflin / The Riverside Press, 1939. Copyright 1939 by Beatrix Cary Davenport. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 30,600 lines and 1.53 MB, from a University of Michigan library copy. Volume II covers November 7, 1790 through January 5, 1793, spanning the French Constitution of 1791, the Legislative Assembly, Morris’s appointment as United States Minister to France in May 1792, the storming of the Tuileries on August 10, 1792, and the opening of the First Republic. The diary proper is suppressed after August 10 — when Morris’s house was being used to shelter royalist refugees — and the remainder of the volume is composed of letters and dispatches, with editorial bridging. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Volume II opens where Volume I left off — Morris returned from his London diplomatic mission in late 1790, still engaged in his business negotiations for Robert Morris while living at the center of Parisian political society. The Revolution has advanced: Mirabeau is dying, the Constituent Assembly is completing its constitutional work, the émigrés are accumulating on the borders, and the king’s position is deteriorating. Morris watches with the same skeptical precision, still predicting — correctly — that the Constitution of 1791 gives the legislature too much and the executive too little to be stable.
The diary through 1791 alternates between the social and the political: dinners with Montmorin and Madame de Flahaut, visits to the Assembly debates, conversations with Lafayette and Talleyrand, his own persistent commercial negotiations, observations on the assignat inflation and the financial chaos. The flight to Varennes (June 1791) is covered through Morris’s letters to Robert Morris — a long retrospective letter written several days after the event, describing the king’s capture at Varennes and the political consequences.
In May 1792 Washington and Jefferson appoint Morris as United States Minister to France — the appointment was controversial because Morris’s sympathy with the monarchy was well-known and the French republicans had lobbied against him. He accepts and presents his credentials. Within weeks the political situation passes the point of no return: the invasion of the Tuileries on June 20, 1792; Morris’s continued contacts with the court; the storming of the Tuileries on August 10; the September Massacres; the abolition of the monarchy; and the opening of the National Convention.
After August 10, Morris’s house on the rue de la Planche shelters royalist refugees — the former minister Monciel, others implicated in royalist counter-conspiracy — and Morris himself is holding funds (5,000 louis d’or) that had been entrusted to him for a royalist defense operation that never took place. The diary is suppressed. What remains is dispatches to Jefferson and later to Thomas Pinckney, and a remarkable accounting he later presents to Madame Royale (Marie-Thérèse) covering what became of the royal funds. The volume closes at the end of 1792 / January 1793, as the trial of Louis XVI is reaching its conclusion. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Full Contents Map
Parts VI–VII — Whales, Nicotine, and the Constitutional Endgame (November 1790 – February 1791)
Morris is back in Paris after his London mission. The diary resumes with his regular social round and business negotiations. Two commercial matters run through this section: the whale oil trade (a major American export to France, the terms of which the Constituent Assembly’s committees are debating) and the tobacco contract with the Farm. He meets with various French ministers and Assembly committee members on these subjects while continuing his social visits.
He observes the declining political vitality of the Constituent Assembly in its final months. Mirabeau is ill and increasingly absent. The constitutional structure being finalized is, in Morris’s view, defective: it will produce legislative tyranny over a passive executive. He records conversations with Montmorin and with the Comte de La Marck (a Belgian who serves as the king’s confidential intermediary) in which they discuss what can be done — Morris’s advice consistently being that the king should hold to the constitution, however flawed, rather than attempt to subvert it, because any attempted escape or coup would fail and worsen his position. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Part VIII — Whales and Nicotine (1 February to 28 February 1791)
This section covers a concentrated period of commercial and diplomatic lobbying — Morris working the Assembly committees on the whale oil and tobacco questions simultaneously. The commercial entries are unusually detailed: the specific tariff rates under discussion, the arguments made by American competitors (the New England whale-oil merchants), the Assembly members most accessible on these questions, the text of memorials Morris drafts or assists. He also notes the political atmosphere: assignat depreciation accelerating, emigration increasing, the king’s aunts attempting to leave France (they eventually succeed, after some public drama). ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Part IX — The French Constitution of 1791 (1 March to 30 September 1791)
The longest single section of Volume II, covering the Constituent Assembly’s final months and the presentation of the completed constitution to the king. The diary’s density increases: Morris is attending more political gatherings, seeing more of Montmorin, Lafayette, and the court intermediaries.
Mirabeau’s death (April 1791). Morris records the impact of Mirabeau’s death on the political situation. The one figure who might have found a constitutional path between royal authority and popular sovereignty is gone. The diary notes the public grief, the political void, and the absence of any successor with comparable ability. The editor’s footnote gives Mirabeau’s last exchange with the king, which Morris had heard from La Marck.
The Constitution of 1791 and Salon of 1791. Morris attends the opening of the Salon — the first opened to all artists regardless of Academy membership, organized by Talleyrand as administrator of the Paris department, with David exulting at the expanded access — while simultaneously observing the Assembly debate the final constitution. He visits Choisy to dine with Marmontel, who contests the droits de l’homme by asking for a definition of the word droit and concluding from it against asserted equality. Morris records these philosophical conversations alongside his business appointments.
The flight to Varennes (June 1791). Morris was at his country property outside Paris when the king attempted to escape. His accounts are given in letters written several days after the fact, reconstructing events from what he has gathered. His analysis: the flight was a political blunder. Public affairs were such that if the king had been quiet he would have soon regained authority as anarchy demonstrated the necessity of stronger executive power; his departure “changed every Thing and now the general wish seems to be for a Republic, which is quite in the natural Order of Things.” He notes the contradiction: the Assembly declared the king inviolable and therefore could not include him in prosecutions relating to his attempted escape — producing intense heat against the Assembly. Lafayette was nearly killed: “a Pistol snapped at his Breast. The Assassin was immediately secured but he ordered him to be discharged.”
The Champ de Mars massacre (July 17, 1791). Morris describes coming from the British Ambassador’s in the evening, meeting a detachment of militia with the red flag flying. He went to a height to see the battle but it was over before he arrived — the militia, being pelted with bricks instead of obeying the order to ground arms, fired and killed “a dozen or two of the ragged Regiment.” He gives a figure of perhaps five or six militia subsequently assassinated in retaliation, and notes that Lafayette was again nearly killed.
The constitution accepted by the king (September 1791). Morris records the king’s formal acceptance of the constitution and the political atmosphere around it. His private assessment is unchanged: the constitution lacks adequate executive authority and will not survive. The Constituent Assembly dissolves; the Legislative Assembly convenes October 1, 1791. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Part X — Legislative Assembly (1 October 1791 to 29 January 1792)
The new Legislative Assembly — composed entirely of men who had not served in the Constituent (the self-denying ordinance Robespierre had proposed) — meets in October 1791. Morris’s diary records the changed political atmosphere: the Girondins gaining influence, the war party growing, Montmorin increasingly uncomfortable in the foreign ministry, the assignat continuing to fall. He observes that the Assembly lacks the experienced constitutional politicians of the Constituent and is more susceptible to radical pressure.
Commercial negotiations continue. Morris is working on the whale oil question, the tobacco accounts, Robert Morris’s debt to French creditors, and various real estate transactions for American speculators. He records the complexity of conducting American commercial business in a country where the political situation changes the legal framework of commercial contracts from month to month. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Part XI — Spring in London (30 January to 5 May 1792)
Morris returns to London for a further period on business — the debt accounts with London bankers, more real estate negotiations, meetings with British ministers. The diary continues from London, recording his observations on British reactions to the Revolution, the progress of the war crisis, and his own commercial work. He notes the appointment discussions that will make him United States Minister to France: the Washington administration has settled on him despite French republican protests. He accepts. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Part XII — United States Minister to France: Transition from Monarchy to Republic (6 May 1792 to 5 January 1793)
Appointment and credentials (May 1792). Morris returns to Paris, presents his credentials as United States Minister, and formally enters the diplomatic corps. His position is awkward: the French republican faction knows he is sympathetic to the monarchy; he is expected to maintain American commercial interests while the political situation is collapsing.
The June 20 invasion of the Tuileries (1792). Morris records the mob invasion of the Tuileries on June 20, 1792, when armed sections forced their way into the palace and the king was compelled to put on a red cap and drink to the nation from a bottle handed to him by a rioter. Morris does not witness it directly but gathers accounts and records his assessment: the king’s behavior was remarkably composed, and the day demonstrated both the degradation of royal authority and the surprising durability of the king’s personal dignity under pressure.
The royalist counter-conspiracy and the 5,000 louis. This section of the diary contains one of its most sensitive and historically significant elements. Morris was drawn into a royalist counter-conspiracy organized by Monciel (a former interior minister) and Brémond (a Provençal agent) to organize armed resistance from inside Paris in the event of an insurrection. Morris held 5,000 louis d’or (convertible gold coin) earmarked for paying reliable men who would rally to the king’s defense at designated points. The money was paid out of royal funds through Brémond; the purses of twenty louis were divided and held at Morris’s house pending the activation of the network. The network was never activated: the storming of the Tuileries on August 10 overtook the plan entirely. The 5,000 louis, which Brémond had by then removed to Swiss bankers, became a prolonged and frustrated effort at recovery that Morris was still pursuing years later. The accounting of what became of this money — written out for the Princess Royale (Marie-Thérèse) when she was finally released from the Temple — is included in the volume and gives the clearest narrative of Morris’s involvement with the royal household’s financial arrangements in 1792.
August 10, 1792 — the storming of the Tuileries. The diary proper is suppressed after August 10. The editor’s note explains: after the Tuileries fell to the insurrectionary sections, former minister Monciel and his family took refuge in Morris’s house on the rue de la Planche, along with others implicated in royalist activities. The diary could not be maintained under these circumstances without endangering the people sheltered there. “The events of August tenth are too well known to admit of repeating their painful story.” What remains is reconstructed from letters and from Morris’s later accounting to Madame Royale.
September Massacres (September 1792). Morris was still in Paris during the September Massacres, sheltering refugees and managing the aftermath of August 10. His dispatches to Jefferson describe the political situation — the abolition of the monarchy, the proclamation of the Republic, the formation of the National Convention. He does not describe the massacres themselves in graphic detail in what survives; his position as US Minister required him to maintain a diplomatic register that restrained his personal assessments.
Louvet’s Robespierride (October–November 1792). Morris’s diary notes, in the compressed style of its final pages: “Robespierre has got thro his Affair with Éclat.” The editor’s note explains: on October 29, Louvet had electrified the Convention by formally accusing Robespierre before the assembly — each charge beginning Je t’accuse! Robespierre’s retreat and comeback are tracked through Morris’s subsequent brief entries. “Nothing in his speeches explains” Robespierre’s growing ascendancy, the editor comments; “unless their lack of eloquence gave an impression of great sincerity to audiences overfed on revolutionary bombast.”
Dumouriez’s campaign (autumn–winter 1792). Morris records the military news from Belgium: Dumouriez’s victory at Jemappes (November 6), the French entry into Brussels (November 14), the opening of the Scheldt. He notes in his dispatches the British reaction to the Scheldt decree and the trajectory toward war between France and Britain. The volume closes in early January 1793 as the trial of Louis XVI is approaching its conclusion. ^[source: raw/morris-diary-french-revolution-vol2-1790-1793.txt]
Key Figures and Running Subjects


Montmorin — The Foreign Minister appears in Volume II as the court’s most accessible and most troubled member. Morris dines with him regularly through 1791, discussing the fiscal crisis, the constitutional situation, and American commercial claims. Montmorin’s position is increasingly untenable; he resigns and will die in the September Massacres.


Madame de Staël — Enters the diary in this volume as a social presence at the British Ambassador’s and at Talleyrand’s salon. Morris records her views on the constitution and on Talleyrand’s career prospects. She and Talleyrand press Montmorin hard on some political subject at a dinner Morris attends; he learns afterward it was a request to revoke the decree barring Talleyrand from the ministry.


The Comte de La Marck — The Belgian prince who served as the court’s confidential intermediary with Mirabeau, and who continued to try to broker a constitutional settlement after Mirabeau’s death. Morris meets with La Marck in a small conciliabule (La Marck, Pellin, Beaumetz, Montmorin, and Morris) to discuss how to manage the political situation. La Marck represents the category of noblemen who genuinely wanted constitutional monarchy and found the choices narrowing around them.


Monciel and Brémond — Former interior minister Monciel and his Provençal agent Brémond are the principal figures in the royalist counter-conspiracy described in Part XII. Their relationship with Morris was commercial and conspiratorial simultaneously; after August 10, Morris sheltered Monciel and managed the fallout from Brémond’s mishandling of the 5,000 louis. The editor traces this story through letters and the later accounting to Madame Royale.


Washington’s watch — A detail that threads through both volumes: Washington commissioned a watch before Morris left for France, Morris bought one in Paris and reported on it with deadpan precision to the General, and the watch recurs in letters as a symbol of the relationship between Morris and Washington that underlies the entire enterprise.


Coverage Guide


The Constitution of 1791 in formation — Morris’s diary provides a continuous view of the constitutional debates from inside the reforming circles: the Constituent Assembly’s late-stage work, the key political choices (single versus bicameral legislature, strength of the executive veto), the king’s acceptance, the Champ de Mars massacre as a turning point in public opinion. His American constitutional experience makes his observations on French constitutional design unusually grounded.


The Flight to Varennes — Covered through Morris’s letters rather than diary entries; gives a clear narrative of what he understood about the king’s motives, the capture, and the political consequences. Cross-reference roland-memoires-vol2-1823 for the Girondin perspective on the same event.


Mirabeau’s death and political vacuum — The diary records the political moment of Mirabeau’s death and the absence of any successor capable of managing the space between the monarchy and the Assembly. Morris had known Mirabeau through the previous volume; his assessment of what was lost is implicit in subsequent entries.


Morris as US Minister during the collapse — Part XII is the most historically consequential section: Morris navigating American commercial interests, maintaining diplomatic relations with an increasingly radical government, sheltering royalist refugees, holding royal funds, and dispatching reports to Jefferson that describe the fall of the monarchy and the opening months of the Republic from an insider-outsider position no other American witness possessed.


The 5,000 louis and the royalist counter-conspiracy — The most sensitive element of the diary and the one most carefully handled by the editor. The accounting to Madame Royale, preserved in full, is a primary document for the royalist resistance operations of 1792 and for Morris’s personal entanglement with them.


August 10 and its aftermath — The diary suppression after August 10 is itself a historical fact. What survives — letters, dispatches, the Madame Royale accounting — documents the event from the perspective of a witness who had refugees in his house and royal gold in his custody.


The September Massacres — Recorded in dispatches rather than diary entries; Morris’s reports to Jefferson describe the political situation without the graphic detail found in French witnesses’ accounts. His role as US Minister requires a degree of diplomatic restraint that is itself historically significant.


Quality
Same University of Michigan copy and 1939 Houghton Mifflin Riverside Press edition as Volume I. OCR quality is equivalent: reliable prose, consistent abbreviations, French passages preserved. The shift from diary to letters in the final sections of the volume creates a somewhat different texture — the letters are more formal, more polished, and more diplomatically restrained than the diary entries. The editor’s bracketed notes are more extensive in Part XII, compensating for the suppressed diary by drawing on other contemporary sources. The index at the end of Volume II (which covers both volumes) is reproduced in the OCR and is readable, giving volume and page numbers for all named individuals.

sources/paganel-histoire-napoleon-1815.title: Paganel — Histoire de Napoléon Bonaparte (1815)
sources/paganel-histoire-napoleon-1815.content:
Pierre Paganel, Histoire de Napoléon Bonaparte, depuis ses premières campagnes jusqu’à son exil à l’isle de Sainte-Hélène. Liège: C. A. Bassompierre, 1815. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 15,750 lines and 644 KB, drawn from a New York Public Library copy. Paganel was a former member of the legislature and former secretary-general of the Ministry of Foreign Relations. This is a political and moral history of Napoleon’s career from the Egyptian expedition through his second abdication and exile to Saint Helena, written in the weeks immediately after Waterloo by an author who had watched the entire period from inside the French state and who was suppressed by it. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Contents at a Glance
The book’s Avant-propos is itself a primary document. Paganel explains that he published a first historical-critical essay on the Revolution of France in 1810. Napoleon read it, was offended by the words souveraineté du peuple and représentation nationale, and ordered the edition seized from the printer’s warehouse by the prefecture of police — without review, after the work had already passed censorship and been printed with ministerial authorization. The seizure, Paganel notes with controlled fury, was a violation of imperial dignity as much as of justice: a great empire did not make itself secure by suppressing books. The preface thus frames everything that follows: this is a judgment delivered by a man who was silenced under the regime and now speaks freely because that regime has fallen.
Paganel writes Napoleon as a historical and moral problem rather than a military epic. He does not deny Bonaparte’s genius; he locates its limits. Bonaparte, in his account, had the scientific knowledge, the cold resolution, and the vast intelligence of a great commander, but lacked a sensitive soul, a calmer head, and the harmony between passion and reason that a great statesman required. A single passion — ambition — consumed all the others. The book traces how this ambition worked through the institutions of the French Republic, wore them down, and replaced them with a military monarchy that by 1815 had exhausted France and was rejected even by the army that had made it.
The structure is chronological across fifteen chapters, moving from the pre-Brumaire moment through the Consulate and Empire to the Hundred Days and Waterloo. The final section of the text is a large chronological table (covering the entire period) and a table of contents, followed by what appear from the OCR to be substantial statistical or documentary tables that may form an appendix to the main narrative.
Full Contents Map
Avant-propos
Paganel explains the circumstances of the 1810 suppression of his earlier work and his reasons for now writing openly. He reflects on the moral position of a historian under despotism: one can give the tyrant patient silence while his authority stands; the moment it falls, justice and freedom of expression require speaking plainly. This preface also contains his central characterization of Napoleon’s soul: a man whose marriage to an Austrian archduchess intoxicated his pride to delirium, who confused being surrounded by sovereigns with being above them, and whose birth and the regime under which he was born had originally ranked him among the subaltern officers of an artillery regiment. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter I — Bonaparte before Brumaire; the Egyptian Expedition
Paganel opens with the central character problem: Bonaparte possessed “a rich fund of positive science,” a vast genius, and an enterprising, cold, resolute character — but lacked a more sensitive soul, a calmer head, and harmony between his passions and his reason. A single passion — ambition — absorbed all the others and gave it long brilliance sustained by brilliant successes, but made him ultimately incapable of the retreat and consolidation that would have preserved his empire. He draws a sharp contrast with Moreau: where Napoleon’s Italian campaigns made him a spectacular offensive commander, Moreau’s Rhine retreat of 1796 showed the art of the strategically wise withdrawal — an art Napoleon never possessed or valued.
The Egyptian expedition is presented as two things simultaneously: a genuine ambition (the Orient as the road to India, the contest with England on its most vulnerable flank) and a flight from the Directory’s failures. Paganel notes that Bonaparte had to choose between watching France drift from Egypt or returning through a British-dominated sea — and chose to return, slipping through the blockade in a gamble that succeeded and that he never admitted was a gamble at all. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter II — 18 Brumaire; the Consular Constitution; Bonaparte as First Consul
Paganel’s account of 18 Brumaire insists it was a personal political achievement of extraordinary craft, not a rescue of France. Bonaparte cultivated a collaborator (Sieyès, whose name Paganel renders as “S…”) whom he intended from the start to use and discard — he “attached himself to S… to deceive him; he deceived him in order not to have to fear him.” He saw his future colleagues as “coarse and inert mud, deprived of feeling, ideas, and will.” From the morning of 19 Brumaire, the coalition of experienced revolutionaries that had made the coup broke its prior confederacy and clustered around Bonaparte “without mission, from various motives” — and from their conceptions emerged the consular republic, whose chief had declared himself its first magistrate “in the manner of Pope Sixtus V.”
Paganel’s sharpest observation is about the reception: military glory was the avowed title of Bonaparte’s elevation; “fear and venality were its true causes.” The court of courtiers that immediately formed at the rue de la Victoire and the Luxembourg is described with contempt: “Women — and what women! — remained in possession of credit and favor.” The Constitution of Year VIII receives a strict verdict: nothing was lacking to guarantee the citizen’s liberty except everything that was lacking in the men who would execute it. The principal danger Paganel identifies is structural: “Everything seemed arranged, men and things, for the advantage of a single man.” The Senate’s “anticipated devotion” merely confirmed a servility already inherent in the design. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter III — The Consul’s Secret Aims; Corruption; Vendée; Émigrés
The Senate’s self-abasements are traced step by step: doubling the duration of the Consulship before it had barely begun; proclaiming the Life Consulship; finally erecting “dictatorial authority” by a single sénatus-consulte without the authentic concurrence of the people. Paganel asks why the first bodies of the State pressed these accelerations on Bonaparte before he could have demanded them. His answer is damning: “The chiefs of intrigue assured themselves thereby of the first dignities, the favors of the master, and the faculty of crushing the most audacious censor of their guilty felony.” The passage of dissidents onto proscription lists — quiet during the Consulate, not yet deadly — is noted.
The alleged conspiracies against Bonaparte’s person (some doubtful, one certain: the Cadoudal-Pichegru affair) produced a great crisis of public silence: “all mouths were shut, all pens chained, all spirits calm, all hearts indifferent” at precisely the moment when the consul was elevated above the law. The Vendée pacification and émigré reconciliation are presented as the first great diplomatic feats of the Consulship — genuine achievements, but achievements whose purpose was as much to remove potential nuclei of opposition as to heal France. Lyon, Paganel notes, received particular protection from the consul because it had been the great martyr-city of the Revolution; winning it over was symbolically and politically essential. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter IV — Interior Administration; Codes; Education; Concordat
This is the chapter where Paganel’s ambivalence toward the Consulate is most concentrated, and where he is most willing to credit genuine achievement. The opening paragraphs are among the most generous he writes about Napoleon: canals, roads over the Mont-Blanc and the Simplon, great public works, engineers who were proud to receive either his criticism or his praise, mountain rivers harnessed for Paris’s water supply. The Legion of Honor — merging military and civil service in a single order of merit — is presented as a genuinely philosophical act: “the great captain seems called upon to repair the ills of war and make the arts of peace triumph.” The education law under Fourcroy, the civil and criminal codes — Paganel grants these their importance. “What a good it was permitted to hope for France and all peoples!”
But the chapter’s second movement traces the corruption of these achievements by the same process — the Senate’s repeated preemptive capitulations to the consul’s presumed wishes, each making the next easier. The famous footnote on the consul’s reported response to General Lannes, who reproached him for trusting only disgraced men: “Imbecile, does one found a monarchy with virtues and men of integrity?” Paganel cannot verify the quotation but places it because it fits so exactly. The Concordat is treated with ambivalence: restoring Catholic worship was necessary; making the clergy agents of the state’s social-control apparatus was something else. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter V — Saint-Domingue; the English Threat; Camp de Boulogne
The Saint-Domingue expedition (1801–02) is the first clear exhibition of the pattern that will define the Empire: an ambition that disregards consequences, announced with the “imposing apparatus of dictatorial authority” against a public opinion that clearly disapproved. Paganel reports the widespread accusation — which he presents without fully endorsing — that the expedition’s actual purpose was to purge France of its most energetic republicans by sending them to die in a tropical climate, while at the same time reasserting colonial sovereignty over the richest of France’s Caribbean possessions. “An army had already undergone numerous reforms under the consular government. The purification reached equally the gown and the arms.” Whether or not this reading is correct, the expedition was a disaster: the army melted, the colony was lost, and the financial and military cost were enormous precisely at the moment France needed to prepare for the renewal of war with England.
The Camp de Boulogne — the assembly of a great army on the Channel coast nominally aimed at invading England — is presented as the period’s signature operation: genuinely conceived as a possible invasion (Paganel does not dismiss it as pure theater), but ultimately serving Napoleon’s organisational purposes as much as any strategic end. It produced a superbly organized army that would fight at Austerlitz. The chapter includes Paganel’s broader verdict on the consular government as a whole: brilliant on the surface, corrupted at its foundation, moving always “toward the advantage of a single man.” ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter VI — Imperial Constitution; Military Despotism; Moreau Trial
The proclamation of the Empire in December 1804 receives a double account: the formal constitutional process (which Paganel finds contemptible in its mechanism) and the broader moral atmosphere that made it possible. He describes the period as one of “singular epidemic” — not just the vulgar who always create supernatural powers, but the educated classes, senators, and men of letters who proclaimed Napoleon’s fortune a certain sign of divine vocation to universal empire: “the most absurd adulation.” He counts on one hand the men who did not descend to this.
The chapter’s specific focus is military despotism as a structural tendency: “every warlike despot is a tyrant; it is a consequence of the regime.” Napoleon dismissed the Imperial Guard’s political significance, but as he concentrated power, his need for his praetorians grew with his distance from public opinion. Special tribunals replaced ordinary law. Paganel deals at length with the Moreau trial: the prosecution of the most distinguished French general after Napoleon himself, whose military reputation was a standing reproach to the claim that only Bonaparte could win France’s wars. Moreau’s conviction on essentially political grounds, and his exile, marks the moment when the Empire moved from institutional despotism to personal vendetta against independent prestige. The chapter closes with the question of how to judge the Senate and Corps Législatif — bodies that had constitutional existence and chose to make it worthless. Paganel’s verdict: not merely cowardly but actively complicit. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter VII — Napoleon and Rome; the Coronation; Italy
Two objects occupy Napoleon in this period: destroying or circumventing British maritime power, and clothing his empire in divine sanction. Paganel traces the negotiations with Rome with notable irony: Napoleon “commands rather than negotiates” the Pope’s presence in Paris. Pius VII comes from the capital of the Christian world to the capital of the political world — and the ceremony that follows reveals Napoleon’s characteristic disdain for subordination to any authority higher than himself. The Pope consecrates the crown; Napoleon takes it from the altar and places it on his own head. The footnote is devastating: Charlemagne had sought the crown from Rome as a favor from the church; Bonaparte, by contrast, “not recognizing any intermediary between himself and Providence, commands.” He contrasts with Charlemagne “as one wishes to distinguish oneself from a man whom one recognizes as great.”
The Italian voyage and the assumption of the Lombard crown complete the picture: Italy is not liberated but organized as an extension of French imperial administration. Paganel notes the lost opportunity — it would have been easy for Bonaparte as general, consul, or emperor to permanently fix Italy’s independence — and attributes the failure to the same family-dynasty logic that drove every decision: “reasons of family prevailed over reasons of state.” ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter VIII — War against Austria; Austerlitz; Confederation of the Rhine
Paganel’s account of Austerlitz (December 2, 1805) is among his most admiring passages: Napoleon reaches his army, harangues it “with the confidence that inspires certainty of victory,” sweeps through Austrian territory, enters Vienna “abandoned by the great men of state, deserted by the government,” and reigns there more through the rights of conquest than by exercising them. The battle of Austerlitz shakes the throne of Emperor Francis; Napoleon reassembles it by signing peace at Pressburg. The generosity shown to Austria — the enemy who had attacked under cover of negotiated peace, who engaged in a coalition “with the secrecy that conspiracies use,” who humbled himself to be a British subsidiary — makes the conquest more brilliant and the magnanimity more conspicuous.
But the political analysis that follows the military narrative is the chapter’s real contribution. Paganel argues that the post-Austerlitz reorganization of Germany into the Confederation of the Rhine was the moment when Napoleon’s structural preference for military government over constitutional life became irreversible: “how many brilliant details” the military historian will find in the campaign; “but then let the philosopher appear on the scene, deplore the fate, claim the rights of humanity.” The Council of State, which had been a genuine deliberative body in the early Consulate, was being emptied of deliberation; every institution was being converted into a transmission mechanism for imperial will. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter IX — War against Prussia; Treaty of Tilsit; Poland; Sciences and Arts
Jena-Auerstedt (October 1806) is presented as the most complete and rapid of Napoleon’s victories: Berlin occupied, Potsdam as imperial headquarters, Prussian fortresses falling in sequence. But the chapter’s moral center is Poland. The Grand Duchy of Warsaw is constituted out of Prussian-held Polish territory; Saxony is enlarged; the Elector becomes a King. And Paganel writes what becomes one of the key passages in his indictment: “It was also the moment that Providence seemed to have marked for the re-establishment of Poland… Under the auspices of Napoleon and his victorious army, under the shelter of a tempered monarchy, she would have risen to the level of free and powerful nations.” The opportunity was missed — not because it was impossible but because Napoleon chose family dynasticism over national liberation: “reasons of family prevailed over reasons of state; honor and liberty were nothing less than Napoleon’s thought.” He kept Polish expectations alive and unfulfilled, needing their manpower while refusing to commit to their national cause — a gamble that would cost him the Russian campaign’s political foundation.
Tilsit and the alliance with Alexander I is read as Napoleon at the height of his power but beginning to overreach: treating Alexander as a partner in European domination while actually preparing to subordinate Russia to French commercial interests. The Continental System against Britain begins here in earnest. The suppression of the Tribunate is noted as another constitutional amputation. The paradox of this period — Napoleon genuinely protecting sciences, letters, and arts while dismantling political liberty — is registered, but Paganel refuses to let the cultural patronage redeem the political destruction. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter X — Invasion of Spain; the Austrian Marriage; Decline Begins
The Bayonne affair (1808) is the hinge of the book and the moment Paganel describes as Napoleon acting most purely as his own worst instinct: seizing the Spanish royal family under pretext of mediation, detaining them, and placing his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne. Paganel apostrophizes the French army that entered Spain as friends of an allied people and would be fought there as hated tyrants: “sublime example of resignation, obedience, and patriotism!” But the armies’ devotion would not compensate for the strategic catastrophe of igniting a national resistance that bled the Empire for six years and gave Wellington his war.
The Austrian marriage of 1810 is examined with the sustained irony Paganel reserves for Napoleon’s gravest self-delusions. He distinguishes himself from the Austrian court’s “truly calculated humiliation” — in offering an archduchess, Vienna was buying time, reducing its own pride to the minimum required to prevent annihilation, while ensuring that Napoleon’s pride would swell to the maximum that would guarantee his eventual ruin. “His marriage with an archduchess exalted his pride to the point of delirium; and such was the foreseen effect, that he alone, among the sovereigns, did not penetrate the true motive of the abasement to which Austrian foresight had decided the monarch’s pride.” Ministers who understood said nothing; courtiers who understood flattered. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter XI — Tyranny Consolidated; the Continental System; Road to Russia
Paganel opens this chapter with a precise diagnosis: “The more Napoleon isolates himself from the nation and concentrates in himself alone the exercise of supreme power, the more he feels the necessity and danger of supplementing the natural limits of power with artificial and tyrannical ones.” The Empire at this point is “a camp, Paris a war-position.” A secret police and an armed police have banished gaiety and pleasure; espionage surrounds the first bodies of the State, “sullies the sanctuary of laws, besieges families, obstructs public places, and daily drags new guests to the dungeons.” Theatre pieces consecrated by two centuries of admiration are subject to imperial revision. Paganel notes that his own 1810 book belongs here — a concrete instance of the suppression he is describing.
The Continental System is analyzed as a strategic conception that was not absurd — cutting Britain off from European markets was a genuine lever — but that was impossible to execute without a continental compliance Napoleon could not maintain. Spain’s resistance had opened the peninsula to British trade and British armies; Russia could not close its Baltic ports without destroying its own economy; every maritime state in Europe had a stake in evading the embargo. The chapter closes with an assessment of Napoleon’s army on the eve of Russia: the Guard superb, the line armies increasingly conscript-heavy, the Emperor’s own physical and intellectual condition showing the first signs of the deterioration that his doctors would later document. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter XII — The Russian Campaign; Moscow; the Retreat
Paganel establishes the political framework before the military one: France believed Napoleon was in Poland organizing a constitution and a government for the Poles; he was in fact entering Russia. Alexander’s reply — a frank and motivated declaration of war, an appeal to his own people, and an invitation to Prussia and Germany to unite against their common enemy — is presented as strategically superior to Napoleon’s proclamation, which “filled the cabinet of Saint James with a secret joy without carrying any alarm into that of Saint Petersburg.”
The Polish question is the chapter’s analytical core. Paganel argues that if, instead of drawing Poland into Russia’s deserts, Napoleon had organized its government, fixed its borders, armed it, and made it capable of defending itself against Cossack raids, Russia would have been forced to respect it — and without Russia’s advance, the entire coalition against France in 1813 would not have formed. The opportunity was lost “because the glory of creating a people would have few attractions for the pretended protector, while he found peoples to subjugate, states to conquer.”
The military narrative — victories in Lithuania, advance to Moscow, the burning of the city — is covered more briefly than the political failure. The retreat from Moscow is described not primarily as a meteorological catastrophe but as the consequence of a campaign that had no exit: having sought a battle the Russians refused to give, an occupation the city’s inhabitants burned rather than concede, and a political settlement with Poland that he had no intention of honoring, Napoleon found himself deep in Russia with an army it was impossible to feed and a political situation it was impossible to manage. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter XIII — The Last Campaign; the Abdication of 1814
The 1813 Germany campaign opened with successes — Paganel calls them “a deceptive prelude to the reverses fortune was preparing.” But he focuses on a structural argument: a peace was available throughout 1813 on terms that, while not restoring the pre-1812 position, would have preserved France and its emperor. Austria offered itself as mediator between Napoleon its son-in-law and the allied powers. “Napoleon could have concluded a treaty no less advantageous than honorable, if he had wanted it in good faith. But he claimed to dictate peace, not negotiate it.” He wanted to be restored to the political and military situation of before the 1812 winter — something the allied powers were not prepared to concede and France’s exhaustion could not support.
The 1814 campaign in France itself — fought on French soil for the first time since 1792 — produced some of Napoleon’s most brilliant tactical improvisations, and Paganel acknowledges them: a commander of his quality, fighting at home with shorter interior lines, produced results that for weeks made the outcome uncertain. But the fundamental political decision — to reject Austrian mediation, to refuse the Frankfurt peace terms — made the military brilliance irrelevant. The abdication at Fontainebleau is presented as the deserved consequence of a politics “in opposition to the lights of the time, the dispositions of the peoples, and local conditions.” ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter XIV — Elba; the Return; the Hundred Days Begins
Paganel describes Napoleon on Elba as “a great error of nature that she cannot commit twice; his system of politics, strongly conceived, is outside human proportions and almost ideal.” He had no model; he will have no imitators. The chapter’s central claim is that the entire Elba period was a fiction that both parties — Napoleon and the restored Bourbon government — chose to maintain, Napoleon because he was gathering intelligence and preparing his return, the Bourbons because they lacked the resolution to prevent it. “He had already reknotted the threads of the plot he had previously woven to subjugate us.”
The return is reconstructed almost scene by scene: the landing at Cannes, the deliberate march through mountain roads to avoid the Rhône valley, the confrontation at Grenoble where the battalion sent to arrest him was won over at pistol range, the entry into Lyon as Bourbon authority dissolved, the triumphal approach to Paris as Louis XVIII fled. Paganel’s verdict on the party that rallied to Bonaparte is carefully calibrated: he distinguishes between those moved by genuine military devotion, those moved by hatred of the Bourbons, and those moved by personal advantage — and declines to treat all three as equivalent. The Acte additionnel, whose appearance is anticipated at the chapter’s close, is already characterized: Napoleon’s proclaimed return to constitutional principles disproved by the evidence of his proclamations, which said what was needed and meant what he always meant. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chapter XV — The Hundred Days; Waterloo; the Second Abdication
The Acte additionnel (April 22, 1815) is analyzed with contempt: “a clandestine work, written by valets under the master’s dictation,” in which “despotism veils itself with some modesty, torments the principles, disguises its venom, and pushes to its last terms the doctrine of Machiavelli.” Its invocation of the Champ-de-Mai — ancient Frankish assembly revived as a Napoleonic electoral spectacle — is described as Napoleon “more blinded about our dispositions, when we are more enlightened about his inflexible character.” He hoped to seduce France with antique dénominations as he had decorated his consular dictatorship with Roman names in Year VIII.
The Chamber of Representatives that emerged from the electoral process is treated more favourably: it “resolved to oppose an inflexible resistance to Napoleon’s despotism” and maintained that resolution. Paganel’s reading is that the constitutional opposition in France was, for the first time, organized and principled — which is precisely what made it politically irrelevant once Waterloo removed the question. The battle of Fleurus (Ligny, June 16) and Waterloo (June 18) are covered in outline; the rout of the French army; Napoleon’s return to Paris; his second abdication — this time in favour of his son, Napoleon II, a constitutional fiction that the Chambers declined to accept and the allied armies dissolved by their advance. The chapter ends with the provisional government, the army cantoned beyond the Loire, and the King’s return to Paris. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Chronological Table and Appendix
A detailed chronological table of the period covered, followed by what appear to be extensive documentary or statistical tables — the precise nature of these appendix tables is difficult to determine from the OCR but they occupy several thousand lines and may include records of campaigns, decrees, or administrative data compiled alongside the narrative. ^[source: raw/paganel-napoleon-1815.txt]
Coverage Guide


Napoleon’s character and political psychology — Paganel is one of the most analytically serious near-contemporary assessments. He was close enough to the imperial government to understand its machinery and distant enough (as a suppressed critic) to describe it without flattery. The Avant-propos and Chapter I are the densest passages for this.


The Consulate’s institutional history — Chapters II through IV give the clearest account of how the Republic was dismantled step by step through the Senate’s willing capitulations. Useful for understanding how constitutional forms survived as shells while actual power concentrated.


The Concordat and religion under Napoleon — Chapters IV and VII touch on Napoleon’s management of the Church: the Concordat as political instrument, the Pope’s visit, and the limits of clerical independence under the Empire.


The Saint-Domingue expedition — Chapter V gives a near-contemporary assessment of the expedition’s logic and failure. Cross-reference with the Statistique’s treatment of Saint-Domingue.


The Spanish catastrophe — Chapter X is the source’s clearest statement of how Spain became the pivot of Napoleon’s decline.


The Continental System — Chapter XI examines the economic warfare against Britain as a strategic concept and as a practical failure.


The Russian campaign — Chapters XI and XII. Paganel is particularly useful on the Polish question and on what Napoleon’s political ambiguity toward Poland cost him in terms of committed allied support.


Waterloo and the Hundred Days — Chapters XIV and XV. Written immediately after the events, by a French political insider, not a military specialist.


Press censorship and intellectual suppression under the Empire — The Avant-propos is the primary source here: a first-hand account of what it meant to have a book seized on imperial order.


Quality
NYPL copy OCR. The text is approximately 644 KB of readable prose, much cleaner than the Almanach because it is narrative rather than tabular. Proper names of people are generally reliable. Place names are consistent. The OCR degrades at page turns and in passages with footnotes (the book has many footnotes, which are picked up mid-sentence by the OCR and interrupt the main text). The chronological table section is heavily garbled because the OCR cannot reliably handle the columnar date-and-event format. Quotations and citations from classical authors (Tacitus, Montaigne) appear in the original Latin or French and are legible. The appendix tables require page-image verification for any precise use.
