sources/pages-histoire-secrete-revolutio.title: pages-histoire-secrete-revolution-6vols-1801
sources/pages-histoire-secrete-revolutio.content:
Histoire secrète de la révolution française (6 vols) — François Pagès (1801–1802)













































FieldDetailsFull titleHistoire secrète de la révolution française; contenant une foule de particularités peu connues, et des extraits de tout ce qui a paru de plus curieux sur la révolution française, tant en France qu’en Allemagne, en Angleterre, etc. etc.AuthorFrançois Pagès (1745–1802)EditionSeconde édition, revue, corrigée et augmentée par l’auteurPublisherDentu, Paris (Palais du Tribunat / Palais-Égalité, galeries de bois, n.º 240)DateAn VIII–An X (1799–1802)Volumes6 tomesOCR sourcePrinceton University Library scans, one volume per zip fileRaw textwiki/raw/pages-histoire-secrete-revolution-tome01-TY.txt through wiki/raw/pages-histoire-secrete-revolution-tome06-IX.txtArchive files6 zip files, one per volume
Overview
This is the second edition of Pagès’ ambitious synthetic history of the French Revolution, expanded and revised by the author just before his death in 1802. François Pagès (1745–1802) was a French man of letters who published several historical, geographical and travel works. The work is titled Histoire secrète — “secret history” — because its aim is to reveal the hidden intrigues, conspiracies and personal machinations behind the public events of the Revolution, incorporating material Pagès claims is drawn from sources across France, Germany and England.
The work runs to 51 numbered books (Livres I–LI) across 6 volumes, covering the Revolution from its deep institutional origins in Merovingian France through the Consulate under Bonaparte and the battle of Marengo (June 1800). Pagès writes in a vivid, dramatic style with a sharp anti-Jacobin, moderate republican perspective: he is contemptuous of the aristocracy (the “party of honnêtes gens”), scathing toward the Jacobins and Robespierre, and broadly favourable to the Directory and Bonaparte as restorers of order. Each Livre is a self-contained narrative chapter covering weeks or months of events, with Pagès’ own personal judgments woven throughout.
Distinctive features:

Character portraits — lengthy personality sketches of key figures (Mirabeau, Marat, Robespierre, Bonaparte, the Directors) with sharp moral judgments
Documents embedded — includes letters (Marie-Antoinette’s farewell letter, Bonaparte’s proclamations), official reports (Courtois’ Thermidor commission report), treaty texts, and witness accounts
“Secret history” angle — emphasizes the Orléans faction, the “Comité autrichien,” hidden conciliatory attempts between courts and revolutionaries, and the role of foreign agents
Military narrative — detailed campaign histories (Italian, Egyptian, Swiss, German) with troop movements, logistics, and tactical decisions
International scope — covers the effect of the Revolution on England, Prussia, Austria, Russia, the Italian states, Switzerland, the Ottoman Empire, and the United States
Analytical summaries — several Livres are synthetic tableaux drawing wider lessons from events

Volume Breakdown
Tome I (An IX/1801) — Livres I–XXIII: Origins to 10 August 1792
This is the longest volume, covering a vast temporal sweep. The first four Livres are a compressed constitutional history of France from the Merovingians through Louis XV, establishing Pagès’ thesis that the estates-general were an ancient institution whose suppression under absolutism created the tensions that exploded in 1789. From Livre V onward the narrative follows the Revolution month by month.





































































































LivreDescriptionIMerovingian origins of French government. Traces the estates-general to the earliest Frankish institutions. Pagès opens with a philosophical reflection: since the origin of societies, despotism has weighed on the universe; the history of human revolutions is the story of usurpations of power, the claims of reason, and vengeance. Describes the four castes of the ancient Franks (nobles, freemen, serfs, clergy).IICarolingian government and estates-general. Charlemagne overshadows Pepin and Charles Martel, acquiring rights to the throne and proving himself worthy by restoring tranquillity. Pagès notes that within seven years seven kings of this house perished, comparing their misfortunes to those of the Stuarts.IIIThird dynasty (Capetian) through Louis XIV. Hugh Capet received the crown from the peers. Pagès reflects that an intermediate body between king and people is less dangerous, even useful under kings — but Louis XI, Richelieu and Louis XIV proved otherwise.IVLouis XIV, the Regency, Louis XV. Louis XIV appeared on the throne when civil wars had carried energy to its highest pitch; his reign became an epoch in the annals of the universe. Covers Choiseul, Madame Dubarri, and the Duke d’Aiguillon.VReign of Louis XVI: ministries of Maurepas, Vergennes, Turgot, Necker, Calonne, Brienne, Lamoignon. Convocation of the notables, exile of the parlement, the royal session (cour plénière), massacres in the rues Mêlée and Grenelle. Pagès notes the exile of the Duke d’Orléans.VIInfluence of writers on national opinion. The estates-general fixed for January 1789. New Assembly of Notables. The parlements, clergy and nobility demand the forms of 1614. Necker grants the Third Estate double representation. Pagès includes Sieyès’ famous pamphlet and the bourgeoisie assigning a guard of honour to their deputies.VIIRéveillon riots. Motives and pretexts of this uprising. Bloody scene in the Faubourg Saint-Antoine. Opening of the estates-general at Versailles; their first session. Pronounced division of the three orders. Conferences on the king’s invitation; his arbitration plan and how it was received.VIIIRoyal session of 23 June 1789. The national hall returned to the people’s representatives. Mirabeau’s “sublime reply” to the grand master of ceremonies (“we are here by the will of the people and will only leave by the force of bayonets”). Homage paid by the people to Necker. The king orders the first two orders to join the Third. Project to dissolve the National Assembly.IXSiege and storming of the Bastille. Pagès provides the most remarkable particulars of this great event, including the fatal misunderstanding of popular vengeance and various acts of magnanimity. Describes the white flag raised on the towers and the crowd who came to speak with the governor.XAftermath of the Bastille. De Flesselles convicted of perfidy and killed by the mob. News reaches Versailles; Liancourt convinces the king to throw himself into the arms of the Assembly. Bailly named mayor of Paris, Lafayette commander-general of the National Guard. Within hours over 150,000 citizens were under arms.XIThe Quincey massacres and the night of 4 August. Horrific events at Quincey (masquerading patriots who turned out to be brigands). The memorable night session of 4 August: destruction of feudalism. Necker proposes a patriotic contribution of one quarter of each citizen’s income. Pagès comments acidly that the oppressive castes “sow for themselves.”XIICharacter of the French people and political writers. Declaration of the Rights of Man with Pagès’ own reflections. Constitutional projects of Lafayette, Sieyès and Mounier. Debates on the royal veto and whether the Assembly should be divided into two chambers. Pagès notes that when reduced to its principles, the Rights of Man produces: “equal rights to justice and humanity.”XIIIFamine in Paris and government monopolies. Plan to abduct the king to Metz. Threats about the royal veto. The king’s observations on the decrees of 4 August. Portrait of Mirabeau — Pagès assesses him as at least a good citizen, but his immorality and ambition limited him to playing a secondary role, that of a principal agitator.XIVArrival of the Flanders Regiment at Versailles. Arrogance of the conspirators. The “orgy” of 1 October 1789 (the famous banquet where royal soldiers trampled the tricolour cockade). Indignation of Parisians. The journées of 5–6 October. Pagès portrays d’Estaing as a courtier by habit and ambition, royalist by prejudice.XVEnd of the October days. The king fixes his residence in Paris. Pagès offers extended reflections on the conspiracies of these two days and identifies the “two first revolutions within the Revolution” — the first being 14 July, the second 5–6 October. Notes d’Estaing’s studied absence during the crisis.XVITerror and emigration of deputies. Lally-Tolendal and Mounier flee. Proclamation of the rights of the French nation. Detailed table of the Assembly’s work on the new constitutional system: the entire internal organisation of the empire and all reforms of the new administration.XVIINew plots and the “Comité autrichien.” Murder of a baker. Conspiracy and heroic death of the Marquis de Favras. Decree establishing equality of punishments for all classes. A noble act by the district of Saint-Honoré toward the family of the two Agasse brothers. Remarkable remark by the Bishop of…XVIIIFinancial operations of the Assembly. Reflections on Necker. A centenarian from Mont-Jura presented to the Assembly. Rejection of the insidious motion to declare Catholicism the national religion. Mirabeau’s brilliant oratorical movement on this subject. Pagès includes the scene of Voltaire’s ashes being transferred to the Panthéon beside Descartes.XIXForeign and colonial affairs. The Brabant Revolution (Belgium). Reunion of Corsica and Avignon with France. Colonial troubles. The Nancy mutiny and the heroic devotion of the young Desille. Honours rendered by the Assembly to the memory of Franklin. Mirabeau’s speech.XXCivil Constitution of the Clergy. General preparations for the Federation of 14 July. Return of the Duke d’Orléans. The Festival of Federation. An eyewitness letter describing the event. The Camp de Jalès (royalist conspiracy in the Midi). European powers solicited to form a coalition against France. A tableau of Europe at this epoch. Retreat of the Duke d’Orléans from the Jacobins.XXIFlight to Varennes (Livre XXI). Details of Louis XVI’s evasion. The queen’s letter to Mme d’Ossun (“I wish I could see you out of here… Leave this city”). Fersen’s central role. Paris’s calm and majestic response — portraits of the king and queen disappeared from signs, their names effaced. Overnight the word “national” replaced “royal.” Arrest at Varennes. Patriotic emulation of the départements. The Pilnitz Conference. Coalition of the powers. The king’s judgment after his return. The Champ-de-Mars affair. Schism of the Jacobins. Revision of the constitution; the king accepts it.XXIILegislative Assembly. Opening session. Sharp division into two pronounced parties. The king vetoes decrees against émigrés and priests. Renewal of the ministry. Disfavour of the new ministers. Troubles in Avignon.XXIIIWar declared and the fall of the monarchy. The Assembly votes war against the foreign powers almost unanimously. Lafayette’s letter to the Assembly. The journée of 20 June 1792. Coalition armies march toward the frontiers. 10 August and 2 September. Suspension of the king; he is transferred with the royal family to the Temple. The Swiss Guard (not more than 900) fought and were overwhelmed. Emigration of Lafayette.
Tome II (An IX/1801) — Livres XXIV–XXXI: Convention, Terror, Thermidor, Directory
The most dramatic volume, covering the Convention, the trial of the king, the Terror, the execution of the principal factions, Thermidor, and the early Directory. Pagès’ anti-Jacobin perspective is most evident here.









































LivreDescriptionXXIVConvention Nationale. First session. Abolition of royalty; establishment of the Republic. Detailed explanation of the divisions within the Convention and the emerging factions. Portraits of Marat and Robespierre — Pagès draws them as the twin architects of the Terror, each with distinct vices. Departmental guard established.XXVCounter-revolutionary uprisings. Movement in the Lozère. Continuation of the Vendée war; Pagès analyses its principal causes and duration. Bombardment of Lyon with reflections on this event. Siege of Toulon and its capture. Tableau of all military operations to the north, west and south.XXVIThe Orléans faction and 31 May. Proofs and interesting details concerning the Orléans faction and the causes of the journée of 31 May (fall of the Girondins). Charlotte Corday assassinates Marat; Pagès portrays her as a heroine, describing her courage and character. Condemnation to death of the proscribed deputies and circumstances of their execution.XXVIICrimes of the decemvirate (Committee of Public Safety). Decrees of accusation against Camille Desmoulins, Hérault de Séchelles, Danton, Philippeaux, Lacroix, Delaunay, Julien de Toulouse, Chabot and Bazire. Their execution. Trial and death of the Duke d’Orléans. Execution of Marie-Antoinette. Incarceration of 73 deputies (the Girondins). Pagès notes the magic and ever-powerful words “patrie, liberté, salut public, conspiration” used to impose on the multitude.XXVIIIRobespierre’s conspiracy. Details of the plot. Events of 8–9 Thermidor. Tallien’s “beau mouvement” at the Convention. Arrest and execution of the conspirators, including 71 members of the Paris Commune. Extract from Courtois’ report to the Thermidorian commission. Pagès mentions the infamous Lebon (“ce peintre affreux”) and Carrier (who disavowed the horrors of the drownings at Nantes).XXIXThe Thermidorian Reaction. New terrorists or “égorgeurs” (throat-cutters). The Companies of Jesus and of the Sun (royalist youth gangs). “Green cravats and black collars.” Troubles over two hymns/songs — the Marseillaise and the Réveil du Peuple. The new Republican Calendar; Pagès proposes his own modifications. A new constitution drafted. Pagès digresses on the state of theatre and literature.XXXEarly Directory. First works of the Council of Five Hundred and the Council of Ancients. Organisation of the Executive Directory. Finances. Debate on the law of 3 Brumaire regarding deputy eligibility (the case of J. Jacques or Job Aymé). Resolution of the Five Hundred approved by the Ancients.XXXI (last of Tome II)Babeuf’s Conspiracy. The conspiracy of Babeuf and Drouet. The grenade camp affair (Camp de Grenelle). New troubles in the Midi; Isnard accused by Fréron. Isnard’s sublime reply to Fréron followed by Fréron’s letter proving he equalled the other proconsuls in ferocity. Republican festivals. Opening of the Italian campaign. Pagès notes that Bonaparte, “like Condé,” was self-taught as a general.
Tome III (An X/1802) — Livres XXXII–XXXVIII: Directory, Italian Campaigns, Treaties
This volume shifts focus from domestic French politics to the external wars, especially Bonaparte’s Italian campaigns of Years 4–5 (1796–97). Pagès includes the full text of several peace treaties.





































LivreDescriptionXXXIIThe 18 Fructidor coup (4 September 1797). Plan of the volume. Annulment of elections in several départements. Condemnation to deportation of two former directors (one of whom escapes), several deputies and writers. Results of the 18 Fructidor journée. Pagès observes that those who had regarded the places with indifference now aspired only to be masters of them.XXXIIIBonaparte’s Italian campaigns (Years 4–5). Portrait of Bonaparte. Recapitulation of the campaigns of 1793, 1794, 1795, especially the last campaign on the Rhine and its connection to Italy. State of Italy and the respective armies at the opening of the campaign. Pagès includes Bonaparte’s proclamation to the Army of Italy (“Soldiers, you are naked, ill-fed…”).XXXIVPavia, Mantua, Castiglione. Revolt of Pavia and its capture. Passage of the Mincio and combat at Borghetto. Capture of Verona. Investment of Mantua. Armistice granted to the Pope. Capture of Livorno. Capitulation of the Castle of Milan. Combats of Salo and Lonado; battle of Castiglione. A “trait of boldness” by Bonaparte.XXXVTreaties and battles of Arcole. Treaty of peace between the French Republic and the King of the Two Sicilies. Treaty with the Duke of Parma. Combats of Saint-Michel and Segonzano. Combat of Caldero. Battle of Arcole. Combat of Saint-George. Battle of Rivoli (or of La Favorite).XXXVIWar with Rome, the Roman Republic, Switzerland. War with the court of Rome; definitive peace. Assassination of General Duphot. Triumphal entry of the French into Rome. Establishment of the new Roman Republic. Events in Switzerland. Brilliant victories by the French. Establishment of the Helvetic Republic.XXXVIISummary of victories (Pluviôse Year 3 – Ventôse Year 6). Pagès catalogues all advantages gained by Republican troops from February 1795 to March 1798, including the battles of Quiberon, Millesimo, Lodi, Arcole, Lonado, Rivoli. Throws in a rhetorical invocation — “they will live forever.” The Congress of Rastadt and its negotiations.XXXVIIIOther peace treaties. Treaties with the King of Prussia. Those preferring to emigrate from Saint-Domingue to Prussian possessions with their property. Treaties with other German states.
Tome IV (An VIII/1799–1800) — Livres XXXIX–XLIII: Egypt, Rastadt, Campaign of Year 7
This volume turns to the Egyptian expedition and the renewed European war of Year 7 (1799). The Egyptian campaign includes extended geographical and ethnographic descriptions.





























LivreDescriptionXXXIXThe Egyptian expedition. General survey of the Revolution. Bonaparte charged with a maritime expedition whose first objective is a descent on Egypt. Savants and artists of all kinds accompany him (the famous “savants” of the Egyptian Institute). Arrival at Toulon; Bonaparte’s harangue to his army. Embarkation. Capture of Malta.XLBattle of the Nile (Aboukir). Combat in Aboukir roads between the English and French fleets; its unfortunate outcome for the French navy. Pagès claims Bonaparte had foreseen this event. General description of Egypt: Cairo, its population and grandeur. Manners, customs, monuments. Bonaparte attends the festival of the Prophet Muhammad’s birth. Reflection on Egyptian mores.XLIRupture of Rastadt and assassination of the envoys. Rupture of the Rastadt negotiations. Causes of the rupture and resumption of hostilities. The assassination of the French plenipotentiaries at Rastadt — one of the most notorious incidents of the Revolutionary Wars. Declarations and other documents related to this assassination. Pagès’ reflections on this “attentat.” Biographical notes on the members of the French legation.XLIICampaign of Year 7: the opening. Reflections on this new war. State of the respective forces of the belligerent powers. Operations of the Army of Helvetia and the Army of the Danube. Jourdan loses the battle of Stockach. Masséna takes command of both armies. The French seize the Grisons.XLIIIYear 7 campaign continued. English naval forces. Table of what England spends on the current war. State and distribution of the coalition armies and those of the French Republic. Capture of Lucien-Steig by the Austro-Russian army. Details of this memorable combat. Pagès notes Suvorov’s attempt to force the Adda crossing while Moreau’s retreat was already underway.
Tome V (An VIII/1799–1800) — Livres XLIV–XLVII: Moreau’s Retreat, 18 Brumaire
The shortest volume, covering the critical transition from Directory to Consulate. Pagès provides “new details” on the 18 Fructidor and 18 Brumaire coups not found in other histories.

























LivreDescriptionXLIVMoreau’s masterful retreat. Savant dispositions and retreat of General Moreau after Suvorov’s passage of the Adda. Capitulation of the commander of the Castle of Milan. Battle in Switzerland on the whole line: Prince Charles wins and seizes Zurich. The famous battle of the Trebia (San Giovanni) lost by Macdonald. Pagès notes that both sides used the forced truce to reorganise.XLVNew details on 18 Fructidor Year 5 and the events of 28–30 Prairial Year 7 (the fall of the Directory). Grievances against the last directors; their means of defence. Decree rendered against them. Victories of the armies of Batavia and the Danube. “Three armies beaten and scattered, 20,000 prisoners, more than 10,000 dead, nine of their generals killed or taken.”XLVI18 Brumaire (9 November 1799). Presentation of twenty captured flags to the Directory by Macdonald. The journée of 18 Brumaire. Creation of a Consulate and other provisional measures. Adjournment of the Legislative Body until 1 Ventôse. Modifications proposed to the current constitution. Pagès reflects on the obstacles that had stopped or favoured great captains during several campaigns being finally overcome.XLVIISummary of the Year 7 and Year 8 campaigns. Battle of Zurich (Second Battle of Zurich, where Masséna defeated the Russo-Austrian army). The Dutch expedition (the Anglo-Russian invasion of Holland, defeated by Brune).
Tome VI (An IX/1801) — Livres XLVIII–LI: Summary, Europe, Egypt, Marengo
The synthetic capstone volume. Pagès steps back from narrative to offer analytical summaries: a tableau of the Revolution’s course, a geopolitical overview of Europe, and a detailed account of the last campaigns through Marengo.

























LivreDescriptionXLVIIITabular summary of the Revolution. Tableau or résumé of the principal political and military events from the first causes through the present day. History of the Directory government (continued from Tome V): public and private lives of the Directors, their character and that of the principal ministers. Pagès notes the extreme penury of the national treasury — needs so great and pressing that the Directory could not borrow at any interest.XLIXPolitical overview of Europe at century’s end. A geopolitical survey of the principal states of Europe and particularly France. Analysis of the effects of the Revolution and the new offensive and defensive system it has introduced among all powers; the system France ought to adopt. Assessment of England’s resources: the attentive observer recognises they are the product of an established system of credit and commerce rather than inexhaustible in themselves.LEgyptian and Syrian campaigns summarised. Résumé of the entire Egyptian and Syrian campaign with new details. Convention for the evacuation of Egypt. Total rout of the Grand Vizier’s army. New details on Bonaparte’s departure from Egypt and his return to France. Formation of a new army. Description of the Alpine snows.LILast campaign on the Rhine and Danube, including Marengo. Battles of Enghen, Oberhausen, Dillingen, Moëskirch and Biberach. Combats of Memmingen and Erbach. Capture of Augsburg and Munich. General Lecourbe seizes the posts of Lucien-Steig and Feldkirch, the Valtelline, and all the Grisons. Battle of Montebello and the Battle of Marengo (14 June 1800). Pagès includes Bonaparte’s proclamation before Marengo: “The result of all our efforts will be: glory without cloud, solid peace.” Describes Lecchi’s extraordinary feat of transporting boats on chariots to cross the Adda. Surrender of Genoa due to absolute lack of food. Pagès’ concluding reflection: blind or ferocious leaders have all been consumed when their time came — Girondins, Maratists, Robespierrists, Hébertists, Dantonists — and he has outlived them all.
Pagès’ Perspective & Method
Pagès writes in the tradition of the histoire philosophique — narrative driven by moral judgment and the extraction of lessons. His distinctive voice emerges in several ways:

Black cockades and “good company”: He repeatedly mocks the aristocracy’s self-description as “honnêtes gens” or “gens comme il faut,” noting that their black cockade was “the symbol of mourning in which they prepared to plunge all France.”
The “secret” revealed: For Pagès, the secret of the Revolution lies in the interplay of factions (Orléanist, Jacobin, royalist) whose hidden machinations drove events far more than public debates. The Orléans faction is a particular target.
Foreign dimension: He consistently frames the Revolution within European power politics — Pitt’s supposed plans, English financial resources, Austrian and Russian military calculations — reflecting the international scope promised in his title.
Anti-Jacobin verdict: The Jacobins are “égorgeurs” (throat-cutters); their Terror is a system of criminal madness. Yet he is no royalist — he blames aristocratic arrogance and the “Comité autrichien” equally. His sympathies lie with the moderate republicans of the Directory and with Bonaparte as the restorer of order.
Personal as political: Pagès consistently reduces great events to the characters and motives of individuals — a “secret history” in the classical sense, where the public transcript conceals private ambition.

Known OCR Issues

Volume numbers for Tome IV and Tome V read as “AN HUITIEME” — likely an OCR misreading of “AN VIII” (Year VIII = 1799–1800). The Anna’s Archive metadata dates the full set to An IX–X (1800–1802).
Roman numeral book numbers occasionally split across lines (e.g., “X XI” for “XXI”, “X L” for “XL”).
Page headers and marginalia mixed into the main text stream.
Title page ornamentation and printer’s marks garbled by OCR.
Livre boundaries sometimes indicated only by bold subheadings rather than explicit “LIVRE” markers (e.g., Livre XXI appears as a section title rather than a book heading).

sources/police-chouans-consulat-empire-d.title: La police et les Chouans sous le Consulat et l'Empire (1800-1815)
sources/police-chouans-consulat-empire-d.content:
La police et les Chouans sous le Consulat et l’Empire (1800-1815)
Ernest Daudet’s 1895 study of the ongoing Chouan resistance after Bonaparte’s consolidation of power, and the police apparatus built to suppress it. Eight self-contained chapters, each a detailed narrative grounded in police archives, examining the persistence of royalist conspiracy through the Consulate and Empire, the methods of the Napoleonic police, and the English networks that sustained the Chouan cause.
Contents
INTRODUCTION: La police de Napoléon
Daudet opens with a survey of the Napoleonic police system after Brumaire. Describes the state of the West at Bonaparte’s accession — Cadoudal in Brittany, Bourmont in Maine, Frotté in Normandy, Châtillon in Vendée — and the First Consul’s strategy: military pacification combined with amnesty offers. The execution of Frotté, the cynical courting of Cadoudal, and the progressive dismantling of open insurgency. The Introduction establishes the central tension of the book: the Chouans, militarily defeated, shift to clandestine operations, and the police must develop new methods to meet the threat.
L’enlèvement d’un sénateur
The kidnapping of Senator Clément de Ris (the “sénateur”) by royalist agents in September 1800. A daring operation orchestrated by Cadoudal’s networks, intended to cripple the government by striking at the Senate. Daudet reconstructs the planning, the execution on the road between Beaugency and Tours, the senator’s captivity at the château de Saut-de-Sabot, and the protracted police investigation. The affair reveals the sophistication of Chouan intelligence and the porousness of Bonaparte’s security; it also triggers a crackdown that reaches deep into the royalist underground.
Le meurtre d’Audrein
The assassination of the constitutional Bishop Yves Audrein in Morbihan (November 1800), killed by Chouans while travelling to his diocese. Daudet traces the motives — Audrein was a repudiator of the oath, a symbol of the Constitutional Church hated by the royalist clergy — and the investigation that followed. The case illustrates the sectarian dimension of Chouannerie: the murder was as much a religious score-settling as a political act.
L’agence anglaise de Bordeaux
An English intelligence and supply network operating out of Bordeaux, coordinated by British agents and local royalists. Daudet details the flow of English gold, arms, and correspondence through the port, the courier routes linking Bordeaux to London via Jersey, and the police’s ultimately successful penetration of the network. A case study in how British support sustained Chouan resistance at the local level.
L’enlèvement de l’évêque de Vannes
The kidnapping of the constitutional Bishop of Vannes by Chouans in 1801. Daudet narrates the abduction, the bishop’s detention in a royalist hideout in the Morbihan countryside, the negotiations for his release, and the police’s failure to locate him despite an extensive manhunt. The incident underscores the limits of state power in Chouan-controlled territory.
L’affaire d’Aché-De Combray
A complex conspiracy centred on the comte d’Aché and the chevalier de Combray, royalist agents attempting to coordinate a new uprising in the West with British assistance. Daudet pieces together the affair from police dossiers: the couriers intercepted, the safe houses raided, the slow accumulation of evidence that led to the conspirators’ arrest and trial. The chapter demonstrates the cat-and-mouse dynamic between the Chouan underground and Fouché’s police.
L’agence de Jersey
The most extensive chapter, covering the Jersey-based English agency that served as the nerve centre of Chouan operations after 1800. Daudet examines the organisation: the British officers running the agency, the French émigré intermediaries, the network of smugglers and fishermen who carried correspondence and supplies across the Channel. The agency’s functions — intelligence gathering, financial disbursement, personnel coordination, propaganda — and the French police’s countermeasures, including the use of double agents and the interdiction of coastal traffic.
La dernière prise d’armes
The final attempted Chouan rising of the Napoleonic period, led by the comte d’Autichamp in 1815 during the Hundred Days. Daudet narrates the mobilisation of royalist bands in the West, the skirmishes with imperial forces, and the rapid collapse of the uprising once news of Waterloo arrived. A coda tracing the last embers of a rebellion that had burned for over twenty years.

sources/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.title: Madame Roland — Mémoires, Volume I (written 1793, pub. 1823)
sources/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.content:
Marie-Jeanne Roland de la Platière (Madame Roland), Mémoires, Tome Premier. Paris: Rapilly, Collin de Plancy, F. Baroyer, 1823. The extracted raw text runs to approximately 15,030 lines and 603 KB, from a New York Public Library copy. This is Volume I — the companion to roland-memoires-vol2-1823. Written in the Abbaye and Sainte-Pélagie prisons between August and November 1793. The two volumes together form the complete published edition; Volume I contains the personal memoir and the first Roland ministry; Volume II contains the second ministry, the imprisonments, the portraits, and the trial documents. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Contents at a Glance
Volume I has a different character from Volume II. Where Volume II is political — prison-written accounts of events Roland witnessed in the corridors of the Girondin government — Volume I is primarily autobiographical. Roland began writing the personal memoir on August 9, 1793, the day she arrived at Sainte-Pélagie, specifically because the political notices she had written during the preceding five weeks at the Abbaye had just been destroyed by the authorities. She started over, this time reaching back to childhood.
The personal memoirs are written under the explicit knowledge that she may not survive. She says so in the opening: “a prisoner, perhaps destined for a violent and unexpected death.” This gives the three autobiographical parts their characteristic quality — the retrospective intenseness of someone deciding what, of her whole life, is worth preserving in the time she has. She covers her childhood in a Paris engraver’s workshop, her years at a convent, her intellectual formation, her reading, her religious crisis and loss of faith, her relationship with her mother and the grief of her death, her long courtship and eventual marriage to Jean-Marie Roland, and her political awakening through the Revolution.
The volume ends with the historical notices on the first Roland ministry (March–June 1792): how Roland came to the attention of the Girondins, his appointment as Minister of the Interior by Louis XVI, the cabinet’s attempt to govern constitutionally under increasing royal resistance, Roland’s famous letter to the king (which Roland partly drafted), his dismissal, and the political deterioration through to August 10, 1792 — the point where Volume II picks up.
Full Contents Map
Notice sur Madame Roland (1823 editors)
The biographical notice by the Rapilly/Collin de Plancy editors provides the external view of Roland’s life: birth on March 17, 1754, daughter of the engraver Gratien Phlipon; her precocious intellectual development; marriage to Jean-Marie Roland in 1780; her role as his intellectual collaborator and political hostess; the two ministries; her arrest; her execution on November 8, 1793 (18 Brumaire, Year II). The editors frame her as a woman of superior intellect and sound judgment who possessed, as a “rare and fatal gift,” an imagination easily exalted — who was a respectful daughter, devoted wife, tender mother, and excellent friend, but who stepped beyond the lines prescribed by those roles out of love of country. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Première Partie — Mémoires particuliers (begun August 9, 1793)
Roland opens the personal memoir with a declaration of method and character that is also a portrait: “The tyrants can persecute me; but debase me? Never, never!” Her political notices have been destroyed; she will write memoirs instead, and “accommodating myself prudently to my own weakness in a moment when I am painfully affected, I am going to speak of myself, the better to distract myself from it.” She will tell the truth about herself, good and bad, with equal freedom: “one who dares not bear good witness to oneself is almost always a coward who knows and fears the ill that might be said of him.” She will apply the same standard to others: father, mother, friends, husband — “I will paint them as they are or as I have seen them.” ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Father: Gratien Phlipon. Her father was an engraver and goldsmith, a craftsman of middling talent but considerable industry, who employed a number of workers on the Pont-Neuf. Roland’s description is precise and unsparing: he was robust, active, vain about his appearance, loved his wife and jewelry, had the superficial taste and knowledge that the fine arts give to those who practice them at a low level. “One cannot say that he was a virtuous man; but he had much of what is called honor: he would have overcharged for a thing more than it was worth; but he would have killed himself rather than not pay the price of something he had bought.” His ambition — the fatal trait Roland identifies in the account — pushed him toward commerce and gem-dealing rather than contenting himself with his craft; he ended by ruining himself. His social world was not merchants but artists: painters and sculptors came to the workshop, and this artistic milieu formed Roland’s earliest aesthetic education. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Mother: Marguerite Bimont. Her mother brought to the marriage “with very little money, a celestial soul and a charming figure.” Eldest of six children, she had been a second mother to her siblings, and married at twenty-six rather late, “to make way for her sisters.” She deserved better: “her sensitive heart, her agreeable mind, should have united her with someone enlightened and delicate.” Instead she had a husband whose ambitions and commercial risks consumed the household. Roland’s portrait of her mother is the warmest in the volume — patient, tactful in her son’s reading supervision, protective without being restrictive. The loss of her mother in middle age is presented as the event that ended the protected world of childhood and forced full personal responsibility. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Childhood reading and Plutarch. Roland’s access to books was early and intensive. She describes reading secretly in her father’s library, her parents tacitly permitting what they did not formally allow: “there seemed to be a tacit convention between us three.” She worked through travel narratives (Regnard’s voyages were the first), then theatrical works, then Dacier’s translation of Plutarch’s Lives. The Plutarch passage is the most celebrated in the memoir: “I will never forget the Lent of 1763 — I was then nine years old — when I carried it to church in place of my prayer book.” From that moment, she writes, dated “the impressions and ideas that made me republican, without my thinking of becoming one.” She read Fénelon’s Télémaque and Tasso’s Jerusalem Delivered — and found herself physically affected: “reading aloud the episode of Calypso’s island, my breath rose, I felt a sudden fire cover my face, and my altered voice would have betrayed my agitations. I was Eucharis for Telemachus, and Herminia for Tancred.” Then Voltaire — she records being reprimanded for reading Candide by a neighbor woman with a “sour face, fat to the belt, grimacing with importance,” while her own mother simply told her to put it back without changing the arrangement that gave Roland access to whatever she found. Her father gave her Fénelon’s Treatise on the Education of Girls and Locke on the education of children — she notes the comedy: giving to the pupil what is meant for the master. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
The convent. Roland entered the Congrégation des dames on the rue Neuve-Saint-Etienne, faubourg Saint-Marcel, on May 7, 1765 — at eleven years and two months. She had asked to go herself, presenting it to her parents as a desire for proper preparation for her first communion. The first night in the convent is described with the precision of someone who has lived with the memory for thirty years: the shared room with four other girls her age, the faint light, her getting up quietly to go to the window, the moonlit garden below, “the most profound silence reigning in these places — I listened to it, as it were, with a kind of respect; great trees projected here and there their gigantic shadow, and promised a sure shelter for tranquil meditation; I raised my eyes toward the sky, it was pure and serene; I believed I felt the presence of the Divinity smiling at my sacrifice.”
The religious life of the convent was intense and genuinely felt. Roland was a sincere Catholic at this period; the discipline, the prayer, the community of women — she found it, she says, not oppressive but nourishing. She describes individual nuns with the same sharp precision she applies to political figures: their characters, their vocations, which ones were genuinely devout and which performed piety. A nun called Sainte-Agathe was her closest companion; their friendship outlasted the convent. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Deuxième Partie — Suite des Mémoires particuliers (begun August 28, 1793)
Roland resumes on August 28 with a passage of political grief before re-entering the personal narrative: France is “only a vast theatre of carnage, a bloody arena where its own children tear each other apart.” The armies advance and flee alternately; able generals are accused of treason because representatives who understand nothing of war find fault with what they cannot comprehend; those who wanted to establish liberty have been sacrificed to intrigue and brigandage. She invokes Brutus: “We have strayed like you. Those pure men whose ardent soul aspired to liberty… flattered themselves, like you, that the overthrow of tyranny would open the reign of justice and peace: it has been only the signal for hateful passions and the most hideous vices.”
Reading after the convent — religious evolution. Back in the personal account: after the convent years, she continued her reading program intensively. Saint Francis de Sales and Saint Augustine’s manual became her favorite meditations; then Bossuet’s works of religious controversy — which, though written to defend Catholicism, acquainted her with objections to it and set her on the path of reasoning her belief. “That was the first step; there was a long way from there to the scepticism I was to reach some years later, after having been successively Jansenist, Cartesian, Stoic, and deist! What roads, to end up with patriotism, which has put me in irons!” She adds Madame de Sévigné’s letters — “her agreeable facility, her graces, her gaiety, her tenderness” — and records the warm domestic scene of her mother and great-aunt Angélique arguing over whether Roland’s education would “spoil” her.
Scene at Madame de Boismorel’s. A vivid social comedy from this period: her mother takes her to visit Madame de Boismorel, a lady of quality, expecting to show off her granddaughter. Madame de Boismorel, sitting with her dog working tapestry, receives them with the automatic condescension of rank: “Come here, my heart, sit beside me. She is timid — what age is she, your granddaughter, mademoiselle Rotisset? She is a little dark, but the complexion is excellent; it will clear before long… You are not a little devout, are you?” The child answers with composed directness at each question. “Take care she doesn’t become a bluestocking, it would be a great pity,” Madame de Boismorel concludes. Roland uses the scene to establish the class humiliation at the heart of her childhood — her mother called “mademoiselle” (unmarried form) rather than “madame” — and her own early formation of a dignity that refused to recognize condescension as legitimate. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Her mother’s death. Her mother was not yet fifty when she died — an abscess in the head, unrecognized until an effusion from the nose and ears at death explained the strange stuffiness she had suffered for a long time. Roland was away for two hours on the afternoon of the day it happened; she came home at five-thirty to find her mother “frappée.” By midnight she was gone. The grief was violent and physical: fainting, arms extended and rigid, losing consciousness repeatedly; unable to fix her attention on anything; seemingly deranged, answering her own thoughts instead of what was said to her. The abbé Legrand, visiting, had the insight that she needed to talk about her mother rather than avoid the subject — he led her through conversations that gradually brought other thoughts alongside. When he judged her ready for a book, he brought her the Héloïse of Jean-Jacques: “its reading was truly my first distraction. I was twenty-one years old… Rousseau made on me then an impression comparable to what Plutarch had made at eight years old; it seemed that he was the nourishment suited to my nature.” The discovery of Rousseau at twenty-one — as intellectual equal rather than childhood food — is the Deuxième Partie’s decisive intellectual event. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Troisième Partie — Continuation des Mémoires particuliers (begun September 10, 1793)
Covers from age twenty-one until she met Jean-Marie Roland.
Young womanhood and the social world. Roland describes the Parisian world she moved in after her mother’s death: visits to relative and friends, observations of the society around her, her judgments of the people she encountered. She is already the sharp character analyst visible in the Portraits of Volume II — she notices vanity, self-deception, and the gap between people’s self-presentation and their actual conduct. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
First encounters with political life. The pre-revolutionary stirrings of the 1780s — the pamphlet literature, the Assembly of Notables, the general atmosphere of reform expectation — are traced as Roland experienced them: through reading, through conversations with her father’s circle, and through her own increasingly formed political opinions. She was not passive: she was already corresponding and forming views. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Meeting Roland. Jean-Marie Roland entered her life through a correspondence that preceded their meeting — he was a manufacturing inspector in the Lyon generalship, contributing to the Encyclopédie méthodique, and came to know her father’s intellectual contacts. When he eventually visited Paris, his brother (a Benedictine prior at the Collège de Cluny) came to see her and communicated the notes Roland was sending from his Italian travels. She read his travel journals and manuscripts: “his soul, his austere probity, his rigorous principles, his knowledge and taste appeared there undisguised.” She found in him, she says, “an ami” — treating him as without sex, as a philosopher who existed purely through reason. A correspondence developed. She was thirty-two years old when she met him; he was forty-six. Three-part personal memoir ends here; the rest is in the Aperçu. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Aperçu de ce qui me restait à traiter
The summary of what Roland would have written. She gives Jean-Marie Roland’s biography from his manuscripts: born to an old family of the robe distinguished for its integrity, whose fortune had already dissolved from disorder and extravagance. The youngest of five brothers who were expected to enter the Church, he alone refused — also refusing commerce — and left home at nineteen without resources. He went to Nantes, placed himself with a shipowner to learn various trades, and planned to sail to India. A hemorrhage stopped him: he was told he would die at sea if he went. He made his way to Rouen, where a relative who was an inspector of manufactures proposed he enter that branch of administration; he distinguished himself there by activity and work and found himself usefully placed. Travels and study divided his time. He published his Italian travel notes, cut into letter form and sent for printing to friends at Dieppe — “an excellent fund, lacking only better composition to be the first-ranked of Italian travel accounts.” She had intended to re-work it with him after their marriage but events overtook them. The Aperçu also names the people she would have written about: cousin Desportes, her old servant Mignonne who died in her arms saying “I am content” — and the entanglement of her father with a questionable associate named Leveilly, whose daughter she had tried to help, and who ended in abasement. These are fragments: “at such a pace I would have a long work ahead, for which I no longer have enough to live.” ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Notes détachées
Scattered notes of varying length, expanding on individuals or incidents mentioned in the three main parts. Some overlap with the Portraits material of Volume II. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Lettres de Madame Roland à M. Bosc
A selection of Roland’s letters to Louis-Augustin Bosc d’Antic, naturalist and longtime friend of the Roland household. The letters, written over several years leading up to the Revolution and into the revolutionary period, are different in register from the memoir: more immediate, more anecdotal, more spontaneous. They show Roland as correspondent — witty, engaged, full of observation — before the political burden of the Girondin years imposed its weight. They cover domestic life in Lyon and Paris, observations on people and events, philosophical reflections, and the gradual intensification of political engagement as the Revolution approached and began. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Notices historiques sur la Révolution — Premier Ministère de Roland
The political historical section, written after the personal memoirs and covering the first Roland ministry.
Arrival in Paris, February 1791 — the Constituent Assembly and Brissot. The Notices begin not with the ministry itself but with the Rolands’ first extended Paris stay in February 1791, when Roland was sent as a municipal deputy by Lyon to present the city’s financial crisis to the Constituent Assembly. Twenty thousand workers had been without bread the previous winter; Roland was tasked with seeking relief. They arrived February 20. She had not seen Paris in five years and had followed the Assembly’s work from Lyon with intense engagement. She went immediately to the Assembly debates: “I saw the powerful Mirabeau, the astonishing Cazalès, the audacious Maury, the astute Lameths, the cold Barnave.” Her footnote on Mirabeau is one of the most quoted in the volume: “The only man in the revolution whose genius could direct men and impose itself on an assembly: great by his faculties, small by his vices; but always superior to the common, and infallibly its master when he took the trouble to command it. He died shortly after: I thought it was at the right moment for his glory and for liberty; but events have taught me to regret him more. The counterweight of a man of this force was needed, to oppose the action of a swarm of curs, and to preserve us from the domination of brigands.”
Brissot came to visit them. She describes their first encounter after their long correspondence: “There is nothing more pleasant than the first meeting of persons who have bound themselves through correspondence, without knowing each other’s faces reciprocally: one looks with curiosity to see whether the features of the face correspond to the physiognomy of the soul.” Brissot’s simple manners, his frankness, his natural negligence, seemed “in perfect harmony with the austerity of his principles; but I found in him a kind of levity of spirit and character that did not equally suit the gravity of philosophy.” She grew to know him better over the following months and years: “It is impossible to unite a more complete disinterestedness to a greater zeal for the public good, and to devote oneself to the good with more self-forgetfulness; but his writings are more suited than his person to effect it, because they have all the authority that reason, justice, and enlightenment give to works, while his person can take none, for lack of dignity.” Her portrait is nearly as detailed as those in Vol II: “The best of men, good husband, tender father, faithful friend, virtuous citizen… confiding to the point of imprudence, gay, naïve, ingenuous as one is at fifteen, he was made to live with sages and to be the dupe of the wicked.” He “judges mankind well and does not know individual men at all. He knows that vices exist; but he cannot believe that someone who speaks to him with a good face is vicious; and when he has recognized people for such, he treats them like fools one pities, without guarding against them.” ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Roland’s route to ministerial office. Through Brissot’s circle the Rolands became part of the Girondin network in Paris during this 1791 stay. Roland was already known through his encyclopédiste writings and administrative record. When the Girondins formed a cabinet in March 1792 under the constitutional monarchy — Dumouriez at Foreign Affairs, Servan at War, Clavière at Finance — Roland was named Minister of the Interior: a genuine reformist appointment of an administrator with deep expertise in French industry and commerce. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
The ministry’s work. Roland describes the Interior Ministry’s actual operations: the breadth of its remit (internal administration, public works, manufactures, communications, education, public relief), the quality and character of the ministry’s staff, the difficulties of governing constitutionally under a king who was constitutionally obliged to accept ministers but not obliged to support them. She covers specific initiatives, specific obstacles, specific moments of political friction with the Tuileries. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Roland’s letter to the king. The most politically significant act of the first ministry: Roland sent Louis XVI a long letter in June 1792 calling on him to promulgate the decrees he had vetoed (on the deportation of refractory priests and on the establishment of a camp of federal volunteers near Paris), warning him that resistance was dangerous to the constitutional order, and arguing in plain terms for the republican and constitutional position. The letter was substantially drafted by Madame Roland herself. She describes its composition, its intent, and the king’s reaction — immediate dismissal of Roland and his Girondin colleagues from the cabinet. The letter was read publicly to the Legislative Assembly and became a political manifesto; she gives her own assessment of its effect. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
The political deterioration to August 10. After the dismissal, Roland describes the period from June to August 10, 1792 as a sustained effort to prevent what they all feared: the court’s counter-revolutionary gamble and the popular explosion it would provoke. The discussions she records — planning with Barbaroux and Servan for a possible southern republic if Paris fell to the court, taking out maps, tracing lines of demarcation, calculating forces — are among the most historically significant passages in the volume. They show the Girondins, before August 10, actively contemplating federalism as a last resort against royalist reconquest: a contingency plan that would later be weaponized against them. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
The Sentinelle. Roland describes the origin of the newspaper La Sentinelle: the Girondin leadership’s decision to fund a placard journal to counteract the court press; Louvet chosen as its writer; the awkward financial arrangement whereby Dumouriez channelled funds from the Foreign Affairs secret account through Pétion as Paris mayor to the Interior Ministry to fund the paper. A minor but revealing passage about how Girondin political operations actually worked. ^[source: raw/roland-memoires-vol1-1823.txt]
Coverage Guide


Madame Roland’s childhood and formation — The Première, Deuxième, and Troisième Parties are the only source in the wiki for Roland’s pre-revolutionary life: her artisan origins, her convent education, her reading of Plutarch and Rousseau, her religious formation and subsequent loss of faith. Essential for understanding the intellectual and moral foundations behind her political role.


The first Roland ministry (March–June 1792) — The Notices historiques are the primary source in the wiki for this period: how a Girondin cabinet formed under the constitutional monarchy, what it tried to do, and how it was dismissed. Cross-reference roland-memoires-vol2-1823 which begins with the second ministry.


Roland’s letter to the king (June 1792) — The political letter that ended the first ministry. Roland describes its composition (she largely drafted it), its content, and its consequences. One of the most cited documents of the constitutional monarchy’s last months.


Girondin contingency planning for federalism — The passages describing the discussions with Barbaroux and Servan about a possible southern republic if Paris fell are historically significant: they show the Girondins actually planning for federalism before August 10, which makes the later Montagnard accusation of federalism more complicated than it is usually presented.


Roland as correspondent (Lettres à Bosc) — The Bosc letters are the most personal and spontaneous of Roland’s writings in the wiki: they predate the political burden and show her voice in a different register. Useful for characterization and for the pre-revolutionary atmosphere in the Roland household.


Complement to Volume II — This volume fills the personal and pre-political background that Volume II assumes but does not provide. Reading the two together gives the complete picture: childhood and political formation (Vol. I), political crisis and prison (Vol. II).


Quality
NYPL copy, OCR from the same 1823 Rapilly/Collin de Plancy print run as Volume II. Quality is identical: readable French prose with running headers (“MÉMOIRES DE Mme ROLAND” / “NOTICES SUR LA RÉVOLUTION”) picked up by the OCR at the top of each page, accent marks sometimes lost, ligatures occasionally split. Editors’ footnotes are marked and readable. The Lettres à Bosc and the Notices historiques sections are somewhat denser with names and political references than the personal memoir sections; the personal memoir prose is the most fluid and readable portion of the volume.
